title_r: Where the Really Hard Problems Went
abstract_r: Many if not all NP problems show a solvability phase transition along a secondary parameter for any fixed input size. These secondary parameters and associated solvability phase transitions have been identified and in many cases, the solving algorithms used for these problems require significantly more time for instances close to this phase transition. This hardness-near-the-phase-transition-phenomenon has profound implications for the NP-completeness of the problems themselves. Being a member of the class \emph{NP} implies that a problem has no exact algorithm of subexponential runtime for the worst case instances for increasing input size. But these worst case instances are rather scarce, and appear to reside around the solvability phase transition. For this reason, further study of this phenomenon is warranted. In this dissertation, we will four different problems in NP: the Hamiltonian cycle problem, the asymmetric traveling salesman problem, the partition problem and the perfect rectangle problem. For the Hamiltonian cycle problem, we show that very rare but super hard instances exist very far from the solvability phase transition. These instances display a degree of universal hardness, requiring vast amounts of runtime for all major published exact backtracking algorithms. But we also replicate earlier results for this problem, showing that in randomly generated ensembles, the hardest instances are all located near the solvability phase transition. We conjecture, by an argument from Kolmogorov complexity, that these super hard instances, which are highly structured, are very unlikely to show up in randomized ensembles, solving the paradox. These results could encourage the community to explore the influence of an instance structure on hardness. For the asymmetric traveling salesman problem, we also replicated earlier results, claiming the standard deviation of the random instance generation function for the values in the cost matrix could be used as a secondary parameter for the problem's instance hardness. These results however, turned out to be flawed. The culprit is an interplay between the lognormal generation function and an ensuing integer roundoff for the matrix values. We show that the hardness difference for the instances almost completely disappears when the roundoff is omitted, but we also show that when the roundoff is preserved, the resulting number of zeroes in the matrix is directly related to the aforementioned standard deviation. For the partition problem, a secondary parameter can be found in the number of bits per integer in the set. If this ratio is low, the instance typically has many perfect solutions, and one is easily found. If this ratio is high, the entire search tree must be traversed to find the optimal split. In our contribution, we show that the problem's algorithmic hardness does not only depend on the absolute magnitude of bits per integer, but also on their actual distribution. The results however do invoke other questions on the hardness of this problem in NP, namely whether a deliberate search for distributions instead of instances can identify hard regions, but also whether easy and hard instances can be separated, as the solution distribution in the instance space might be fractally structured. For the perfect rectangle packing problem, we identified a secondary parameter in the parameter `randMax', which determines the maximum side length of the rectangles in an instance. The midpoint of this phase transition lies very close to O(n sqrt(n)), which is very different from other phase transition midpoints. It begs further investigation, but the problem is much harder than the other NP-complete problems in this thesis, and demands significantly more time and space.

title_r: Orangutans (<I>Pongo pygmaeus</I> and Hybrid) and Gorillas (<I>Gorilla gorilla gorilla</I>) Modify Their Visual, but Not Auditory, Communicative Behaviors, Depending on the Attentional State of a Human Experimenter
abstract_r: The ability to judge the visual attention of others is a key aspect of human social cognition and communication. While evidence has shown that chimpanzees can discriminate human attention based on eye cues alone, findings for gorillas and orangutans have been less consistent. In addition, it is currently unclear whether these gorillas and orangutans attempt to attract the visual attention of inattentive recipients using attention-getting behaviors. We replicated and extended previous work by testing whether six orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus and hybrid) and six gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla) modified the use of their visual and auditory signals based on the attentional state of a human experimenter. We recorded all communicative behaviors produced by the apes for 30 s while a human experimenter stood in front of them with a food reward in a variety of postures, both visually attentive (facing the apes) and inattentive (body and/or head facing away or eyes covered). Both species produced visual behaviors more often when the experimenter was looking at them than when she had her face turned away, but only the orangutans discriminated attention based on eye cues alone. When we removed human-reared apes from the analyses (N = 3), mother-reared apes showed sensitivity to eye cues from the experimenter. However, further analyses found that the orangutans and gorillas relied more heavily on the body and head orientation of the experimenter than on her eye cues. Neither species produced more vocalizations or nonvocal auditory behaviors, such as mesh and object banging, mesh rubbing, or clapping, in the inattentive, than attentive, conditions. Our results reveal that while orangutans and gorillas preferentially use visual gestures when a human is attending to them, they do not appear to produce auditory behaviors, including vocalizations, with the intention of manipulating the recipient s attention state.

title_r: Estimating the accuracy of early life predictors of 11-year language outcome: A replication study
abstract_r: Background: Early identification of language disorders can help provide support to children who need it most to improve development and quality of life outcomes. A previous study identified 6 preschool indicators that predict 11-year language outcome with 75% sensitivity and 81% specificity using data from the Early Language in Victoria Study (ELVS). These items relate to sentence complexity, vocabulary and gross motor skills. This study aims to replicate these methods in the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) birth cohort. Method: Between 0-3 years of age, LSAC collected parent surveys, direct assessments and investigator observations relating to the child. At 11 years the children completed the sentence recall task of the Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals, 4th Edition as a potential indicator of Language Disorder. Here we use SuperLearner to estimate the accuracy of the set of 6 questions identified by the previous ELVS study in predicting 11-year language outcome (dichotomised as sentence recall score &gt;1.5SD below the mean). We also use random forests to identify whether any additional variables relating to families’ socioeconomic status, parents’ or children’s general health and development arise as predictive of language outcome. Expected results: We expect that the accuracy of the 6 items will attenuate in comparison to the results of the previous study. We may find that the items relating to children’s morphosyntax, vocabulary and motor skills predict with “fair” (&gt;70%) accuracy which children will have language difficulties in late childhood, replicated across two population-based cohorts.

title_r: Translated instructions.
abstract_r: <div><p>In this paper, we investigate how technology has contributed to experimental economics in the past and illustrate how experimental economics can contribute to technological progress in the future. We argue that with machine learning (ML), a new technology is at hand, where for the first time experimental economics can contribute to enabling substantial improvement of technology. At the same time, ML opens up new questions for experimental research because it can generate previously impossible observations. To demonstrate this, we focus on algorithms trained to detect lies. Such algorithms are of high relevance for research in economics as they deal with the ability to retrieve otherwise private information. We deduce that most of the commonly applied data sets for the training of lie detection algorithms could be improved by applying the toolbox of experimental economics. To illustrate this, we replicate the “lies in disguise-experiment” by Fischbacher and Föllmi-Heusi with a modification regarding monitoring. The modified setup guarantees a certain level of privacy from the experimenter yet allows to record the subjects as they lie to the camera. Despite monitoring, our results indicate the same lying behavior as in the original experiment. Yet, our experiment allows an individual-level analysis of experimental data and the generation of a lie detection algorithm with an accuracy rate of 67%, which we present in this article.</p></div>

title_r: Prefrontal-Amygdala Interactions in Social Learning
abstract_r: This R01 renewal application proposes functional neuroimaging studies with human subjects to elucidate the role of the prefrontal cortex and amygdala in the processing of facial identities and expressions that predict critical social outcomes. Presentations of facial expressions of emotion in neuroimaging studies have proven particularly robust stimuli for activating amygdala and prefrontal regions involved in processing biologically- relevant social cues. Here we propose to further develop our novel structural and functional neuroimaging methods to better understand how the amygdala interacts with reciprocally connected prefrontal areas when such expressions are encountered. Specifically, following up on our previous findings that the structural integrity of an amygdala-prefrontal pathway predicts individual differences in reported anxiety - we replicated this effect in > 250 subjects and observed an exciting sex difference this effect is compellingly stronger in females than in males. Here we propose to follow up on this effect with higher resolution DTI methods and to extend it to functional resting state data to see if the same sex difference is observed functionally. In addition, we propose a new mathematical model where we believe we can disentangle the effects of valence from arousal in brain imaging data, a confound the field continues to struggle with. Finally, we propose the development of a new facial expression stimulus set where we record the psychological status of the models posing for the expressions so we can determine any interaction this might have with the psychological status of the our subjects of study. The field can then usefully compare these data to complementary developmental research (i.e., with children and adolescents) and will be amenable to direct translation to clinical populations (e.g., anxiety and depression).

title_r: Hybrid models of cognition: The influence of modal and amodal cues in language processing tasks
abstract_r: In recent years, a growing amount of evidence has been accumulated suggesting that at least some part of our cognition and especially language comprehension is embodied in actions, perceptions, and emotions, and is therefore multimodal in nature. While the debate in previous decades was focused on whether cognition indeed is embodied, today the discussion revolves more around the question when and how embodied representations are used and what their exact role is. The present dissertation is aimed at shedding light on this discussion, investigating the presence and the role of multimodal representations across different tasks and contexts. At first, a series of anagram-solving tasks investigating the influence of different modal cues on subsequent solving of anagrams of words associated with either the ocean (e.g., shark -> SARHK) or the sky (e.g., cloud -> CUOLD) was conducted. Combining a background picture depicting an ocean-sky scene with a shift of attention towards the upper half of the computer screen resulted in faster solution times for words associated with sky compared to words associated with ocean, while the reverse was true for a downward attentional shift. This finding was extended to emotional valence, using pictures either associated with a positive or negative emotional valence to prime words with a matching emotional valence. Indeed, anagrams were solved faster when the emotional valence of the picture matched the associated emotional valence of the solution word. Going back to the domain of vertical space, we tried to replicate the findings of the first set of experiments with another set of stimuli and the use of linguistic cues in the form of adjectives or sentences preceding the anagrams, paired with a vertical shift of attention. In contrast to pictorial cues, these linguistic cues did not influence solution times. In another set of anagram-solving experiments, we directly compared the influence of linguistic (amodal) and pictorial colour (modal) cues, using written colour words or coloured rectangles as primes for solution words associated with a certain colour (e.g., specific types of fruit or vegetable, such as “cherry”). These were solved faster when a matching colour cue was presented before the anagram, regardless of whether the colour cue was linguistic or pictorial. Combining both cues by showing a written colour word inside a coloured rectangle only facilitated anagram solving of anagrams when both cues matched the solution word, e.g. the word “green” written inside a green rectangle facilitating solution of an anagram for “cucumber”. Neither a symbolic, amodal colour word, nor a colour patch seem to be responsible for this match effect exclusively, but instead both cues seem to activate the same superimposed conceptual colour representation. In a last line of research, it was investigated in how far hemispheric differences come into play during embodied word representations. A divided visual field study by Zwaan and Yaxley (2003a), who found a match effect regarding visual-spatial relations between objects to be confined to the right hemisphere in a semantic-relatedness judgment task was replicated - with the addition of the factor response side. Word pairs were shown very briefly either to the left or right visual field in a vertical arrangement on the screen either matching or mismatching the canonical spatial relation between the word’s referents (“nose” being above “mustache” in a canonical view of a face, thus seeing “nose” written above “mustache” would be a match). In contrast to the original study there was no interaction between visual field and the spatial compatibility effect. Instead an interaction between response side and visual field and an additional main effect of match - independent of visual field - was found. This leads us to assume that multimodal concepts are not confined to either hemisphere but instead seem to be spread over large scale networks across the whole brain. Taking all of these results together, a hybrid-view of cognition seems to be the most fertile: superimposed conceptual representations seem to be at the core of semantic meaning, and can be influenced by both modal and amodal contextual information, with neither type of information exerting clear dominance over the other.

title_r: Critical evaluation of LOCO dataset with machine learning
abstract_r: Purpose: Object detection is rapidly evolving through machine learning technology in automation systems. Well prepared data is necessary to train the algorithms. Accordingly, the objective of this paper is to describe a re-evaluation of the so-called Logistics Objects in Context (LOCO) dataset, which is the first dataset for object detection in the field of intralogistics. Methodology: We use an experimental research approach with three steps to evaluate the LOCO dataset. Firstly, the images on GitHub were analyzed to understand the dataset better. Secondly, Google Drive Cloud was used for training purposes to revisit the algorithmic implementation and training. Lastly, the LOCO dataset was examined, if it is possible to achieve the same training results in comparison to the original publications. Findings: The mean average precision, a common benchmark in object detection, achieved in our study was 64.54%, and shows a significant increase from the initial study of the LOCO authors, achieving 41%. However, improvement potential is seen specifically within object types of forklifts and pallet truck. Originality: This paper presents the first critical replication study of the LOCO dataset for object detection in intralogistics. It shows that the training with better hyperparameters based on LOCO can even achieve a higher accuracy than presented in the original publication. However, there is also further room for improving the LOCO dataset.

title_r: Experiment 1D: Replication of the head nodding and shaking effect in a web-based experiment
abstract_r: Given that nodding and shaking head motions are used as communicative signals, such as signals of approval (and denial), these motions might be expected to modulate perceived trait impressions of model faces. We used movie clips of nodding and shaking head motions of computer-generated figures and examined the modulation effects of these motions on perceived trait impressions. Results showed that the nodding head motion significantly increased ratings of subjective likeability and approachability compared to the shaking or control conditions, whereas the shaking motion did not affect ratings. However, previous studies have primarily examined this effect using laboratory-based experiments with Japanese university students, which limits the generalizability and replicability of the results. Therefore, the present study examined whether this effect can be observed in a web-based experiment and for crowdsourcing service workers. In this experiment (Experiment 1D), we re-examined the effects of nodding and shaking motions on perceived likeability about appearance.

title_r: Modulations of stimulus-response binding and retrieval (SRBR) by performance-dependent affective consequences: A follow-up
abstract_r: We aim to study the modulating role of performance-dependent affective consequences (positive, neutral, or negative consequences consisting of visual, auditory, and monetary events) on stimulus-response binding and retrieval (SRBR). In a colour categorisation task with a sequential prime/probe design, we will use an orthogonal variation of response relation (colour repetition vs. change) and stimulus relation (word repetition vs. change) to investigate SRBR effects. Previous studies have demonstrated that not only targets (colour), but distractors (word) too, can retrieve previously executed responses from event files in episodic memory, when faced with the same distractor again. Known as the Retrieval Effect, distractor repetition – in conditions where the response must be repeated – leads to facilitation, whereas with response change – leads to interference. Our goal is to investigate the influence of affective consequences on this Retrieval Effect in S-R binding. Based on the assumption that SRBR is the underlying mechanism of learning and operant conditioning (law of effect), we would expect that the Distractor Repetition (DR) * Response Repetition (RR) interaction should be strengthened (weakened) in cases of positive (negative) consequences after the prime episode. In our previous experiments, however, we did not find any evidence for an affective modulation of performance-based (error rates (ER) and reaction time (RT)) retrieval effects, indicating that these effects are fully automatic and independent of feedback, but instead might reflect simple effects of behaviour repetition and episodic memory retrieval (“law of exercise”, “law of recency”). Thus, we do not expect to see any moderating role of affective consequences on the retrieval effect in the data from this experiment. Furthermore, we expect to replicate the null effect of affective consequences on retrieval effects from our previous studies.

title_r: Does test difficulty moderate the forward testing effect with educationally-relevant text materials?
abstract_r: Retrieval practice has been shown to be more effective than restudy or no-interim practice to reduce proactive interference and thereby to enhance subsequent learning of new information (for a meta-analysis, see Chan, Meissner, Christian, & Davis, 2018). The main objective of this study is to test the encoding effort hypothesis of this forward effect of testing (FET). According to the encoding effort hypothesis, taking a test on previously studied information enhances subsequent learning by encouraging participants to sustain effort and attention while encoding new information (Cho, Neely, Crocco, & Vitrano, 2017; Szpunar, Khan, & Schacter, 2013; Weinstein, Gilmore, Szpunar, & McDermott, 2014). Experiencing a difficult test with retrieval failure may enable participants to experience that their previous encoding was insufficient and therefore dedicate more effort to subsequent studying (Cho et al., 2017; Lee & Ahn, 2018). If a test is easy, participants will not experience difficulty or failure and therefore will not increase their subsequent study effort accordingly. The encoding effort hypothesis is analogous to the retrieval effort hypothesis account of the backward testing effect. Previous research has demonstrated that more difficult retrieval practice enhances memory for previously learned information to a greater degree (Carpenter, 2009; Finley, Benjamin, Hays, Bjork, & Kornell, 2011; Pyc & Rawson, 2009; Rawson, Vaughn, & Carpenter, 2015). Therefore, the main objective of this study is to test the analogous prediction that more difficult retrieval practice will enhance subsequent learning, leading to a larger FET, than easier retrieval practice. The second objective of this study is to examine another prediction of the encoding effort hypothesis of the FET. If experiencing retrieval failure encourages participants to dedicate increased attention and effort to subsequent studying, then these changes should be observable in how long participants choose to study subsequently presented information. Indeed, prior research has demonstrated that failing to retrieve previously learned information encourages participants to adapt their study times and study strategies when the information is presented for review again (Pyc & Rawson, 2010, 2012; Koriat & Bjork, 2006; Soderstrom & Bjork, 2014). Therefore, the second objective of this study is to examine whether more difficult tests lead to longer study times for subsequent materials than easy tests or restudying (Yang, Potts, & Shanks, 2017). Our goal is to test the encoding effort hypothesis using educationally-relevant materials, namely instructional texts. This study is a conceptual replication of our previous research using English word pairs and Swahili-English translations (Hausman et al., 2020). Participants will read a text, split into three sections. After reading Section 1 and after reading Section 2, participants will complete a 2-minute distractor task and then will complete one of three review tasks: 1) Difficult retrieval: Participants will answer difficult multiple choice questions about the section they just read. 2) Easy retrieval: Participants will answer easy multiple choice questions about the section they just read. 3) Restudy: Participants will re-read select facts from the passage. Finally, all participants will then read Section 3 at their own pace, complete a 2-minute distractor task, and then take a cued recall test on information from Section 3.

title_r: Effects of Informed Dissonance
abstract_r: As useful as hypocrisy interventions are, their use in the “real world” outside the laboratory has been limited. In previous researjh ch, participants were of course unaware that they were in a hypocrisy study; knowing so may have changed their behavior. While deception is understandable and a sound science practice, it still involves misleading the participants. It would be easier to employ dissonance on a wide scale if there was no deception involved; that is, if people could willingly employ dissonance in their own lives to change their behavior. The purpose of this study is two-fold. Primarily, we seek to understand what happens if we tell participants about the effects of induced hypocrisy. Secondarily, we seek to replicate a previous study that increased hypocrisy participants’ intentions to exercise, but this time in an online format.

title_r: No so different in present attitudes and behavior, but expected future membership - A technical replication of a study of party youth in six European democracies
abstract_r: Based on the statistical analysis of an original survey of young party members from six European democracies, Bruter and Harrison (2009) conclude that three types of young members differ systematically regarding their membership objectives, activism, efficacy and perceptions of the party and self-perceived political future. We perform a technical replication of the original study correcting four deficiencies that lead us to a different conclusion. First, we discuss substantive significance in addition to statistical significance. Second, we run significance tests on all comparisons instead of limiting them to an arbitrary subset. Third, we perform pairwise comparisons between the three types of members instead of using pooled groups. Fourth, we avoid the inflation of the type-I error rate due to multiple testing by using the Bonferroni-Holm correction. We find that most of the differences between the types lack substantive significance and that statistical significance only coherently distinguishes the types of members in their future membership, but not in their present behavior and attitudes.

title_r: The role of similarity perception in recall dynamics
abstract_r: There is evidence that emotional events – or, in an experimental setting, emotional items – are better remembered than their neutral counterparts in free recall tasks, a phenomenon called the Emotional Enhancement of Memory (EEM) (Cahill & McGaugh, 1998; Hamann, 2001; Yonelinas & Ritchey, 2015). The mechanisms underlying the EEM are still under investigation, with retrieved context theories of memory (e.g., Howard & Kahana, 2002a; Polyn et al., 2009) providing some insight into these processes. Broadly, these propose that contiguity effects (i.e., certain items being recalled in succession due to a range of factors) arise due to a “mental time travel” which occurs during memory search, whereby the context associated with a given recalled item is reinstated, increasing the likelihood that items which share this context will be recalled subsequently. One such context, we hypothesize, might arise from the emotional content of emotional memories: the emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model targets emotional memory specifically (Talmi et al., 2019). The model suggests that emotional items are preferentially bound to their emotional context during encoding; thus emotional items from a list tend to be recalled first. Once this encoding context is retrieved, upon recall of the first emotional item, it will bring to mind other emotional items, which were associated with the same emotional context; thus, a second prediction of the model is thus clustering of emotional items. Naturally, the model also predicts that more emotional than neutral items will be recalled from a list. In other words, the eCMR model can provide a mechanistic explanation for the EEM, and suggests additional processes which, if empirically observed, would offer insight into the organization of emotional memories when they are recalled. The eCMR and the follow-up CMR3 (Cohen & Kahana, 2019) models remain limited in that they have never been tested empirically with material that had true personal significance for participants. In a previous study conducted in our lab, we were unable to demonstrate that recall of more and less emotional real-world images was organised based on emotional similarity. The present study aims to test this hypothesis in a more sensitive way by moving beyond binary categorization of stimuli. While the previous study used lists that included both more and less emotional items (mixed lists), this study will also include pure lists. This will allow us to examine whether we can replicate previously-obtained emotional list composition effects. It will also allow us to test whether the emotionality of the list influences the temporal organisation of recall, a key question for the development of the eCMR model and its potential to explain associative memory effects. How similarly events are represented likely comprises several dimensions (Prince & Konkle, 2020) including emotional similarity, visual similarity and semantic similarity. Emotional similarity refers to the tendency to group stimuli together on the basis that they evoke the same feelings (e.g. two images that evoke sadness), regardless of perceptual and/or semantic similarity (e.g. two images of city streets). Semantic similarity itself likely encompasses many different factors, such the spatiotemporal context (e.g., time of day or location shared by two images); the characteristics of people in the scene (e.g., two images displaying older people, or people of a particular gender); or the activities performed in the image (e.g., a sports game). In a study investigating the extent to which these dimensions could predict overall object-level similarity ratings, Iordan et al. (2018) showed that ratings on various dimensions of semantic similarity were not weighed equally in predicting object-level similarity ratings. In addition, in Tomita et al. (2021; unpublished), action-purposive properties (e.g., “playing football”, “eating”) of autobiographical events were the second most predictive factor of overall similarity perception of these autobiographical memories, after emotional properties. Together, these findings suggest that certain features of stimuli seem to contribute to perception of similarity more so than others. Particularly relevant to the present discussion, semantic similarity has been shown to have an influence on memory and recall of stimuli, including emotional stimuli (Mandler & Ritchey, 1977; Tulving & Pearlstone, 1966; Talmi et al., 2007). Semantic contiguity refers to the tendency to organize recall of items based on pre-existing semantic associations between those items, and has been demonstrated in research on recall organization. For instance, Polyn et al. (2011) found that taxonomic categorization of items within a list played a substantial role in these items being subsequently recalled in close temporal proximity – even when the categorized items were not presented in successive list positions. Using latent semantic analysis to manipulate the semantic structure of item lists, Healey & Uitvlugt (2019) have also found that the influence of temporal processes (i.e., recency, primacy, temporal contiguity effects) were reduced in lists that with strong semantic associations, particularly when participants were specifically asked to focus on recalling items that were related to one another, but also in an unspecified free-recall condition. Pre-existing semantic associations likely play a role in perception of similarity between events or items – it is thus important to disentangle the involvement of different similarity dimensions in overall perception of similarity between items, as this can have downstream effects on how these items are organized in memory. In sum, the present investigation aims to understand the involvement of similarity perception in memory recall dynamics. Organizational aspects of memory, such as clustering and context retrieval, may stem from similarities between contiguously recalled items along multiple dimensions. In order to investigate this in complex, ecologically valid emotional stimuli, different dimensions of similarity must be accounted for. We will investigate the relative contributions of emotional, visual, and semantic similarities in recall of complex events, with the goal of further developing the eCMR model.

title_r: Boosting working memory pro- and retroactively: Interactions of statistical learning and retro-cueing
abstract_r: We study the effects of statistical learning and retro-cueing on visual working memory in a task that requires participants to encode four shapes and later report whether a probe matches the shape presented at this position before. In an existing experiment (Experiment 1), we found main effects of statistical learning (now referred to as stimulus probability) on sensitivity (i.e. d') such that high probability locations were associated with better sensitivity. Further, we found a main effect for retro-cueing such that retro-cued locations were associated with higher sensitivity. We also found an interaction between retro-cue and stimulus probability such that the retro-cue had no additional benefit in the high probability condition, but had an additional benefit on sensitivity in the low stimulus condition. Response times were found shorter for the retro-cue compared to the neutral cue. The main effect of probability as well as the interaction between probability and retro-cue were non-significant. In the first experiment (Experiment 2) associated with this pre-registration, we aim to replicate these findings. Importantly, two parts of the original experiment were changed. 1) The number of trials is going to be doubled. 2) The stimulus probabilities for high/low chance of being retro-cued change from 67-11% to 40-20%. We also now ask whether participants were able to indicate which of the locations was the high stimulus probability location after the experiment. In the second experiment (Experiment 3) associated with this pre-registration, we aim to follow up on these findings. This experiment is identical to Experiment 2, but the statistical probabilities are as follows: high 30, 30. 30%; low 10% Also, we ask whether participants are able to indicate which of the locations was the low stimulus probability location (instead of the high probability location in Experiment 2, again after the experiment).

abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Baxter et al. (2015) is that becoming a parent leads [men] to more strongly support a traditional division of labor in relation to the care of children. title_r: The etiology of primary and secondary callous-unemotional traits
abstract_r: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, such as reduced empathy and remorse, develop in childhood and predict chronic and escalating trajectories of antisocial behavior and psychopathy. It has been proposed that the etiological origin of CU traits may vary depending on whether such traits are accompanied by anxiety or not (Viding & Kimonis, 2018), roughly corresponding to designations of ‘primary’ (thought to be more genetically driven) and ‘secondary’ (thought to reflect coping mechanisms in response to trauma and harsh environmental conditions) risk for psychopathy (Cecil at al., 2018). Examining whether anxiety moderates the relative importance of genetic and environmental factors on CU traits will enable us to examine the theoretical proposition that the etiology of CU traits varies depending on whether such traits are accompanied by affective symptomatology or not. This study represents a conceptual replication in the Twins Early Development Study (TEDS, UK) of analyses conducted in the Michigan State University Twin Registry (MSUTR, USA). These analyses will shed light on potentially distinct etiological pathways to CU traits that may require distinct preventative and treatment approaches.

title_r: Effects of Message Framing on Engagement with News Headlines
abstract_r: ​​Negative information captures attention and drives engagement with online news (Robertson et al., 2023; Soroka & Nir, 2019). However, consuming negative news can bias memory and increase distress, anxiety, and depression (de Hoog & Verboon, 2020; Shaikh, McGowan, & Lydon-Staley, 2022; Pfefferbaum et al., 2014; Kensinger, 2009). A potential alternate route to increasing engagement is to emphasize action (i.e., highlighting what people are doing to address a problem, as opposed to fixating on the problem itself). In a prior study, we created alternate versions of news headlines and found that emphasizing either crisis or action increased engagement, increasing intentions to read and share the news articles (relative to the original headlines, as published). Crisis and action framing strongly modulated emotional responses (increasing negative and positive affect, respectively). Both positive and negative affect predicted intentions to read and share news. In the present study, we aim to replicate these findings and extend our paradigm to investigate new outcome measures. To investigate effects of message framing on prosocial action, we will provide participants with a small endowment that they may optionally donate to causes associated with issues described in each news article. We will also include a next-day surprise memory test to assess memory for the headlines and associated images.

title_r: The relationship between vigilance and cue utilisation in driving
abstract_r: Motor vehicle driving is one of the riskiest activities that people undergo on a daily basis. In Australia between 2015 and 2017, driving-related accidents accounted for 22% of deaths in people aged 15 to 24 years of age, higher than any older age group (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, 2019). This suggests that less experienced drivers are more susceptible to road accidents than more experienced drivers. The four most common causes of driving fatalities in 2016 were alcohol consumption, speeding, driver fatigue and inattention (Budget Direct, 2019). Safe and responsible drivers must remain vigilant and attend to critical threats in the driving environment both inside and outside the vehicle. Often, this involves sustained monitoring and scanning of the road for potential and unexpected obstacles that may occur (e.g., monitoring the open highway at night). As human error is at the core of driving accidents, understanding the relevant cognitive processes such as vigilance that may distinguish driver ability means that steps can be taken to improve driver skill and thereby reduce accidents. According to attentional resource theories, cognitive resources are drawn from an observer’s capacity-limited working memory during the process of sustained attention (Baddeley, 2000). This means that, over an extended period of time, cognitive resources are depleted to the point where the capacity to respond accurately and rapidly is diminished (Kahneman, 1973). However, with repeated exposure to stimuli, associations can form that enable predictive cues. Sturman et al. (2010c) showed that behaviour associated with cue utilisation, which is the degree to which people are able to effectively use associations or patterns within data, is related to differences in the rate at which cognitive resources are consumed during a sustained attention task. Previous research has shown that there are individual differences in how drivers respond to environmental cues (Sturman & Wiggins, 2019c; Yuris, Wiggins, Auton, Gaicon, & Sturman, 2019). Cues comprise an association between environmental features, such as a green traffic light, and an event or outcome, such as ‘release the brake’. With exposure, these associations become specialised, automated routines in memory that, on activation, reduce the demands for cognitive resources. The residual resources can be directed towards other tasks, including secondary tasks (Brouwers, Wiggins, Helton, O’Hare, & Griffin, 2016; Sturman et al., 2019c). Brouwers and colleagues (2016) measured cue utilisation using the driving battery of EXPERTise 2.0, and included a novel rail control task as an independent measure of sustained attention. In this task, participants were asked to monitor multiple rail lines simultaneously and intervene to re-route trains on 50% of trials. The results indicated that behaviour associated with a relatively greater capacity for cue utilisation in driving was associated with an increased capacity to adapt to the demands of this novel railway task. This suggests that a capacity for cue utilisation may constitute a domain-general capability that can be generalised across tasks. However, the inference that cue utilisation (as measured by EXPERTise 2.0) predicts performance on vigilance tasks remains unclear, since the target prevalence in the railway task was 50%, rather than < 10% as is typically the case in vigilance tasks. In many real-world scenarios, including highway driving and semi-autonomous vehicle driving, participants are asked to monitor a scene over an extended period of time, and to remain attentive even when the likelihood of a response being required (target prevalence) is low. This is a special case of sustained attention: vigilance. The Multiple Object Monitoring Task (MOM: Karimi-Rouzbahani, Woolgar & Rich, 2020) is a new paradigm designed to measure vigilance in a lab context with features of real-world monitoring scenarios: moving items, selection of relevant from irrelevant information, and extended time periods, with either frequent (active condition: 50%) or infrequent (monitoring/vigilance condition: ~6%) targets. As one of the major theories of vigilance decrements in performance over time is the depletion of cognitive resources (Helton & Russell, 2011; Helton & Warm, 2008), and high cue utilisation has been proposed to reduce cognitive load, if there is a domain-general effect, it should be evident in performance on the MOM task. This research is designed to test the contribution of cue utilisation in a driving context to vigilance as measured by the MOM task (Karimi-Rouzbahani, et al., 2020). As cognitive ability predicts performance on vigilance tasks (e.g., Shaw, Matthews, Finomore, & Warm, 2009), the participants’ score on a fluid intelligence test will be included as a covariate. We define performance in terms of (a) accuracy on detecting potential collisions (% hits vs misses) and (b) reaction time (RT) to detect potential collisions (average RT on detected targets, known as correct RTs). We compare performance based on the average of the first 5 blocks (‘early’) compared to the final 5 blocks (‘late’). We also look at performance in each block over time, but due to the small numbers of trials in each block under monitoring conditions, the major inference will be based on the averages across early and late blocks. We address four main questions in the current study: 1. We test whether we replicate the original findings on the MOM task (Karimi-Rouzbahani, et al. 2020): we predict a greater decrease in performance over time in monitoring compared with active conditions, and a significant decrease in performance from early to late blocks, primarily in the monitoring condition. 2. We test whether the findings of Brouwers et al. (2016) replicate with a domain-general test of sustained attention (a condition of the MOM). We test whether cue utilisation predicts baseline performance in the active condition of the MOM task reflecting the maintenance of attention over time when responses are frequent. We predict that in early blocks, cue utilisation will not differentiate performance, but in late blocks, those with lower cue utilisation will have poorer performance compared with people with higher cue utilisation, controlling for cognitive ability. 3. We will examine whether cue utilisation differentiates performance on the MOM task in the vigilance (monitoring) condition, as a type of sustained attention when targets are infrequent. We predict that in early blocks, cue utilisation will not differentiate performance, but in late blocks, those participants with lower cue utilisation will record poorer performance compared with participants with higher cue utilisation, controlling for cognitive ability. 4. Based on cognitive load theories of vigilance, we test whether participants with higher cue utilisation are better able to maintain performance when targets are rare over and above their ability to sustain attention in general, than participants with lower cue utilisation. We test this by comparing the performance of participants with higher and lower cue utilisation on active vs monitoring conditions in the late blocks.

title_r: Coronavirus Mitigation
abstract_r: This study will attempt to replicate and extend a previous study on coronavirus mitigation efforts. In that study, we found that providing contextual information about social distancing increased people's perceptions that such measures were unnecessary and more harmful than helpful, but not when described as being from a similar location (New Jersey vs Brazil). Political affiliation was strongly correlated with these judgments as well such that conservatives saw mitigation efforts as both unnecessary and more harmful than helpful. Interestingly, participants did not differ in terms of whether they thought mitigation efforts were effective or whether the projections are wrong. Thus people who disagree with mitigation efforts seem to be disagreeing with their value and not the actually efficacy of such efforts. Here we seek to replicate this effect and to show that it is primarily driven by the political nature of the topic; we expect not to see the same pattern of results in a less politicized area, seat-belt use. Further we expect that reactance, cultural world views, populism, and political orientation to moderate these effects of politicalization.

title_r: CROWN Act: Exploring natural hair as an identity-safety cue among Black women
abstract_r: The goals of the present investigation are two-fold. Foremost, the current experiment will examine whether organizational norms celebrating natural hair will signal identity-safety for Black women. Specifically, participants will view company news that either celebrates the state senate passing the CROWN Act – an act that extends legal protection against hair-based discrimination, or the passing of the CRAFT act – an act that provides legal protection against appearance-related discrimination (i.e., tattoos and piercings). Second, we will also examine whether a Black man (versus white woman) employee with a natural (versus traditionally worn) hairstyle signals identity-safety for Black women. The current study is an extension of a previous study exploring natural hair as an identity-safety cue (see pre-registration here: https://osf.io/c3h4z/?view_only=0bb8527f187843ec8c803855f8ecbe82 ). In this previous work, we found that a Black man employee promoted greater organizational safety than a white woman employee. Likewise, we found that a Black man employee with natural hair promoted the highest levels of authenticity. In the current study, we sought to replicate this finding, while also examining the presence (versus absence) of an organizational norm celebrating natural hairstyles and prohibiting hair-based discrimination.

title_r: Insights into Diagnosing Cognitive Engagement – A Replication Study in the Context of Technology-Supported English Lessons
abstract_r: Cognitive engagement supports efficient learning and is one of the most important aspects of good teaching (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Kunter & Voss, 2011). We conceptualize cognitive engagement with the ICAP framework (Chi & Wylie, 2014) which proposes the four levels of cognitive engagement: Passive (P), active (A), constructive (C) and interactive (I). Digital media has proven to be very efficient in initiating cognitive engagement (Stegmann, 2020). Therefore, it may be beneficial for teachers to know how to cognitively engage their learners, using technology. This skill includes diagnosing cognitive engagement in a technology-related context (DCB, 2017), indicating that teachers need technology-related diagnostic skills. As teaching does not only include giving lessons but also planning them (DCB, 2017), the technology-related skills are needed when planning (panning phase) and when giving lessons (implementing phase). Acquiring complex skills like these can be facilitated by using simulations as they approximate practice and reduce its complexity (Grossmann et al., 2009; Chernikova et al., 2020). We created a simulation which aims at fostering technology-related diagnostic skills regarding cognitive engagement in the context of technology-related English lessons. Participants diagnose cognitive engagement in lesson plans and students’ activities within a technology-related context (i.e., lesson plans and students’ tasks are technology-related). With the study we aim at systematically inspecting the difficulty of the levels of cognitive engagement (passive, active, constructive, interactive), proposing that levels that require inferential processes (i.e., levels cannot be diagnosed merely by observing learners but require further information like a learning product) in order to determine them (active, constructive and interactive) are more difficult to diagnose accurately. This present study follows a similar simulation study, in which we inspected the difficulty of diagnosing the levels of cognitive engagement for the first time. Therefore, we aim at replicating the following research question of the preceding study: To what extent does the difficulty of diagnosing levels of cognitive engagement depend on differences in the levels of cognitive engagement (inferring vs. no inferring) within the phases of teaching (i.e., planning phase, implementing phase)?

title_r: Relative task demands and demand preference
abstract_r: This study investigates the relationship between relative task demands, ability, and demand preferences. We aim to replicate results found in a previous experiment that suggested relative task demands can influence demand preferences and the association between ability and demand preferences. This experiment will have three conditions using a spatial working memory task: high vs low, low versus no-task, and high versus no-task. High- and low-demand levels will be set using a staircase algorithm for each subject, with the low-demand aiming at 90% accuracy and the high-demand aiming at 75% accuracy. After these levels are set, participants will be given the choice between two options: in the low/high condition this will be between performing the low- or the high-demand levels, in the task/no-task conditions, the options will be between performing either a low or high-demand level versus sitting quietly for the same duration as a block (no-task). Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the three conditions. We predict that in the low/high condition, the low-demand will have higher accuracy than the high-demand level. We also predict that accuracy will be associated with task choices in the task/no-tasks conditions.

title_r: Utilitarian moral judgment, reflection and moral leniency (2)
abstract_r: There are two aims to this study. First, we wanted to replicate the findings of the previous study (Utilitarian moral judgment, reflection and moral leniency) regarding the "Moral Leniency Hypothesis", and address some of its limitations. This ML hypothesis states that what is commonly called an "utilitarian" answer to moral dilemmas, is not actually participants showing a committment to utilitarianism but a result of their "Moral Leniency". For this we will again investigate the link between Cognitive style, Moral Leniency and "Utilitarian" moral judgement. Compared to the first study, some measures of Cognitive style have been changed and moral dilemmas were replaced with pairs in order to use a process dissociation approach. More precisely, our main hypotheses are : (i) That a more analytic cognitive style will predict more utilitarian moral judgment, (ii) That a more analytic cognitive style will predict higher moral leniency (iii) That a higher moral leniency will predict more utilitarian moral judgment (iv) That moral leniency will mediate the relationship between cognitive style and moral judgment This study also investigates the link between Utilitarian moral judgment and animal ethics, more specifically speciesism. Some studies (Bègue & Laine, 2017) found that Utilitarianism is positively correlated with negative attitudes towards animals. This finding is surprising considering the history of the animal advocacy movement, in which some arguments clearly rely on utilitarian thinking. However, in these past studies, Utilitarianism was assessed by classic moral dilemmas, which may not be a good measure of Utilitarian tendencies. Thus, we will investigate whether true Utilitarianism, as assessed by (i) the process dissociation approach and (ii) asking whether the utilitarian answer is the best one and a moral duty, is negatively correlated with instrumental attitudes towards animals and speciesism. Then, we will see if the puzzling results of previous experiments can be explained by the fact that the "utilitarian" answers in these classic dilemmas are in fact a sign of moral leniency. Thus, the positive link between an instrumental representation of animals and "utilitarian" judgments would come from the fact that an "utilitarian" answer in these dilemmas is linked with more moral leniency, which leads to stronger endorsement of instrumentalization of animals. title_r: Effects of target frequency on the temporal dynamics of attentional selection
abstract_r: Attention can be focused on specific locations in our visual field (space-based attention), but also spreads along objects (object-based attention). However, object-based effects are prone to large individual differences and seem not as prevalent as previously assumed. In a previous study, we investigated individual differences in the temporal dynamics of attentional selection. Our results showed that individual differences in the temporal aspects of attentional selection are not the underlying cause for the low-prevalence of object-based effects. We further assessed the rhythmic sampling of visual space underlying object- and space-based effects. Our data suggest that the rhythmic sampling depends on the target frequency and is particularly enhanced for targets with a low frequency (invalid targets: 10% validity for invalid same and different targets) and robust for those with a high frequency (valid trials: 80% cue validity). In three experiments, we further assess the effects of target frequency on attentional selection and the rhythmic sampling of visual space. Experiment 1 is a direct replication of our previous study. However, we will collect data for all three experiments online. In Experiment 2, we change the target frequency to be 50% (50% valid, 25% invalid same- and different-object target locations). In Experiment 3, target frequency was balanced across valid, invalid same- and different-object target locations.

title_r: Rhetorical Effectiveness of Insinuations: Interaction between Explicitness and Fallaciousness - Experiment 3 (Justificatory role of Argument; Character)
abstract_r: In this project, we present an experiment that seeks evidence on whether the explicitness/implicitness of a personal attack in ad hominem constructions is likely to have a different effect depending on its fallacious/non-fallacious nature. We aim to replicate the exploratory results of previous experiments, where preference for insinuations was only present when the attack was fallacious, and open up further reflections on the interaction between pragmatics and argumentation. Indeed, our preliminary observations show that pragmatic variations can affect rhetorical effects insofar as they are consistent with normative considerations in argumentation. In the first two preregistered experiments (Experiment 1 and Experiment 2), we observed results that contradicted our hypotheses. Firstly, we did not find any interaction, as indicated by our exploratory analyses. Additionally, the interest of insinuation was found solely for the perceived benevolence of the opponent. We attribute these inconsistent findings to the type of attack used in the first two experiments, which targeted the proponent’s lack of knowledge or expertise in a specific domain. Nonetheless, ad hominem attacks are not restricted to pointing out a lack of knowledge; they may also include personal attacks on the proponent’s personality, morals, or values. This perspective of also addressing attacks on personality aligns more closely with the exploratory analyses’ experiments. In fact, by conducting further exploratory analyses differentiating between personal attacks based on a lack of expertise in a field and those targeting the proponent’s integrity, the previously observed interaction appears to only apply to the latter type of attack and is not present for the former. Therefore, in the subsequent two experiments (Experiment 3 and Experiment 4), we hypothesise that the interaction between degrees of explicitness and fallaciousness only (or mainly) plays out in the case of an attack on the integrity of the proponent.

title_r: Good-enough production: priming influences production
abstract_r: We expand our previous preregistration and predict an influence of priming on the accessibility of lexical items during language production. Specifically, priming should increase accessibility, and thus influence the selection between general category labels and specific-level labels. By priming general category labels (flower, weed), we expect participants to produce these labels more often compared to specific labels, even though specific labels provide twice the reward. This would indicate that participants are balancing an accessibility—informativity trade-off. We will replicate our previous experiment structure (https://osf.io/4kbrc). Once again, during the Intermediate phase (24 trials), participants in a Prime condition will be asked to respond to images by identifying each as a flower or weed (flowers and weeds will each appear 12 times each). In a No-priming condition participants will be asked to respond to images by responding whether each is a canine or feline (dogs and cats will each appear 12 times each). The rest of the experiment is the same. Responses will be required within a 3 second window (the Speeded condition of the previous experiment) and with non-confusable images to allow us to focus on the main variable of interest: priming. Finally, we will include specific instructions that tell our participants that four-character responses are acceptable at all stages of the experiment.

title_r: Visual similarity effects in complex span: A replication of experiments with articulatory suppression and size-judgement tasks
abstract_r: The contribution of visual codes in working memory has been confirmed by the fact that serial order memory performance is better for a sequence that consists of visually dissimilar items than visually similar items. This is called the visual similarity effect. This diagnostic phenomenon has been tested so far in immediate serial recall of verbal materials (e.g., Logie et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2008). In our previous experiments (Saito et al., 2020), we found the visual similarity effects in a complex span task, which is one of the most prevalently used working memory tasks. In those experiments, English speaking participants were required to remember a series of six monosyllabic English words drawn from a visually dissimilar or visually similar set, with each word followed by a 4,800 ms retention interval. Specifically, we reported that the visual similarity effects appeared in an articulatory suppression condition in which participants were required to utter "1, 2, 3" repeatedly during every retention interval, while the effect disappeared in a size judgement condition in which they were required during the retention interval to judge whether a presented drawing represents an object that smaller than, equivalent to, or larger than a soccer ball in the real world. This judgement is assumed to require participants to generate visual images of a soccer ball and another object. In this preregistration study, we attempt to replicate the findings in our previous experiments. Therefore, the hypotheses we will test are identical to those we tested in the previous study. One practical advantage of testing the visual similarity effect with complex span tasks is that we can manipulate several factors efficiently by changing the characteristics of processing tasks between memory items in the span task. Then we can examine the sensitivities of the visual similarity effect to the processing task manipulations. References Logie, R. H., Saito, S., Morita, A., Varma, S., & Norris, D. (2016). title_r: Personal Memories and Social Associations: How Positive Emotions Influence the Activation of Implicit Prejudice
abstract_r: Recent research has shown that attitudes can be influenced by induced emotion states (DeSteno, Dasgupta, Bartlett, & Cajdric, 2004; Cottrell & Neuberg, 2005; Dasgupta, DeSteno, Williams, & Hunsinger, 2009). The purpose of this study is to examine the effects of two positive discrete emotions, awe and nurturant love, on implicit prejudices. In a previous study, we hypothesized that nurturant love would increase the strength of negative evaluations of Arab individuals and positive evaluations of White individuals, whereas awe would decrease the strength of these negative evaluations when compared to a neutral condition. However, in Study 1 we found, surprisingly, that both awe and nurturant love increased negative implicit prejudices toward Arab individuals when compared to the neutral condition. The current study is a direct replication of Study 1. After completing an emotion induction task, participants will complete Implicit Association Test blocks where they pair photos of Arab and White individuals with “good” and “bad” evaluations. Reaction times, demographic information, and answers to questions about the participants identities and attitudes towards others will be recorded for analyses.

title_r: Character Interdependence
abstract_r: The proposed research will investigate the importance of prior character behavior when audience members form moral perceptions of subsequent characters and a narrative as a whole. Participants will read a story where one character has behaved in a moral or immoral fashion followed by a second character behaving in a morally neutral fashion. Individuals will then rate their moral perceptions of the story and characters, along with demographic and psychographic measures. The proposal seeks to provide a more holistic explanation of how audiences form moral perceptions of characters when attending to a narrative. The principal investigator and key personnel have completed related studies at their previous institution. This work has been presented at conferences and published in journals in the Communication field. This work suggests that audiences make moral judgments of characters based on their perceptions of preceding characters (Character A influences perceptions of Character B through priming). The basis of this work was visual impressions using pictures absent of character behavior. The studies that will come from this proposal will examine whether the previously stated phenomena are also dependent upon character behavior in a narrative. Toward this goal, narratives have been written specifically for this study in order to examine the proposed hypotheses. The narratives present a story about two scientists trying to understand the Yellowstone Super Caldera. The narratives present either Character A being a good person or a bad person while Character B is always described neutrally (see attached Narrative Stimuli document for the narratives). By creating new narratives that are similar to extant narratives, this study will provide stimuli that is more representative of extant entertainment narrative and provide a more accurate estimation of results when generalizing. Additionally, we hope to replicate the findings from previous work to demonstrate robust results and provide evidence towards this framework. We did not have any adverse or unwanted effects reported by any previous participants, and we believe that the opportunity to collect worthwhile information with minimal risk to participants is very high. Specific scholarly aims of this research are to develop a new framework for understanding how audiences form moral judgments of characters within a narrative, to understand whether using more ecologically valid stimuli will provide similar effects to past work, to replicate previous findings offered in the moral media literature, and to understand the impact of character dynamics on narrative outcomes and processes (i.e., transportation, character liking, etc.).

title_r: BB-PRIME Phase II: Synergistic Episodic Simulation Interventions for Climate Action
abstract_r: Prior studies have demonstrated that episodic simulation (e.g., in the form of a guided imagination exercise that illustrates future or hypothetical scenarios) can increase patient decision-making, prosocial intentions and behaviors, perceived risk, and future-oriented thinking (Sinclair et al., 2021; Gaesser & Schacter, 2014; Gaesser et al., 2020; Bulley et al., 2016; Schacter et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2020). In particular, prior studies have shown benefits of two-part interventions: episodic simulation can enhance subsequent learning from feedback in intervention tasks that correct misconceptions about risk (Sinclair et al., 2021) or the impact of climate action (Lee et al., 2020). In a prior study, we found that an episodic simulation exercise (imagining oneself experiencing a negative future scenario that could arise from climate change) increased intentions to engage in pro-environmental behaviors and influenced emotions related to climate change (e.g., increasing anger and perceived risk). In this prior study, we also tested multiple other intervention strategies and identified other approaches that had similar or complementary effects (e.g., increasing the perceived impact of climate action, increasing hope and self-efficacy, correcting misconceptions about which mitigation actions matter most). In the present study, we aim to replicate our prior findings and test novel multi-part interventions, combining strategies that target different psychological mechanisms. On the basis of prior research (described above), we expect that episodic simulation will induce a state that will enhance the effectiveness of subsequent intervention tasks.

title_r: Students’ attitudes towards mental health and physical health problems
abstract_r: Because in a previous study conducted by our team (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/MQSZW), we found the surprising result that students have more positive attitudes towards mental illness than to physical health problems using the VAAST, we aim to replicate this study. Indeed, our finding contradicts past literature. That’s why, we have conducted a complementary exploratory study evaluating threat based on the Sociofunctional Model of Prejudice (Cottrell & Neuberg, 2006) testing the same etiquettes used in our VAAST adaptation (physical health conditions and mental health conditions). In this second study, we found no difference in threat in these two categories. So, we hypothesize that our surprising result (more positive attitudes towards mental health conditions as opposed to physical health conditions) may be related to the period in which the study was conducted: just after the covid confinements. title_r: Uncertainty, low-dimensional meaning and affects. A mediational model
abstract_r: This study aims to provide further empirical evidence in support of the Semiotic Dimensionality Model (SDM), according to which uncertainty triggers affective activation that reduces environmental complexity in order to allow the individual to provide an interpretation of events/objects in the external environment. The SDM conceptualizes uncertainty as the inability of individuals to produce a stable interpretation of their context, leading to the adoption of simplified and affect-laden meanings. According to SDM, uncertainty reduces the dimensionality of mental representations, focusing on basic affective dimensions (e.g., valence, arousal) to manage complexity. This process is rooted in embodied cognition, where affective meanings serve as fundamental, low-dimensional structures for interpreting destabilizing experiences. Previous preliminary studies have shown, for example, that destabilizing the sense of national identity (which the authors define theoretically in terms of domain meanings) leads to low-dimensional interpretations, measured through linguistic and cognitive tasks (Salvatore et al., 2023); or that inducing constructive uncertainty (i.e., lack of contextual cues) leads to greater affective activation and lower semantic dimensionality in narratives, further validating the computational approach of SDM. The present study aims to test the hypothesis that exposure to constructive uncertainty (i.e., stimuli lacking contextual cues) influences affective responses and meaning dimensionality at the physiological, linguistic, cognitive, and belief system levels. By experimentally manipulating uncertainty, we seek to validate the SDM hypothesis that affect-laden low-dimensional meanings emerge as a coping strategy under conditions of uncertainty. An experiment will be conducted by randomly assigning participants to three groups (experimental: prime without context; control 1: prime with context; control 2: neutral prime) and pre-post measures of affective, linguistic, and cognitive responses will be employed. Specifically, we expect that: H1. Constructive uncertainty (prime without context) will trigger greater affective activation than control conditions (prime with context and neutral), measured using self-report measures (Positive and Negative Affect Schedule [PANAS; Watson et al., 1988]) and physiological indices (heart rate). H2. This uncertainty will reduce the dimensionality of meaning, measured at the linguistic level (Affective Saturation Index [Gennaro et al., 2021]) and cognitive level (Meaning-Making Dimensionality Index [Reho et al., under review], PANAS). With this study, we plan to replicate and extend previous SDM findings, demonstrating that uncertainty systematically shifts meaning-making toward affective and low-dimensional modalities. This will strengthen the explanatory power of the model for socio-cognitive responses to uncertainty in real-world contexts (e.g., polarization, threats to identity). title_r: Group dynamics between young girls. A replication of Sherif’s Robbers Cave study with girls.
abstract_r: The original study’s key goal was to examine how the nature of intergroup relations impact intergroup behaviours and attitudes in an experimental manner. Such behaviours and attitudes could be discrimination and prejudice (Sherif, M., et al. (1961). Sherif and his colleagues made sure to secure “homogeneity of subjects as to sociocultural and personal backgrounds” (Sherif, M., et al. (1961). The goal was to acquire a sample of participants who were least likely to have familial, psychological or sociocultural traits that might befoul the study’s findings (Sherif, M., et al. (1961). The study consisted of 22 participants, and they were all white boys around the age of 12. They all were of protestant background and their psychological and physical development was ordinary. Moreover, interviews were conducted with the caregivers of the participants, school records were evaluated and psychological tests were administered. In short, one could say that, according to the standards of the time, the boys were normal (Sherif, M., et al. (1961). The experiment itself consisted of three different phases (McLeod, S. A. (2008)). Phase 1 lasted about five to six days and focused on in-group formation. In this phase, the members of each of the two groups got acquainted, developed social norms and found their spot in the group. After a while, the group developed a structure and leadership appeared. In this phase, the two groups were kept separate from each other and did not know the other group existed. It was of importance for the two groups to bond as individual groups first (McLeod, S. A. (2008)). Phase 2 focused on conflict within the individual groups and lasted about four to five days. The two groups came into contact with each other, competing in different games and challenges, and also for control of territory. The purpose of this phase was to bring the two groups into competition with each other in order to create frustration between them(McLeod, S. A. (2008)). In phase 3 the focus was on the reduction of the intergroup conflict and it lasted about six to seven days. Sherif and his colleagues used various means to lessen the animosity and low-level violence between the two groups. Different improvised reconciliatory opportunities, such as showing a film or shooting firecrackers as a celebration of the fourth of July, did not lead to any reduction of the tension between the groups. Instead, they arranged a couple of situations with superordinate goals which could not be easily ignored by members of both groups, like getting drinking water and securing a movie (McLeod, S. A. (2008)). The study found that competition between groups leads to prejudice and hostility, whereas intergroup cooperation reduces it. Sherif and colleagues specifically found that superordinate goals, which are goals that are so large that achieving them requires more than one group. It is important to replicate this study to find out if there would be a different outcome if it would be all girls instead of all boys and if there would be any gender differences. It is also important to replicate in terms of different social norms in today's society than it was in Sherif’s time. In this replication we predict that the results are going to show a difference in behaviour due to gender differences. Modern stereotypes makes us expect that the girls competitive behaviour and feelings of Group identity will possibly be more verbal and emotional, than the boys behaviour in the original study where they acted out a bit more physical.

abstract_r: Stroop effect is the delay in reaction time between congruent and incongruent stimuli. title_r: Replication: CIE - Social Endorsement
abstract_r: An initial experiment (see https://osf.io/vt7p6/) investigated whether high vs. low endorsement (i.e., number of “likes”) of misinformation posts and corresponding fact-checks modulated people’s belief in misinformation. Results suggested that level of misinformation endorsement affects misinformation belief, both before and after exposure to fact-check information. However, in contrast to both predictions and past research (see Vlasceanu & Coman, 2021) the results of this experiment suggested that the influence of fact-check endorsement on belief may be limited, with there being weak evidence of an effect of fact-check endorsement after a short delay. The current study aims to directly replicate this experiment to provide additional evidence for the role of social endorsement in both belief in misinformation and belief updating in the face of corrective information. Further, the current study will also include an additional no-endorsement control condition. The control condition is included because although Experiment 1 suggests that people appraise (mis)information differently based on level of endorsement, it does not provide specific evidence for what is driving this effect. Specifically, from the results of Experiment 1 it remains unclear whether high endorsement increases belief, and/or whether low endorsement decreases belief compared to when people receive no endorsement information. Thus, in addition to a direct replication, the current experiment aims to tease apart these possibilities.

title_r: Why does the darkness promote cheating III: The effect of the ambiguity in task outcomes
abstract_r: A previous study showed that darkness environment could increase cheating by creating a sense of “illusory anonymity” that let individuals expect that they would be difficult to be perceived by others (Zhong et al., 2010). We have successfully replicated the phenomena reported by Zhong et al. (2010) in an early study (https://osf.io/nkjq5). However, the perceived anonymity of participants in our results did not support the explanation by Zhong et al. (2010). According to our results, we proposed another hypothesis that the outcomes of the task in a dark environment could present a kind of “ambiguity”. It means that it was difficult for participants (and also for experimenters) to visually confirm the outcome because of the dark illumination conditions. We considered participants tended to believe that the outcome was in their favor and reported it without a closer check of the true outcome in this situation. Thus, we designed a non-visual task to ensure that participants could know the outcomes, then used the task to check participants’ cheating indicators in different illumination conditions (See more details in https://osf.io/p6j4t). In contrast to the earlier study, we found that in terms of illumination, there was no significant difference in the cheating indicators, and the effect size was considerably smaller (d = 0.1) than in the study using a visual task (https://osf.io/nkjq5, d = 0.37). To further confirm the effect of ambiguity of the task outcomes on cheating, we decided to conduct an experiment by directly manipulating this factor in the present study.

title_r: Continuous state-space transitions shape mental state concepts
abstract_r: This study is a direct replication of a pilot study. It aims to replicate the central finding of the earlier behavioral studies - that transition dynamics shape mental state concepts. In this case, the alien's states will not be directly provided in the form of word labels. Instead, participants must infer the state from a noisy indicator: the alien's eye colors. These manifest indicators reflect the latent state of the alien, which exists in a continuous state space. Four attractor basins within this state space compose the alien's discrete states, and the alien makes nonlinear transitions between them in accordance with a pre-specified transition probability matrix. As in previous studies, we will test whether these transition predict subsequent judgements of the similarity between states.
