title_r: The Effects of Facial Attractiveness and Trustworthiness in the Sharing Economy
abstract_r: Online peer-to-peer markets, such as Airbnb, often include profile photos of sellers to reduce anonymity. Ert and colleagues (2016) found that more trustworthy-looking, but not more attractive-looking, Airbnb hosts charge higher prices for similar apartments. This suggests that people are willing to pay more for a night in an apartment if the host looks trustworthy. Here, we present a pre-registered replication testing how photo-based impressions of hosts’ attractiveness and trustworthiness influence rental prices. We extend previous investigations by (a) controlling for additional features related to price (e.g., the apartment’s location), (b) testing for an influence of other host features, such as ethnicity and facial expression, and (c) analyzing a substantially larger sample of apartments. An analysis of 1,020 listings in New York City showed that more attractive-looking, but not more trustworthy-looking, hosts charge higher prices for their apartments. Compared to White hosts, Black (but not Asian) hosts charge lower prices for their apartments. Hosts who smile more intensely in their profile photo charge higher prices. Our results support the general conclusion that people rely on profile photos in online markets, though we find that attractiveness is more important than trustworthiness.

title_r: Spatial correlates of coherence follow-up
abstract_r: In this project, we aim to examine whether the perception of coherence is mentally represented on the vertical dimension. Previous studies revealed that when two concepts are objectively coherent or they "fit together" (e.g., two concepts that come from a valid versus invalid syllogism), people see them as spatially close to each other (von Hecker et al., 2016). Extending these findings, we will test whether coherence is represented on the vertical dimension when people reason about coherence in the context of situations that are relevant to themselves. The rationale behind this question is that, in perceptual terms, higher verticality is usually associated with higher perceptual scope, which in turn leads to greater visual coherence. Based on this principle, Slepian et al. (2015) suggested that such greater perceptual scope should be also associated with conceptual coherence, or in other words higher construal levels (thinking about how elements fit together). Indeed, they found that the experience of high verticality leads to more abstract processing and more meaningful associations between concepts and categories than low verticality, and the nature of this relationship is bidirectional. That is, abstract processing also influences the experience of verticality (Slepian et al., 2015). Given that there is a bidirectional causal relationship between verticality and levels of processing, in the current study, we hypothesise that spatial processing associated with verticality supports people’s mental representation of coherence. That is, verticality is utilised to reason about coherence. We obtained initial evidence for the vertical representation of coherence across two studies that used socially meaningful (Study 1) and abstract syllogisms (Study 2). In the current study, we aim to replicate our previous findings using a different population.

title_r: FallingDroppingUnmoderated
abstract_r: This is an attempt at an unmoderated online conceptual replication of a previous study evaluating children's ability to calculate probabilities from imagined possibilities. We created digital "plinko" boxes, where one or two balls fall through a series of obstacles into bins at the bottom of the screen. Children have two "cushions" that can be placed in the bins. They are trained, in deterministic situations, that when there is one place for balls to go (because there is one ball following a deterministic path) they should put both cushions in that bin. When there are two places for balls to go (because there are two balls following deterministic paths to two different bins), they should put one cushion in each place. At test, these two trial types are repeated 3 times; a third trial type is added: trials where there is one ball that can go either of two places, each with 50% probability. The research question is: do children stack their cushions up, as though there is only one place for the ball to go? Or do they spread them out, as though there are two place for the ball to go? This is the fourth study in this line of studies. Earlier studies showed that 4-year-olds tend to stack their cushions in one possible bin. In this study we add age, testing children from age 4;0 to 8;11 to see when children start taking both possibilities into account when placing their cushions.

title_r: Triplett’s Social Facilitation Experiment: A Registered Replication Report
abstract_r: A seminal study by Triplett provided initial evidence for the social facilitation effect, and over the last century research has demonstrated this effect across a range of settings. However, despite the importance of Triplett’s study no research has replicated the original study paradigm. Furthermore, in the context of research advances and methodological rigour, some elements of the original study weaken the validity of the observed findings. We address these critical limitations and replicate the original study, employing a standardized study protocol to minimise potential confounds, such as practice effects. A minimum of 400 school-aged children will be recruited. Using a purpose-built apparatus, participants will complete each trial twice — once alone and once in competition with another participant. Trial order will be standardized. The results of this study will extend research on social facilitation by replicating the original study paradigm and exploring potential age and gender effects.

title_r: The role of culture and ideal affect in romantic relationships: A replication
abstract_r: Cultural differences in ideal affect, or the emotions people want to feel, have been associated with different conceptions of romantic love. Specifically, a previous study found that European Americans value partner attractiveness and romantic relationship excitement more than Japanese, and these differences are explained by European Americans valuing excitement and other high arousal positive (HAP) states more than Japanese. Additionally, among participants who reported being in a relationship, we found cultural differences in the extent to various partner response styles to good news predict relationship satisfaction: For European Americans, an enthusiastic and involved response style predicted greater relationship satisfaction, whereas passive and/or critical response styles predicted lower relationship satisfaction. In contrast, among Japanese, while enthusiastic and involved responses also predicted relationship satisfaction, none of the other response styles (passive and/or critical) predicted lower relationship satisfaction. We seek to replicate these results in a separate sample of Japanese (N = 200) and European Americans in the U.S. (N = 200).

title_r: Underlying Mechanisms of Nature’s Effect on State Authenticity: A Replication in Western Community Sample
abstract_r: In our previous studies, we showed that nature can enhance state authenticity, across various nature manipulation, such as exposure to both real nature settings and digital nature pictures (vs. urban nature and digital ones) and engagement with nature-related activities (vs. control ones). We also found that this effect is mediated by need for autonomy, positive affect, self-esteem, and mindfulness, independently. In the current experiment, we ask participants to view a 5-minute video depicting nature scenes (vs. urban ones) and to immerse themselves into the scenes. Subsequently, we ask participants to fill out scales measuring—at the state level—the four plausible mediators (autonomy satisfaction, positive affect, self-esteem, mindfulness) and the dependent measure (i.e., authenticity). We aimed to replicate and extend the prior findings by testing these four mediators (i.e., autonomy satisfaction, positive affect, self-esteem, mindfulness) both independently and in parallel. title_r: The facilitators and barriers to transferring Cued Congruency effects in The Flanker and Simon tasks
abstract_r: Everyday goal-directed behaviour depends on the flexible use of cognitive control, allowing us to adapt to changing demands and resolve conflict. One proposed mechanism for this flexibility is the formation of learned control states, where cues become associated with high or low conflict, enabling proactive adjustments before a task begins. While these cue-based adaptations have been observed within tasks like the Flanker or Simon paradigms, it is still unclear whether they reflect general learning that transfers between tasks, or task-specific strategies. In a previous study we found cued congruency effects within both the Flanker and Simon tasks, but no evidence of transfer between them. However, in an unpublished PhD thesis, Vasta N. (2024) found transfer from a letter Flanker task to a letter Simon task. While there were methodological differences between our studies, the underlying concept was the same. Vasta used highly predictive cues during training and then tested transfer in a separate block using non-predictive cues, while we interleaved both tasks and trained separate cues for each simultaneously. Their findings raised the possibility that control learning may be more generalisable than our study suggested. To clarify the conditions under which cue-based control transfers between tasks, the current project includes two experiments. Experiment 1 is a direct replication of Vasta’s Flanker to Simon design. Experiment 2 reverses the task order, testing whether a Simon to Flanker transfer is also possible. Together, these studies aim to clarify the nature, scope, and directionality of learned control states.

title_r: Meaningful versus Pleasurable Popular Music Video Exposure
abstract_r: Research suggests that entertainment media consumption can produce positive emotions, such as feeling meaningful and pleasurable (de Leeuw et al., 2022; Oliver et al., 2012). Specifically, when viewing entertainment media such as meaningful movies, people not only feel inspired and moved but also enjoyable (Haidt, 2000; Oliver et al., 2012). While several studies have focused on inspiring movies and speeches, recent research reveals that music videos can be a powerful media content making people feel inspired and joyful (de Leeuw et al., 2022; Raney et al., 2018). However, little research has considered popular music video consumptions typically shared on social media (e.g., YouTube). The literature suggests two types of music that have intrinsic features that can lead to either inspiring or hedonic feeling, including meaningful music and pleasurable music (de Leeuw et al., 2022). While the first type refers to sentimental music that is experienced as beautiful and inducing feelings of inspiration, the second pertains to music that leads to positive affect, such as feeling joyful and upbeat (de Leeuw et al., 2022). As such, classic and film music are regarded as meaningful music (e.g., Chopin’s classical music) and popular music (e.g., pop and rock songs) tend to be viewed as pleasurable music (Ji et al., 2021). However, it is possible that even music of the same genre (e.g., pop music) can lead to different audience emotional responses depending on its features. For example, pop music videos with fast tempos, dancing scenes, and upbeat lyrics might produce more pleasurable feelings than meaningful feelings. Vice-versa, pop music videos with moderate tempos, portrayals of human kindness and love, and lyrics containing insights about life might lead to audience feeling emotionally moved and meaningful. While there is still more work to learn about the intrinsic features of entertainment media types leading to these different emotional states, scholars have recently argued that entertainment media content that focuses on depicting humans’ threatened needs, life struggles, and virtue likely arouse meaningful feeling (Graaf & Das, 2023). The goal of this proposed study is to examine whether viewing popular music videos bearing different message features can lead to different audience experiences (pleasurable vs. meaningful experiences), and how such experiences might lead to prosocial motivation, hedonistic motivation, universal orientation, and thoughts about living a flourishing life. We extend and, to some extent, replicate prior research (de Leeuw et al., 2022) to add to the literature of media psychology and eudaimonic media effect. We expect that meaningful pop music videos will induce higher elevation, more physical responses indicative of transcendent emotions than pleasurable music (Oliver et al., 2012). We also expect that pleasurable pop music videos will induce higher pleasurable feelings and more physical responses indicative of enjoyment than meaningful music. We will replicate prior studies by testing the proposition that elevation induced from meaningful pop music videos (vs. pleasurable pop music videos) will lead to higher prosocial motivation and universal orientation, and lower hedonistic motivation. To add to the existing literature, we further hypothesize that experiencing elevation from viewing meaningful pop music videos will evoke thoughts about living a meaningful life and thoughts orienting toward building lasting social relationships with others. As guided by prior research, several important covariates are included to account for confounds and better interpretations of data: emotional contagion as part of trait empathy, need for affect, nostalgia, and engagement with beauty. While this project is part of a larger project and its original aim is to test a series of stimulus materials (i.e., pleasurable pop music videos vs. meaningful pop music videos), this project itself can be an independent study because the study’s design, hypotheses, and sample size allow for addressing both of these purposes. The steps taken in this project includes: 1. The research team use the Billboard 100 site to create a list of popular music songs in the recent 30 years. 2. The team view the song videos posted on YouTube site and use the criteria of tempo speed, portrayals of characters in the videos, and lyrics to categorize pleasurable versus meaningful pop music videos. 3. The team then randomly select 5 songs of each category and collect the top 100 comments posted to these videos on YouTube. 4. Two coders independently code the comments of each song. Results are used to confirm audience responses on YouTube are indicative of music video types in line with the categories identified in Step 2. Intercoder reliability is calculated to confirm the matches between the songs’ intrinsic features (Graaf & Das, 2023) and audience responses (Oliver et al., 2012). 5. An online experiment is conducted to test the proposed hypotheses.

title_r: Exploring a Cascade Model of Urgency: Momentary Dynamics of Stress, Affect, and Impulsivity and their Correlates
abstract_r: Negative urgency, as part of the four-factor model of impulsivity, refers to rash action taken in response to negative emotions (Whiteside & Lynam, 2001). Positive urgency or action taken in response to strong positive affect, has been suggested as a potential fifth factor contributing to impulsivity (Cyders et al., 2007). Sperry and colleagues (2018) have strongly argued against considering positive urgency as a distinct entity and instead suggest that all manifestations of impulsivity in the context of strong emotions be subsumed under a single factor of urgency (without valence modifier). However, we believe further research on these constructs is warranted, especially when directly assessed as dynamic processes. Urgency refers to an if… then process (“If I experience strong negative (or positive) emotion, then I will engage in risky behaviors.”) which dispositional scales can, at best, only approximate. Following this, we considered a cascade model from which stressful experiences lead to affective reactions, which in turn lead to both impulsive actions and impulsive urges in the absence of discrete risk behavior engagement (in individuals with personality disorders; Sharpe, Simms, & Wright, under review). At the daily level, our results were consistent with the hypothesized links between affect, stress, and impulsivity. Stress enhanced impulsivity both directly and through negative and positive affect. Parts of this process (namely the connections between stress and impulsivity and negative affect and impulsivity) are amplified in individuals who report stronger impulsive traits. The presence of independent effects for both regression pathways in the same model, as well as a lack of association among within-person links in PA, NA, and impulsivity suggest that the cascade of negative urgency and positive urgency operate as separate processes. In the present study, we will use multilevel structural equation modeling to examine within- and between-person predictors of momentary impulsivity with a particular focus on testing a cascade model of affect and momentary stress in a 10-day ambulatory assessment study of non-undergraduate community members. We seek to replicate our previous results from analyses at the daily level by modeling a cascade from stress to impulsivity through both positive and negative affect at the momentary level by regressing momentary impulsivity on the severity of lagged stress, positive affect, and negative affect. At level 2 (i.e., between-person) we will include trait impulsivity as measured by Impulsivity facet scores at baseline on the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5; Krueger, Derringer, Markon, Watson, & Skodol, 2012) as a between-person predictor. Additionally, we will extend the nomological network of the urgency cascade by examining associations of individual differences in within-person paths with other pathological traits (Negative Affect, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism) and externalizing behaviors (alcohol consumption and drug use). title_r: Does Information Predicting “When” and “What” Facilitate Target Detection Interactively? (Experiment 3)
abstract_r: Human responses to environmental stimuli are crucial for adapting to surroundings, particularly when cues accurately predict the occurrence of events requiring a response. In contexts involving interaction with assistance systems, such as driving with Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), cues about forthcoming events can enhance task performance. Additionally, the extent to which people predict the timing of events (i.e., timing predictability) is related to their responses to events because predictable timing enables us to anticipate the onset of forthcoming events implicitly. Despite the importance of these factors, the interactive effects of cue informativeness and timing predictability on human responses remain unclear. This study aims to investigate whether these two factors interact to influence target detection. A cued go/no-go task will be conducted via a crowdsourcing platform, manipulating two variables: timing predictability and cue informativeness. The constant delay between the cue and the target in one block is defined as the timing predictable condition. A variable delay is introduced in the other block, named the timing unpredictable condition. Cue informativeness will be varied across three levels: an informative cue indicating a high probability of a go target, a noninformative cue with an equal probability of signaling a go or no-go target, and a reverse informative cue suggesting a low probability of a go target. ## Our previous experiment did not reveal a significant interaction between the two factors. In this study, we aim to replicate these findings by employing multiple go targets that require action and implementing shorter delays between cue and target presentation.

title_r: Age Differences in Emotional Memory for Moral Dilemmas
abstract_r: Recent research highlights the importance of memory for moral behaviors in the formation of personal identity (Stanley et al. 2020). However, prior approaches to understanding memory for previously engaged moral and immoral behaviors involved autobiographical memory retrieval methods. Although this approach provides rich narratives of previously engaged behaviors, it is unclear how different individuals remember the emotionality of a commonly engaged moral behavior, following previous emotional valence ratings for these behaviors. Furthermore, it is unclear whether the emotional memory for these moral dilemmas change across the adult life span. Indeed, older adults rate proposed resolutions to first-person sacrificial moral dilemmas more negatively than younger adults (McNair et al., 2019). As such, it is possible that older adults will similarly recall these behaviors as more emotional than younger adults, suggesting a boundary effect on the commonly observed positive memory bias in older adults (Mather & Carstensen, 2005). However, given that older adults tend to show positivity biases in memory, it is possible that although they tend to rate first-person moral dilemmas more negatively than younger adults, they may remember previous moral dilemmas less negatively (i.e. more neutral), or no differently than younger adults. Previous work also links shortened temporal horizons in older compared to younger adults as assisting positivity biases. These shortened temporal horizons are thought to be associated with motivational shifts to focus on positive information in the present moment (Lang & Carstensen, 2002). This shortened temporal horizon is also thought to assist older adults in engaging in emotion regulation strategies, such that they avoid (i.e. expressive suppression) or engage in cognitive reappraisal to regulate their emotions away from negative and towards positive information. As such it is possible that individual differences in future time perspective or subjective emotional regulation strategy use may partially account for the relationship between age and emotional memory for previously engaged moral behaviors. Even in the absence of a significant effect of age, it is possible that emotion regulation relates to the relationship between valence ratings immediately following moral dilemmas, and emotional memory at a later time. That is, subjective reports of emotion regulation abilities may interact with valence ratings immediately following a moral dilemma to predict emotional memory ratings at a later time. Given the previous literature, here we seek to elucidate the following Aims: First, we seek to replicate previous findings demonstrating that older adults rate first-person sacrificial moral dilemmas as more negative than younger adults using a purely older adult sample. Second, we seek to determine whether there are age differences in emotional memory for previously engaged first-person sacrificial moral dilemmas. Third, we seek to determine whether initial emotion ratings of moral dilemmas can predict emotional memory of these same dilemmas, and whether initial emotional ratings interact with age. Finally, we seek to determine whether subjective reports of emotion regulation strategy use or future time perspective can account for the relationships between initial emotional ratings or age to predict emotional memory for moral content.

title_r: Media Bias on Perceptions of Radicalism of Muslims Can Impact Collective Punishment (Study 2)
abstract_r: This is a pre-registration for a second study of a larger project looking at the role of mass media bias (in particular, voice). This is a conceptual replication of Study 1 with two major changes: 1) we changed the context of the news coverage we used in Study 1 as the main manipulation. While in Study 1, we used a news coverage of a terrorist attack, we wondered if the analysis we found for Study 1 would still hold (and, indeed, perhaps be more robust) in a more ambiguous context involving (political) violence during a protest. 2) we include a Muslim-students versus students condition to examine if the voice effects will impact Muslim perpetrators more. 3) we include measures of perceived legitimacy of the news coverage as a potential moderator on the role of passive versus active voice. We expect this should moderate the effect of voice on collective punishment towards Muslims. Specifically, we believe that participants who view the media portrayal of Muslim protestors as legitimate and accurate may be more likely to be influenced by voice bias. Conversely, those that find the media to be illegitimate should be more wary and cognizant of media bias tactics (such as voice). This awareness may either lead to no effect of media bias, or even a backfiring effect. We believe these changes are necessary to expand our previous Study 1 findings, specifically, by looking at the boundary conditions of the effect of media voice on perceptions of radicalism of Muslims and subsequent trickle down effects on anti-Muslim policies and collective punishment. You may find the pre-registration and more details about the first Study in the link below: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CXG32

title_r: SPR 2019 Symposium: Methodological Rigor and Multi-Site Replications in Psychophysiology
abstract_r: The reproducibility, replicability, and robustness of findings in psychological science have led to a perceived crisis. The purpose of this symposium is to identify barriers to the replicability of psychophysiological data and to provide recommendations for improving psychophysiology research practices. The symposium begins with Carbine reporting the sample sizes and statistical power that are common in studies of event-related brain potentials (ERPs) and highlighting the importance of a priori power calculations. Clayson then discusses how researchers are not reporting all the necessary data collection and processing steps outlined in the ERP methodology guidelines published in 2014, which is a barrier to replication studies. Sandre provides an example of the impact of various processing pipelines on error-related negativity (ERN) scores, psychometrics, and relationships with external correlates. One recommendation for improving replicability and robustness of research to is to conduct large multi-site studies. The symposium concludes with two presentations that cover the results and challenges of such studies. Bauer presents on a multi-site replication of the relationship between intolerance of uncertainty and threat generalization using skin conductance responses (SCR) and ERPs. Moser reports on a multi-site replication of the relationship between ERN and worry. Together, these presentations highlight challenges to the reproducibility, replicability, and robustness of psychophysiological findings and provide recommendations for best practices moving forward.

title_r: Extreme weather, climate change, climate action and uncertainty distress: A replication study using network analysis.
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

Both extreme weather and climate change have been linked to distress and at times mental health problems. Pro-environmental actions have often been related to higher distress.  The uncertainty distress model (Freeston et al., 2020) proposes that in real-world situations, perceptions of threat and uncertainty contribute to distress.  Freeston, Sermin-Read, et al. (2023) recruited a community sample (N = 327) who completed an online survey.  Network analysis was used to analyse the relationships between the variables. Exposure to extreme weather, perceptions of climate change, climate change distress and pro-environmental action were measured along with symptoms of adjustment disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, and uncertainty intolerance and behaviours.  They reported there was variable exposure to extreme weather, but greater exposure was associated with more severe post-traumatic symptoms. Pro-environmental action was associated with greater severity of adjustment disorder symptoms.  The perception that climate change was happening now was linked positively to pro-environmental action and negatively to perceptions of uncertainty about whether climate change was happening.  The results replicated several findings from the emerging climate change distress literature and are consistent with some predictions of the uncertainty distress model, but not others.  

Aim: The main aim of the current study is to conduct a replication using network analysis with 1) improved measurement in some areas (see above and in measures section), 2) a larger and more diverse sample (see recruitment methods). The network analysis will follow the previous analysis as much as possible to facilitate comparison. 

Methods: The study will essentially replicate the previous study with the following modifications: inclusion of heatwaves; expand the type, timescale and impact of warnings; differentiated assessment of disruption; fuller range of emotional responses; shortened/improved versions of other measures. A larger sample will be sought, recruited to increase not only the diversity and representativeness of the sample, but also the geographical distribution and so the range of experiences of extreme weather. 

Results: Descriptive analyses of the participants, the experiences of extreme weather, and network analysis will be reported, based on the previous study.

title_r: The Dynamics between Physical Activity and Positive Affect: Investigating Potential Mechanisms and Predictive Pathways
abstract_r: Physical activity is widely recognized for improving mood and alleviating symptoms of mental health conditions like depression, anxiety, and stress. However, not everyone experiences mood enhancements from exercise, and the mechanisms behind this are unclear. This study aims to identify who benefits most from physical activity, exploring the links between physical activity, mood, emotional memory, and biomarkers in a healthy population. We define physical activity as continuous movement (e.g., steps, cycling) and exercise bouts (combining movement and heart rate data). First, we will replicate previous findings from a sub-sample of the Healthy Brain Study data (Healthy Brain Study consortium et al., 2022) by examining whether more physical activity is associated with improved positive mood. We will then explore whether we can develop a model to predict an individual’s mood in subsequent weeks during the year based on intra-individual variability in the relationship between physical activity and mood during the first week. Second, we will investigate how physical activity influences mood, hypothesizing that exercise enhances emotional memory processing4, promoting more positive appraisals of past emotional events. We found this relationship in the first part of the HBS data, and will try to replicate this finding in the second part of the data. Finally, we will examine whether neural plasticity biomarkers like brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and endocannabinoids (eCB) levels influence the relationship between physical activity and mood. Although studies have indicated associations between neural plasticity biomarkers and mood improvements, these findings are mixed and based on widely different samples (e.g., mentally affected, healthy) and generally rather small sample sizes. Therefore, we will examine the relationships between neuroplasticity biomarkers, emotional memory, physical activity, and mood to gain further insight into possible mechanism of the mood-enhancing effect of physical activity. Our findings may improve understanding of how exercise enhances mood and inform personalized interventions to optimize mental and cognitive health.

title_r: Replication of Against Empathy Bias: The Moral Value of Equitable Empathy (2021) at BYU-I Winter 2023
abstract_r: Research related to empathy and morality has focused on empathy's effect on our morality. People have been shown to express more empathy towards those that are close to them or similar to them. But does morality have an effect on how empathy is expressed rather than just empathy impacting our morality? The original study sought to find possible answers to this question. The study was conducted on Amazon's Mechanical Turk with 604 participants. Study 1 focused on how participants judged hypothetical situations in third person, while study 2, the study we replicated, explored how people judged their own hypothetical empathetic reaction in various situations. Study 2 presented six different situations with six possible empathetic expressions: empathy felt only for a socially close individual, only for a socially distant individual, more for the socially close than the socially distant, more for the socially distant than the socially close, neither, and equally for both. Results from this study found that participants preferred empathy expressed to those that are socially close rather than those that are socially distant. It was found that empathy felt equally for both groups was viewed as the most moral position. There were two major deviations in our replication study from the original. Our replication was done at Brigham Young University - Idaho, a private religious institution, using students in General Psychology or Research Methods courses while the original was done at Amazon's Mechanical Turk. Secondly, our participants were incentivized with class credit while the participants in the original study were incentivized with a small monetary reward.

title_r: Age effects on perceptual and conceptual priming
abstract_r: The aim of this study is to systematically manipulate perceptual/conceptual processing at encoding in young and older adults prior to measures of perceptual and conceptual priming. It is a close replication of the prior registered experiment using line drawings of everyday stimuli, but will not include a concurrent recognition judgement at test to limit the possibility of contamination. Participants will perform two counterbalanced encoding blocks, one involving perceptual processing (orientation judgements), and one involving conceptual processing (pleasantness ratings), prior to a blocked test phase to measure perceptual and conceptual priming. Test phase tasks will be matched on all characteristics except processing – participants will judge whether objects are angular or rounded (perceptual) or smaller/larger than a shoebox (conceptual).

title_r: Using Magnetoencephalography Source Localization to Examine Temporal Latencies of Responses to Symbolic and Non-Symbolic Bodies in the Functionally-Localized EBA
abstract_r: Previous studies have claimed some successes in combining fMRI and MEG to obtain spatiotemporal maps of human brain activity (Dale et al. 2000; Cichy et al. 2016). However, these methods have not been examined in detail for category-selective regions of the visual ventral cortex until recently, in a study which suggests that it is possible to functionally localize the EBA using fMRI and transfer this spatial map to find MEG responses from this region with millisecond temporal resolution (Lydic & Kanwisher, unpublished). In the present study we ask two questions. 1. Can we replicate our earlier finding that MEG source localization can be used to extract the time course of responses in fMRI-localized regions of the VTC, specifically the EBA? The motivation for the second (main) question is as follows. A recently-published CNN-based model of the EBA accurately predicts the response of this region to photographic stimuli, but incorrectly predicts low responses to stick figures of bodies and line drawings of bodies. That prediction appears false based on our previous study showing similar fMRI responses in the EBA to photographs of bodies and to line drawings of bodies and stick figures (Downing et al., 2001). We hypothesize that the discrepancy between the reported fMRI responses and the predictions of the otherwise highly accurate CNN-based model results from the low temporal resolution of fMRI, which combines feedforward and feedback responses. According to our hypothesis, the high response to stick figures and line drawings of bodies reflects feedback from higher cognitive regions not modeled by CNNs. This hypothesis predicts that selective responses to the more abstract body stimuli (compared to non-body control stimuli) will arise at a longer latency than selective responses to photographs of bodies (compared to control non-body photographs). Therefore, our second question, which can only be asked if we are able to replicate our previous finding regarding MEG source localization of the EBA, is as follows: 2. Does the EBA respond selectively to stick figures and line drawings of bodies at a later latency than its selective response to photographs of bodies?

title_r: Effect of Exposure to Corruption on Beliefs about Vaccination through Distrust of Institutional Information
abstract_r: In a previous Study (https://osf.io/hwk2v), we showed a causal link between the perception of corruption and vaccine confidence. Specifically, high salience of corruption leads to less vaccine confidence than low salience of corruption. In the current study, we aim to replicate the test of this causal relationship as well as to examine one potential mechanism responsible for this effect: distrust of institutional information. The literature shows that the degree of corruption measured by experts negatively predicts institutional trust (e.g., Catterberg & Moreno, 2006). This distrust in institutions leads individuals to reject institutional information (e.g., Fairbrother, 2017). This leads us to suggest that exposure to corruption should result in a greater tendency to reject institutional information. Since vaccine confidence is based on institutional communications, this tendency to reject institutional information should explain the link between exposure to corruption and low vaccine confidence. Since we are interested in the effect of corruption on beliefs around vaccination, such as the belief in the safety and efficacy of vaccines, we also wanted to replicate this result on other types of beliefs around vaccination, in this case conspiracy beliefs on the vaccination. A conspiracy theory can be defined as a belief concerning the existence of a malicious, hidden and intentional action by a group of individuals (e.g., Lantian et al., 2016). Here, we hypothesize that exposure to corruption is likely to increase belief in conspiracy theories about vaccination through distrust of institutional information. This hypothesis is in line with data in the literature. Firstly, studies tend to show that the level of corruption objectively measured by experts is linked to belief in conspiracy theories (e.g., Cordonnier et al., 2021). On the other hand, other studies also show that institutional distrust leads to greater belief in conspiracy theories (e.g., Abalakina-Paap et al., 1999). These results should extend our previous results showing that exposure to corruption leads to believing the vaccine to be less safe and efficient to other conspiracy beliefs around vaccination. title_r: Replication of Grauepner & Comin (2017), Part 3
abstract_r: This is a replication of our previous replication attempt (Part 2), with the following changes: 1) We have reduced the 40-item AIM scale to 15 items (randomly chosen items using a random number generator) 2) We have removed the General Conspiracy Beliefs measure, as the results from Part 2 suggested it was redundant with the other two measures of conspiracy beliefs. 3) We have added a number of demographics measures (ethnicity, income, education, political party, political ideology) 4) We added an Emotion Regulation Scale, to test the hypothesis that low emotion regulation is related to conspiracy beliefs (and thus might explain why emotional arousal measured via the PANAS and other measures is related to conspiracy beliefs) 5) We added Trust in Science and Trust in Government scales, so as to demonstrate that emotional arousal is either unrelated or negatively related to these types of beliefs, while still being positively associated with conspiracy theory beliefs.

title_r: An investigation of the time course of the lexical tonal encoding in Mandarin word production: A replication EEG study of picture naming
abstract_r: Lexical tones, which refer to pitch information used to distinguish lexical meanings, are an important phonological property in tonal languages (M. Chen, 2000; Yip, 2002). In recent years, a vast majority of behavioral and electrophysiological studies on speech production were conducted to investigate the encoding of phonological segments and syllables in tonal languages such as Mandarin (e.g., Cai et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019; Qu et al., 2012, 2020; Wang et al., 2018; You et al., 2012; M. Yu. et al., 2014; Zhang & Damian, 2019) and Cantonese (Wong et al., 2012, 2016, 2018, 2019; Wong & Chen, 2009), but it remains unclear how lexical tones are planned at the phonological encoding stage of word production among native speakers of tonal languages. Several models have been proposed to incorporate the encoding of lexical tones (Alderete et al., 2019; J. Chen, 1999; O’Seaghdha et al., 2010; Roelofs, 2015). Some researchers proposed that lexical tones are independently retrieved and encoded in ways similar to segments in production (Alderete et al., 2019; Wan & Jaeger, 1998), whereas other researchers proposed that lexical tones are retrieved as part of the metrical frame of the syllables like lexical stress in non-tonal languages (J. Chen, 1999; J. Chen et al., 2002; O’Seaghdha et al., 2010; Roelofs, 2015). However, the proposed models were mostly drawn upon the analysis of behavioral data, including tonal errors in natural speech corpora (Alderete et al., 2019; J. Chen, 1999; Wan & Jaeger, 1998) and in error-induced experimental paradigms in the lab (e.g., tongue-twisters, Kember et al., 2015), and implicit priming or picture-word-interference studies (J. Chen et al., 2002; Wong & Chen, 2008; Zeng, 2022), but these corpora or behavioral studies did not yield fully consistent conclusions. In addition, another hotly debated question is about the relative encoding timing of lexical tones, compared to the encoding of the syllable and segments. Currently, most models of Mandarin speech production proposed that the syllable is the proximate unit (the first unit selected during phonological encoding) and segments are later specified in Chinese word production (O’Seaghdha et al., 2010; Roelofs, 2015), which has been supported by several recent EEG studies on the word production in Mandarin (Cai et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019; Zhang & Damian, 2019) and Cantonese (Wong et al., 2016). As for the lexical tonal encoding, these models mostly assumed that the tonal encoding consists of two stages: the retrieval or selection of the lexical tonal information (either treated as independent segments or as part of the metrical or word-shape frame), and the tone-to-atonal syllable mapping process (i.e., assigning the lexical tone to the syllabic or segmental contents) (Alderete et al., 2019; J. Chen, 1999; O’Seaghdha et al., 2010; Roelofs, 2015). However, the exact time course for the lexical tonal encoding relative to the other phonological information is still not clearly specified. For example, Roelofs (2015) assumed that the lexical tonal information is retrieved as part of the metrical frame simultaneously with the syllabic contents and later assigned to the syllabic frame with specified segments. O’Seaghdha et al. (2010) also implicitly assumed that the lexical tonal information is retrieved as part of the word-shape frame and assigned to the syllabic frame before segments are further specified. In contrast, Alderete et al., (2019) proposed that the lexical tones are firstly retrieved simultaneously as segments, and the segments later form the atonal syllabic frame, and the tones are then linked to the atonal syllabic frame. Moreover, a few behavioral studies (Wong & Chen, 2008; Zeng, 2022; X. Zhou & Zhuang, 2000) also attempted to use the picture-word interference task (or a similar variant paradigm such as the picture-pinyin interference task) and manipulated the SOA (Stimulus-onset asynchrony, the time interval between the presentation of distractors and the presentation of the picture) to probe into the time course of lexical tonal encoding. The results of these studies suggested that the retrieval of the lexical tone seemed to occur at a very early stage, possibly in parallel with the syllabic information. In contrast, two earlier EEG studies (Zhang & Damian, 2009; Zhang & Zhu, 2011) made use of the Go-NoGo judgment task to implicitly infer the time course of the encoding of the segmental and tonal information in covert speech production and their results suggested that the encoding of the lexical tones occurred later after the retrieval of the onset consonant but simultaneously with the central vowel encoding in covert production. As previous EEG studies showed that the encoding of the segments occurred later than the syllabic encoding in Chinese (Cai et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019; Wong et al., 2016; Zhang & Damian, 2019), the findings from Zhang and her colleagues (Zhang & Damian, 2009; Zhang & Zhu, 2011) seemed to indicate that the lexical tonal encoding occurred at a later stage of the production, at least after the syllabic encoding, but this is not consistent with those behavioral findings (Wong & Chen, 2008; Zeng, 2022; X. Zhou & Zhuang, 2000). Thus, there is no consensus regarding the time course of the lexical tonal encoding during Chinese word production. Since there is still no available study that directly explores the neural processes underlying the encoding of lexical tones using an overt naming task, we therefore recently conducted an EEG experiment using a phonologically-primed picture naming task to investigate this issue. We asked native Mandarin speakers from North China to produce the disyllabic names of 104 target pictures and 52 filler pictures while their oral responses and EEG signals were recorded. Each picture was preceded by a monosyllabic visual prime, presented together with its auditory form. We manipulated the tonal relatedness and syllabic relatedness of the primes in relation to the initial morpheme of the target picture names (e.g., 鹦鹉, ying1-wu3, ‘parrot’), resulting in four prime conditions: (1) homophone prime (e.g., 英, ying1, sharing the syllable and tone); (2) syllable-overlap prime (e.g., 营, ying2, only sharing the syllable); (3) tone-overlap prime (e.g., 纲, gang1, only sharing the tone); (4) unrelated prime (e.g., 悖, bei4, phonologically unrelated). The behavioral results revealed that there was a significant interaction between tonal and syllabic relatedness. The syllable-related primes (homophone and syllable-overlap prime) yielded significantly shorter naming latencies than the other syllable-unrelated primes. Moreover, the homophone primes yielded significantly shorter naming latencies than the syllable-overlap primes, but the tone-overlap primes exhibited significantly longer naming onset latencies than the unrelated primes. This suggests that additional tonal overlap facilitated the production only when the syllabic information could be prepared but hampered the production when the syllabic information was not readily prepared. Regarding the EEG data, our ANOVA analysis of the stimulus-locked ERP (i.e., ERP time-locked to the picture onset) revealed there was an early tonal relatedness main effect in the 250~350 ms time window (with more negativity in left frontocentral regions for the tonally related primes than the tonally unrelated ones), and a later syllabic relatedness main effect in the 350~500 ms time window (with larger negativity in left frontocentral regions but more positivity in the right frontal region and bilateral posterior regions for the syllable-related primes than the syllable-unrelated ones). In contrast, our ANOVA analysis of the response-locked ERP (i.e., ERP time-locked to the speech acoustic onset) revealed an early syllabic relatedness main effect in the -450~-250 ms time window (with larger negativity in frontocentral regions but larger positivity in posterior regions for the syllable-related than the syllable-unrelated primes), and a significant interaction between tonal and syllabic relatedness in the -250~-100 ms time window. Further analysis showed that the homophone primes elicited larger negativity in left frontocentral regions than the syllable-overlap primes, but no difference was observed between the tone-overlap primes and the unrelated primes. These results indicate that lexical tones can be independently retrieved in an earlier time window than the syllable at the phonological encoding stage, but need to be planned and integrated with the syllable at the later phonetic encoding stage. However, the results described above still need to be further replicated and confirmed, in particular, for the main effect of the tonal relatedness in the 250~350 ms time window of stimulus-locked ERPs and the interaction effect between the tonal and syllabic relatedness in the -250~-100 ms time window of response-locked ERPs, which seemed to be focal effects only restricted to a narrow time window and the left frontocentral regions. Thus, this study aims to replicate the result of the EEG experiment we described above and used the same design and task by manipulating the tonal and syllabic relatedness of the preceding primes to the target names of pictures. The only difference is that we choose to use the monosyllabic target names as the stimuli in this planned experiment. Unlike the disyllabic items that involve the encoding of the lexical tonal information of two syllables and thus possibly introduce some interference, when producing the monosyllabic items, only the lexical tonal information of one syllable needs to be retrieved and encoded in production. If the tonal relatedness effect found in our previous EEG experiment is real, it is supposed to come up again in our replication EEG study using the monosyllabic items.

title_r: Study 2: Effects on Political Participation
abstract_r: As civil society organizations such as churches, civic associations, and voluntary organizations decline and the ones that remain become more politically homogeneous, work remains one of the main environments where Americans participate in in-person conversation across political, racial, or other demographic lines (Putnam 2000, Mutz and Mondak 2006). Given the centrality of the workplace in individuals' ordinary lives, interactions with coworkers play an important role in providing information about broader societal news and politics and an opportunity to express views to others. Yet, at the same time, corporations have shown greater willingness to take public stances on political issues and engage in politically controversial actions. In addition, following Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010), corporations have been free to dedicate unlimited funds, employees, and resources to support their preferred causes and candidates. While almost 50% of companies report working to engage workers politically, scholars do not yet understand the impact of such political activity on the types of cross-cutting political discussion workplaces have often enabled (Hertel-Fernandez 2016). On one hand, corporate political messaging could increase discussion by signaling that politics is an appropriate topic at work and normalizing views aligned with the company’s publicized position. On the other hand, it could chill discussion by discouraging individuals with opposing views from expressing them. The previous study established that corporate political messaging has an impact on citizens’ intention to discuss politics in the workplace. In this study, we replicate Study 1's treatment and overall design. However, we modify our dependent variables to include a wider range of political actions. This will help us get a baseline understanding of subjects' propensities for political participation, compare actions in the workplace to more general actions to isolate the effect of being at work, and get an understanding of whether corporate actions act as in-kind donations to their preferred political causes. We use a survey experiment of US employees to measure the extent to which corporate position-taking on political issues influences workers' willingness to engage in a range of political actions with varying degrees of connections to their careers. The survey first asks respondents to describe their occupation and the company they work for, identifies political issues they care about, and asks their positions on those issues. Then, we use a large language model to generate mock statements from an employer in the subject's industry. These mock statements take a stance on a political issue that the respondent cares about and manipulate whether the corporation agrees or disagrees with the respondent’s stated attitudes. This personalized experimental manipulation will allow us to estimate the effect of corporate position-taking on willingness to engage in political actions in a manner that is more organic than a standard survey experiment. The survey closes by measuring six dependent variables: discussing politics at work, discussing politics with family and friends, posting about politics on social media, writing to Congressional representatives, voting, and donating to a non-profit organization. These variables enable a repeated measures design, as we also ask a version of these items pre-treatment. We will also examine whether treatment effects are moderated by factors like workplace viewpoint homogeneity, job security, and socioeconomic status.

title_r: Assessing manifestations of depressive behavior during the Rorschach task - Study 3
abstract_r: This preregistration focuses on a follow-up study, Study 3, of this current project. In our initial studies (https://osf.io/sxkgv) we introduced three Rorschach variables as potential markers of depression or its conceptual antithesis, Self-Critical and Helpless Behavior (SCHB), Elevated Mood States (EMS), and Pleasant or Appealing Expressions (PAE), and compared them to a previously validated marker of depression, Morbid content (MOR). EMS, PAE, and MOR are coded dichotomously as absent or present on each Rorschach response, while SCHB is coded at three levels as absent, present to a mild extent, and present to a notable extent (0, 1, or 2). In Study 1, we used an archival dataset of adult male inpatients (n = 70) with interview-based clinician ratings of depressive symptomology. Results showed that clear instances of SCHB (i.e., Level 2) may be associated with guilt feelings and degree of depressive diagnostic features (i.e., both r = .27, p = .02). In follow-up Study 2, we used an extreme group design to compare the inpatients (n = 70) to nonpatients (n = 70) matched as closely as possible on their number of responses (R) to the Rorschach and level of education. With very large effect sizes, the total SCHB scale differentiated nonpatients from inpatients (delta = 1.39, p < .001) and just the subset of patients with depressive disorders (n = 29, delta = 1.74, p < .001). MOR, EMS, and PAE were unrelated to the depressive indices used in these studies (ps > .05, Study 1 rs from -.07 to .20, Study 2 ds from -0.24 to 0.20). We also found that even though the SCHB scale was elevated in the inpatients, the inpatients had less rich and more simplistic protocols, as indicated by the percentage of responses that were just based on the form (F%) features of the inkblots, rather than based on color, achromatic color, shading, dimensionality, symmetry, or form suggesting movement. From those results (not yet published), we found that SCHB might be useful for evaluating depression and differentiating between nonpatients and patients, especially those with depression. We also observed that EMS and PAE did not show a connection to depressive symptoms or the general demoralization experienced by inpatients. However, results from studies 1 and 2 were based on a sample in which MOR, a validated marker of depressive demoralization, surprisingly did not demonstrate validity, and the effects for Level 2 SCHB among the inpatients were not hypothesized a priori. Therefore, as a follow-up, in Study 3, we aim to replicate our previous analysis using a different sample of patients and nonpatients. We use a dataset that has been used in prior publications (e.g., Meyer, 1997), but not yet coded for the three new variables or analyzed for all four variables. We will code all variables and attempt to replicate our previous analysis as well as extend the findings to evaluate these variables relative to an alternative criterion that previously showed supporting evidence for a Rorschach indicator of depressive propensity. Specifically, Meyer (1997, 1999) and colleagues (2000) found that the Rorschach Depression Index (Exner, 2003) was correlated with MMPI-2 depression scales when analyses were limited to patients with similar response styles on both measures, with response styles defined as open, spontaneous engagement with each task.

title_r: Situational pressure as a moderator of followers preferences for considerate versus initiating structure leaders. Replication of earlier findings.
abstract_r: In this study we will try replicate our earlier results that situational pressure moderates the preference of "followers" for one of two leadership styles. In order to achieve this, we will present participants with the description of a company aswell as its economic and social situation and ask them to imagine being an employee of the described company. Afterwards we present them with the profiles of two potential group leaders that differ in their leadership style, these leadership styles are based on the two most important behavioural styles identified by the Ohio State leadership studies ("consideration" and "initiating structure"). Then participants will choose for which of the two leaders they would prefer to work for and rate both of them regarding their qualification and their liking of them

title_r: How different types of data and narratives affect attitudes and trust in data
abstract_r: In a previous study, we presented participants four types of data materials (data-only, story-only, data-story, and data-walkthrough) explaining the risk of a COVID-19 positive person being present at a Thanksgiving dinner with 10 people in total. We measured the rating of concern for contracting COVID-19 given individuals' thanksgiving plan in 2020 before and after providing data materials. We found that, consistent with current literature, a story describing a negative outcome of a risky decision or a short narrative accompanying the data had a bigger impact on people’s perceptions of risk than quantitative data representing the risk alone. Furthermore, when people were provided a visual narrative that explained how the risk data are generated, they are more likely to change their attitudes and intentions to avoid risky decisions. We also found that by adding a step-by-step walkthrough explanation to the data, we could mitigate the “backfire effect” of the data-only intervention material and affect people’s attitudes and decisions to the same extent as story-only or data-story materials. In this study, we aim to replicate our previous findings and test whether different materials affect people’s comprehension and trust in cumulative risk data. To achieve this, we create a hypothetical scenario where we assume that there is a new respiratory disease virus that is immune to all of our current vaccines and we ask people questions about plans for the upcoming holidays. We use the same four conditions from the previous experiment (data-walkthrough, data-only, data-story, story-only).

title_r: Old Habits May Die Hard, But How Are They Born? The Role of Context in Habit Formation
abstract_r: A crucial feature of habits is their automaticity, meaning habitual actions are executed irrespective of their immediate consequences, whether costs or benefits (Wood & Ruenger, 2016, Yin & Knowlton, 2006). A common paradigm in the study of habits in previous human and animal research is the outcome devaluation paradigm. This entails a learning phase consisting of instrumental response-outcome training, followed by a devaluation phase where the previously valued outcome becomes devalued, and then a test (outcome devaluation test or Slips Of Action Task (SOAT)) phase to measure the persistence of behaviours after the associated outcome is devalued. According to these findings (deWit et al., 2007, 2012, Watson & deWit, 2018), when an action continues to be sensitive to its outcome, it is considered goal-directed. If, however, it is repeated even after its consequence becomes devalued, it is considered habitual (also refer to Wood & Neal, 2007). These paradigms measure the relative balance between the two systems (goal-directed and habitual) based on the Devaluation Sensitivity Index: ((N valued responses/N total responses) - (N devalued responses/N total responses)). As a result, there is no direct, independent measure for the study of habits, rather a relative one. Additionally, even though we have some hints about the role of repetition/extensive training (Adams, 1982), or recency (Giesen et al., 2020) in habit formation, the precise factors (mechanisms, timing, duration, etc.) for the formation of habits is presently still exploratory. The aims of our study, then, are thus: 1. We wish to replicate the findings from previous studies by deWit et al. in an experimental set-up by employing the outcome devaluation paradigm in a Slips of Actions Task (SOAT: "Go No-go" task procedure), to elicit habitual responses in an experimental set-up. 2. Importantly, with the aim of identifying the contributing factors in the formation of habits, we wish to systematically measure the role of context stability in the strength of habit formation. 3. Next, we wish to test whether habits express themselves more automatically in situations of stress (compared to baseline, non-stressful situations) as has been previously demonstrated (Schwabe & Wolf, 2010, Soares et al., 2012). 4. Lastly, we would like to ascertain whether habit strength influences habit expression differentially in high compared to low stress situations. Thus, we wish to validate the efficacy of the outcome devaluation paradigm in a modified experimental set-up with the aim of determining the role of context and stress in habit formation and habit expression.

title_r: Dissociation between Size and Distance effect in decimal numbers with a fixed referent task
abstract_r: The idea that a joint approximate numerical magnitude code underlies both symbolic and non- symbolic numerical information has been challenged. A joint code implies that intra-individual behavioral signature effects such as size and distance effects correlate significantly with each other in both notations. In contrast, recent studies employing a numerical magnitude comparison task (e.g. Krajici et al., 2017 Psych Bull Rev), have shown such correlation for non-symbolic quantities but not for symbolic stimuli. This lends support for the hypothesis of two different systems. However, the use of a limited stimulus range (0 - 9) may have mitigated the behavioral variance and hence masked potential correlations. Here (N=44), we (a) replicated and (b) extended previous results with symbolic and non-symbolic quantities using less familiar symbolic stimuli (two-digits decimals numbers ranging from -0.99 to 0.99) in a numerical magnitude comparison task. We previously did a magnitude comparison task with pair of numbers and now we want to replicate these results using a fixed referent comparison task.

It is proposed that psychological flexibility plays a pivotal role in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy as a means of undermining excessive adherence to verbal rules. This project aims to explore whether self-reported 'pliance', a form of rule-governed behaviour, is predictive of sensitivity to changing contingencies as measured by Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST). title_r: Tonic LC-NA Arousal and Implicit Pattern Abstraction
abstract_r: In order to meet the challenges of a complex and constantly changing world, organisms must manage the balance between exploiting known sources of reward and exploring the environment for potentially more fruitful opportunities. The locus coeruleus-noradrenaline system (LC-NA) mediates this trade-off through a synergistic interplay between phasic and tonic modes of noradrenergic firing. Phasic activity reflects bursts of task-oriented arousal favouring exploitative behaviour, whereas increased tonic firing facilitates task disengagement and promotes exploration of alternative reward avenues when tasks are no longer remunerative (e.g., when task utility wanes). Although reliably demonstrated to initiate exploratory behaviour, less is known about the broader adaptive utility of this tonic LC-NA mode. Prior research has revealed associations between LC-NA arousal and subsequent compensatory efforts to alleviate this arousal (e.g., affirmation and abstraction behaviours), but no study has yet converged inductions of AGT-predicted LC-NA activity and subsequent exploratory efforts indicative of such compensatory strategies. Employing a mixed, two-task paradigm, we aim to extend our preliminary investigation into the relationship between tonic LC-NA activity and exploratory behaviour by once again revealing a novel association between elevated tonic arousal and subsequent implicit pattern detection. That is, utilising pupil diameter as an indirect proxy for LC-NA activity, we aim to replicate our initial evidence that (a) tonic LC-NA activity tracks intrasubject utility-induced transitions between exploit/explore control states and (b) variations in inconsistency-evoked pupil size are differentially related to implicit learning performance, insofar as increased tonic activity is associated with enhanced implicitly-learned grammar retrieval, consistent with an exploratory mode of reward detection. Crucially, we aim to augment these aims by introducing a between-subjects manipulation, whereby an experimental group (Escape DUT) will be instructed to execute an 'escape' response when task utility wanes (e.g., behavioural indices of task disengagement / exploration), thus resetting task difficulty, whereas a control group (Automatic DUT) will not be asked to commit an 'escape' response and the difficulty will automatically reset after a given number of trials, thus removing behavioural indices of task disengagement and associated exploratory processes (e.g., increased LC-NA arousal). As such, it is hypothesised that aforementioned relationships between tonic LC-NA arousal and subsequent implicit pattern abstraction will only be evident for Escape DUT participants, as tonic LC-NA activity should only manifest during active task disengagement. We also aim to replicate our preliminary study that dispositional mindfulness - a proposed tonic capacity - is positively associated with tonic LC-NA activity, moderating the relationship between tonic arousal and implicit learning for the experimental group only. These findings will further demonstrate the adaptive nature of tonic arousal by directly replicating prior results and consolidating previous interpretations of these results that there exist robust AGT-predicted inter-task arousal-performance relationships, by providing direct experimental manipulation. Our project will also provide further evidence for the interactive qualities of trait tonic capacities and elevated tonic states in facilitating adaptive outcomes. One such capacity is mindfulness, so an individual difference measure of trait mindfulness (Mindfulness Attention Awareness Scale, MAAS) will also be incorporated.

title_r: Intuitive and Reflective Foundations of Free Will and Scientific Determinism Exp. 2
abstract_r: In this project, we attempt to replicate our previous study (see OSF link: https://osf.io/p7gnz/?view_only=4f5d2f2d795642f0957e1685e4a5342e). The experiment in the previous study yielded mixed evidence regarding the relationship between reflective cognitive style and scientific determinism. Contrary to our initial hypothesis that reflection would increase the endorsement of scientific determinism while decreasing the endorsement of free will, the research showed that reflection decreased support for both free will and scientific determinism. This unexpected finding allowed us to propose a novel hypothesis called the reflective doubt hypothesis based on Yılmaz and Isler’s previous finding (2019), showing that reflection increased belief in God for non-believers, but it tended to decrease it among believers. Yılmaz and Isler (2019) argue that reflection leads to an increase in doubt in one’s initial or intuitive judgments. Hence, we assume that the decrease in scientific determinism when using reflection could be a result of doubt. Hence, we aim to confirm this unexpected finding with improved methodology.

title_r: Spatial cueing of attention by rotational motion — Floors and ceilings, with different SOAs and rotation speeds
abstract_r: In a previous experiment, we found that viewing a rotating object oriented observers’ spatial attention, and that the nature of this spatial cueing depended on how the object was touching another surface (a horizontal line drawn above or below it). For example: if an object is shown touching a surface below it, then clockwise rotation would normally cause the object to move rightward — and, accordingly, in the floor-touching condition, clockwise rotation produced faster response times to targets presented on the right than on the left (and counterclockwise rotation vice versa). Conversely, if an object is in frictive contact with a surface above it, then clockwise rotation would normally cause the object to move leftward — and, accordingly, in the ceiling-touching condition, clockwise rotation now produced faster response times to targets presented on the left than on the right (and counterclockwise rotation vice versa). In this experiment, we aim to replicate and extend the previous results. To allow other factors to be manipulated, the present experiment will replicate only the previous study’s floor-touching and ceiling-touching conditions, and not include trials in which the object does not touch the line. Furthermore, the present study will introduce two new factors to study how the ceiling-touching cueing effect and floor-touching cue effect depend on (1) object rotation speed (using object rotation speeds of 120°/sec, 240°/sec, and 360°/sec) and (2) duration of stimulus exposure (using object-target SOAs of 100ms, 200ms, and 300ms).

title_r: Investigation of Inequity Avoidance from the Perspective of Morality as Cooperation Theory
abstract_r: Fairness and reciprocity had been proposed as two fundamental moral sensitivities to display inequity avoidance (Fehr & Schmidt, 1999). Empathy was also found another important motivation to show altruism toward others who are in the disadvantageous situations (Batson, 1991). However, some social contextual factors might create discrepancy between self-reported attitudes and moral actions. It is important to explore which social contextual factors might decrease the importance of self-reported attitudes and lead people to display less inequity avoidance (IA) to have a deeper understanding about moral decision making processes. We expect that individuals would display less AIA, specifically in a social context in which they are used to be unable to refuse disadvantageous unequal allocations. Therefore, in this study, we aim to create a situation where the norm is to accept inequality with a novel manipulation technique. This hypothesis had been tested in the previous study (raw data; Aktas et al., in prep) but manipulation did not work in the expected direction. For this reasno, in the current investigation, we aim to replicate previous study by making a change which let participants to be informed that their responses will be fully anonymous. To sum up, in the present study, we aim to investigate the impact of a specific social context for displaying inequity aversion while considering the impact of individual differences about moral values regarding reciprocity and fairness (Curry et al., 2019) and the role of empathy (Batson, 1991).

title_r: Can Exposure to Memes Trigger Stereotype Threat and Lift Effects on Physical Activity? An Expansion and Replication with Women and Men
abstract_r: This study investigated how stereotype threat and lift messages delivered as memes -a popular form of online communication- influenced physical activity performance. A pilot test of memes to be used for subsequent studies with a Latin square design (n = 32; men = 16, women= 16) found that the experimental memes activated stereotype threat and lift effects on expected psychological mechanisms. Data collection has begun for a between-subjects design experiment which randomly assigned physically eligible women to one of three conditions (meme exposure: stereotype threat vs. stereotype lift vs. control). Participants were exposed to stereotype threat, lift, or a control condition and then engaged in a running task on a treadmill. Accelerometers recorded anteroposterior (forward-backward movement), mediolateral (sideways balance), and vertical body acceleration (upward-downward movement). Additionally, we examined the influence of mediators, such as state anxiety, task motivation, and gender identification on physical activity after meme exposure. This study expanded and replicated the results of a previous study and discusses theoretical and practical implications of how memes that convey stereotypes can influence physical activity performance.

title_r: Taking moral uncertainty into account: The relationship between utilitarianism and moral hedging
abstract_r: Data from the first study of this project indicated an interaction between subjective probability of consequentialism and the degree of moral uncertainty on the personal moral evaluation of an action. In this study, we try to replicate this finding in a simplified paradigm. In this study, participants respond to the Oxford Utilitarianism Scale (OUS; Kahane et al., 2018), before rating the response options in sacrificial dilemmas. The dilemmas are taken from Christensen et al. (2014): - Transplant 1 (personal - instrumental - avoidable death), - Transplant 2 (impersonal - instrumental - avoidable death), - Switch (impersonal - accidental - avoidable death), - Shipyard (personal - accidental - avoidable death). For each scenario, participants indicate on 11 items, how uncertain they are in the moral evaluation of the different actions. The previous study showed that these items are related to normative rather than empirical uncertainty.

title_r: The effect of behavioral complexity, consistency and individual differences on habit formation. A Multi-Centre Replication.
abstract_r: This pre-registration is part of a larger replication effort of the influential study by Lally et al. (2010) ​​in which they tracked the subjective automaticity of a novel, daily (eating or exercise-related) routine, using the Self-Report Habit Index across 12 consecutive weeks. The replication of the main finding (that it takes 66 days to form a new habit) has been addressed in a separate pre-registration (https://osf.io/bj9r2). In the current extension of this basic replication, we will investigate potential causes of interindividual variability, including the consistency and complexity of the habit, as well as individual differences in impulsivity, personal need for structure (PNS), conscientiousness, effort, intention, and reward. Consistency and complexity were already explored by Lally et al., but they could not draw strong conclusions due to their small sample size. Individual differences in impulsivity, PNS, and conscientiousness were not included in the original publication, but they were part of the original study protocol. In addition to addressing the research questions of the original study, we will also investigate how anticipated effort, intention, and reward influence habit formation.

title_r: Privilege-Reframing Bias: Study 5
abstract_r: Framing inequality in terms of in-group privilege (vs. out-group disadvantage) can be threatening to group-based beliefs, leading to various defensive reactions. We hypothesize that privileged group members more often misremember in-group privilege than out-group disadvantage.
