title_r: Common and Specific Neural Mechanisms of Perseverative Thought in Real-World Contexts
abstract_r: Despite a growing push toward transdiagnostic conceptualizations (e.g., Harvey et al., 2004), clinically-relevant thought is overwhelmingly conceptualized in terms of discrete categories (e.g., “worries;” “obsessions”) in clinical practice and most research settings. These categories are typically defined on the basis of the underlying features of thoughts (e.g., temporal orientation; valence; form; content). These categorical conceptualizations play a major role in clinical conceptualization and treatment planning. However, previous work interrogating the existence and nature of these categories has been overwhelmingly conducted within the constraints of established theories and models, which limits the extent to which that work has the ability to falsify or confirm those categories. In our previous work (Hallion et al., 2022) we directly challenged the existence of discrete categories or subtypes. Applying multilevel exploratory factor analysis and multilevel latent class analysis to naturally-occurring (i.e., theoretically unconstrained) patterns of covariation in the underlying features of idiographic thoughts, we demonstrated and replicated a dimensional (five-factor) latent structure that outperformed a latent categorical (subtype) structure in two samples (cross-sectional data; three thoughts per participant). The present study will first establish whether the five factor latent structure observed in our previous work replicates when thoughts are sampled repeatedly in ecologically valid contexts. Next, we will replicate the direct comparison between a dimensional versus categorical (subtype) latent structure. We will then identify the latent dimensions of perseverative thought that show the strongest concurrent and prospective relationships to momentary distress and impairment. Additionally, previous research has rarely investigated momentary experiences of subjective difficulty concentrating, despite the theoretical and conceptual overlap with clinically-relevant thought and the presence of this symptom in many criteria for mood and anxiety-related disorders (American Psychological Association, 2013). The present study will therefore also quantify the relationship between momentary perseverative thought and concurrent and prospective experiences of difficulty concentrating. A secondary aim of the present study is to begin to characterize the latent structure of mindfulness. Although an extensive body of work supports a five factor model for trait mindfulness (Baer, 2018), this structure has never been tested using a momentary design.

title_r: The effects of statistical learning on visual awareness
abstract_r: This is a replication study. We have already conducted three experiments exploring the effects of statistical learning on visual awareness. In the first two experiments, we observed that statistical learning facilitates the conscious access of high-probability compared to low-probability items. Specifically, we found shorter reaction times to initially suppressed items when these items appeared at high-probability locations compared to low-probability locations (e.g., left versus right hemisphere) or with high-probability features compared to low-probability features (e.g., downwards versus upwards pointing triangle). In Experiment 3, we employed the detection-discrimination dissociation paradigm (Stein & Peelen, 2021) to confirm that our probability manipulation impacted processing of the items when they were still suppressed, rather than impacting response times through processes that occurred after suppression was (partially) resolved. In epoch 1 (the first 96 trials of the main experiment), participants’ ability to discriminate the manipulated dimension (i.e., distinguishing between the low and high probability stimulus feature) was at chance level. That is, the signal-detection theory sensitivity index - d’ - was not different from 0 in the feature discrimination task. At the same time, participants had better localization performance (a higher d’ in the localization task) when the target items comprised a high-probability feature compared to a low-probability feature. The goal of this preregistered replication study is to (1) confirm the ‘null effect’ on the discrimination task, and (2) confirm the difference in performance on the localization task. In the detection-discrimination dissociation paradigm, we render the target item invisible by using sandwich masking, and by adjusting the presentation time of the target. Our primary aim is to show the effects of statistical learning on the processing of stimuli that are not consciously perceived. To this end, our hypotheses focus on a short presentation time (8.3 ms) condition. Besides, we also include two other presentation times (16.7 ms, and 33.3 ms followed by an 8.3 ms blank, which reduces masking effectivity) to keep participants motivated to respond to the – otherwise mostly invisible - stimuli.

title_r: Truth Sensitivity and Belief Bias in Responses to Misinformation about COVID-19 Vaccines: III. Self-Feelings vs. Self-Confidence
abstract_r: This study is part of a broader project that aims to investigate how people determine whether COVID-19 vaccine information they encounter is correct or incorrect. Using Signal Detection Theory (SDT), the research focuses on two aspects of such judgments: (a) overall truth sensitivity in responses to correct versus incorrect information and (b) belief-congruency bias involving a tendency to accept information that is congruent with one’s beliefs about COVID-19 vaccines and dismiss information that is incongruent with one’s beliefs about COVID-19 vaccines regardless of veracity. In the current study, we will investigate associations of self-feelings and self-confidence with truth sensitivity and belief-congruency bias among participants who hold favorable versus unfavorable attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccines. We are especially interested in whether (a) positive self-feelings are negatively associated with belief-congruency bias (as predicted by motivational accounts of belief-congruency bias) and (b) greater self-confidence is positively associated with belief-congruency bias (as predicted by cognitive accounts of belief-congruency bias). In addition, we aim to replicate findings from two earlier studies regarding (1) differences in truth sensitivity and anti-vaccine belief bias (i.e., a tendency to accept anti-vaccine information and dismiss pro-vaccine information regardless of veracity) between participants who hold favorable versus unfavorable attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccines and (2) the relative contributions of anti-vaccine belief bias and lack of truth sensitivity to COVID-19 vaccine misinformation susceptibility.

title_r: Perspective of Player A in the transport game (Experiment 2)
abstract_r: This experiment is part of a larger project focused on investigating the role of perspective-taking in coalition formation dynamics. In a previous correlational study conducted by Cantiani et al. (2023), participants engaged in a coalition formation game (i.e., the Transport Game). The game involved three logistics companies, namely A, B, and C, with A carrying 4 tons, B carrying 3 tons, and C carrying 2 tons. The primary objective was to form a coalition comprising at least 5 tons, allowing them to utilize a larger truck and thereby gain an additional monetary reward. During the negotiation process, participants were tasked with determining which partners to share the truck with and how to distribute the reward. Engaging in perspective-taking to a greater extent during negotiations predicted being more often included in the winning coalition and earning more money. To establish causal evidence, we conducted an experimental study where participants were assigned the role of company A, and were either instructed to adopt the perspective of the other players before initiating negotiations (perspective-taking condition) or to focus on themselves (egocentric condition). In both conditions, players B and C were instructed to determine their negotiation approach independently, without emphasizing either perspective-taking or egocentrism. The results showed that although player A's behavior aligned with the findings of the observational study, and the manipulation of perspective-taking was effective, there was no significant difference in inclusion in winning coalitions between the two conditions. We argue that inclusion may have been influenced by the behavior of the other members of the triad (players B and C), whose actions did not align with those observed in the observational study. Notably, their initial offers and proposed coalitions demonstrated a significant bias against player A (e.g., we observed a 10% increase in BC-proposal relative to the correlational study), suggesting that the supposedly neutral instructions may not have been as neutral as intended. This study is a conceptual replication of the experiment described above, with the modification of removing the neutral instructions, hoping to remove their biasing influence. This will potentially provide greater clarity on the causal role of perspective-taking in coalition formation.

title_r: Avoidance of Switch Between Attentional Control States & Proportion Congruence - Follow-up
abstract_r: The current study builds on our previous pre-registered work (https://osf.io/u6zky), where we examined the effects of proportion congruence (PC) and switch rate (SR) on demand avoidance using a Demand Selection Task (DST) paradigm. In that study, we found that, when PC and SR were manipulated simultaneously, there was no inherent preference for mostly congruent (MC) options over mostly incongruent (MI) options when SRs were equal. However, preference for MC options over MI options varied based on the relative SRs: specifically, when the MI option involved fewer switches than the MC option, participants showed a reduced preference for MC options, suggesting that SR had a stronger influence on demand avoidance than PC in this task. In the present study, we aim to replicate our previous study conceptually by using a parametric flanker task. Here, participants view a 3x3 grid of arrows and respond to the orientation of the center arrow, with the surrounding (flanker) arrows varying in congruency. By adjusting the number of mismatching flanker arrows, we introduce varying levels of distracting information. By using the parametric flanker task, we are able to create stronger PC and SR manipulations simultaneously. Even though we did not observe an inherent preference for MC over MI options when SRs were equal in the previous study, it could be possible to observe the influence of both PC and SR in the present study with a stronger manipulation.

title_r: Study 2- The Effect of Mindfulness on Heart Rate: The Moderating Role of Narcissism
abstract_r: The current study is a replication of an exploratory study that demonstrated that people high in trait vulnerable narcissism (as revealed using the NPI-40, vulnerable narcissism was computed using an average of the subscales Exhibitionism and Vanity) in a mindfulness condition showed increased heart rate, compared to people high in trait vulnerable narcissism in a control condition. Here, we will measure trait vulnerable narcissism with both the NPI-40 and the MCNS. Notably, we did not find a main effect for mindfulness condition (vs a control condition) on heart rate. Thus, we do not expect to find a main effect of condition in this replication. Description of original exploratory study: Our study compares individuals who are high in trait narcissism with individuals who are low in trait narcissism on how a short mindfulness exercise affects them. More specifically, because it can be difficult to get an accurate measure of how narcissistic individuals are feeling based on self-report, we decided to use the physiological measure of heart rate. We are interested in the potential negative effects of mindfulness measures (Britton, 2019). In particular, we are interested in narcissism and how these measures might backfire. The mindfulness exercise may encourage the participants to turn inwards and, for the narcissistic individuals, this may potentially cause feelings of distress (Morf & Rhodewalt, 2001). We are also interested in the effects of mindfulness meditation on those who are high and low in trait narcissism. To measure these effects we will be using the participants resting heart rate before and after a mindfulness exercise. Because this study is being completed during COVID-19, there are additional restrictions that make it difficult to collect heart rate information directly from participants. Instead, we will use the “Instant Heart Rate'' app, participants will download the app and then report their heart rates before and after the mindfulness exercise. We can use changes in heart rate to infer mental states. The usage of increased heart rate as a measure of anxiety in studies looking at the effects of panic attacks and anxiety disorders demonstrates its reliability as a measure of anxiety (Hoehn-Saric et al., 2004). Half of the participants will not participate in a mindfulness exercise, but will instead listen to an audio recording educating them about mindfulness and will act as our control group. As mindfulness has been observed to lower measures of anxiety we seek to replicate these findings within the low trait narcissism group (Razon et al., 2017).

title_r: Digital Immunity: consciousness as antidote to digital harms
abstract_r: We hypothesize that individuals with psychological traits typical for self-transcended individuals show natural protection from psychological harms from online social media. We theorize that this phenomenon is a manifestation of psychological freedom within people's consciousness and call it 'digital immunity'. Between May and September 2021, we carried out a previous study where we identified characteristics of the human psyche/consciousness that correlate negatively with digital harms from social media, including mental health issues, misinformation, social tensions, and economic manipulation. The 1.5h experiment with 1,164 participants produced 29 measures describing the human psyche (128 questions), and 28 measures of digital harms (97 questions). Using integrative modeling (Hofman et al., 2017, 2021), we identified a much smaller subset of variables on both sides that show a strong negative correlation (half a dozen for the human psyche and a dozen digital harms). Here we test if and what aspects of our results hold up in a replication study.

title_r: Pupil Dilation as a Function of Pitch Discrimination Difficulty: A Replication of Kahneman and Beatty, 1967
abstract_r: In this paper, we carry out a replication of a seminal paper by Kahneman and Beatty [1] for using pupillometry as an implicit measure of auditory processing load. Specifically, non-verbal auditory processing. While numerous papers since have supported the notion that pupillometry is a fairly reliable index of processing load in general [6, 5], they typically have relied on memory recall, and/or more sophisticated cognitive tasks such as language comprehension or split attention. This paper, despite that it was published more than 50 years ago, continues to be the primary citation to support the claim that pupillometry is a reliable index of task difficulty for a simple nonverbal pitch discrimination task therefore giving us an implicit measure for listening effort (e.g., [2, 4, 3]). This type of task takes very little explicit memory, is non-verbal, and relies heavily on more low-level, automatic perceptual processing. We therefore aimed to replicate the 1967 experiment using modern pupillometry hardware and techniques.

title_r: Does social context (really) modulate the own-group bias in face recognition? A test of the social categorization hypothesis
abstract_r: The term “own-group bias” (OGB) refers to the human tendency to better discriminate and memorize own vs other-race faces. Socio-cognitive theories assume that categorizing someone as an out-group member decreases the motivation to individuate that person, leading to worse recognition performance. The current research aims to replicate a study reported by Bataille (2018, unpublished master’s thesis), which was a replication attempt of Shriver, Young, Hugenberg, Bernstein and Lanter’s (2008) experiment 1a. Supporting socio-cognitive accounts, Shriver and colleagues (2008) demonstrated that socio-economic context (impoverished vs wealthy backgrounds) impacts own-race face recognition for middle-class White perceivers. Bataille (2018) expanded the original paradigm by adding new stimuli and varying participant group (i.e., White and Black), and found that stimulus group affected recognition for faces, with better memory for own- vs other-race faces, suggesting the presence of the OGB for both White and Maghrebi participants. Socio-economic context however, had no effect on face recognition performance. The present study aims to extend Bataille’s (2018) findings, adapting her study conducted in France, to the South African context. Stimuli group are kept identical: White, Black and Maghrebi, considering Maghrebi faces as being part of an infrequently represented group in South Africa. While Bataille’s study (2018) included White and Maghrebi participants, the present study includes Black, White and Coloured participants [South African race terms might not be familiar to readers. They date from the defunct Population Registration Act of 1950 (and perhaps before), but are still in official use in South Africa in order to audit change and the process of corrective actions]. The study aims to contribute to the knowledge of the effect of context on face recognition in particular. To sum-up, propose an extension of the study conducted by Bataille (2017) in France. Differences consist of (a) a translation of all written content; (b) different stimuli for the background context and combinations of faces and contexts (from Cape Town and suburbs); (c) a new population as participants, including Black, White and Coloured participants.

title_r: Fostering maker engagement in a summer vacation workshop: The role of autonomy and utility-value
abstract_r: Preregistration for the study: Fostering maker engagement in a summer vacation workshop: The role of autonomy and utility-value. An experimental study In the study, we investigate how adolescents can be motivated to engage in making activities. Making refers to the creative design and production of innovative products and artistic works using 3D printers, laser cutters or even single-board computers. For this purpose, we will conduct one experiment with a control group and an experimental group. The theoretical background is the theory of planned behavior (TPB; Ajzen 1991). In a manipulation check, we will examine if the intervention designed to be perceived as fostering autonomy and providing high utility value is really perceived that way. Afterwards, we examine whether high depicted autonomy and utility value in the video vignettes causes high values in the dependent variables (behavioral beliefs related to making activities, e.g. intrinsic value, and intention to participate). As covariables, we adjust for differences in self-efficacy, normative and control beliefs according to the TPB. This studiy is a conceptual replication of a similar experiment, which was preregistered here: https://osf.io/bkq2e/?view_only=1445720b40c94985ba2b586845f8f0ef. Since in that study, childrens’ intention to participate in a further workshop did not increase from pre- to posttest, we decided to redesign the underlying intervention and to conduct another experiment. The redesign of the intervention had the following focus: Instead of having discussions about the usefulness of making, we decided to allocate time for exploring what can be done through making. This applied to the experimental group. In the control group time was allocated for exploring how material (e.g. filament when printing) can be saved.

title_r: Predicting 17- and 24-month vocabulary from 12-month-olds’ prelinguistic communication and their caregivers’ responses
abstract_r: Language development is argued to be built on a foundation of infant-caregiver interactions. While there is robust evidence that infant prelinguistic acts and caregiver talk separately predict later child vocabulary, recent exploratory work suggests that, around children’s first birthdays, the strongest predictor of vocabulary growth over the second year is the dyadic combination of vocal and gestural infant communication (thought to be intentional) with relevant caregiver responses (Donnellan et al., 2020). The goal of the current study is to build on this exploratory work in two ways. First, we propose to create a single count measure of infant communicative behaviours that were observed by Donnellan et al. to be more or less valuable positive predictors of later language (namely gaze-coordinated vocalisations, index finger points and give and show gestures). This measure is relatively quick-to-code by observing interactions collected remotely via mobile phone and should, in a conceptual replication of Donnellan et al.’s exploratory study, be a positive predictor of later language. Second, we propose to test theoretical proposals regarding the roles of different socially contingent interactions in driving early language learning. In particular, we would like to differentiate the value of vocally responding to infants’ communicative acts in any way (including ‘content-light’ responses such as imitating the child’s babble or making minimal remarks like ‘oh’, for example) versus responding in a way that provides linguistic content that is semantically contingent on the infant’s focus of interest. The former should reinforce infants’ communication whereas the latter should additionally provide linguistic content to learn from. Therefore, the primary aims of the current study are to 1) produce a conceptual replication of key elements of Donnellan et al.’s exploratory work to confirm the specific predictive value of infants’ intentional, prelinguistic communicative acts and caregivers’ responses to them for predicting later vocabulary outcomes and 2) compare the predictive value of different types of caregiver response (no responses, any vocal response, ‘content-light’ response, specifically semantically contingent response for later vocabulary). Background: Donnellan et al. (2020) reported a novel procedure for predicting vocabulary development in the second year of life via multi-model inference over a comprehensive set of infant behaviours produced at 11 and 12 months. This established the relative predictive value of different infant communicative acts that were hierarchically organised by level of granularity. The set of infant communicative acts (vocalisations and gestures) considered is reproduced from their paper in the attached PDF preregistration (Figure 1). Also measured was how often infants combined one of these acts with a gaze to their caregiver (a proxy measure for communicative intent that was almost always present for infants’ gestural communication but only sometimes present for vocalisations). Finally, in addition to counting infant communicative acts, Donnellan et al. counted how often caregivers replied to them with a response that was related to what the infant appeared to be attending to and thus likely communicating about. Of all the communicative acts infants produced, Donnellan et al. found that the frequency with which infants produced gaze-coordinated vocalisations (where the infant vocalised and looked to the caregiver within one second of doing so) was identified as the most valuable predictor of expressive vocabulary. Other positive predictors included the infants’ production of give and show gestures and index-finger points. These four types of infant communicative act were assumed to be especially predictive because they were likely to have been produced intentionally (as opposed to non-gaze-coordinated vocalisations that may be produced purely for vocal play with no intention of having an effect on a communicative partner). When caregiver responses to infants’ prelinguistic communicative acts were also considered, the dyadic combination of infant gaze-coordinated vocalisations with caregivers’ prompt and semantically contingent responses was revealed to be an even more valuable predictor. It was assumed that this was the case because this measure reflected how often an infant intended to communicate with their caregiver and received a prompt response that contained linguistic content that was semantically relevant to what they had been trying to convey. Finally, the dyadic combination of infant vocalisations of any type (gaze-coordinated or not) and caregiver responses was also among the best predictors. For this count measure, it was not assumed that the infant necessarily had any communicative intent since they were not necessarily looking to the caregiver when producing the vocalisations, and it is known that infants often babble to themselves without appearing to want to communicate ostensively by doing so. Nonetheless, it would appear that this sequence of vocalisation and contingent response was a valuable predictor of infant language learning (albeit not as strong as the count restricted to only those vocalisations that were gaze-coordinated and responded to contingently). This perhaps suggests that even when infants’ vocalisations are not necessarily produced ‘for’ a caregiver (to initiate or continue communication with them), responding contingently may nonetheless be helpful for language learning (a simpler instance of reinforcement and associative learning). On the theoretical front, this exploratory study suggested that specific, socially-contingent sequences of behaviour are important for driving language learning. On the practical front, it suggested that if one sought to predict vocabulary growth from 12 to 24 months, one could observe a child interacting with their caregiver at around 12 months and count specific infant acts and infant-caregiver behavioural sequences. While some infant behaviours are incredibly time consuming to code (e.g., all infant vocalisations, which are produced at very high frequency), the most valuable positive predictors observed in this study are relatively quick to count from a 5-minute video. To recap, these behaviours and sequences are as follows: Infant Prelinguistic Communicative Acts (PCAs) that positively predict language outcomes: - Gaze-coordinated vocalisations - Index finger points - Give gestures - Show gestures Infant-caregiver dyad sequences that positively predict language outcomes: - Gaze-coordinated vocalisations + semantically contingent response - Any vocalisation + semantically contingent response This study seeks to build on Donnellan et al.’s exploratory study to test whether we can usefully predict variance in expressive vocabulary size at 17 and 24 months by coding 5-minute home videos of 12-month-old infants playing with their caregivers for infant prelinguistic communicative acts and caregiver-infant dyadic sequences of interaction. Importantly, this is a confirmatory test of the claims that arose out of Donnellan et al.’s exploratory study. To test theoretical accounts, we seek to establish whether semantically contingent caregiver responses to communicative acts were especially valuable. We also seek to explore the relative value of ‘content-light’ caregiver responses, which includes those that were prompt but not semantically contingent. To address these questions, we will analyse a new dataset with participants from socially diverse areas of the four nations of the UK (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). For these infants and their caregivers, we have measured: - the frequency of infants’ Prelinguistic Communicative Acts (PCAs: gaze-coordinated vocalisations and index-finger pointing gestures and give gestures and show gestures) - the frequency of PCAs that elicited a caregiver response that was either a) semantically contingent or b) ‘content-light’ (i.e., not semantically contingent). - the frequency of PCAs and infants’ non-gaze-coordinated vocalisations that elicited a caregiver response that was either a) semantically contingent or b) ‘content-light’ (i.e., not semantically contingent). By testing the predictive value of these 12-month measures, we will verify the conclusions of the exploratory Donnellan et al. study and theoretical proposals regarding the role of different types of social contingency in early language learning. On a practical level, we will also test whether a relatively quick-to-code measurement of socially contingent interactions during naturalistic play derived from home videos collected remotely is useful in predicting early child language development. The new cohort of 125 families (whose data we will analyses here) took part in a larger Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) which tested the effects of an early language intervention (see clincialtrials.gov and https://osf.io/kme68/ for pre-registration). Approximately half of the participants in the current study (N = 61) took part in the intervention while the other half (N = 64) took part in an active control condition. Condition did not have an impact on caregiver reported vocabulary (the outcome variable here). Nonetheless, we control for intervention condition in all analyses. We will also explore the relation between caregiver education (undergraduate degree/no degree) and predictor variables. title_r: The Contributions of Positive Outgroup and Negative Ingroup Evaluation to Implicit Bias Favoring Outgroups
abstract_r: In an initial set of studies, we investigated the contributions of positive and negative evaluations to implicit biases in favor of outgroups. Among members of lower-status groups (i.e., Asian, Black, older, gay and lesbian people), their outgroup favorability biases reflected positive evaluations of the higher-status outgroup more than negative evaluations of their ingroup. Among members of higher-status groups (i.e., White, younger, straight), their outgroup favorability biases reflected a more mixed pattern of positive and negative evaluations. In a separate set of analyses, we also investigated the contributions of positive and negative evaluations to implicit biases in favor of ingroups. We found that ingroup favorability biases reflected positive evaluations of ingroups more than negative evaluations of outgroups – and this was true for members of higher-status groups as well as for members of lower-status groups. In the present research, we seek to replicate our initial findings in new samples, using different analytic methods, and including additional measures of bias.

title_r: Effects of sensory feedback location on response effectiveness ver.1
abstract_r: Several previous studies have shown that immediate feedback could enhance reaction time (e.g., Eitam, Kennedy, & Higgins, 2013; Tanaka, Watanabe, & Tanaka, 2020). In Tanaka et al., two conditions were immediate (0 ms) and lagged (600 ms). After the button press, feedback (i.e., flash) was given immediately in the immediate condition, while it was given after 600 ms in the lagged condition. title_r: "He came from a good family": Vicarious moral licensing via family members of criminal offenders
abstract_r: This study is a replication and extension of a previous study, which examined whether criminal offenders can receive moral license from their family members. Participants will read a description of a criminal offender that includes some information about their family. Their family description will be edited to either be moral, immoral, or neutral. The offender will either be biologically related to the family, or adopted into the family. Participants will then be asked to evaluate the crime and the offender. We expect to replicate our previous findings, that individuals receive vicarious moral license from their family, so that those from an immoral family are judged more harshly than those from neutral or moral families. Furthermore, we expect this effect may be stronger for offenders who are biologically related to their family.

title_r: Listening to a rhythm to enhance grammatical processing during reading
abstract_r: The aim of this study is to investigate the influence of the listening of different rhythmic background on the grammatical processing during reading. Previous studies have shown that a regular rhythmic priming improve the detection of grammatical errors in sentences presented auditorily (Chern et al., 2018; Canette et al., 2020). However no study have tested this effect on reading yet. To address this issue, a first study was conducted in 2021. In this study, 42 4th graders performed a grammatical judgement task in three background conditions (silent, regular rhythm, irregular rhythm). The results revealed that the participants were faster when they listening a regular rhythm compared to the two other conditions. We aim to confirm this result by conducting a replication study using the exact same procedure.

title_r: Is it just the font? Effects of different font types (Verdana vs. Times New Roman) on successful learning in digital vs. analogue reading formats.
abstract_r: Digital learning today is essential and has become an integral part of knowledge transfer alongside analogue learning materials (Mortler, 2018). The Corona pandemic has even increased and speeded up the use of digital learning, with its advantages and disadvantages (e.g. Engels, 2020; Müller, Lalive & Lavanchy, 2020). In this context, previous research has largely focused on the question whether different reading formats lead to different learning successes (e.g. Kong, Zeo, Thai, 2018; Mangen, Anda, Oxborough & Bronnik, 2015; Sackstein, Spark & Jenkins, 2015; Singer & Alexander, 2017). For example, learning material was examined which includes the arrangement of text and images. Some studies in turn investigated learning material only in one of the two reading formats. For example, the effect of fonts on learning (e.g. Ali, Wahid, Samsudin & Idris, 2013; Hojjati & Muniandy, 2014; Josephson, 2011). Josephson (2011) showed in an eye tracking study that the font Verdana increases learning and reading speed more than the font Times New Roman in digital reading. Ali et al. (2013) showed that Verdana proves viable for digital learning and Times New Roman for analogue learning. On the issue, if analogue or digital reading formats are more benefitting for learning, a number of meta-analyses show somewhat mixed results (e.g. Clinton, 2019; Delgado, Vargas, Ackerman & Salmerón, 2018; Dillon, 1992, Kong, Sik Seo & Zhai, 2018, Singer-Trakhman & Alexander, 2017). Overall however, a tendency towards better learning results from analogue formats can be expected. To the best of our knowledge, no studies were conducted on the combination of the two influencing factors on text-based learning: The effect of digital vs. analogue reading in addition to the font. Moreover, studies have been conducted on the reading process itself. More specifically, two approaches were used to examine reading processes comparing digital and analogues reading: reading time and cognitive load (Clinton, 2019). For example, Rapp and van den Broek (2005) measured reading time. They postulated that when reading for a longer period of time, the the working memory capacity is reduced, and , in turn the cognitive load increases. Chen and Catrambone (2015) associated longer reading time with an increase of cognitive load (Chandler & Sweller, 1991). Hahnel, Kroehne, Goldhammer, Schoor, Mahlow and Artelt (2019) showed that high cognitive load is associated with a longer and more difficult texts. Moreno and Park found that ”the Cognitive Load Theory has mostly focused on how the objective characteristics of the task affect cognitive load and, in turn, learning” (p. 11). According to the Cognitive Load Theory teachers should match the learning material in an optimal way to reduce cognitive load to increase learning. With this study, we aim to add to previous research. We aim to replicate the results from Josephson (2011) in an experimental setting and more importantly we will extend the results from Josephson (2011) and Ali et al. (2013), comparing the effect from the fonts Verdana and Times New Roman on learning between analogue and digital reading formats. Furthermore, we want to investigate, if there is any effect on cognitive load (e.g. Sweller, van Marrienboer & Paas, 1998; Mayer, 2005) and learning in different reading formats, when using more suitable fonts as shown by Josephson (2011) and Ali et al. (2013). When using the suitable fonts within the correct reading format, we expect that the learning material will be designed in an optimal way for learning. Accordingly, learning will be easier and more successful. Cognitive Load As stated above, cognitive load can have an impact on text-based learning. The Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) (Sweller, van Marrienboer and Paas, 1998) and the Cognitive Load Theory of Multimedia Learning (Mayer, 2005) both address how learning materials can influence cognitive processes and which factors affects this process while in turn learning. Sweller et al. (1998) developed their theory to design learning material in a way that readers can retrieve their optimal learning performance. Sweller et al. (1998) postulated three assumptions: Based on the theory of Baddely (1986) and Atkinson and Shiffrin (1971) as well as Sweller (2005), (1) the capacity of the working memory is limited, (2) the capacity of the long-term memory is unlimited and (3) the processing of learning information depends on stable cognitive structures, called schemata (Chi, Glaser & Rees, 1982). The Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) suggests that effective learning is only possible, when the capacity of the working memory is not overloaded. Based on these assumptions, Sweller et al. (1998) postulated three types of cognitive load: Intrinsic Cognitive Load (ICL), Germane Cognitive Load (GCL) and Extraneous Cognitive Load (ECL). The ICL depends on the complexity of the learning material (Klepsch, 2020). The interactivity of the learning elements represents the scale of the ICL (e.g. Sweller & Chandler, 1994; Paas, Renkl & Sweller, 2003). The GCL postulates activities that help to understand the impact of learning materials and effective schemata on the long-term memory (Sweller et al., 1998). Schemata are constructs to organize information in the long-term memory. The GCL postulate that deep learning can increase the understanding of the learning material and activate and form schemata for the long term memory (e.g. Sweller et al., 1998; Bannert, 2002). The ECL is affected by the design of the learning material (Klepsch, 2020). For example, if the design includes irrelevant information or a complicated structure, the ECL increases, because the reader must shield against disturbing design elements to learn effectively. Accordingly, there are a number of design principles to organize the learning material in an optimal way and to reduce the ECL (Klepsch, 2020). We go into more detail on the ECL down below. The Cognitive Load Theory of Multimedia Learning (Mayer, 2005) explained, how individuals are able to learn with text and pictures. Mayer (2005) postulated three assumptions, based on previous findings: (1) that information are processed in a visual and a verbal way (i.e. Paivio, 1986; Baddeley, 1992), (2) that both ways are limited (Baddeley, 1992; Chandler and Sweller, 1991) and (3) that active processing of learning is important for effective learning (Mayer, 2008). As well as Sweller et al. (1998), Mayer and Moreno (2010) postulated three types of cognitive load. The Essential Processing, which correspondents to the GCL. The Incidental Processing, which correspondent with ECL and the Representational holding, which correspondents with the ICL. Mayer (2005) postulated the challenge is to design the learning material without overloading the individual. In the present investigation, we focus on ECL as one important aspect of cognitive load (Klepsch, 2020). There are some principles to reduce the ELC and increase learning: The redundancy principle (Sweller and Chandler, 1994), the coherence principle (Mayer, 2009, Mayer & Moreno, 2010) and the split attention principle (Ayres & Sweller, 2005). The redundancy principle suggest that people learn deep from graphs and narration than from graphs, narration and text on display. The rationale behind the redundancy principle is that people waste processing capacity by trying to reconcile the different information streams and, in turn, the cognitive load increases. For example, Moreno and Mayer (2002) showed that students performed better in an experimental setting when they received a narrated animation than the same narrated animation with concurrent text on display. The coherence principle (e.g. Mayer, 2009, Mayer & Moreno, 2010) suggest that all decorative information, such as decorative sentences, increase the cognitive load. The rationale of the coherence principle is that individuals are more able to focus on essential information, when learning information are presented without decorative sentences. For example, Mayer, Griffith, Jurkowitz, and Rothman (2008) showed in an experimental setting with students that learning increases when no irrelevant information were presented. So only the important information for the learning tasks at hand should be included. The split attention principle (Ayres & Sweller, 2005) postulates that learners benefit by the spatial integration of information. So, deep learning is possible when corresponding words and graphs are as close together as possible. The reason for this is that spatial contiguity supports learners to build connections between corresponding words and graphs. For example, Moreno and Mayer (1999) showed in an experimental setting that students showed better learning performance, when text and animation were presented closely together. What consequences can we thus assume for learning? For effective learning it is important to reduce the cognitive load. One aspect to increase learning is to reduce the ECL. The ECL depends on the design of learning materials. As shown earlier, we can design learning material by specific criteria and thereby reduce ECL. Josephson (2011) and Ali et al. (2013) showed, that using suitable fonts (Verdana and Times New Roman) in digital and analogue reading formats can increase learning. In this study we will use the fonts as one aspect to design the learning material and investigate the ECL it in the context of learning. title_r: Exploring the role of long-term memory in residual working memory performance
abstract_r: Working memory provides two fundamental functions, the processing and the temporary storage of a limited amount of information. Some models of working memory suggest that there is a sharing of resources between these two functions, which means that when we perform one at our maximum level, the performance in the other decrease. We recently carried out a series of experiments, the results of which support this hypothesis (Barrouillet et al., in revision). Participants were asked to perform a dual-task with memorizing letters and processing the parity of digits in a complex span task. They were asked to prioritise one of the two components of the task to ensure that they performed at their maximum level in one of the two components. The number of items to be memorised and processed was adapted to each participant's span. In addition, participants performed a concurrent articulation during trials to prevent the use of articulatory rehearsal for letter maintenance. The results showed that performance decreased considerably for the component not prioritised. However, performance residual in the non-prioritised task remained high, which suggests that there is a partial sharing of resources. As a result, the origin of this performance residuals in the non-prioritised task needs to be explored, since under a complete resource-sharing, the residual should be null. We suggest that long-term memory is involved in letter maintenance. In the present study, we will measure whether the residual can be explained by long-term memory. We will replicate the previous described experiments, adding a new recall condition. In some trials, before the recall of letters, participants will be asked to perform a backward counting task, to erase the content of their working memory. We will only examine residual performance in the memory component of the task, with a prioritization on processing. If the participants will be able to remember the letters as much in delayed recall as in immediate recall, this would support the involvement of long-term memory in residual memory performance.

title_r: Congruency effect in face recognition for masked perpetrators with real-life images under low memory load
abstract_r: Masked perpetrators pose unique challenges for people to recognize since occlusion of facial features impairs recognition. To address this challenge, previous studies have suggested that contextual congruency can facilitate recognition performance for masked perpetrators and this congruency effect can still be available even with low-quality face images. However, this improvement in performance does not necessarily extend to confidence. Earlier research found no clear relationship between confidence and accuracy (the CA relationship) in recognizing masked faces, but when the number of faces to memorize is reduced, a CA relationship emerges, suggesting that it may be influenced by memory load. However, the impact of memory load has primarily been explored under optimal viewing conditions, leaving it unclear when viewing a face image of low quality. Here we aim to replicate and extend this finding with a reduced number of studied targets to explore whether the potential influence of cognitive and memory load can affect recognition performance in real-world scenarios.

title_r: Helping Predicts Within-person Changes in Empathic Sensitivity
abstract_r: Previous research shows that people who help more than others experience more positive changes in their trait empathic concern over time, and also experience higher levels of empathic concern when they help more than usual (Guevara Beltran et al., under review). However, an outstanding question is whether changes in empathy lead to changes in helping or whether helping leads to changes in empathy over time. The primary goal of the present study is to conduct a pre-registered direct replication of a previous non-preregistered study. We examine whether helping cultivates changes in empathy over time, and whether there might be bidirectional associations between helping and empathy. We tested this idea across two studies, predicting that helping others in need would cultivate changes in empathy (i.e., affect sharing, concern) over time because helping provides a context in which people can deploy, experience, and practice their empathy within the context of mutual support relationships. We found that helping was associated with positive within-person changes in empathy, but empathizing was not associated with changes in helping. Moreover, while we expected helping to specifically lead to positive changes in emotion sharing and concern (i.e., facets of empathic concern), we found that helping only predicted noticing (i.e., having) a greater number of opportunities to empathize. However, secondary data analysis (Study 2; Depow et al., 2021) shows that (a) people empathize most of the time in which they notice an opportunity to do so (88% of cases), and (b) when they empathize, they report feeling concern most of the time (94% of empathy experiences) (Depow et al., 2021). Combined, these findings suggest that helping may cultivate an empathetic disposition over time not because it intensifies empathy itself (e.g., emotion sharing, concern), but because regularly practicing empathy through the act of helping increases one's attunement to others' thoughts and feelings.

title_r: Artwork as a catalyst for Nature's mind attribution
abstract_r: In the current study, we aim to deepen our understanding of the potential of Art as an intervention tool to raise mind attribution towards natural resources (specifically the Ocean) and examine if such mind attribution translates into a stronger moral commitment towards pro-environmental actions. The theoretical background of this project is two-folded. First, art theorists and experts in the field of Art psychology have argued that non-living entities portrayed in artworks are perceived by the observer as having vitality and a sense of purpose (Eck, 2016; Ioviono, 2015; Mitchell, 2006). Moreover, art is an especially powerful means of eliciting emotions (Chatterjee,2014), and as emotions are essentially human, it is argued that the evocation of emotions by art could spill over and generate an inference of mind towards the main motifs of the artwork. The second main theoretical argument relates to the role of art as one of the main cultural diffusion mechanisms. Throughout history, natural resources have been depicted as deities and anthropomorphized beings (Campbell, 1991; Dehouve, 2020), a symbology recurrently depicted in many artworks across the world and throughout history (Beard, 2018). We argue that contemplating an artwork featuring a natural resource could make this narrative of 'sentient Nature' accessible, without the need for the art to actually depict anthropomorphized representations of nature. Supporting these claims, we have found evidence that observing art increases mind attribution towards the ocean in a previous study. Specifically, we presented people with either a regular picture of the ocean or artwork in which the ocean is the main motif (specifically, the Great Wave Off Kanagawa by Japanese painter Katsushika Hokusai). As hypothesised, observing the artwork produced a significant, positive main effect on mind attribution towards the ocean. However, the previous study is subject to some limitations that limit our claims. Although variables like directionality and valence were controlled, important differences remained between the two experimental conditions in terms of stimuli. Especially, differences in colour and size of the objects portrayed, as well as a potential familiarity effect due to the artwork being a very well-known piece preclude us from making a more confident assertion of an effect of art contemplation. Therefore, the present study aims to constitute a more stringent test to that claim. In order to accomplish this, we will use two almost identical visual stimuli. More specifically, we will use the same photograph as the one used in Study 1. The control group will observe the target photograph while being told it is a picture of the ocean. The experimental group will observe the same picture while being told that it is an artwork (i.e., oil painting) featuring the ocean. In this way, we will isolate the effect caused by the participants' belief that they are contemplating art rather than an unspecified photograph. Finally, we aim to examine mind attribution using an additional, more nuanced, multidimensional scale and we also intend to examine if the hypothetical effect on mind attribution would be generalizable to an effect on mind attribution towards Nature. We expect to replicate the effects found on mind attribution in Study 1 as well as the mediational path that explains the increase of moral obligation for those who observe art through mind attribution.

title_r: “Grandma, what gray hair you have!”: How children think about 'grandmothers'”
abstract_r: Despite the importance of family during early life, current literature suggests that kinship terms are challenging for children: explicit understanding of these words does not fully develop until late childhood (refer to Steele & Thomas, 2024 for review). However, recent literature suggests that young children have the ability to identify specific relationships in their family network (Steele & Thomas, in press) and that even infants can recognize that some social interactions provide evidence of family-like relationships (Steele et al., 2024; Thomas et al., 2022). In this project, we aim to investigate children’s knowledge about the kinship term “grandmother”. We build on a study conducted by Landau (1982), in which, when shown images of different families and asked which images they believed to contain a grandmother, young children identified elderly women without children as grandmothers, but failed to identify middle-aged women depicted alongside two younger generations as grandmothers. For Condition 1, we do a conceptual replication of this study, giving only explicit information about the age of the people in the pictures. We also add a Condition 2, in which we provide a definition of grandma and then give information about the relationships of the people in the pictures. Across both conditions, we test if children tend to use perceptual features of age, or relationships information (or both). We expect that, in condition 1, children will tend to rely on physical traits (age) to identify their grandmother, while in condition 2, more children use the definition of “grandma” to identify grandmothers. Likewise, we expect children will say that there is a grandmother in a picture containing childless old women less frequently in the second condition and will say there is a grandmother more often in an image containing a middle-aged grandmother in experimental condition than in the control condition.

title_r: Colorblind ideology/Assimilation and Perception of a Bleak Future on Anti-immigration attitudes and White Nationalism: Replication and Extensions
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

In our first pre-registered study titled “Re-categorization and Perception of a Bleak Future”, we assess whether (1) the perception of a bleak future for one’s racial group by the majority (Whites) will predict anti-immigration policies, (2) not recategorizing targets of prejudice as having a shared identity will lead Whites to show higher anti-immigration attitudes, especially when they perceive a bleak future. Our analysis showed that anti-immigration attitudes were not dependent on recategorizations, i.e participants who recategorized and those who did not showed higher anti-immigration attitudes when they perceived a bleak future. However, the trend for low recategorizers was more steep than for the high recatgeorizers. Hence, the effect of perceived bleak future on anti-immigration attitudes was more pronounced in low recategorizers. In our previous study, we acknowledge that the item we used to measure recategorization was actually a measure of assimilation (a facet of colorblindness) which explains the result. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to see if the result found in our earlier study would replicate using explicit measures of color blind ideology (CBI)/assimilation. We expect a similar pattern with support for white nationalist ideologies.

title_r: Effects of nicotine deptivation on value processing in smokers
abstract_r: The planned study examines the effects of nicotine deprivation in smokers on metacognition, motivation for mental effort, and reward-guided attentional capture. For this, nicotine-dependent smokers will perform a battery of computer-based tasks either in a deprived or in a saturated state in separate experimental sessions. The study addresses four main research questions. 1. Metacognitive insight into time preferences in an intertemporal cigarette decision task In previous studies, the high relapse rate in tobacco dependence was associated with deficits in decision-making and increased impulsivity (Sheffer et al., 2014), which are further enhanced in the state of nicotine deprivation (Heckmann et al., 2017). Moreover, Soutschek, Bulley, and Wittekind (2022) found that smokers (relative to non-smokers) suffer not only from increased impulsivity but also from poorer metacognitive insight into their impulsivity. In this follow-up study, we will examine whether nicotine deprivation influences metacognition. To test this, we will use a cigarette intertemporal decision task with confidence ratings after each choice as an indicator for metacognition (Soutschek, Bulley & Wittekind, 2022). Participants will perform this task once in the ad-libitum state and once in the deprivation state. This will provide insights into the influence of nicotine on metacognitive processes as well as whether nicotine deprivation affects metacognitive insight into their impulsiveness. We hypothesize that nicotine deprivation increases the preference for immediate rewards and reduces metacognitive accuracy. 2. Motivation for rewarded mental effort Unpublished data from our group suggest that smokers have a lower motivation to engage in goal-directed mental effort compared to non-smokers (Soutschek & Wittekind, submitted). Based on these findings, we test whether the motivation for rewarded mental effort in smokers is further reduced in craving states, which may compromise their motivation to engage in demanding control processes to remain abstinent due to the effortful nature of control processes. We measure smokers' motivation to engage in mental effort with effort-based decision tasks where participants have to decide between a monetary reward for which they have to perform a demanding mental task an effort-free monetary or cigarette rewards (Soutschek et al., 2017). We hypothesize that smokers will exhibit a stronger preference for effort-free rewards in the deprived compared with the saturated state. 3. Sensitivity to distractors in the value-modulated attentional capture (VMAC) task The value-modulated attentional capture task measures the influence of reward-associated distractors on attentional allocation (Le Pelley et al., 2015). It has been shown that reward-associated stimuli can capture attention, thereby interfering with goal-directed behavior and that persistence of value-modulated attentional capture is associated with risky alcohol consumption (Albertella et al., 2019). However, the influence of deprivation (either of nicotine or any other substance) on value-based attentional capture as well as on the persistence of learned value-distractor associations remains unknown. A further goal of this study is to investigate whether nicotine deprivation enhances the impact of distractors associated with high rewards. 4. Influence of nicotine deprivation on smoking lapses Approximately 90 percent of smokers experiencing a first relapse continue to smoke (Brandon et al., 1990). The identification of precursors to relapses is therefore crucial for the clinical understanding of smoking cessation failures (Heckmann et al., 2017). The lapse task measures the ability of participants to resist nicotine consumption (McKee, 2009). Within a 30-minute delay phase, the time of the first cigarette consumption (i.e., lapse) indicates participants' ability to resist smoking. We expect to replicate previous findings that nicotine deprivation leads to faster lapses. Moreover, depending on the effects of deprivation on the other task, we will explore whether deprivation-induced changes in the other tasks statistically explain the deprivation effects on the lapse task. Research Questions Q1: Does nicotine deprivation reduce smokers' metacognitive insight into their impulsiveness? Q2: Does nicotine deprivation reduce the motivation to engage in goal-directed effort? Q3: Does nicotine deprivation increase value-modulated attentional capture and lower the ability adapt to distractor-value reversals? Q4: Do lower cognitive abilities (i.e., less metacognitive insight, less motivation, higher value modulated attentional capture) shorten the time to the first cigarette?

title_r: Experiment on indirect rebound - study 2
abstract_r: At the end of 2018 we carried out this study for the first time by means of an online experiment. At the end of 2020, we will replicate the study. One of the main reasons for replicating this study is that we found a result (interaction effect) that we find difficult to interpret. In hindsight we see a number of limitations in the first study that could possibly have led to the effect we found. By improving the study on these aspects we aim to filter out unwanted noise and improve our investigation of the indirect rebound effect. In short the study consists of a number of questions on personal traits, a priming task, a second task in which participants choose a reward, and finally a number of questions on states and demographics. We adjusted the study in four main ways: 1) In the second task of our first study participants could make a choice out of a set of 13 rewards, which were selected based on their value ($13), their environmental impact and category (food, leisure, technology). In the initial study we provided rewards that would appeal to many people, without having one reward standing out so much that people would only want that reward. We did not pre-test how people would assess our rewards, and although we asked questions on the characteristics of the rewards we are not sure about the role initial preferences played. In addition we included a number of low environmental impact rewards, but did not offer the option that people would not receive an award or would choose a reward that would reduce their CO2 impact. Moreover, the variation of CO2 impact of the rewards lacked some structure: sometimes what we defined as a high CO2 impact reward in one category, we defined as low in another. In other words, it happened that a reward that we considered high within one category actually scored lower than the lowest scoring reward in a different category. Thus, it was impossible to distinguish whether people were choosing the lowest impact options within categories or the lowest impact options overall. To improve the dependent variable in the replication study, we performed a pilot study to test people’s preferences of rewards and their perception of the provided environmental information. Based on the pilot results we selected eight rewards (four pairs) of which all low impact rewards indeed had a lower impact than the high impact rewards (see table 1). Moreover we checked the clarity and credibility of the information on environmental impact associated with each reward; both clarity and credibility proved to be good for the eight rewards. Finally, in study 2 we also included a reward that would allow participants to positively impact the environment / reduce CO2. 2) Overall we kept the questionnaire as similar as possible to the questionnaire we used in study 1. The measurement of traits at the beginning and the priming task were left unchanged. The reward task was changed as described under bullet 1. A main difference was that at the end of the questionnaire we added a question on moral self-concept (state) and we checked one of the manipulations more explicitly, in particular whether respondents noticed the information on environmental impact. 3) The power of the effects we found in study 1 was on the low side. Therefore we will include a larger sample in our second study. 4) In our first study we collected our data via the MTurk platform, which is known for a fast and easy way to collect survey data, but it is also known for being a way for people to make fast and easy money without much attention. As our experimental study asks for concentration and attention for at least 20 minutes, we expect that recruiting participants via another platform will lead to better quality responses. We will therefore recruit participants via Prolific.

title_r: Does native language promote access to visual consciousness?
abstract_r: Can the language we speak influence what we consciously perceive? While evidence accumulates that language modulates visual discrimination, little is known about the relation between language structure and access to visual consciousness. In two previous experiments we employed EEG and the attentional blink paradigm in which targets are often unnoticed. In Experiment 1, native Greek speakers, who distinguish categorically between light and dark shades of blue, showed higher hit rates for this contrast compared to a verbally unmarked green contrast. Electrophysiological signatures of early visual processing (P1 component) predicted this behavioral advantage. Experiment 2 replicated the study with German speakers who place the “Greek” blues into one category, yielding no differences between the blue and the green contrast in behavior and electrophysiological signatures. The present study is a pre-registered behavioral replication in which we will test Russian native speakers, who also distinguish categorically between light and dark shades of blue. We expect to replicate the behavioral effects found in Experiment 1.

title_r: Effect of spatial attention on egocentric and allocentric spatial judgments. A replication with oculometric measures
abstract_r: In previous pre-registered experiment (detailed at length here: https://osf.io/egs7b) conducted on healthy participants, we studied the effect of spatial attention on the line bisection and visual straight-ahead tasks. We found that shifting spatial attention to the left or the right by means of exogenous visual cues could bias the subjective line midpoint (in the line bisection task), as classically reported in the literature (e.g., Sosa et al., 2011). Moreover, a similar and congruent effect of visual cues was also observed in the straight-ahead task. However, this latter effect might have been triggered by ocular saccades automatically directed toward the visual cue (just before performing the straight-ahead judgement). The aim of the present experiment is to test the effect of this potential confounding factor, by replicating this experiment with eye-tracking measures. This way, we will be able to measure the mean eye position of each participant for each visual cue condition. We will analyze the main effect of this factor, both for the straight-ahead and line bisection tasks.

title_r: It's your game..keep it real in South Carolina: A group randomized trial evaluating the replication of an evidence-based adolescent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infection prevention program
abstract_r: Objectives. To evaluate the effectiveness of an evidence-based HIV/sexually transmitted infection (STI)/pregnancy prevention program for middle schools implemented by school staff in South Carolina. Methods. Twenty-four schools, representing 3143 youths, participated in a randomized trial from 2011 to 2014. Students completed surveys before programming (fall of seventh grade), after completing the 2-year It's Your Game..Keep It Real program (spring of eighth grade), and 1-year postprogram (spring of ninth grade). Results.There was no statistically significant effect on initiation of vaginal sex between baseline and eighth grade. Significantly fewer students in the comparison condition reported initiating sex at ninth grade, relative to the intervention condition. No group differences existed on other behavioral outcomes that addressed sexual activity in the past 3 months at ninth grade. Seven of 26 psychosocial outcomes (3 knowledge, 1 attitude, 1 self-efficacy, 2 personal limits) were positively affected at eighth grade; 4 remained significant at ninth grade. Conclusions. The original studies' behavioral effects were not replicated in this population, possibly as a result of this being an effectiveness trial instead of an efficacy trial, counterfactual exposure design issues, or postprogram exposure to evidence-based programming.

title_r: Agreeableness as Predictor of Induced Scratching in Patients with Atopic Dermatitis: A Replication Study
abstract_r: In patients with atopic dermatitis agreeableness and public self-consciousness have previously been shown to be significant predictors of induced scratching, while depression was significantly related to induced itch. This study aimed to replicate these findings. Itch and scratching were induced by videos of crawling insects or skin diseases. Induced itch was measured using a visual analogue scale. Scratching behavior was evaluated by two raters. Psychological variables were assessed using validated questionnaires. Induced scratching could be predicted significantly by agreeableness (corrected R2 = 15.5% or 38 % after exclusion of one outlier): Patients scoring low on agreeableness showed a higher increase in scratch movements than patients scoring high on this scale. No associations between induced scratching/itch and public self-consciousness/depression were found. One clinical implication that arises from this study could be to offer patients scoring low on agreeableness certain psychological interventions.

title_r: Open-label placebo effects on psychological and physical well-being: a conceptual replication study
abstract_r: Background: Contrary to traditional placebos, open-label placebos (OLP) abstain from deception, i.e., participants are openly informed to receive an inert substance. Studies in clinical and healthy samples evidence the efficacy of OLPs. This study aims to conceptually replicate and expand findings of a recent OLP study in healthy participants while implementing a within-subject design and daily instead of retrospective assessments. Additionally, the effect of a brand name on the medicine container is tested and possible predictors of the OLP effects are explored. Methods: Healthy participants (N = 75) received OLP and no placebo for 5 days each (randomized sequence) and answered daily questionnaires on sleep quality, bodily symptoms, mental well-being, and psychological distress. The medicine container of half the participants had a brand name, the remaining did not. Different personality traits and situational factors were assessed. Results: Mental and physical well-being did not differ between OLP and control phase, i.e., overall, no OLP effect emerged. Contrast analysis indicated that an OLP effect emerged for sleep quality and psychological distress when no brand name was present. Further, an OLP effect emerged in persons with higher expectations for bodily symptoms (r = .23, p = .046) and psychological distress (r = .24, p = .037). Conclusions: Methodological differences to the original study are discussed as an explanation for the failure to induce overall OLP effects. Future studies should continue to replicate previous findings and determine the exact conditions of successful implementation of OLP effects in healthy as well as clinical samples.

title_r: Divide Tariffs and Prosper? A Focus on the Role of Need for Cognition
abstract_r: This study presents a conceptual replication of the effect of partitioned prices on consumer responses in a subscription service setting. Contrasting Morwitz/Greenleaf/Johnson’s (1998) seminal article, the results of an online experiment reveal that consumers are more likely to buy a subscription service with a partitioned tariff (i.e., a pay-per-use tariff) than with a combined tariff (i.e., a flat rate). This effect occurs even though all consumers are aware of the correct billing price and the billing price is identical in both conditions. However, the negative effect of the partitioned (vs. the combined) tariff on consumer responses is mitigated by high levels of need for cognition. Intriguingly, consumers extremely high in need for cognition show a reversed effect pattern when examining perceived price fairness as the dependent variable, that is, they perceive the partitioned tariff to be fairer than the combined tariff.

title_r: TESS Experiments: Proposal to Replicate and Extend Seven TESS Studies - Part 2
abstract_r: Time-sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS) offers researchers the opportunity to capture the internal validity of experiments. Investigators submit proposals, and TESS fields successful proposals for free on a representative sample of adults in the United States. This 2-wave multi-experiment study was conducted to test the persistence of framing effects. In experiment 1, Wave 1 respondents were randomly assigned to one of three framing treatments in which they were asked to read an article on the popularity of a television show (Control), partisan agreement, or political polarization. Respondents then indicated their stance and what they believed the stance of the typical Democratic and Republican voter would be, on capital gains taxes, undocumented immigrants, free-trade agreements, and election financing. In experiment 2, Wave 1 respondents were randomly assigned to one of eight conditions which varied arguments presented for or against international trade (none (Control), pro, con, or both pro and con) and either omitted or included expert consensus on the benefit of and need to increase international trade. Respondents were then asked to report their support/non-support of increased international trade. A total of 2,123 respondents participated in Wave 1. Wave 2 (n=1865) resurveyed respondents 10 days later. This allowed for comparison of immediate and longer-term effects of framing.

title_r: Re-examining factors in AR/VR teacher training: A replication study
abstract_r: This study aimed to replicate and extend Buchner and Hoffman’s (2022) research on the Tell-Show-Enact-Do (TSED) approach to integrating augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) into teacher training. We conducted non-parametric Mann–Whitney U tests on the original dataset to examine the impact of age and learning design on the participants’ attitudes, skills, and access. Our results diverged from the original findings. TSED only increased two scores more than TSE (Tell-Show-Enact): Will (attitude) and Tool (availability). In addition, younger participants felt more strongly about the accessibility of digital tools. Overall, TSED appears more effective than TSE, though its specific benefits still need to be identified. This replication study highlighted the need to tailor teacher training based on age and confirmed the promise of AR/VR for professional development. Its insights will contribute to ethical, evidence-based AR/VR integration and enhance teacher training. The study also demonstrated that replication is useful for re-examining conditions and demographics in educational technology research to refine its conclusions. As technology evolves, further replication studies will be necessary.

title_r: Making Decisions with Limited Information: Forming and Updating Ambiguous Beliefs
abstract_r: Introduction: How individuals deal with outcomes under unknown risks (I.e. ambiguity) can be important for understanding decisions in the real world. One commonly applied model for ambiguous decisions, maxmin expected utility (MMEU), suggests that people only focus on the range of probabilities. However, other models, including subjective recursive expected utility (SREU), suggest that instead of thinking about the range, people construct a belief about the probabilities as a distribution, based on their experiences or intuition. MMEU has been used to relate ambiguity preferences to clinical disorders, including autism spectrum disorder. However, if SREU models are a better reflection of decisions under ambiguity, these differences may be related to beliefs instead of preferences. Methods: To investigate the role of beliefs in ambiguous decisions, we collected choice and personality data from an online sample (N=298) utilizing a novel task. In our task, participants make decisions under ambiguity after learning about the distribution of probabilities during a previous decision task. We test if variance in beliefs influences decisions under ambiguity, interacts with reward feedback, and accounts for individual differences related to a clinical variable, the Autism Quotient (AQ) to explore the bounds of the MMEU model. Results: Participants preferred ambiguous stimuli associated with high variance distributions and made larger changes in response to feedback information when applied to high variance distributions. We did not replicate results showing that ambiguity aversion decreased with AQ but did find AQ decreased with the believed variance of probabilities. Conclusions: Our results provide experimental evidence that decisions under ambiguity are influenced by beliefs, violating a key axiom of MMEU, suggesting previous results should be revisited by incorporating beliefs to better understand the mechanisms of ambiguous choice.

title_r: Can losses help attenuate learning traps?
abstract_r: Recent work has demonstrated robust learning traps during learning from experience – decision-making biases that persist due to the choice-contingent nature of outcome feedback. In two experiments, we investigate the effect of outcome valence on learning trap development. Participants chose to approach or avoid category exemplars associated with rewards or losses, and, to maximize reward, must learn a categorization rule based on two stimulus dimensions. We replicate previous findings showing that when outcome feedback was contingent upon approaching exemplars, people frequently fell into the trap of using an incomplete categorization rule based on only a single dimension, which was suboptimal for long-term reward. Notably, learning trap development was attenuated in an environment with frequent loss outcomes, even when participants received explicit information about the base rates of gains and losses. The implications of these findings for theoretical models and future research are discussed.

title_r: Willingness to Interact Increases When Opponents Offer Specific Evidence
abstract_r: In polarized political climates, debate is ubiquitous but minds rarely change. This raises a question: what causes people to update their views? Recent work has shown that people are persuaded more by experienced-based explanations rather than factual ones. Yet, facts surely play (or ought to play) an important role in political discourse. Is it possible to leverage the persuasive power of personal experiences without sacrificing factual information? In Experiments 1 and 2, we replicate and build on previous findings showing that people who offer experienced-based (vs. fact-based) explanations are perceived as more rational and worthy of respect. In Experiment 3, we show that more complex explanations combining factual information with personal examples reveal more nuanced results. Collectively, this work sheds new light on how experienced-based and fact-based evidence can be used to persuade.
