title_r: An experimental replication and extension to “sexual communal motivation and self-determined sexual motivation in romantic relationships”
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

The following pre-registered study is an experimental replication and extension of previous studies in this project

summary: 1) Hypotheses. What are the main question being asked or hypotheses being tested in this study?

Communal theories of sexual motivation suggest that romantic partners experience higher satisfaction and desire when they are responsive to each other’s sexual needs (i.e., high sexual communal strength); however, doing so at the expense of attending to one’s own sexual needs (i.e., high unmitigated sexual communion) has been associated with mixed outcomes. To distinguish sexual communal strength from unmitigated sexual communion, we are interested in examining whether autonomous sexual motives (i.e., inherently choiceful and meaningful) and controlled motives (i.e., pressured and obligated) for engaging in sex mediate the effects of sexual communal strength and unmitigated sexual communion on relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction, and desire. 

In two cross sectional studies—one with people in relationships and the other with couples—we found that people higher in sexual communal strength and their partners endorsed more autonomous sexual motivation, and in turn reported higher relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction, and sexual desire. In contrast, people higher in unmitigated sexual communion and their partners endorsed more controlled sexual motivation and in turn reported lower satisfaction and desire. 

The current pre-registration is for an experimental study designed to manipulate sexual communal motivation (i.e., sexual communal strength vs. unmitigated sexual communal vs. control) using a false feedback paradigm and to test whether autonomous and controlled sexual motives mediate the associations between sexual communal motivation and sexual and relationship outcomes. To manipulate sexual communal motivation, we will provide participants with false feedback about their levels of responsiveness to their partner’s sexual needs as well as their levels of assertiveness with their own sexual needs. Participants will either be oriented to high sexual communal strength (i.e., provided with feedback about their high responsiveness to a partner’s needs + high assertiveness of own needs), high unmitigated sexual communion (i.e., provided with feedback about their high responsiveness + low assertiveness), or receive no feedback (i.e., control). Relative to participants in the unmitigated sexual communion and control conditions, we expect that people in the sexual communal strength condition will endorse more autonomous sexual motives and less controlled sexual motives, and in turn, will report greater satisfaction and desire. Compared to participants in the control condition, those in the unmitigated sexual communion condition will endorse less autonomous sexual motives and more controlled sexual motives, and in turn report poorer sexual and relational outcomes.

2) Independent variable. Describe the key independent variable(s) specifying how they were measured.

The primary independent variable, sexual communal motivation, will be manipulated. However, we will include the following baseline measures as potential covariates and moderators for secondary analyses.

Baseline measures 

Sexual communal motivation. Sexual communal strength (Muise, Impett, Kogan, & Desmarais, 2013) will be assessed with 6 items (e.g., How far would you be willing to go to meet your partner's sexual needs?) using a 5-point Likert scale (0 = not at all to 4 = extremely). Unmitigated sexual communion will be measured with 7 items (e.g., I always place my partner’s sexual needs above my own) using a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree).

Sexual assertiveness. Sexual assertiveness will be measured with the sexual assertiveness subscale of the Multidimensional Sexual Self-Concept Questionnaire (Snell, 1998). Participants rate their sexual assertiveness with 5 items (e.g., “I am very assertive about the sexual aspects of my life.”) using a 5-point Likert scale (1= not at all characteristic of me to 5= very characteristic of me)

Relationship satisfaction.  Relationship satisfaction will be measured with the 16-item version of the Couple Satisfaction Index (Funk & Rogge, 2007). Participants rate their relationship satisfaction with their partner (e.g., “In general, how often do you think that things between you and your partner are going well?”), on 5-point scales with anchors tailored to specific items (e.g., 0 = never, 5 = All the time)

Sexual satisfaction. Sexual satisfaction will be measured with the Global Measure of Sexual Satisfaction (Lawrence & Byers, 1998). Participants’ rate their sexual satisfaction with five bipolar items on a 7-point scale (e.g., My sex life is “very bad” to “very good”).

Sexual desire: Sexual desire will be measured with the dyadic subscale of the Sexual Desire Inventory-2 (Spector, Carey & Steinberg, 1996). Participants rate their sexual desire for their partner with seven items (e.g., “When you have sexual thoughts, how strong is your desire to engage in sexual behaviour with a partner?”) on 9-point scales with anchors tailored to specific items (e.g., 0 = no desire, 8 = strong desire).

3) Dependent variable. Describe the key dependent variable(s) specifying how they were measured.

Self-determined sexual motivation. Nine items were adapted from the Sexual Motivation Scale (SMS; Gravel, Pelletier, & Reissing, 2016) to measure participants’ current autonomous motivation (4 items., e.g., “Because I feel that having sex is meaningful.”) and controlled motivation (5 items, e.g., “To prove to myself that I am a good lover.”) to engage in sex, on a 7-point scale (1=Not at all, 7= Extremely).

Relationship satisfaction. Relationship satisfaction will be measured with the 4 item Couple Satisfaction Index(see above) and adapted aft to reflect participants’ relationship satisfaction at the present moment (i.e., “right now”).

Sexual Satisfaction. Sexual satisfaction will be measured with the Global Measure of Sexual Satisfaction (see above) and adapted to reflect participants’ sexual satisfaction at the present moment (i.e., “right now”). 

Sexual desire. Sexual desire will be measured with one item (“I feel a great deal of sexual desire for my partner right now.” using a 7-point scale (1=Not at all, 7= Extremely).

4) Conditions. How many and which conditions were participants assigned to?

Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three conditions. Based on a false feedback paradigm previously used in relationship and sexuality research (Balzarini et al., 2021; Maxwell et al., 2017) participants will receive false feedback about their levels of sexual responsiveness and sexual assertiveness in their relationship under the guise of an algorithm that calculated results from participant’s baseline measures, which in reality are ostensible scores used to manipulate sexual communal motivation. Participants will be randomly assigned to the sexual communal strength (i.e., high sexual responsiveness + high sexual assertiveness), unmitigated sexual communion (i.e., high sexual responsiveness + low sexual assertiveness) or the control (i.e., no false feedback) conditions. 

A pilot study was conducted to test the sexual communal motivation manipulation. The sample for the pilot study included 150 participants recruited from Prolific, an online crowd sourcing platform, who were in a relationship for at least 6 months, sexually active, and 18 years or older. After the manipulation, participants responded to one item manipulation checks measuring their sexual responsiveness (“To what extent are you responsive to your partner’s sexual needs?”) and sexual assertiveness (“To what extent are you assertive with your own sexual needs?), using a 7-point scale (1=Not at all, 7= Extremely). There was a significant effect of condition on both sexual responsiveness (F2,147 = 3.217, p = .043, ηp2  = .042) and sexual assertiveness (F2,147 = 25.55, p <. 001, ηp2  = .26). Post hoc analyses with a Tukey adjustment revealed that participants in the SCS condition (M = 5.96, SD = .96) reported significantly higher sexual responsiveness (t = .50, SE = .21, p =.045) than the control condition (M = 5.46, SD = 1.20). There were no significant differences between SCS and USC (t = .10, SE = .21, p = .87), which was expected given that they were both manipulating high responsiveness. However, there was also no significant difference between USC and control (t = .40, SE = .21, p =.15) on sexual responsiveness, but the mean responsiveness score was higher in the USC condition (M =5.86, SD= .96) compared to control. Participants in the SCS condition (M = 5.14, SD = 1.31) reported being significantly more sexually assertive than those in the USC (t = 1.85, SE = .26, p < .001) and control (t =.62, SE = .26, p= .051) conditions as expected. Participants in the USC condition (M = 3.29, SD = 1.32) also reported less sexual assertiveness (t = -1.23, SE =.27, p <.001) than those in the control condition (M = 4.52, SD = 1.31). Overall, the pilot study suggested that our manipulation was successful in shifting people’s feelings of sexual responsiveness and assertiveness as intended. 

Participants in the SCS and USC conditions also responded to item gauging the accuracy and believability of feedback in terms of sexual responsiveness (e.g., “The feedback accurately captured my levels of sexual responsiveness” and sexual assertiveness (e.g., “The feedback accurately captured my levels of sexual assertiveness”). The effects of condition on sexual responsiveness and sexual assertiveness were not significant (F1,98 = .0.43, p = .836; F1,98 = .2.24, p = .137). Although participants in the SCS and USC conditions did not statistically differ on the extent to which they believed the feedback, the average scores in both conditions were relatively high for both sexual responsiveness (M = 5.55, SD = 1.46; M = 5.49, SD = 1.39) and sexual assertiveness (M = 5.25, SD = 1.53; M = 4.76, SD = 1.80). Additionally, only a small number of people guessed the hypothesis (4.6%) based on open ended responses (e.g., “What do you think this study is about?”; “Do you have any comments about the study in general?”), suggesting that overall, the manipulation was believable. 

5) Analyses. Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct to examine the main question/hypothesis.

We will use Hayes’s (2013) SPSS macro-PROCESS (Model 6) with 95% bias corrected confidence interval (CIs) based on 20,000 bootstrap samples to test for total, direct, and indirect effects in our proposed mediation models. Sexual communal motivation will be entered as a multicategorical independent variable in the model (Hayes & Preacher, 2014) with the control condition as the reference group for comparisons with the sexual communal strength and unmitigated sexual communion conditions. The unmitigated sexual communion condition as the reference group for the comparison with the sexual communal strength condition. Autonomous and controlled sexual motives will be simultaneously entered as mediators in the model.

6) More analyses. Any secondary analyses?

We will test for differences across groups in key demographics such as age and relationship length. If these differ across groups, we will control for them in subsequent analyses. We can also assess if any of the primary effects are moderated by participants’ baseline sexual communal strength, unmitigated sexual communion, sexual assertiveness, relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction, and sexual desire reported at baseline.

7) Sample Size. How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size?

In the pilot study, we also included one of our key outcomes—sexual satisfaction—in order to provide an estimate of the effect size. A small to medium effect of condition on sexual satisfaction was found (ηp2  = .048). We then used this estimate as the effect of condition on the account and the correlations from our previous study (ranging from +/- .58 to .17) for the associations with the mediators variables to input into a monte carlo power analysis for our proposed model with parallel mediators (Schoemann, Boulton, & Short, 2017). The power analysis indicated that 500 participants would be needed to estimate a small to medium effect with 80% power. To account for incomplete surveys and exclusion criteria, we will oversample by 20% to account for the potential exclusion of inattentive responders, participants who do not believe the false feedback based on open-ended responses, and those who are outliers on our key outcomes. Approximately 600 participants will be recruited from Prolific. To be eligible for this study, individuals will have to provide informed consent, be 18 years or older, be involved in a romantic relationship of at least six months and be sexually active with their partner.

8) Other. Anything else you would like to pre-register?

title_r: Talker variability and learning distinct novel words follow up
abstract_r: This is a preregistration for a follow-up to our originally preregistered study with 14 month olds. The original study tested the effects of within- and between- talker variability (compared to no talker variability) on learning two distinct words (neem and lof) in a traditional switch task. We found that participants in the within- and between- talker variability conditions did not increase their looking time to the switch trial relative to the same trial, but they did increase their looking time to the visual control which featured a completely novel image. However, contrary to predictions and previous research, participants in the no-variability-condition did not show differences in looking time from the same to the switch trial, or to the control trial. Since the no-variability-condition with dissimilar words is the standard version of the switch task, this pattern of results is surprising. Exploratory analyses revealed that, in the no variability condition, participants with larger productive vocabularies (as measured by the CDI) were more likely to increase their looking time to the switch trial relative to the same trial. This is consistent with Chan et al., 2011, who found that english learning 14 month olds with larger vocabularies increased their looking time to the switch trial when learning novel word-object mappings, while 14 month olds with relatively smaller vocabularies did not. In this follow-up study, we test another group of 18 14-month-olds on the no-variability condition of the switch task, not making any changes relative to the original version. If our previous findings were a statistical anomaly, we expect to find the predicted pattern of results (infants should increase their looking time to the switch and control trials, relative to the same trial). Instead, if the previous findings were not a statistical anomaly, we expect to replicate the effect of vocabulary on looking time to the switch relative to the same trial.

title_r: Weight-Based Vigilant Coping and Spontaneous Self-Affirmation in Predicting Eating Outcomes Replication
abstract_r: Weight stigma (stereotyping and devaluation of an individual because of their body weight) is associated with maladaptive eating outcomes. People may use different techniques to cope with weight stigma, and depending on the technique, may experience different outcomes. This study plans to replicate our previous study in which we found: weight-based vigilant coping was associated with greater maladaptive eating behaviors (i.e., cognitive restraint, uncontrolled eating, emotional eating, eating to cope with stress), and lower in an adaptive eating behavior (i.e., intuitive eating) and spontaneous self-affirmation was associated with lower maladaptive eating behaviors (i.e., cognitive restraint, emotional eating, eating to cope with stress), and greater in an adaptive eating behavior (i.e., intuitive eating). We plan to replicate this study and change two things: 1) only examining participants who report experiencing weight stigma and 2) adapting the spontaneous self-affirmation questionnaire to be in response to weight stigma.

title_r: Replication of the consequences of stereotype threat on the academic performance of white and non-white lower income college students
abstract_r: Harrison et al. Examined the effects of socioeconomic stereotypes on college students from different income backgrounds. They essentially wanted to expand their understanding of stereotype threat on participants with varying income backgrounds and determine whether it influences academic performance of white and non-white college students and additionally the influence on test anxiety, academic identification, and state self-esteem. In order to do this Harrison et al. Recruited 269 participants who were randomly assigned to either math or verbal test first and then randomly assigned to the diagnostic or non-diagnostic condition. The diagnostic condition was the control group where stereotype threat was placed and assessed. Participants completed various assessments after math and verbal tests to determine effort, identification, test anxiety, self-esteem, and demographic (SES, gender, ethnicity). Overall, the results suggest lower income students performed worse when stereotype threat was activated, had higher test anxiety scores, and experienced less academic identification with either math or English compared to middle and upper income students. However, lower income students self-esteem was not effected by the stereotype threat. Middle income students performance, test anxiety, and identification were not affected by stereotype threat in anyway. While upper income students performed better with the stereotype threat in math and verbal tests and academic identification. These results have led me to want to replicate stereotype threat on lower and upper income college students, specifically wanting to examine how it affects their math performance and test anxiety scores. I plan to exclude the middle income group and they were not significant different across the entire study. title_r: Memory for offloaded information: Related vs. unrelated word pairs
abstract_r: Cognitive offloading Individuals are often faced with situations where they must remember large amounts of information, and that information may vary in its importance to remember to achieve one’s goals. To illustrate, one may need to remember a list of both essential and non-essential items to pick up at the grocery store, or a student may need to remember multiple chapters worth of class material for a final exam. Offloading information to an external store (e.g., a smartphone application) is one self-regulation strategy that can ease cognitive demands on internal memory storage (Hamilton & Benjamin, 2019; Hu et al., 2019; Risko & Dunn, 2015). Prior work has shown that cognitive offloading can be beneficial to performance on a variety of memory tasks such as remembering cue-target word pairs (Hu et al., 2019), an item’s location (Grinschgl et al., 2021), or to complete a task (Ball et al., 2021). However, offloading can also come with decrements in memory for the information that was offloaded, particularly when access to the external resource is not available when needed (Sparrow et al., 2011) or when individuals must retrieve that information unexpectedly (e.g., a surprise recognition test; Hargis, Castel, & Bjork, under review). To use external memory aids effectively, it is important to understand how offloading influences one’s memory for both internally and externally stored information. When given the option to rely on internal or external memory stores, individuals are generally biased towards offloading behavior (Gilbert et al., 2020). Despite the ubiquitous availability of offloading devices in our daily lives (i.e., pen and paper, smartphones), individuals are sometimes limited in the amount of information they can offload. For instance, students taking notes in a class lecture may not be able to offload everything the professor said (e.g., when under time constraints); instead, students may have to strategically decide what material to offload. Prior work has demonstrated that factors such as item difficulty (Hu et al., 2019) and item value (Dunpont et al., 2021) can influence offloading behavior. Associative memory Both inside and outside of the classroom, learners often need to explicitly bind associated items together in memory. For example, learning that the Spanish translation for “pencil” is “lápiz” requires binding “pencil” with “lápiz” in memory; similarly, learning the name of a new colleague requires binding the name “Mark” to Mark’s face. Researchers have found that factors such as semantic relatedness can influence associative memory (Arbuckle & Cuddy, 1969; Soderstrom et al., 2015; Undorf & Erdfelder, 2015). Undorf and Eldfelder (2015) showed that participants not only had better memory for related than unrelated word pairs, but when given the option to self-pace their study, participants tended to spend more time studying unrelated than related pairs, perhaps reflecting participants’ awareness of item difficulty (i.e., it can be advantageous to spend more time studying a difficult item than an easy item). For example, participants may study cue-target word pairs during a learning phase, such as: “dog : cat” or “dog : spoon”. Here, “dog” is the cue (that will be used in a later testing phase to probe associative memory), while “cat” is a highly semantically related target. On the other hand, “spoon” is much less similar to the cue “dog” than is “cat”. During the testing phase, participants would then be probed with the cue and asked to recall the associated target they learned previously (e.g., dog : __). Similarly, in an offloading study, Hu and colleagues (2019) instructed participants to study related and unrelated word pairs and rate the word pairs in difficulty before taking a test on the studied pairs. During learning, participants had the option to offload some of the word pairs by selecting to save them to the computer, to later use as hint cues (e.g., an item with a hint may appear as “dog : sp___” vs. an item without a hint, which may appear as “dog : ___”) on a final memory test. Participants indicated they were less confident in remembering unrelated word pairs than related word pairs and tended to offload more difficult (i.e., unrelated) pairs than easy (i.e., related) pairs. On the test, participants asked for more hint cues on difficult items than on easy items, and they recalled more offloaded than non-offloaded itms when supplied with the hint cue. However, when participants were forced to recall the target without any hint cues, they recalled more non-offloaded than offloaded words (Hu et al., 2019). Current study While research has illustrated the effects of offloading and semantic relatedness on recollection-based memory (e.g., cued recall), little is known on how these two factors may interact with one another to influence later, familiarity-based memory such as on a recognition test. The current study serves as a conceptual replication and extension of Hu and colleagues’ work (2019) investigating offloading and associative memory using an adapted version of the paradigm introduced in Hargis and colleagues (under review). We also take a more conservative approach to offloading than Hu and colleagues (2019), such that participants may only save up to 6 of the 30 items, and therefore, must be more selective when choosing which items to offload. We argue that this restriction better reflects real-life situations in which offloading is limited, such as when students are allowed to fill one side of a note card with information to use as a “cheat-sheet” for a Spanish vocabulary exam. Additionally, we will present the word pairs simultaneously (in contrast with sequential presentation used in Hu et al., 2019), which may influence participants’ awareness of item difficulty given that prior work has shown that studying items simultaneously allows for more strategic encoding of the to-be-learned information compared to studying items sequentially (Middlebrooks & Castel, 2018; Schwartz et al., 2020). When studying cue-target pairs simultaneously, participants are afforded more flexibility in the cognitive control mechanisms they recruit (i.e., attention allocation) to strategically encode the most valuable/important information, out of the entire set of competing to-be-learned information, to achieve their goals. Thus, limiting the number of cue-target pairs participants are allowed to offload, while presenting the pairs simultaneously, may drive participants to selectively offload only the more difficult (i.e., unrelated) pairs. Uncovering how these factors influence later memory is informative given that individuals sometimes need to remember information unexpectedly, such as when students take a “pop” (i.e., surprise) quiz in the classroom or when someone’s external storage device becomes unavailable (e.g., forgetting one’s grocery list at home, a phone’s battery dying, or being in a place with no cellular or internet connection). Overall, the current study aims to examine the effects of offloading and semantic relatedness on recall and recognition, using a free-choice paradigm in which participants have the option to either offload or not offload items while studying paired associates. Specifically, we examine how semantic relatedness influences offloading decisions and how learners’ offloading decisions affect downstream recollection and recognition for the previously learned cue-target pairs. During the task, participants will study a list of 30 simultaneously-presented cue-target word pairs, half of which are semantically related (e.g., dog : cat, with strong associative strength; M = .67, SD = .10) and half of which are semantically unrelated (e.g., dog : spoon, with weak associative strength; M = .02, SD = .01; Nelson, McEvoy & Schreiber, 2004). Word pairs were taken from a database of 4000 associates created by Nelson et al.(2003, 2004) in which an average of 149 participants (SD = 15) were asked to provide an associate for each of 120 words (e.g., swim - __). Associative strength was subsequently determined by the connectivity (associate-to-associate links) and resonance (associate-to-target links) among participant responses. Participants will be told that immediately after studying each list of paired associates, they will take a cued recall test in which they will be given the cue for each of the studied pairs, simultaneously, and asked to provide the associated target (e.g., filling in the blank in “dog : __”) for as many items as possible within 60 seconds. During the study phase, half of the participants will have the option to offload a limited number of word pairs by saving them to the computer and will be told that the saved words will automatically count as correct on the test. The other half of participants will not have the option to offload any of the word pairs and will instead, have to rely on their internal memory for each test (Hargis et al., under review, Experiment 1). Following each study session, participants will complete a 60-second distractor task before taking the cued-recall test. Participants will repeat this task (study-test) for 8 different word-lists; afterwards, they will be given a surprise recognition test in which they will be asked to identify all previously seen word pairs among new (i.e., not previously studied) word pairs. During the recognition test, participants will view all 240 studied pairs along with 160 previously unstudied words and be asked to indicate whether the paired associate is “old” or “new.” Reaction times on the recognition test will be recorded to provide insight into whether offloading and semantic relatedness also influences how long it takes participants to retrieve the target.

abstract_r: In recent years, much attention has been paid to the superior political performance of either democracies or authoritarian governments. title_r: Replication on Closeness Regulation in Couples
abstract_r: The present study will be a conceptual replication and extension of a study on dissociations in the regulation of closeness discrepancies (i.e., deviations of experienced closeness from the desired amount of closeness with a romantic partner) by Hilligloh and Hagemeyer (in revision). In the original study, the authors conducted continuous time structural equation models on daily-diary data (n = 240 individuals, t = 12) of mixed-gender couples. Based on a set-point perspective and the Intimacy Process Model (Reis & Shaver, 1988), the authors hypothesized that the regulation of closeness frustration (i.e., a desire for more closeness with the partner) is slower and more dependent on the partner than the regulation of closeness surfeit (i.e., a desire for less closeness with the partner). Additionally, effects of personal and situational conditions on closeness regulation were explored. As personal conditions, implicit and explicit motivational orientations (IMO; EMO) were examined, constructs that reflect whether communal or agentic motive dispositions were predominant in the individual. The couple’s daily contact duration was analyzed as a situational condition. Continuous time models approach an estimation of effects that are independent of the measurement interval. In the continuous time framework, the rate of change in a criterion is estimated instead of the absolute change. In the present case, the rate of change can be interpreted as regulatory speed. A greater rate of change denotes a faster regulation and a smaller rate of change denotes a slower regulation. Additionally, the great flexibility of the models allows a separate estimation and comparison of the processes of closeness frustration and closeness surfeit in the same model. The results indicated that the regulation of closeness frustration was slower and more dependent on partner contact than the regulation of closeness surfeit. However, more partner contact than usual was associated with a faster regulation of closeness discrepancies in general. IMO and EMO moderated the effect of partner contact on closeness regulation. Regardless of the kind of the closeness discrepancy, communally oriented individuals regulated faster on days with more partner contact than usual compared to agentically oriented individuals. Conversely, agentically oriented individuals regulated faster on days with less partner contact than usual. Only for EMO of the male partner did the interaction not become significant. Nevertheless, we will test the moderation hypothesis in the replication study for this case as well. In the present manuscript, two studies (Study 1: n = 510 individuals, t = 28 days; Study 2: n = 130 individuals, 70 measurements over 14 days) will be conducted to conceptually replicate and extend the findings of the original study. In Study 1, we aim to replicate the findings on a day-to-day level using the same direct measurement approach as in the original study. In Study 2, we will extend the replication to the momentary level by assessing closeness discrepancies through difference scores, a measurement approach more commonly represented in the literature. Please note that the original study is still undergoing review, and changes in methods and results may occur. We preregister the expected hypotheses and methods (as they appear in the current version of the manuscript at the time of preregistration). In case of changes in the original study, we will deviate from the preregistration and follow the original study. To ensure that preliminary analyses for the replication study do not influence the review process of the original study, such analyses will be conducted with scrambled data up until the acceptance of the original manuscript.

title_r: Does Information Predicting “When” and “What” Facilitate Target Detection Interactively? (Experiment 3-1)
abstract_r: Human responses to environmental stimuli are crucial for adapting to surroundings, particularly when cues accurately predict the occurrence of events requiring a response. In contexts involving interaction with assistance systems, such as driving with Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), cues about forthcoming events can enhance task performance. Additionally, the extent to which people predict the timing of events (i.e., timing predictability) is related to their responses to events because predictable timing enables us to anticipate the onset of forthcoming events implicitly. Despite the importance of these factors, the interactive effects of cue informativeness and timing predictability on human responses remain unclear. This study aims to investigate whether these two factors interact to influence target detection. A cued go/no-go task will be conducted via a crowdsourcing platform, manipulating two variables: timing predictability and cue informativeness. The constant delay between the cue and the target in one block is defined as the timing predictable condition. A variable delay is introduced in the other block, named the timing unpredictable condition. Cue informativeness will be varied across three levels: an informative cue indicating a high probability of a go target, a noninformative cue with an equal probability of signaling a go or no-go target, and a reverse informative cue suggesting a low probability of a go target. ## Our previous experiment did not reveal a significant interaction between the two factors. In this study, we aim to replicate these findings by employing multiple go targets that require action and implementing shorter delays between cue and target presentation.

title_r: Exaggerated Meta-perceptions between Israeli Jews and Arabs
abstract_r: Meta-perceptions refer to how in-group members think that outgroup members perceive them (e.g., Frey & Tropp, 2006). For example, previous findings showed that both Democrats and Republicans in the U.S. erroneously perceive that the outgroup dehumanizes and dislikes them at least twice as much as they actually do (Moore-Berg et al., 2020). In this study, we aim to replicate these findings in the context of Arab and Jewish relations in Israel. Previous findings have shown that between competitive groups each group has skewed (in fact, negative) meta-perceptions regarding the outgroup (Carlson, 2016; Chambers, Baron, & Inman, 2006; Lees & Cikara, 2020; Moore-Berg et al., 2020; Ruggari et al., 2021). Therefore, we assume that these patterns of results will replicate in the context of the relations between the Jewish majority and the Arab minority in Israel. Nevertheless, while previous research has examined meta-perceptions in various contexts, it did not examine whether different groups are more or less meta-accurate, and whether power relations affect this meta-accuracy. Thus, in the present research we aim to examine whether the extent to which the discrepancy between perceptions and meta-perceptions is dependent upon the degree of power each group has in this context. We have two opposing hypotheses, which we detail below. Briefly, on the one hand, according to Galinsky (2006) low-power groups (in this case, Israeli Arabs) would be more accurate regarding the high-power group’s (in this case, Jewish-Israelis) perceptions, as it was found that high-power group members tend to engage in perspective taking less than low-power group members. On the other hand, Lees and Cikara (2020), and later Ruggeri et al. (2021), showed that high-power group members were in fact more accurate in their meta-perceptions than low-power group members. According to Lees and Cikara (2020), this is likely because the low-power group members (in their case, women) were more affected by a specific policy that was examined, and therefore, men were able to be more accurate. The meta-perceptions of men and women in their study were equally negative. Put simply, this meta-accuracy might have been an artifact of using (meta-)support for policies (as opposed to meta-dehumanization and meta-prejudice in Moore-Berg et al., 2020).

title_r: Online replication of Fan et al. (2016)
abstract_r: In this study we use a procedure introduced by Fan et al. (2016). Participants are presented with visual stimuli in the periphery. They have to identify whether the stimuli are different or identical. At fixation a mask is presented. The main variable is the delay between stimulus onset and mask onset. A feedback signal specific to the foveal cortex has been proposed. The evidence comes from neuroimaging studies showing that when observers are presented with an object in the periphery, object category information can be decoded from the foveal retinotopic cortex (Williams et al., 2008) and that performance is affected by transcranial magnetic stimulation applied to the foveal cortex (Chambers et al., 2013) after target presentation (350-400ms) consistent with the hypothesis that feedback to the foveal retinotopic cortex is crucial for extra-foveal perception (Chambers et al., 2013). In addition to the neuroimaging studies, psychophysical experiments have manipulated the information presented in central and peripheral vision. The results show that processing of visual objects in the periphery is modulated by masking information at the fovea (Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2016; Yu & Shim, 2016). These psychophysical studies therefore support the feedback hypothesis. In the paradigm used by Fan et al. (2016) observers performed a task on peripheral stimuli, and noise was presented in fovea at different stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). Observers maintained fixation on a central mark. Importantly, the noise caused impairment only for SOA of 250-ms, and only for tasks that required processing of object shape. The study also included fMRI data showing shape representation in the foveal cortex. Fan et al. reported several experiments in their study. In the first one, two objects either the same or slightly different were presented for 100 ms in diagonal quadrants on two sides of the fixation point (either in upper right and lower left or in lower right and upper left). Subjects were asked to make a same or different decision based on the detailed feature of objects. A dynamic noise patch was presented for 83 ms in the foveal region at stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs) of 50, 150, 250, 350, and 450 ms after the onset of the object images. The stimuli were 3D rendered abstract shapes, known in the literature as spikies (de Beeck et al. 2006). Our experiment is a conceptual replication of the first experiment reported in Fan et al. (2016). We have kept as close as possible to the original design. In particular, we will use a same or different decision task, we will use the same class of stimuli (spikies) as Fan et al. and the stimuli will be randomly presented either in upper right and lower left quadrants or in lower right and upper left quadrants. The mask will also be similar and include a dynamic set of random dots changing over time. The SOA levels will be as in Fan et al.: 50, 150, 250, 350 and 450 ms plus the no-noise baseline condition.

title_r: Modal and amodal representations and inhibition in hungry and satiated individuals (follow up)
abstract_r: Metabolic state is an important periodic driver of food intake. In a fasted state, individuals attend quicker and display lowered inhibition to food stimuli compared to a satiated state. It is, however, unknown if the representation of food facilitates such a loss of inhibition. These representations can take a highly abstract, amodal form (words) or rather be modal and in line with how food is represented in everyday life (pictures). Here, we follow up on our previous study. As such, this study ask the question whether food cues leads to greater disinhibition problems compared to abstract, amodal food cue representation in individuals in a fasted state, compared to a satiated state, which was partly confirmed by the initial study. In this second part, we aim to replicate this finding and to extend the research by using neutral stimuli.

title_r: Preregistration of replication and extension study
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

In humans, attitudes can be learned when initially neutral stimuli (Conditioned Stimuli, CSs), such as faces of unfamiliar persons or brand names, are merely presented together (i.e., paired) with valent stimuli (Unconditioning Stimuli, USs), for example beautiful faces or pleasant scene images (Hofmann, De Houwer, Perugini, Baeyens, & Crombez, 2010). It is debated whether this phenomenon—evaluative conditioning (EC)—can occur unconsciously. While there is little evidence supporting EC in the absence of awareness during learning (for review, see Corneille & Stahl, 2019), some studies report EC in the absence of participants’ memory of the CS-US pairing at the time of retrieval (e.g., Hütter, Sweldens, Stahl, Unkelbach, & Klauer, 2012; Waroquier, Abadie, & Dienes, 2020).

In a recent study, Stahl, Aust, Mierop, Béna, and Corneille (2020) used an improved assessment procedure and came to the opposite conclusion: In their study, whenever participants reported not remembering the valence of the US, they did not show EC effects. This finding suggests that EC and memory are strongly related, and that there is no EC in the absence of memory. Here we aim at replicating this finding with a larger sample.

A second goal of this study is to extend the study of the EC-memory relation by asking, reversely, whether there is memory in the absence of attitudes towards the CS. If EC and
memory are tightly related, then participants should always have acquired an attitude whenever they remember a CS-US pairing. If, on the other hand, CS-US pairing memory is
merely a precondition for establishing an attitude, one would expect to find cases of memory without learned attitudes.

title_r: Adults’ Prediction of Emotions in Cooperative versus Competitive Resource Sharing Contexts: An Online Approach to Interview Studies for Developmental Psychological Research
abstract_r: This is the Master's thesis project of Ronja Schiller. Prof. Dr. Marco F. H. Schmidt and Bianca Dietrich, M.Sc., are the project's supervisors. Already young children have first precedents of moral understanding of their own and others’ behaviour as they expect certain behaviours, such as helping or sharing, in certain situations (e.g., Schmidt & Sommerville, 2011; Geraci & Surian, 2011). From the age of about three years, children clearly show normative expectations about resources being fairly distributed (e.g., Rakoczy et al., 2016). Moreover, young children expect other individuals to benefit from sharing in cooperative but not in competitive sharing situations (e.g., Wang & Henderson, 2018). Children in turn also associate certain emotional states with certain contexts and understand that prosocial behaviour such as sharing is followed by positive emotions (Paulus & Moore, 2017). Thus, the prediction of potential recipients' emotions could also be expected to differ between cooperative versus competitive sharing contexts. However, expectations of others’ emotions in cooperative versus competitive resource sharing contexts have hardly been empirically studied with either children or adults. Dietrich, Petersen, and Schmidt (2022) have addressed this by showing children picture stories in which characters play a game for resources either as a team or against each other but only one of them (“lucky” individual) obtains the resources. Children were then asked to predict the emotion of the other character who did not obtain the resources but is a potential recipient in this situation (“unlucky” individual). Results of Dietrich et al. (2022) show that older (5.5 – 6.2 years), but not younger (3.5 – 4.2 years) pre-schoolers were more likely to predict the potential recipient to be happy in the cooperative than in the competitive condition in the target task of the study, suggesting that in cooperative situations they assume that there are benefits from sharing resources also for the character who did not obtain them. In the control task, which serves to rule out that participants use inherent features of the target task in their prediction of emotions, the “lucky” individual announced not to share resources despite a common goal or to give away resources even though they were playing against each other. Consistent with the assumptions about sharing expectations and associated emotions, according to which the expectation that resources will be shared should be associated with positive emotions, participants predicted the potential recipient (“unlucky” individual) to be happy more often in the competitive than in the cooperative context of the control task. But while the Dietrich et al. study focuses exclusively on children, the question arises how adults would predict the emotions of potential recipients and whether differences from the child sample could be observed. For completeness for the developmental psychological classification of the findings, it is necessary to also consider results on adults. Thus, this project aims to investigate adults’ prediction of others' emotions in cooperative versus competitive resource sharing contexts. A second aim of this project is to look at different possibilities of online research in developmental psychology. Like the children's study by Dietrich et al., the study with adult participants is also conducted online. The current pandemic has severely limited many scientific projects. Since many studies could no longer be conducted in the laboratory due to contact restrictions, online formats gained attention in the last two years. While these forms of studies may present many other challenges, the potential of online formats has also become increasingly apparent not only in terms of presence-independent study conduction, but also in terms of saving resources and efficiency in scientific work. While the Dietrich et al. (2022) study was conducted live and interactively with a present experimenter, there are also ways to fully automate online studies. This could further increase the efficiency of interview studies conducted online, since, for example, advantages in sample acquisition can be expected especially for adult samples and no interaction with interviewers is required. To examine how applicable different forms of online studies are in developmental psychology, the emotion prediction study will be conducted using two different formats. On the one hand, the study will be conducted interactively via the videoconferencing platform BigBlueButton (Study A), just as in the child sample of Dietrich et al. (2022). On the other hand, it will be conducted in a fully automated way via the software Labvanced (Study B). Study B is designed in order to attempt a conceptual replication of Study A.

title_r: Do babies use accent to infer who caused distress?
abstract_r: Background. This replication study builds on the pre-registered hypotheses outlined here: https://osf.io/kjt83. In our previous study, we tested whether 13-to-18-month-olds expect same accented characters to comfort each other compared to differently accented characters. Based on prior research suggesting that infants expect speakers of the same language to affiliate (Liberman, Woodward, & Kinzler, 2017) and anticipate imitators to respond to each other’s distress (Kudrnova, Spelke, & Thomas, 2024), we predicted that infants would look first or longer at the side character whose accent matched the protagonist’s during the distress event. However, contrary to our predictions, infants looked first at the differently accented character during the distress event–but only when the protagonist had an American accent. These unexpected findings raise the possibility that infants use accent not to predict who will respond to distress but rather to infer who caused it. To explore this alternative explanation, the current study seeks to further investigate this possibility by replicating our first experiment. Current Study. The current study aims to replicate the findings from Study 1 with a new sample to assess the robustness and reliability of the observed effects. Thus, we will use the same study design and stimuli as Study 1. We hypothesize that infants will look at the differently accented character first or longer during the distress event–but only in the condition where the protagonist speaks with an accent that matches the participant's accent (i.e., US American accent). If we successfully replicate these findings, this would suggest that infants do not use accent to predict who will respond to distress but instead use it to infer who caused distress. Overall, this replication study aims to broaden our understanding of infants’ expectations about social interactions based on accent, advancing our ability to assess whether infants exhibit early sensitivity to intergroup dynamics shaped by language.

title_r: The Influence of Risk-Taking Tendencies and Personality on Deviant Behavior
abstract_r: The aim of this research is to further investigate the influence of risk-taking tendencies and personality on deviant behavior. A conceptual replication of Zimerman, Shalvi and Bereby- Meyer (2014) is conducted to test the influence of ethical risk-taking tendencies on dishonesty using a private coin tossing task. Additionally, the influence of Honesty-Humility on dishonest behavior is investigated. Deviant behavior, such as dishonesty, can lead to substantial costs on the societal level and thus holds a major threat to society (Mazar & Ariely, 2006). Therefore, it is of special interest to investigate the underlying traits which lead individuals to dishonest decision making. The assumption, that risk preferences influence unethical behavior was already addressed in previous research, the findings suggesting that the ethical risk-taking subscale of the domain-specific risk-taking scale (DOSPERT, Blais & Weber, 2006) mediates the relationship between regulatory focus and unethical behavior such as stealing, cheating and dishonesty (Gino & Margolis, 2011). Zimerman, Shalvi and Bereby-Meyer (2014) explored the influence of ethical risk-taking tendencies, using the DOSPERT-scale (Blais & Weber, 2006), on dishonesty, using a private coin tossing task (Shalvi, 2012). The study was conducted in an online format to enable cheating in a private setting. The participants were asked to grab a coin they had at home and flip it 20 times. Before flipping the coin the participants had to predict the outcome of the toss, hold the prediction in mind, flip the coin and then report if their prediction was correct. The participants were assigned to one of the two conditions of the private coin tossing task: the incentivized versus the non-incentivized condition. The task description either gives an incentive to lie, informing the participants that five out of every 100 participants can win money according to their performance on the coin tossing task, every correct prediction giving 5 ILS (Israeli new shekel, approximately 1,25 Dollar, approximately 1 Euro). Alternatively, the task description only contained the information that five out of every 100 participants will randomly be chosen to win money, thus no incentive to lie was given in this condition. Afterwards the participants were asked to fill out the DOSPERT, of which only the ethical subscale was of interest. Results could reveal a positive relation between self-reported unethical risk-taking tendencies and dishonesty. The results indicate that dishonest individuals know about their dishonest tendencies and are willing to report them, too. According to Shalvi, Dana, Handgraaf and DeDreu (2011) one factor that influences the decision to act dishonest is justified ethicality, the internal process which justifies the individual’s behavior. The authors postulate, that individuals will lie up until the extent that they can self-justify their lies is reached. Such justifications can occur before, pre-violation justification, or after the decision to act dishonest, post-violation justification, is made. Thus, dishonest behavior can be executed, for example in the coin tossing task, and reported, for example in the ethical risk-taking subscale, if it can be justified by pre- or post-violation justifications to maintain a positive image of the self. To explain individual differences in dishonest behavior, previous research furthermore focused on linking unethical decisions in cheating-paradigms to personality traits in general and the dimension Honesty-Humility of the HEXACO Personality Inventory (Ashton & Lee, 2007) in special (Heck et al., 2018). Results indicate a negative relation between Honesty- Humility and dishonest behavior in cheating paradigms (Heck et al., 2018; Schild, Moshagen, Scigala & Zettler, 2020). Based on the underlying trait theory, postulating that traits are aspects of personality that influence human behavior (Fajkowska & Kreitler, 2018), and previous findings, the following hypotheses were derived.

title_r: The effect of pain on optimistic belief updating and its mechanisms
abstract_r: Optimism bias refers to the common expectation that good things will happen in the future, while bad things are unlikely to occur (Weinstein, 1980; Sharot & Garrett, 2016). In the context of belief updating, this phenomenon manifests as greater adjustments in response to desirable news compared to undesirable news (Sharot et al., 2011). Despite some controversy (Shah et al., 2016), this effect has been replicated and supported by increasing evidence from brain imaging studies (Sharot et al., 2011; Moutsiana et al., 2015; Kuzmanovic et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2024) and computational models (Kuzmanovic & Rigoux, 2017, 2017; Palminteri & Lebreton, 2022). Previous studies have demonstrated that under conditions such as pressure (Czekalla et al., 2021), uncertainty (Beron et al., 2024), and threat (Garrett et al., 2018), the asymmetrical updating pattern associated with optimism bias tends to disappear. As a physically aversive experience, pain may similarly disrupt the optimism bias. Clinical research has also provided evidence that pain, especially chronic pain, is highly correlated with depression, which is often characterized by pessimism (Korn et al., 2014; Fonseca-Rodrigues et al., 2021; Dudeney et al., 2024; Campbell et al., 2003). Therefore, the main aim of the current study is to examine the potential disruptive effect of pain on optimism bias. We will explain the phenomenon of belief updating in optimism bias from a Bayesian perspective. First, we seek to replicate previous findings to confirm the belief updating pattern of optimism bias. Second, we aim to investigate the underlying role of confidence monitoring in shaping this bias. Third, we explore whether pain disrupts optimism bias and examine the potential mechanisms through which this effect may occur.

title_r: Return-To-Player vs No-Info Study 2
abstract_r: This is a follow-up study to https://osf.io/sgk3c. The aim is to strengthen the results found in the previous study, by (1) testing new hypotheses, (2) replicating the results with a new population, and (3) addressing some minor limitations. (1) Previous research had shown that a House Edge type of return-to-player information is clearer, easier to understand, and should be more effective in informing participants of the true risks of gambling. We will therefore test the responses of participants to House Edge information in comparison to Return-to-Player information. (2) We aim to replicate the study with the same population as Study 1 (slot players in the UK), but also extend it to a new population of slot players in the US. (3) It was also possible that in study 1 the ordering of the questions being asked (scenario first, followed by PGSI, for all participants) might have influenced PGSI scores as these were asked after a scenario about gambling. We will counterbalance the blocks to avoid this potential limitation, by asking PGSI first for half of the participants. We will also remove some unnecessary wording from both conditions, for being repetitive and potential also influencing participants. We will therefore replicate that previous study with the following changes: - Add two new experimental conditions: House Edge (Keeps) and House Edge (Costs) - Extend the study to US slot players - Counterbalancing the presentation of the scenario (and message + chances question) and PGSI blocks - Remove the sentence "Only a percentage of all the money bet gets paid back out as winnings" from all experimental conditions Everything else in the study will remain the same as in Study 1 (https://osf.io/sgk3c).

title_r: The Impact of Gender Bias and Evidence Type on Men’s and Women’s Engagement with HEED (health care, elementary education, and domestic roles)
abstract_r: A growing body of research has 1) demonstrated women’s underrepresentation in STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) fields, 2) identified the factors contributing to women’s underrepresentation, and 3) developed interventions designed to boost women’s representation in STEM (e.g., Cheryan, Plaut, Davies, & Steele, 2009; Diekman, Steinberg, Brown, Belanger, & Clark, 2017; Moss-Racusin, Sanzari, Caluori, & Rabasco, 2018; Murphy, Steele, & Gross, 2007; Nosek et al., 2009; Stout, Dasgupta, Hunsinger, & McManus, 2010). However, virtually no work has considered the factors responsible for men’s underrepresentation in HEED (health care, elementary education, and domestic roles) fields, nor the factors that could boost men’s engagement in these important domains. This is ironic, given that men participate in many HEED fields in even lower numbers than women participate in many STEM fields (Block, Croft, & Schmader, 2018). Unfortunately, evidence suggests that people are generally less concerned with men’s underrepresentation in HEED than they are with women’s underrepresentation in STEM (Block, Croft, De Souza, & Schmader, 2019). However, researchers have identified that men’s underrepresentation in HEED has serious negative consequences for men themselves, women, children, and society at large (Croft, Schmader, & Block, 2015). For example, the lack of male early education teachers reinforces existing gender stereotypes in children, and suggests that women are more adept at care-oriented work relative to men. Thus, we argue that it is critical to gain a better understanding of the factors contributing to men’s underrepresentation in HEED, in order to ultimately enable their full participation. Of importance, some existing evidence suggests that men encounter negative reactions when they violate gender stereotypes broadly (for a discussion, see Moss-Racusin, 2014), and specifically, when they engage with HEED. For example, one experiment found that participants rated a male applicant for an elementary education position as less likeable and posing more of a safety threat than the identical female applicant (Moss-Racusin & Johnson, 2016). In this research, we replicate and extend the previous research conducted in our lab about the idea that existence of gender bias targeting men may be one factor driving men out of HEED. Of interest, prior work suggests that this is the case for women in STEM. Specifically, when exposed to the reality of gender bias targeting women in STEM, women expressed significantly less enthusiasm for, sense of belonging, and interest in STEM than did men (Moss-Racusin et al., 2018). However, when told that gender bias does not exist in STEM, this gender gap in STEM engagement vanished. These results suggest that the existence of gender bias (targeting women) is one factor driving women out of STEM. In the current work, we seek to determine whether the existence of gender bias (targeting men) is one factor driving men out of HEED. Additionally, we manipulate the type of evidence used to present the information about gender bias against men in early education. Previous research suggests that certain types of evidence may be more impactful than others when presenting novel information (Parker et al., 2018; Pietri et al., 2017). In the case of bias against men in HEED, we are curious about whether anecdotal or research evidence will influence participants’ engagement in early education more significantly. Importantly, inequality in women’s and men’s changing gender roles may lead to a stalled revolution in which men’s lack of flexible gender roles impedes women’s progress toward equal pay and hiring in STEM (Thébaud & Pedulla, 2016). Thus, creating awareness about gender bias against men in HEED may ultimately benefit both men and women. Therefore, understanding which type of evidence is the most meaningful may improve our ability to increase awareness of this inequality. To our knowledge, no previous research has been conducted examining the impact of gender bias on gender gaps in HEED. The proposed experiment will be a 2 (existence of gender bias: yes, no) x 2 (participant gender: male or female) x 2 (evidence: anecdotal, research) between-subjects experimental research design. We will assess the following four outcomes: 1) positivity towards early elementary education, 2) sense of belonging in early elementary education, 3) aspirations to participate in early elementary education, 4) anticipated discrimination in early elementary education. Specifically, we predict that: Hypothesis 1: Existence of gender bias and participant gender will interact, such that men will demonstrate less engagement with early elementary education (i.e., less positivity, sense of belong, and aspirations, as well as more anticipated discrimination) relative to women only when participants are exposed to the reality of gender bias targeting men in early elementary education (i.e., the gender bias condition). In the gender equality condition, men and women will express equal levels of engagement with early elementary education. Exploratory Research Question: There was insufficient prior literature to warrant an a-priori prediction regarding whether anecdotal or experimental evidence would produce a more substantial gender gap in HEED engagement in the gender bias condition. Because the current research is the first (to our knowledge) to explore this novel question, we will examine any differences as a function of evidence type manipulation.

title_r: Effect of spatial attention on spatial judgments. A replication with oculometric measures
abstract_r: In a previous pre-registered experiment (detailed at length here: https://osf.io/xvna5) conducted on healthy participants, we studied the effect of spatial attention on line bisection and visual straight-ahead tasks, with oculometric measures. We found that shifting spatial attention to the left or the right by means of exogenous visual cues could bias the point of subjective equality (PSE) in the line bisection (for a similar result see, e.g., Sosa and al., 2011) and straight-ahead (new result) tasks. However, oculometric measures also revealed an effect of ocular saccades on the PSEs, as a confounding factor. The aim of the present experiment is to limit as much as possible the influence of ocular saccades on the line bisection and straight-ahead tasks. For this, we will replicate our previous experiment with the following modifications: (1) testing the influence of visual cue on a representational space task such as the number line bisection task (e.g., Nicholls & McIlroy, 2010) ; (2) randomizing the presentation of the visual cues (left, right, none) to avoid anticipatory saccades toward the cue, as observed when cues are presented by blocks. We will analyze the main effect of visual cues and ocular position for the line bisection, straight-ahead, and number line bisection tasks.

title_r: Is conscious perception necessary to direct attention? A replication of Jiang et al. (2006) with gaze-contingent crowding
abstract_r: The relationship between attention and consciousness has been debated for the past few decades. Observing attentional biases induced by visual stimuli below the conscious threshold is one way of providing evidence for the independence of attention and conscious perception. Among such studies, Jiang et al. (2006) found a strong priming effect below the objective conscious threshold with high sensitivity, in showing attentional biases to nude images suppressed by continuous flash suppression (CFS). This study aims to replicate the results from Jiang et al. by employing the gaze-contingent crowding paradigm with the original materials and Bayesian analytical approaches.

title_r: Is there an Action-Outcome Effect? (PC is inaction | joint causation) (replication)
abstract_r: This is a replication of our previous experiment. For that project, we presented participants with videos of a joint-causation scenario where there are inactions as the potential causes (i.e., the switch staying in its position). We manipulated whether the outcome is an inaction (the light stays on) or an action (the light turns on). We found that people judge inactions in the outcome of a causal scenario as more causal than actions in the outcome of a causal scenario. Because the p value was .04 in that experiment, we aim to replicate that finding in this experiment.

title_r: Moral Change Beliefs - In-Lab Study
abstract_r: This is a very close replication of Study 2, but with five modifications: 1. For this reason, we now refer to the low current level variable as “lowlevel” (rather than “deficiencies”, as per the Study 2 preregistration). We will adjust for both operationalizations of perceived deficiencies when estimating the effects of moral relevance on perceived consequences for various valued outcomes (RQ1), and when estimating the effects of various predictors of change goals (RQ2). 4. title_r: The Development of Negotiation in Children: Follow Up Study
abstract_r: When do children show preferences compatible with negotiation? Negotiation is an interpersonal process that can be used to accomplish goals one cannot achieve on their own, by generating value through exchange (Thompson, Wang, & Gunia, 2010). An ideal negotiation outcome involves the efficient allocation of resources, such that parties end up with more of what they want. In this sense, capacity for negotiation reveals another avenue for human cooperation and collaboration, and is currently an understudied in the developmental domain. We aim to address this limitation by observing the age at which children show preferences for mutual gain, and spontaneously engage in attempts for mutually beneficial exchange. Our prior study demonstrated that even three-year-olds can engage in negotiation when prompted to do so. However, children won’t engage in spontaneous negotiation until they reach the age of five. title_r: Visual display for communicating COVID-19 forecasts
abstract_r: Our previous study (https://osf.io/u9g84) showed that when communicating probabilistic influenza forecasts, a bar chart performs best in term of participants’ comprehension and perceived helpfulness, compared to a tree map, PDF, or 90% confidence interval. There was no difference between these four displays in participants’ confidence in decisions informed by the forecasts. We partially replicate this experiment with a larger nationally representative sample, in collaboration with Stanford’s Coastal Region study. The new study adapts two of the four influenza-related decisions to analogous COVID-19 decision scenarios, (a) whether to go on a trip to visit grandparents and (b) whether to send a child back to school. It uses the most successful display, the bar chart, to visualize the probabilistic COVID forecasts for new cases. Results will show the replicability and generalizability of the initial study of influenza forecast displays. The previous study found that comprehension was poorer for some participants for whom one might expect it to be superior: those who report being more familiar with a display, those with more education, and those with medical backgrounds. These participants also completed the task more quickly. We will study how fluency and exposure are associated with the dependent measurements of comprehension, confidence, decision, and perceived helpfulness. With the manipulation of exposure frequency, we will examine its causal relationship with dependent measurements as well.

title_r: The neural correlates of implicit emotion regulation through affect labeling as reflected in EEG
abstract_r: Affect labeling, an implicit emotion regulation (ER) strategy, involves using words to label emotions, whether by speaking, writing, or selecting among the provided words (see review, Torre & Lieberman, 2018). Increasing evidence supports its effectiveness in immediately reducing negative affect (Constantinou et al., 2014; Levy-Gigi & Shamay-Tsoory, 2022; Lieberman et al., 2011). Some studies have shown that this regulatory effect persists during reexposure to previously labeled stimuli. Specifically, some studies have found such an effect during immediate or short-interval reexposure but lacked follow-up assessments (Huang et al., 2013, Liang & Lin, 2023). In contrast, others have observed long-interval effects without finding significant results in earlier stages (Kircanski et al., 2012; Niles et al., 2015; Tabibnia et al., 2008). While these findings suggest that affect labeling may produce a lasting down-regulating effect, the precise time course of this regulatory process remains unclear. Our recent study (Chen et al., in prep) has provided preliminary evidence that the effects of affect labeling can persist over different reexposure phases; however, the existing evidence remains limited and warrants further investigation. We plan to replicate and extend on these findings by adding measures of neural activity during the different phases of reexposure. There are two cognitive processes relevant to emotion processing that will be analysed in this study. One reflects the emotion processing and expression process (emotion reactivity), which is evident in EEG markers such as the LPP at centroparietal sites and theta oscillations at parieto-occipital regions. The other reflects top-down control processes (like emotion regulation), which we expect in the frontal regulation LPP (Doornweerd et al., 2024) and possibly in frontal theta oscillations (Ertl et al., 2013). Additionally, the alpha asymmetry is also considered a valuable marker of both emotion reactivity (overall activity) and emotion regulation (lateralized patterns) (Parvaz et al., 2012). Emotional reactivity – LPP Only one recent study has examined neural responses during reexposure to emotion stimuli following affect labeling (Liang & Lin, 2023), by measuring EEG and focusing on the Late Positive Potential (LPP). The LPP is widely marked as reflecting emotional arousal. It begins approximately 400 ms after stimulus onset and peaks at central and parietal sites (see reviews, Hajcak & Foti, 2020; MacNamara et al., 2022). Consistent findings showed that LPP amplitudes are larger for emotional stimuli than for neutral ones, reflecting heightened emotional engagement (Hajcak & Foti, 2020; MacNamara et al., 2022). Importantly, LPP amplitude is sensitive to the perceived significance of stimuli and can be modulated by ER strategies (Chen et al., 2024; Hajcak & Foti, 2020; MacNamara et al., 2022). For example, numerous studies have demonstrated that reappraisal resulted in reduced LPP amplitudes in response to negative stimuli compared to passive viewing (Hajcak & Foti, 2020; MacNamara et al., 2022). Emotional regulation – LPP In line with this effect, Liang & Lin (2023) observed reduced LPP amplitudes to negative stimuli after affect labeling during both immediate (versus affect matching) and short-interval reexposure (versus passive viewing). However, in this study, they used emotion-category words (e.g., ‘neutral’ or ‘negative’) as labels, rather than the emotion-specific words that are used in other affect labeling research (Constantinou et al., 2014; Kircanski et al., 2012; Levy-Gigi & Shamay-Tsoory, 2022; Niles et al., 2015; Sun et al., 2025; Yue et al., 2024). Although we have evidenced at the behavioral level that affect labeling with emotion-specific words (e.g., ‘fear’ or ‘sad’) can also have lasting effects across different reexposure phases (Chen et al., in prep), it remains unclear whether these effects are still supported by regulatory signals as witnessed in the LPP at the neural level. Emotional reactivity – theta oscillations Like the LPP, theta-band activity is sensitive to emotional valence. Previous research has demonstrated that theta power increases in response to negative stimuli compared to neutral stimuli, particularly over parietal–temporal–occipital regions during the first second after stimulus onset (Aftanas et al., 2001, 2004, 2005; Sulpizio et al., 2021). To date, no study has investigated oscillatory activity during reexposure after affect labeling. Due to the nature of emotional stimuli, the processing of negative emotional valence can be expected to evoke theta oscillatory activity also during reexposure. Emotional regulation – theta oscillations Affect labeling and reappraisal share overlapping neural mechanisms, including engagement of prefrontal regulatory regions and reductions in amygdala activity (Burklund et al., 2014). Reappraisal has been linked to increased frontal theta power when comparing ‘decrease’ versus ‘maintain’ conditions (Ertl et al., 2013). Based on the shared neural mechanisms, it is plausible that affect labeling, because of its regulatory function, may also be associated with increased frontal theta power. However, it is unknown whether this regulation-related theta would also still be present during reexposure. Emotional reactivity and regulation – alpha oscillations Furthermore, ER involves inhibitory control to suppress the emotional response. Given its role in engaging executive functions, including inhibitory control, the PFC may therefore act as a mediator during ER. Inhibitory processing in the PFC has been associated with a decrease in alpha oscillations. Indeed, a previous study on reappraisal found that while processing of negative emotional stimuli relative to neutral stimuli was associated with increased frontal alpha power (8–13 Hz) across both hemispheres, alpha power decreased with reappraisal (Parvaz et al., 2012). Notably, this regulatory effect of reappraisal was evident primarily in the left hemisphere, where alpha power decreased following reappraisal (Parvaz et al., 2012). This alpha asymmetry is consistent with findings from fMRI studies on reappraisal, which show greater activation in the left PFC (Johnstone et al., 2007; Ochsner et al., 2002). Given that affect labeling appears to engage a similar left-lateralized cluster of prefrontal brain areas (Burklund et al., 2014), a similar pattern of alpha asymmetry might be expected during affect labeling. However, it is unclear whether this regulation-related alpha would also still be present during reexposure. Summing up, few studies have investigated the lasting effects of affect labeling and the associated neural activity. To address this gap, our study investigates the lasting effects of affect labeling. We assess emotional responses (arousal and valence ratings) at three reexposure time points: immediately after labeling, after a short-interval delay (~15 minutes), and after a long-interval delay (one week). EEG data are recorded during immediate and short-interval reexposure to examine the underlying neural mechanisms. Additionally, given the variation in word types used in previous studies, it remains unclear whether the regulatory effects are driven by the labeling process itself, the emotional content of the words, or both. To clarify this, we will use emotion-specific words in the affect labeling condition to reflect participants' subjective feelings. A content labeling condition will be included, using perception-specific words (e.g., ‘colorful’, ‘wide-view’) to describe image features. This will allow us to test whether the effect of affect labeling is specific to the emotional content of the labels. An affect matching condition, requiring participants to choose between emotional images to best reflect their subjective feelings, will serve as a control for the processing of emotional content without a linguistic component. This will help determine whether the down-regulation of negative affect arises specifically from linguistic processing, and to tease apart perceptual, linguistic and emotional contributions in the EEG. Generally, due to its greater engagement of linguistic emotional processing, we hypothesize that affect labeling will reduce negative emotions more effectively than content labeling or affect matching. We will use subjective arousal and valence ratings as behavioral indices to measure perceived emotional intensity and unpleasantness. At the neural level, we will use event-related potentials (specifically the midline LPP and frontal regulation LPP) and EEG oscillatory activity (power in the theta and alpha frequency bands) as indices to reflect changes in emotional processing and stimulus significance associated with the different regulation strategies, particularly during the reexposure phases (for more specific hypotheses see Study Infromation_Hypotheses).
