title_r: Exploring the role of long-term memory in residual working memory performance: releasing constraints from the concurrent articulation
abstract_r: Working memory provides two fundamental functions, the processing and the temporary storage of a limited amount of information. Some models of working memory suggest that there is a sharing of resources between these two functions, which means that when we perform one at our maximum level, the performance in the other decrease. We recently carried out a series of experiments, the results of which support this hypothesis (Barrouillet et al., in revision). Participants were asked to perform a dual-task with memorizing letters and processing the parity of digits in a complex span task. They were asked to prioritise one of the two components of the task to ensure that they performed at their maximum level in one of the two components. The number of items to be memorised and processed was adapted to each participant's span. The results showed that performance decreased considerably for the component not prioritised. However, performance residual in the non-prioritised task remained high, which suggests that there is a partial sharing of resources. As a result, the origin of this performance residuals in the non-prioritised task needs to be explored, since under a complete resource-sharing, the residual should be null. We suggest that long-term memory is involved in letter maintenance. In the present study, we will measure whether the residual can be explained by long-term memory. We replicated the previous described experiment, adding a new recall condition. In some trials, before the recall of letters, participants were asked to perform a backward counting task, to erase the content of their working memory. We examined residual performance in the memory component of the task, with a prioritization on processing. In a first experiment, we asked participants to perform a concurrent articulation during tasks. In this second experiment, this constraint will be release, and participants will be enabled to use articulatory repetition as a mechanism for letter maintenance.

title_r: ALAS Move (Active Learning About the Self - Move) - Training Decisions in Motor Sequence Learning: Follow-up 1
abstract_r: This is a registration of the first follow-up experiment to the study "ALAS Move (Active Learning About the Self - Move) - Training Decisions in Motor Sequence Learning", available at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/K3V65 We aim to replicate the results of this first experiment on an older participant sample of 8-10-year-old children. All methods and statistical data analyses are identical to those specified in the previous preregistration. In previous experiments, we found that children (ages 4-8) make effective decisions about what to practice in light of distinct goals (Serko et al., 2022). However, it is unclear whether young children can make adaptive training choices in motor skill learning. In the previous study of the ALAS Move project, we investigated in a motor sequence learning task whether 4- to 8- year-old children make effective training choices depending on the task characteristics, with the final goal of maximizing their performance at a final test phase. In particular, we studied whether participants tailor their learning strategies to boost their strengths (i.e., maximizing wins) or compensate for their weaknesses (i.e., minimizing losses). DESCRIPTION OF THE METHODS Participants play three different game blocks (=conditions) presented to them on a tablet screen. In each block, participants are presented with two frog-catching games (SRT tasks). Children see a frog jump between the cells of a 4x4 grid on the screen, and they are instructed to tap on the frog at each jump with their index finger as quickly as they can. Crucially, in each block, one frog jumps in a fully predictable spatial sequence (e.g., jumping from one grid cell to the next) in what we call an Easy game, while the other frog jumps in a partially random manner, which we call the Difficult game, as it is not trivial to predict where the frog will jump next (every second jump happens to a random grid cell). The temporal sequence - i.e., the inter-stimulus interval between the frogs' appearances - is fixed across game difficulty levels. During an initial familiarization phase, participants try to play the Easy or the Difficult frog game first (order counterbalanced across conditions and participants), in which they try to catch the frog 16 times and receive feedback about their performance defined as the number of hits. After this, we ask participants to indicate how difficult they found the game on a 4-point Likert scale (absolute difficulty rating). Then participants proceed to play the other frog game and are asked to indicate its absolute subjective difficulty level on the same 4-point Likert scale. Additionally, we ask participants to indicate which of the two games they just played was easier, and which one was more difficult than the other (binary difficulty rating). To visualize this and provide memory aid throughout the task, we ask participants to place the image of a person lifting small and heavy weights next to a picture of the frog game they found easy or difficult, respectively. After the familiarization phase, we tell participants that eventually, they will be tested on one of the two games they just played (the Easy or Difficult game). We incentivize children by promising them to get one small goodie item if they catch the frog at least 15 out of 16 times. Critically, we manipulate whether we tell participants that eventually they will be tested on the Easy game (Easy game condition), the Difficult game (Difficult game condition), or a randomly chosen game (Random game condition). Participants then decide which game they want to practice for one round before the test. This choice is our dependent variable. In this practice phase, participants have to catch the frog of their choice, who jumps in the same spatial sequence as it jumped during the familiarization phase (i.e., the Easy game is exactly the same sequence as before, as is the Difficult game). After this, participants enter the testing phase, where they are tested either on the Easy game (in the Easy game condition/Random game condition) or on the Difficult game (in the Difficult game condition/Random game condition). After the test phase is over, participants move on to the second and third game blocks presenting the rest of the three experimental conditions. The order of conditions, games within a condition (i.e., whether the Easy or Difficult game is presented first), and the colors of the frogs assigned to each difficulty level are randomized.

title_r: Distinct phenotypes of suicidal ideations in high-risk psychiatric in-patients
abstract_r: Suicidal ideation is the strongest predictor for suicide attempts, and yet reliable prediction models for suicide risk are still lacking. One possible explanation for this is that suicidal ideations are not a uniform symptom. A recently published study by Kleiman and colleagues (2018) suggests that there are five distinct phenotypes that vary in mean severity and variability of suicidal thoughts. The presence of such phenotypes is intriguing considering that suicidal ideations have so far been investigated as a single construct. Based on the study by Kleiman and colleagues (2018), we aim to replicate the statistical approach in a psychiatric inpatient sample, and hypothesize that there are five distinct subgroups of people with suicidal ideation that differ in mean severity and variability of suicidal ideations. Exploratory part The Kleiman and colleagues (2018) paper provided a meaningful contribution to understanding subtypes of suicidal ideation. Here we expand on these analyses. The authors collected longitudinal (i.e., dynamic) ideation data and summarized it into person level means and variances in a cross section analysis. One caveat to this approach entails the the loss of information induced by the summary use of discrete latent outcomes. Such a model can only provide classes which discriminate cases based on a mean and variance. For example, a case which exhibits a stable level of ideation followed by a period of high variability would be classified the same as someone who has a similar mean but a lower variance that is consistent across time. We believe there is a clinically relevant distinction between these two situations. By utilizing Dynamic Latent Class Structural Equation Modeling (DLC-SEM) information will not be reduced to investigate latent classification. By retaining the temporal dimension with a DLCSEM, we will investigate subtypes of suicidal ideation in the context of time. While the analysis is exploratory, we do anticipate the identification of several distinct classes. Specifically, classes which exhibit a relatively stable level of ideation followed by high variability, one class with a high mean and one with a low mean.

title_r: Two-digit number processing in low-literacy adults
abstract_r: Processing Arabic digits is critical for success in our society. In daily-life activities, we are constantly required to understand and compare the magnitude of Arabic digits (e.g., if a meal costs $12.75 in a restaurant and $13.20 in another, where is the cheapest meal?). Although processing Arabic digits seems trivial, it is complex and requires informal and formal training. When processing Arabic digits, people may adopt a componential rather than a holistic heuristic, which is marked by the unit-decade compatibility effect (Nuerk et al., 2001). In a study with German-speaker adults, Nuerk and colleagues (2001) have found that when comparing two-digit numbers, people are influenced by the distance of units and decades separately rather than by the holistic distance of the numbers alone. For instance, people are slower and less accurate when comparing incompatible (i.e., the larger number has a smaller unit, e.g., 36 vs. 52 - 3<5 but 6>2) than compatible pairs (i.e., the larger number has a larger unit, e.g., 32 vs. 56 - 3<5 and 2<6). This effect has also been found in adults and children from other cultures (e.g., Ganayim & Ibrahim, 2015; Macizo et al., 2011; Nuerk et al., 2005). It is still unclear how formal training shapes the unit-decade compatibility effect. Wood and colleagues (2006) found that this effect may be robust and prominent, as it is observed in adults with low literacy. In their study, 19 Brazilian adults who abandoned school in childhood completed a two-digit number comparison task. Participants were from an urban region, received between 1 and 4 years of formal schooling as children, and all of them were functioning in society, working regular jobs, and dealing with money. Results indicated that participants had worse performance in incompatible trials contrasted with compatible trials. Further, their performance was shaped by the distance between decades. Interestingly, these signatures in participants’ performance were not significantly correlated with their years of formal education. These results suggest that adults with low literacy may be able to access the semantics of two-digit numbers and process them in a componential way. However, it is still unclear to what extent these results emerge from the years of formal schooling participants received as children or their informal experiences with numbers. In this study, we conduct a secondary data analysis with three main goals: 1) Perform a conceptual replication of findings from Wood and colleagues (2006); 2) Investigate how the compatibility effect differs between adults with low literacy, adults who completed basic education, and elementary-school children; 3) Investigate how participants’ familiarity with Arabic-digits (e.g., number transcoding skills) relate with their performance in a two-digit number comparison task.

title_r: Modulations of stimulus-response binding and retrieval (SRBR) by performance-independent affective consequences: a follow-up study
abstract_r: We aim to study the modulating role of performance-independent affective consequences (positive, negative, or neutral consequences consisting of visual, auditory, and monetary events) on stimulus-response binding and retrieval (SRBR). In a colour categorisation task with a sequential prime/probe design, we will use an orthogonal variation of response relation (colour repetition vs. change) and stimulus relation (word repetition vs. change) to investigate SRBR effects. Previous studies have demonstrated that not only targets (colour), but distractors (word) too, can retrieve previously executed responses from event files in episodic memory, when faced with the same distractor again. Known as the Retrieval Effect, distractor repetition – in conditions where the response must be repeated – leads to facilitation, whereas with response change – leads to interference. Our goal is to investigate the influence of affective consequences on this Retrieval Effect in S-R binding. Based on the assumption that SRBR is the underlying mechanism of learning and operant conditioning (law of effect), we would expect that the Distractor Repetition (DR) * Response Repetition (RR) interaction should be strengthened (weakened) in cases of positive (negative) consequences after the prime episode. In a previous experiment, however, we did not find any evidence for an affective modulation of RT-based retrieval effects, indicating that these effects are fully automatic and independent of feedback. We did find, however, an indication that with regard to the accuracy of their responses, participants tended to benefit from the condition “response change” after having received negative feedback in the prime. We hypothesise that (at least some of the) participants interpreted negative feedback as indicating that their previous response was erroneous, which elicited a tendency to change their response after trials with a negative consequence, rather than reflecting an actual effect of negative feedback on retrieval. To eliminate strategic effects due to an interpretation of affective consequences in terms of performance feedback, we modified the experiment design and instructions (details in the methods section). We thus do not expect to see any moderating role of affective consequences on the retrieval effect in the accuracy data in the current study. Furthermore, we expect to replicate the null effect of affective consequences on retrieval effects in the RT data.

title_r: Study 2: Targeted Follow-up Pre-reg
abstract_r: Study 2: Targeted Follow-Up on LGBTQ+ Aging Attitudes This preregistration outlines the methods, hypotheses, and analytic plan for a follow-up study (Study 2) that builds on our original investigation of ageism and aging anxiety among LGBTQ+ and heterosexual/cisgender individuals. Study 2 was conducted in response to editorial and reviewer feedback requesting greater representation of exclusively gay men and lesbian women in order to clarify subgroup-level patterns that could not be confidently interpreted in Study 1. To address this, we used updated Prolific screening tools to recruit a new sample that includes increased representation of gay men and lesbian women. The goal of Study 2 is to replicate key findings from Study 1 and evaluate whether patterns generalize across subgroups with improved demographic representation. Note: Data collection began on June 27, 2025, but no data have been accessed or analyzed at the time of this preregistration. This preregistration was created to transparently document our hypotheses and analytic plan prior to data inspection, in line with open science best practices. Hypotheses These hypotheses are informed by the results of Study 1, which was exploratory in nature. Study 2 is designed to test whether those results replicate and extend to specific subgroups. Gender and Ageism: Men will score higher than women on interpersonal ageism, defined as a composite of hostile, benevolent, and prescriptive ageism scales, regardless of sexual orientation. Sexual Identity and Aging Anxiety: LGBTQ+ individuals will report lower comfort with aging (i.e., higher aging anxiety) than heterosexual individuals, regardless of gender. Intersectional Subgroup Exploration (Exploratory): We will explore whether gay men report greater ageist attitudes than other subgroups (e.g., bisexual men, heterosexual men), consistent with themes in prior literature and media discourse. These subgroup contrasts are exploratory and will be interpreted cautiously. Planned Analyses We will conduct two 2×2 ANCOVAs: (1) Gender (men vs. women) × Sexual Identity (LGBTQ+ vs. heterosexual) predicting ageism composite scores; (2) Same model predicting comfort with aging scores. Age and social desirability will be included as covariates, as in Study 1. We will conduct additional planned contrasts comparing gay men, bisexual men, and heterosexual men to evaluate whether gay men show uniquely elevated ageist attitudes. We will also replicate our prior use of principal component analysis (PCA) to create the composite outcome variables unless the structure meaningfully changes. All additional exploratory subgroup comparisons (e.g., lesbian vs. bisexual vs. heterosexual women) will be reported but clearly distinguished from confirmatory analyses. Clarification (posted June 28): Our planned sample size for Study 2 is approximately 50 participants per cell (N ≈ 200 total), matching the original Study 1 design. This allows for adequate power to detect medium-sized effects using 2×2 ANCOVA while accounting for budget and population constraints. This plan was in place prior to analysis but inadvertently omitted from the preregistration text. which was powered to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25, η²ₚ ≈ .06) with 80% power at α = .05 using 2×2 factorial ANCOVA. This sample mirrors the original design of Study 1, which was powered to detect medium-sized effects (f = .25, η²ₚ ≈ .06) with 80% power at α = .05 using 2×2 factorial ANCOVA.

summary: Replication of Rochefort et al. (2017) on Discriminant Validity of AAQ-II and MEAQ from Neuroticism/Negative Affect 
Study Registration

Research Questions: 
1. Do the most commonly used measures of experiential avoidance (MEAQ and AAQ-II) demonstrate appropriate discriminant validity from neuroticism (IPIP-NEO-N and BFI-2-N) and trait negative affect (TAI) at the scale, subscale, and item levels? 

2. Are the results from Rochefort et al. (2017) replicable using different neuroticism and trait negative affect measures? 

Hypothesis:
We hypothesize that the AAQ-II will continue to be overly saturated with neuroticism and trait negative affect variance, such that it will function as an indicator of neuroticism and negative affect instead of experiential avoidance at the scale, subscale, and item levels. In addition, we hypothesize that the MEAQ will demonstrate appropriate discriminate validity from neuroticism and negative affect, and will demonstrate appropriate associations with another third-wave behavior therapy construct, mindfulness. 

Participants and Recruitment Method: 
We are planning to collect cross-sectional data from 500 adult participants recruited from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk and a minimum of 300 undergraduates. In recruiting undergraduate participants, we will not stop data collection at 300 participants, but will instead continue to collect data until the end of the semester in which we reach 300 participants. 

Procedure and Measures: 
Participants will complete questionnaires online, including the Multidimensional Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (MEAQ), the Action and Acceptance Questionnaire-2 (AAQ-II), IPIP-NEO Neuroticism scale (IPIP-NEO-N), Big Five Inventory-2 Neuroticism scale (BFI-2-N), Temperament and Affectivity Inventory (TAI), and the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ). 

Analytic Overview:
Similar to the analyses conducted in Rochefort et al. (2017), we will:
	- Examine Pearson correlations between all scales and subscales
	- Conduct significance tests for dependent correlations to determine differences in strength between the correlations
	- Conduct exploratory factor analyses with promax rotation at the scale, subscale, and item levels 
	- Conduct parallel analyses to determine the maximum number of factors to extract in the scale, subscale, and item level extractions
	- Present item level results using Goldberg’s (2006) bassackward approach 
	- Conduct exploratory structural equation modeling to determine the optimal solutions at the scale, subscale, and item levels 
All analyses will be conducted in the MTurk and undergraduate student samples separately in order to examine replication of our results.

title_r: A Multi-site German Validation of the Interoceptive Accuracy Scale and its Relation to Psychopathological Symptom Burden
abstract_r: Processing of internal bodily signals (i.e., interoception), and associated impairments are thought to be implicated in the development of psychopathology. Recent proposals highlight the need to differentiate between dimensions of interoception (i.e., accuracy and attention) to better understand its relation to mental health. In the current study, we validated the German version of the recently developed Interoceptive Accuracy Scale (IAS; Murphy et al., 2020) and investigated its relation to clinical outcomes, across seven samples from four research centers (Ntotal = 3462). The German IAS version was best explained by a one-factor structure that showed acceptable psychometric properties. Concerning clinical outcomes, we replicated previous findings showing a negative association between IAS scores and measures of alexithymia. Furthermore, we found that IAS scores were negatively related to measures of clinical symptomatology (e.g., anxiety, depressive, and somatoform symptoms) and neurotic traits. These findings suggest that the German validation of the IAS is a reliable and valid instrument for measuring subjective interoceptive accuracy and emphasize the importance of distinguishing between dimensions of interoception to understand its modulatory and protective role in the existence of psychopathology.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from de Langhe et al. (2014), from the Journal of Consumer Research
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from de Langhe et al (2014) is the Study 2 claim that consumers base their predictions of quality given price on perceived covariation, in particular the presence of a price region where quality is locally consistent increases the predicted quality at high price: experiencing consistently low quality products at lower prices should lead to more extreme price-based quality predictions at higher prices. This reflects the following from the paper’s abstract: “Consumers inappropriately conﬂate the conditional mean of quality with the predictability of quality.” Participants’ estimates were modeled with a mixed general linear model (see p. 9) with predictors for condition, slope and intercept for the condition in which quality was never consistent, and fixed effects indicating differences in slope and intercept for the two conditions containing a price region with a strong quality/price consistency. The parameter delta 1A = 0.32, and is significantly greater than 0 (p < 0.05). This implies that, relative to the condition where quality is never consistent, the regression slope for price is steeper in the conditions where quality is locally consistent. Specifically, for the same unit increase in price participants who consistently encountered low quality at low price expect a 33% greater increase in quality than participants who never encountered consistent quality.

title_r: Relative Deprivation in Groups - Study 2 Materials
abstract_r: Relative Deprivation in Groups OVERVIEW Inequality has been linked with numerous negative consequences at the societal and individual levels. The detrimental effects of inequality are proposed to operate at the individual level through social comparisons, where perceived unfair disadvantage leads to the experience of personal relative deprivation (i.e., subjective feelings of anger and resentment), which in turn causes psychosocial stress. To date, little empirical work has investigated how individual differences in personal relative deprivation influences group dynamics. In a prior study, greater feelings of personal relative deprivation were associated with reduced group engagement. Personal relative deprivation explained 9% of variance in group exercise engagement over and above demographic and situation-related variables (e.g., stress, perceived competition, role fit), and the overall regression model accounted for 58% of total variance in group. These findings suggest that such negative socioemotional comparison reactions as personal relative deprivation have important implications for group-based decision making and small group dynamics. Following up this study, we will investigate if feeling of relative deprivation are associated with reduce participation in self-reported recollection of teamwork in organizations. Project goals: 1) To replicate the effect from study 1 2) To investigate how voice/silence influence participation 3) To better understand the mechanisms and contextual factors that lead to lowered participation by high-RD participants 4) To identify the points of comparison for RD in groups (which aspects of comparison are important for this relationship) Hypothesis and predictions: We hypothesize that people who experience higher feeling of relative deprivation will also report participating less in their groups. Specific predictions: i. Predict higher relative deprivation scores will be associated with lower group participation a. We predict that this relationship will be robust after accounting for demographic variables (age, gender, income) ii. Predict higher relative deprivation scores will be associated with lower promotive and prohibitive voice participation a. We predict that this relationship will be robust after accounting for demographic variables (age, gender, income) iii. We predict that higher relative deprivation scores will be associated with higher acquiescence and quiescence subscale scores on the Employee Silence Scale (adapted), but not associated with the opportunistic or prosocial subscales Additional predictions: We will also investigate possible mechanisms that mediate/moderate the relationship between relative deprivation and group participation. We posit four possible issues: self-efficacy, expectancy, psychological safety, and engagement. Below, we posit that the following variables (with specific predictions) will provide evidence of each possible mechanism, although they are not mutually exclusive. 1) Self-efficacy Moderators: - Group size o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in larger groups (may fear more repercussions from sharing in large groups) - Team composition (Likert scale, seniority compared to self) o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in groups where members are more senior than respondents (may be more critical of ideas in more senior groups) Mediators: - Concern for reputation scale o Greater RD will be associated with greater concern for reputation in the group, which will be associated with lower participation (may be reluctant to share ide-as with high concern of reputation) - Self-efficacy proxy (see analysis section below) o Greater RD will be associated with lower perceived self-efficacy, which will be as-sociated with lower participation 2) Expectancy Moderators: - Group size o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in larger groups (may be less likely to be listened to in large groups) - Team composition (Likert scale, seniority compared to self) o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in groups where members are more senior than respondent (may be less likely to be listened to in more senior groups) - Virtual meeting (vs in-person meeting) o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in in-person groups (lower expectancy to participate in virtual groups, also fewer points of comparison for RD in virtual groups) Mediators: - Acquiescent silence o Greater RD will be associated with greater acquiescent silence (lower perception of being listened to), which will decrease participation (low expectancy) 3) Psychological Safety Moderators: - Group size o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in larger groups (may fear more consequences from sharing in large groups) - Team composition (Likert scale, seniority compared to self) o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in groups where members are more senior than respondent (may fear more consequences in more senior groups) - Cooperative vs competitive goal o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in competitive (compared to cooperative groups; may fear more consequences in competitive groups) Mediators: - Concern for reputation scale o Greater RD will be associated with greater concern for reputation in the group, which will be associated with lower participation (may fear sharing ideas with high concern of reputation) - Quiescent silence o Greater RD will be associated with greater quiescent silence (fear of contribu-tion), which will decrease participation (if low psychological safety, there may be greater fear of contribution) 4) Engagement Moderators - Virtual meeting (vs in-person meeting) o Stronger relationship between RD and participation in in-person groups (less committed to virtual groups, or lower expectancy to participate in virtual groups; also fewer points of comparison for RD in virtual groups) Mediators: - How valuable is it to you to be part of this group? o Greater RD will be associated with lower valuation of the group, which will be associated with lower participation SAMPLE Based prior data, we estimate the effect size will be a Cohen’s d of 0.63. Based on a power calculation for linear multiple regression (alpha = .05, two-tailed) for 95% power, we require 216 participants. We will oversample to account for bots and participants who fail our attention check. Our final sample will at least 216 participants. Data will be collected from Prolific, restricted to participants from the US and Canada who work full-time. PROCEDURE Survey methods (see question document for greater detail of questions) After consenting to participate in the study, participants will describe their most recent group work experience at their workplace. They will describe in detail the group characteristics (size, participants, purpose, how often they meet, duration etc) and how much they participated in that group (see Survey document). Following this description, participants completed a series of questionnaires in the following order: • Randomized scales o Group participation (see below and Survey document) o Personal relative deprivation (revised; Callan, Shead, & Olson, 2015) • Group experiences and comparisons (from Study 1 and created for this study) • Randomized scales o Employee silence scale (adapted from Knoll & Van Dick, 2013; see Survey document) o Promotive and prohibitive voice scale (Liang, Farh, & Farh, 2012) • Concern for reputation scale (de Cremer & Tyler, 2005) • Workplace questions (see Survey document) Participants will also complete an attention check question during the survey and fill out demographic information. title_r: BB-PRIME Phase II: Longitudinal effects of an action planning intervention promoting collective climate action
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate and extend prior research testing whether an action planning intervention can increase intentions to engage in collective climate action. In our prior study testing this intervention, we found that an action planning intervention that specifically targets collective climate action increased intentions to engage specifically in collective climate actions, including both the target behavior for the action planning task as well as other collective behaviors, as compared to an individual-action focused version of the task and the no-task control group. The collective action planning task also increased the perceived impact of both individual and collective climate actions. (Prior preregistration: https://osf.io/7rwbz). In the current study, we seek to replicate these findings, test hypotheses with new outcome measure (including e.g. policy support), and evaluate longitudinal effects on intentions as well as day-to-day self-reported behavior.

title_r: Intersectional invisibility - social cognition approach | Study 1b
abstract_r: Authors call for the embedding of gender dimension in racism experimental psychology or race dimension in sexism experimental psychology (Else-Quest & Hyde, 2016). For example, a non intersectional approach could tend to exclude women of color from research scope either in sampling or measured concepts, while subsequently overgeneralizing (e.g. research on racism towards Black Americans while only using male Black Americans). Using McCall’s (2005) typology of empirical application of intersectionality, this research would fall within intercategorical intersectionality, which assumes that categories (e.g. race) are socially constructed (vs. biologically) but are associated with inequalities and discrimination. In contrast with a color/gender-blind approach, race and gender are considered as meaningful – but non exhaustive – dimensions to understand discrimination processes. Building on previous contributions on intersectional invisibility (Purdie-Vaughns, 2008; Sesko and Biernet, 2010/2018; Neel & Lasseter, 2019), this research will investigate the interpersonal invisibility of Black women through an attentional blindness paradigm. Sesko and Biernat (2010, p. 360) state that “in using the term ‘invisibility’, we do not mean to suggest Black women literally go unnoticed”. In contrast, this is exactly what we suggest. We will replicate Brown-Iannuzzi’s et al. (2014) procedure, while including Black and White women. In their study, these authors often refer to ‘African-Americans’, when they actually mean ‘male African-Americans’. Hence, we propose to further explore interpersonal invisibility bringing an intersectional approach. As we mobilize an attentional blindness paradigm, our main focus are attentional processes, in contrast with Sesko and Biernat (2010/2016) who focused on memory-based tasks. Through this study, we will evaluate the effect of race and gender on invisibility, which are visually cues (and often non-concealable). This first study is a conceptual replication of Brown-Iannuzi et al. (2014) and aims to establish a difference in invisibility between Black men, Black women, White men and White women.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Zhu & Meyers-Levy (2009), from Journal of Marketing Research
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Zhu & Meyers-Levy (2009: Experiment 1) is that, because interdependents should rely on holistic processing, an assimilation effect should emerge, such that they will evaluate a neutral product as more modern and less natural when it is displayed on a glass table than when it is displayed on a wood table. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: “The authors theorize and find that people’s use of holistic cognition, as prompted by an interdependent self-view, produces an assimilation effect.” Following a self-view mind-set task that prompted holistic or analytic processing, participants were asked to view the target product, a mug, displayed on either a glass or a wood table, and participants evaluated the mug on the trendiness and naturalness items. Participants’ evaluation of the mug’s trendiness constitutes the dependent variable used by the SCORE program (trendiness index score). It was analyzed with a 2 (self-view: interdependent/holistic processing versus independent/analytic processing) x 2 (table surface: glass versus wood) x 2 (evaluative dimension: trendiness versus naturalness) ANOVA. Following the discovery of a significant two-way interaction between self-view and table surface for the trendiness outcome, the authors performed planned contrasts between interdependents’ evaluation of the mug’s trendiness when viewed on the glass table vs the wood table. Interdependents evaluated the mug as more trendy (F(1,37) = 13.57, p < .001) when it was viewed on a glass table (M = 4.53, SD = 1.37) than when it was viewed on a wood table (M = 2.55, SD = .97).

title_r: The Effect of Game Difficulty on Player Experience, Engagement and Enjoyment: An Extended Replication
abstract_r: Grounded in flow theory, numerous researchers and practitioners have proposed that the relationship between game difficulty and engagement follows an inverted U curve, with optimal engagement at a ‘goldilocks’ midpoint where game difficulty ‘matches’ player skill. Existing empirical studies have found mixed support for this relationship, but also show high variance in operationalising the proposed relationship. Maybe even more importantly, contrary to flow theory, game difficulty is typically theorised and operationalised as a fixed, subject-independent construct, rather than as a subject-environment ratio or relationship. That is, optimum ‘medium difficulty’ is construed as a population-level aggregate medium, rather than as an individual-level match with skill. One likely reason prior research has found mixed results is that it did not operationalise difficulty on an individual level, producing higher variance in the data overall and biased results due to unrepresentative samples with non-normally distributed playing skills for the game under study. In a prior large-scale, pre-registered study, we used a novel dynamic difficulty adjustment technique based on Monte Carlo Tree Search that allows us to give an AI opponent a target player win margin, which in a points based game is the players’ score after subtracting the AI opponents’ score. We created three levels of game closeness: - The player wins decisively, targeting a player win margin of +15 - The AI wins decisively, targeting a player win margin of -15 - The match is close, targeting a draw with a player win margin of 0. Thus, closeness or objective winning likelihood as an individual-level, relative measure will be operationalised as the target win margin of the AI agent. Our first study found no difference in player self-reported enjoyment and player engagement behaviour (operationalised as voluntary games played after the experiment is called over). Among other factors, we identified two potential reasons why this may be a false negative: (1) The game was novel and polished, and the enjoyment and engagement effect of that overshadowed any differences in difficulty. We hypothesise that playing the game more often before taking measurements should address this issue, if it exists. (2) Omnibus enjoyment ratings may not be sensitive to actual differences in player experience for the same reason. We hypothesise that measuring differentiated player experience constructs, including those closer to underlying theories (Flow, SDT), should address this issue, if it exists. With this study, we therefore plan to run an extended replication of the original study where we will - create the same three difficulty conditions - require player to play the game multiple times before measuring experience and behaviour - measure additional player experience constructs # Experimental Procedure # Participants will be informed that this is a study about the design of digital games. They will then fill out a consent form and if they agree to the conditions, the study will then start. The experiment starts with a tutorial on how to play the game “Explorers vs Owls”. This is a cut down version of the full game with only one piece per player and a 4 x 4 board. During this game the opponent AI is configured to aim for a draw. They will then play 5 games with 3 pieces per player and a 7x7 board. title_r: Resting state cortico-limbic functional connectivity and dispositional use of emotion regulation strategies: A replication and extension study
abstract_r: Neuroimaging functional connectivity analyses have shown that the negative coupling between amygdala and cortical regions is linked to better emotion regulation (ER) in experimental task settings. However, less is known about the neural correlates of ER traits or dispositions. The present study aimed to (1) replicate the findings of differential cortico-limbic coupling during resting state depending on the dispositional use of ER strategies. Furthermore, the study aimed to (2) extend prior findings by examining whether differences in cortico-limbic coupling during resting state predict behavioral and neuronal emotion regulation success in a standard emotion regulation task. To this end, N=107 healthy adults completed the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ), underwent an 8-min resting-state fMRI acquisition and completed a reappraisal task during fMRI. Functional connectivity maps of basolateral and centromedial amygdala nuclei were estimated with a seed-based approach regarding associations with regions of the prefrontal cortex, and were then correlated with ERQ scores as well as behavioral and neuronal ER success. All hypotheses and the analysis plan are preregistered at https://osf.io/8wsgu. Opposed to prior findings, we were not able to replicate a correlation of habitual ER strategy use with functional connectivity between amygdala and PFC regions. Furthermore, there was no association of behavioral and neuronal reappraisal success with functional connectivity between amygdala and insula as well as PFC. The present preregistered study calls into question the reported association between individual differences in resting state cortico-limbic connectivity and habitual use of ER strategies. However, ongoing advances in functional brain imaging and distributed network approaches may leverage the identification of reliable functional connectivity patterns that underlie successful emotion regulation.

title_r: Can multiple visual working memory representations simultaneously indeed capture attention?
abstract_r: Can we look for multiple objects simultaneously? Previous studies have proposed that the representation of an item in visual working memory (VWM) can bias the deployment of attention to memory-matching items in visual search. However, it is still controversial whether multiple VWM item representations are able to capture attention. In the present study, we will adopt an eye-tracking technique to reveal this issue. In Experiment 1, we will replicate Chen and Du’s Experiment 2 and adopt an eye-tracking technique to determine whether multiple VWM item representations are able to bias attention. In Chen and Du’s paradigm, the memory test is always followed by the search test, and the participants may intentionally prepare for the search task, which can affect the results of the research. Thus, in Experiment 2, we will prevent participants from predicting the temporal occurrence of the visual search task by randomly conducting a search test or a memory test after memoranda. The findings of the present study suggest whether multiple VWM items can capture attention simultaneously and whether temporal expectancy can affect the search test.

title_r: Is the influence of contextual modulation of the spatial variance of visual signals on audiovisual spatial binding mediated by the change of perceived visual variance?
abstract_r: Previous models of multisensory binding assumed that the brain integrates multimodal inputs weighted by sensory reliability estimates based on the noises of current sensory signals (Alais & Burr, 2004; Ernst & Banks, 2002). However, recent studies about audiovisual spatial binding (i.e., the ventriloquism effect) demonstrated that visual bias is stronger than predicted by the models, indicating the possibility that the visual reliability estimates may be affected by the prior experience that vision is the more reliable modality for spatial location than audition (Arnold et al., 2019; Meijer et al., 2019). A recent study (Beierholm et al., 2020) reported that the sensory reliability estimates in multisensory binding depend not only on the sensory noises of the current signals but also on those of the past signals. We conceptually replicated the effect of contextual modulation of visual noise on the ventriloquism effect (https://osf.io/b6qtd/). In this study, we will attempt to directly replicate the results of our previous experiment under identical conditions but with fewer trials. We will also investigate whether the change of perceived visual variance mediates the effect of contextual modulation of visual noise on the ventriloquism effect. Before running the study, all procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Sophia University (Reference number: 2023-40).

title_r: VSLMEM_Py_2
abstract_r: This study intends to investigate the transfer of learning from one task to another. Participants will complete a learning phase, in which they will be exposed to paired regularities in the presentation of stimuli, a procedure known to produce “visual statistical learning” (VSL) of those regularities. In a second task, these learned pairs and unlearned items will be used as the stimuli in a memory recall task. In a previous study we found that the paired stimuli from the VSL sequence were remembered more accurately than paired items consisting of the unlearned items, as reflected by differences in participants’ working memory capacity (k). This study will serve as a preregistered replication of that work with minor differences (removing an explicit recognition phase). We expect to see an initial performance advantage of learned items during the VWM task, compared with unlearned items. The initial task will be the visual statistical learning task where participants will be required to view a stream of visual images and indicate when there is a repetition of the stimuli (1-back). The second task is a cued memory recall task where participants will be presented an array of 8 shapes and after a brief interval are cued to recall the item that appeared at the cued location. Stimuli in the experiment will consist of sixteen Ndjuka characters. The sixteen stimuli will be randomly divided into two uniquely random groups for every participant. In the first group, referred to as the learned group, the stimuli are assigned to pairs. These stimuli will appear in their respective pairs side by side in the memory array 100% of the time. The other set of eight stimuli, referred to as the unlearned group, will appear in randomized pairs on every trial (appearing in consistent pairs only 25% of the time) during the learning phase. On each trial four sets of two reference boxes are displayed as the memory array (above, below, right, and left of fixation). Stimuli will appear side by side inside the reference boxes, presenting eight stimuli in total on each trial. Paired trials consisted of the presentation of the paired stimuli randomly presented at the possible reference locations. Randomized trials consisted of the randomized stimuli presented at the reference locations. In the paired condition each pair is spatially consistent, (e.g. item A always appears in the right box while item B appears in the left). I controlled for this in the randomized condition by having four items consistently presented on the right and the other four on the left, however the pairing of these stimuli was randomized. For the training phase, participants will be tasked with a rapid stimulus visual presentation cover task. The cover task used will be a 1-back memory task in which participants indicate with a spacebar keypress whenever the current set of items on the screen matches the last pair of items that had appeared previously. During this training phase, the RSVP of stimulus pairs, will be presented randomly in one of the four reference locations used in the testing phase. Half of the item sets will appear in consistent pairs 100% of the time, while the other half will appear in randomized pairs. The display consisted of a fixation cross in the center of the screen, and four reference locations on the top, bottom, left, and right consisting of two black outlined boxes side-by-side. Each set of paired items will be shown forty times during familiarization while each randomized pair is only presented ten times during familiarization. Participants are also required to make sixty 1-back responses which are randomized throughout the stream. The total stimulus presentation stream is 380 presentations in total. During the secondary cued memory task participants are shown at the beginning of each trial of the testing phase the same display as in VSL training is displayed This screen is presented for 1000 msec. Eight memory items then appear in all of the reference locations on the screen for 3000 msec. The stimuli then disappear, while the boxes remain on the screen for 1000 msec, then one of the reference boxes will be highlighted in green, prompting the participant to recall the shape at the cued location. Participants make a keyboard response using the 1-8 keys at the top of the keyboard to indicate their response based on a randomized response map displayed at the bottom of the screen. On half of the trials the paired set is displayed with the four pairs being shuffled around the different locations. On the other half of trials, the randomized stimulus set will be presented in consistent pairs at the four reference locations just like the paired stimulus set. This way we are allowing learning to occur in the testing phase in both stimulus conditions. This will allow us to look specifically at the benefit from the pairing during the training phase.

title_r: Effects of sensory feedback delay on response effectiveness in a within subject design ver.1
abstract_r: Several previous studies have shown that immediate feedback could enhance reaction time (e.g., Eitam, Kennedy, & Higgins, 2013; Tanaka, Watanabe, & Tanaka, 2020). Eitam et al. found that reaction times were shorter in the group that was given feedback (i.e., flash) immediately after the button press than in the group that was given feedback 600 ms after or no feedback. On the other hand, there was no significant difference in the reaction time between the group given feedback 300 ms after the button press and the group that was given feedback immediately after or 600 ms after. title_r: Is Pluralistic Ignorance More Likely to Occur in Low Mobility Society? The Moderating Effect of Society Size
abstract_r: In Japan, few male employees take paternity leave. Why do many male employees in Japan refrain from taking paternity leave? One of the reasons is pluralistic ignorance. Pluralistic ignorance refers to the situation where each group member mistakenly estimates that other members support the norm, although most of them privately reject it. It is demonstrated that Japanese male employees mistakenly estimate that other employees are against males taking paternity leave, although they are privately in favor of them. Pluralistic ignorance is more likely to occur in lower relational mobility societies. In higher mobility societies, when they deviate from norms and lower their reputation in their group, they can move to another group and construct new relationships. Contrarily, in lower mobility societies, even when they lower their reputation and are excluded from their groups, they cannot easily move to another group and construct new relationships. Therefore, the cost of reputation damage is larger in lower mobility societies. It is demonstrated that people in lower mobility societies overestimate reputation damage incurred by deviating from the norm, and thus they are more likely to conform to norms. In this study, we try to replicate previous studies which demonstrated that the norm of not taking paternity leave in Japan is maintained in pluralistic ignorance. In addition, we try to examine whether society size moderates the relationship between social mobility and normative behavior. As societies are composed of groups, companies are composed of workplaces. We focus on companies and workplaces as societies and groups, respectively. We examine the following hypothesis: (1) In companies with more employees, those in lower mobility companies would estimate greater reputation damage incurred by taking paternity leave, and thus are more likely to refrain from taking paternity leave, and (2) in companies with fewer employees, there is no relationship between them.

abstract_r: In two previous studies, we asked participants how positive or negative, how vivid, and how important they imagine an election to be (future thinking) and followed up with the same participants and items after the election (remembering). This was done first with German participants and the EU parliamentary elections, and then with UK participants of the UK general elections. In both studies, we found evidence for a self-protective bias where people who supported parties that lost ascribed less importance to the election afterwards than they had before, while the opposite was true for people who supported winning parties. A similar effect was found for vividness. We aim to replicate this apparent self-protective bias in a separate nationality and also investigate to what extent participants show a consistency bias in their remembering. We will therefore ask participants to imagine the US presidential elections and will afterwards follow up on how they feel about it now, as well as, as an additional aspect, how they remember imagining it (memory for the simulation). Importantly, in this study, we control the timing of the two surveys more tightly, by collecting imagining data on one single day (one week prior to the election) and collecting remembering data mainly on one single day (one week after the election). This is in contrast to the first two studies, for which data was collected over periods of two weeks (for both imagining and remembering). Furthermore, we aim to recruit equal numbers of Democrats and Republicans so that we can observe differing effects based on political allegience and candidate preference within the same election.

title_r: TIPS (Team-Initiated Problem Solving) Evaluation: An Effectiveness Replication of a Widely-Used Problem-Solving Process for Data Teams Implementing Schoolwide Behavior Supports
abstract_r: Team Initiated Problem Solving (TIPS) is a problem-solving framework with standardized training and coaching protocols that has demonstrated positive impacts on problem-solving of school level PBIS teams. Improved problem solving positively affected student outcomes in a previous randomized controlled trial (RCT) funded by the Institute of Education Sciences (IES). This five-year project intends to replicate and extend the findings from the previous IES-funded RCT, which demonstrated, under ideal conditions, the initial efficacy of a professional development and coaching package for school teams using universal behavioral data for decision-making. The need for this replication project arises from (a) the rapid growth in data available to school teams, (b) repeated findings that under-prepared teams are not effective in their use of data, (c) documentation that the IES-funded Team Initiated Problem Solving (TIPS) framework delivered through training and coaching can improve team decision-making and student outcomes, and (d) the wide-spread use of Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS) currently being used by over 25,000 schools across the United States. This replication will be conducted under routine conditions. Specifically, this project will accomplish the following objectives in each phase: Effectiveness & Replication Aim: Conduct a randomized controlled effectiveness trial to assess the impact of TIPS training on (a) evidence-based problem-solving procedures and (b) student behavioral and academic outcomes. Investigators will conduct a replication analysis that compares the impacts of the current routine-conditions study, using typical school and district resources, to those of the original ideal-conditions study, which provided more intensive research support. Implementation Aim: Monitor the implementation process and conduct focus groups with treatment teams after one year of TIPS implementation to document implementation facilitators and barriers. Economic Evaluation Aim: Conduct a comprehensive estimate of the resources needed to implement the TIPS training and coaching with the ingredients method and assess the program costs relative to its effectiveness. Dissemination Aim: Disseminate the findings in a multimodal approach tailored to stakeholders including participants, partnering state agencies, national technical assistance center partners, district and school administrators, teachers and other relevant school staff members.

title_r: Do other forms of minimization lead to pragmatic inferences of leniency?
abstract_r: Having found no evidence that the minimization tactics we tested in Studies 1, 2, and 3 cause people to draw explicit inferences that the suspect will receive more lenient treatment (despite having an apparently reliable effect on sentencing expectations), we have decided to test an alternative form of minimization: one in which the interrogator develops a theme about the value of honesty and makes references to how other people, including the courts and prosecutors, may view honesty favorably. Such tactics were employed in the high-profile interrogation of Brendan Dassey. Indeed, we have derived the language of this condition from a transcript of Mr. Dassey’s interrogation. We expect to replicate our previous results that participants in the moral minimization condition will not draw inferences about lenient treatment of the suspect, and we predict that participants in the honesty theme condition will draw such inferences. We are also interested in testing a possible mechanism for the effects of moral minimization on sentencing expectations. It is possible that this form of minimization influences expectations by changing people’s perceptions of how severe the crime was. That is, perhaps moral minimization makes people view the crime as less blameworthy and therefore less likely to be punished severely. We will assess this possibility using a measure of perceived crime severity.

title_r: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine: assessing clinical impact and potential harm from overuse in a Swedish setting.
abstract_r: Globaly imaging for lower back pain has increased over the last decades, especially the use of MRI. This trend is true for Sweden as well. A previous study by Wnuk et. al. found that 13% percent of outpatient MRI´s of the lower back had actionable findings. With a rather high rate of false positive findings. The rate of actionable findings in a Swedish context is unkown thus we intend to replicate the study done by Wnuk et al. but in a Swedish setting. Methods This study is a retrospective cohort study of lumbar spine MR imaging. The study is descriptive in nature. Simple descriptive statistics will be used to summarize data. Two reviewers will independently go through radiological reports and patient journals manually to note findings and whether they led to a change of treatment or new diagnoses. In the case of disagreement a third senior reviewer will be used to settle the case. Independent manual assessment will be used instead of automatic text search engine in order to mitigate risk of over or under-assessing any of the study endpoints. The outcomes of the study are "actionable exams", "potentially harmful findings" and appropiateness as descriped below. Actionable exams: Examinations will be classified as either “actionable,” or “non-actionable” using the definitions created by Wnuk et. al. An examination could satisfy more than one set of criteria but would contribute only once to the overall total of actionable examinations. An actionable examination is one which either: 1. Contributes to planning of an anatomically specific treatment; 2. Contributes to a new diagnosis of fracture, cancer or infection; 3. Is performed to follow known lumbar spine pathology (other than degenerative conditions). Examinations that do not meet any of the three criteria are classified as non-actionable. Anatomically specific treatment: An examination is classified as actionable if a spine procedure occurred within 12 months following the examination, without an intervening lumbar spine MRI, for which the anatomical imaging information might be used in planning. Procedures considered included laminectomy, foraminotomy, resection, drainage, decompression, discectomy, vertebral fusion, vertebroplasty and radiation therapy performed at spinal levels from T12 through S1, inclusive. Furthermore we will also note less invasive treatments (nerve root block, facet joint injection,) and of more doubtful efficacy. They will be presented in aggregate and separate. Contribution to a new diagnosis: New diagnoses of cancer, infection, acute fracture of the spine or other clinically significant disease requiring treatment. For all positive reports, clinical notes will be examined up to one year following the examination. A finding will be considered a “true positive” if confirmed by subsequent imaging, blood tests or biopsy, or if treatment was initiated based on the imaging findings. Treatment might include surgery, chemotherapy or radiation therapy for cancer, and treatment with antibiotics or drainage for infection. A finding will also considered a true positive if accepted as real by the clinician as indicated in the clinical chart. False positives (see below) were considered as harmful. Following a known condition: Examinations are classified as actionable if they are used to follow known condition (other than degenerative disease). Potentially harmful: When the suggestion of cancer or infection raised in the report is not substantiated by subsequent events the finding was considered a “false positive,” and the examination is classified as potentially harmful since it may lead to further evaluations, incorrect treatment and/or patient anxiety. Appropriateness: While not formally used in our setting we asses this in a smaller random sample in order to benchmark our referrals to the findings in the previous study by Wnuk et al. Appropriateness scores, based on ACR criteria, from 1-9 will be assessed based on information given in the referrals. Study population: Outpatient adult lumbar spine MRI performed in Skane county between 20220101 and 20230101. Imaging protocols vary to some extent but generally include sagittal T1 and T2 weighted images covering the lower thoracic spine through the sacrum. Usually there is also a coronal T2 TIRM sequence covering the whole abdomen and pelvis. Exams were performed on either 1.5 or 3.0 Tesla and interpreted by radiologists of varying training and subspecialty, some by musculoskeletal radiologists or neuroradiologists. Exams were read at non-academic institutions. Demographic information, indications for the study, and appropriateness scores will be obtained from the radiology information system(PACS). Examinations will be excluded if they were incomplete or if the patient is younger than 18 years of age.

title_r: Intergroup Bias towards Robots?
abstract_r: In a series of three studies (N = 495), we replicated a study on social categorisation of robots: German participants evaluated a robot better that was supposedly from Germany than a robot ostensibly from Turkey. The authors conclude that an intergroup bias caused the effect. In our replications, we intend to understand how an intergroup bias towards robots evolves and investigate the role of ingroup identification on the moderation of intergroup bias. Additionally, we explore alternative explanations for different ratings of the robot: stereotypes and attitudes towards people and manufactured products from both countries. In all three studies, we were not successful in replicating the original effect: participants did not rate the ingroup robot better than the outgroup robot. We did not find an intergroup bias. We did, however, find evidence for our alternative explanations: participants were influenced by attitudes towards people and products from both countries in their ratings of the robots. In this paper, we discuss why we found no intergroup bias, why there was probably no intergroup bias in the original study, if and when ingroup identification and intergroup bias towards robots evolve, and how both concepts are different in all-human interaction and human-robot interaction.

title_r: Drift and Selection in a Language Change Experiment: A Replication
abstract_r: Frequently occurring words tend to have lower rates of regularization. One possibility is that this pattern is driven by selection; another possibility is that it is driven by drift. We will conduct an experiment to shed light on this question, testing whether drift and selection play a role in the lower rate of regularization of more frequently occurring words. The experiment will have a mixed 2x2 design, with word frequency as a within-subjects independent variable and selection as a between-subjects variable. Participants will be asked to learn an artificial language composed of nouns and plural markers. Nouns will belong either to the low- or the high-frequency class. As the high-frequency noun will occur three times more often than the low-frequency noun, the low-frequency noun will be under stronger drift than the high-frequency noun. In the Drift Condition, plural markers will occur in a 1:1 ratio. As both plural markers will be equally common, there will be no directional pressure for participants to use one plural marker over the other. In the Selection Condition, plural markers will occur in a 1:5 ratio. As one plural marker will be more common than the other, there will be directional pressure for participants to use the more common plural marker (the "regular" marker) and not the less common one (the "irregular" marker). We will then measure how participants regularize low- and high-frequency nouns in the presence and absence of selection. We predict that if the frequency of word use affects regularization rate, then the number of irregular nouns (i.e., nouns that occur with both plural markers) will decrease at a faster rate in the low-frequency class than in the high-frequency class.

title_r: Shared History - Country cohesiveness rating study (Replication)
abstract_r: In a recent theoretical paper, Sijilmassi, Safra & Baumard (2024) suggested an account to explain why portraying a group's history as ancient is a recurrent feature of nationalist discourse. In this account, such historical narratives are created because they are thought to activate specific social cognitive mechanisms in their audience--in particular, cognitive mechanisms dedicated to identify fitness interdependence relationships. This account makes two fundamental assumptions. First, individuals should indeed have an intuition that other individuals who perceive themselves as sharing an ancient history (vs. more recent history) should be more likely to cooperate with each other. Second, individuals should indeed have an intuition that other individuals who perceive themselves as sharing an ancient history (vs. more recent history) should also perceive themselves to be more fitness interdependent. We confirmed these hypotheses in a previous preregistered study (see https://osf.io/zv8gc). In this study, we seek to replicate these findings using the same design but a different set of vignettes.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Becker & Cropanzano (2015), in Journal of Organizational Behavior
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Becker & Cropanzano (2015) is that the effect of individual deep acting on job performance would be moderated by team-level deep acting dispersion such that the relationship between deep acting and performance would be positive and stronger in teams with low dispersion, which reflects the following statement from the abstract: "Our findings suggested that team-level deep acting effects can foster benefits for team members (lower emotional exhaustion and higher satisfaction) and organizations (higher job performance)." The study fits a multi-level linear regression model to data from nurses nested in work teams. Job performance is regressed on the cross-level interaction between individual deep acting and team-level deep acting dispersion; the model also includes the separate terms for individual deep acting and team-level team acting dispersion, as well as controls at the individual level for age, team tenure, surface acting, and emotional exhaustion, and a control at the team level for deep acting level. Following the finding of a significant interaction, the authors performed a simple slopes analysis. The evidence for the claim used by the SCORE program is the interaction term alone. The coefficient on the interaction of individual deep acting and team-level deep acting dispersion is -0.40 with a p-value less than .05.

title_r: Quadrisyllabic Word Segmentation in Finnish Speakers: A Focus on Replication
abstract_r: It is suggested that participants during quadrisyllabic word segmentation tasks successfully learn words only when aided by 25 millisecond pauses between words but not if the exposure stream is continuous (Benjamin et al., 2023). The study by Benjamin et al. (2023) was completed on French participants, where the average word length in French is shorter than Finnish. Nevertheless, pauses help with word-form extraction also in Finnish speakers. This project aims to replicate the Finnish-stimuli results with attention toward stimuli, methodology, and further analysis and discussion. title_r: Semantic and action prediction
abstract_r: Theoretical frameworks for language prediction (Pickering & Gambi, 2018; Pickering & Garrod, 2013) and action prediction (Wolpert et al., 2003) suggest that these two predictive processes may rely on shared mechanisms. The idea for this study arose from a previous study that investigated whether there is a link between semantic and action prediction abilities in toddlers. In addition, we tested a group of 21 adults as a control for the main study with toddlers. While we found no evidence for an association between semantic and action prediction in toddlers, the study revealed an association between these predictive abilities in adulthood. We, therefore, decided to examine whether we could replicate this finding in adults in a well-powered replication of the initial study with toddlers and adults. The objective of the present study is to compare adults' abilities to predict semantic meaning and action movements. Using an eye-tracking visual world paradigm, participants are exposed to auditory sentences containing semantically constraining verbs (e.g., "eat"), along with four pictures (where only one is edible). This setup aims to assess their ability to predict semantically. To evaluate their capacity for predicting action movements, the same participants are presented with videos featuring four objects, with two pairs of objects that "belong" together (e.g., spoon and bowl of soup). A hand will grab one object and move it to the corresponding object.

title_r: Threat Sensitivity and Authoritarian Leadership Preferences followup 1
abstract_r: This is a close replication and extension of the forked registration. In the previous study we focused on the relationship between threat sensitivity and support for political candidates who exhibited dominant leadership styles. We manipulated, between subjects, the party affiliation of the candidates. We found that, regardless of the political identity of participants and the political affiliation of candidates (whether they were in or outparty to the participant), heightened threat sensitivity was associated with stronger support for dominant candidates. That is, threat sensitivity did not interact with candidate party affiliation status or participant political identity, nor was there a three way interaction among these predictors. We make a minor adjustment in the current design. Previously, candidate party affiliation was listed at the end of the vignette describing their leadership style. Thus, candidates were possibly evaluated primarily through the lens of their leadership style. Here we will first introduce the candidate's affiliation before describing their leadership style. In this case, candidate's leadership style may be evaluated through the lens of their party affiliation. Our main hypothesis is, again, that individual differences in sensitivity to physical threat are positivity associated with attitudes and voting intention towards hypothetical political leaders who take on an dominant and authoritarian leadership style.

title_r: Trust in Simulated Automated Facial Recognition Systems
abstract_r: The current study will be the first pre-registered experiment in our project investigating how trust in automation affects an operator’s reliance on decisions made by a simulated Automated Facial Recognition System (AFRS) when completing a one-to-one face matching task. This project follows from our previous paper (Carragher & Hancock, 2022), which investigated changes in human face matching performance when assisted by a simulated AFRS. Across five experiments, we showed that while participants significantly improved their own face matching performance when shown the identification decisions of a highly accurate AFRS, the performance of the collaborative human-AFRS pair was sub-optimal, failing to reach the level of performance that the AFRS achieved alone (i.e., human operators tended to overturn correct decisions from the AFRS, while failing to correct errors). This consistent pattern of results demonstrated that, at least in this simplified model of human AFRS oversight, the human operator is a factor limiting the performance of the collaborative system (Carragher & Hancock, 2022; Heyer et al., 2018; White et al., 2015). At the end of several of these experiments, we asked participants some exploratory questions that were designed to gauge their beliefs about the accuracy of humans and algorithms on the face matching task. Participants were also asked whether they thought they were more accurate than an AFRS at face matching, and whether they would they prefer a human or AFRS partner if they were to do the task again. While it was beyond the scope of our first paper to examine how attitudes toward the AFRS might affect collaborative performance, we asked these questions with the intention of informing our future work in this space. The aim of the current project is to investigate how an operator’s trust in automation might influence their reliance on the AFRS decision-aid. Following the publication of this first paper (Carragher & Hancock, 2022), we re-analysed selected performance data alongside the responses to these exploratory questions. This re-analysis revealed that responses to several questions, which could be seen to indirectly measure “trust” in the AFRS, were related to the level of collaborative performance participants achieved when using the AFRS as a decision-aid. For example, participants who indicated that they would rather complete the task again with an AFRS partner achieved a greater increase in performance when using the AFRS as a decision-aid than participants with a preference for a human partner. Likewise, participants who indicated that an AFRS was likely better at face matching than they were (when asked directly) also experienced greater benefit when using an AFRS as a decision-aid, compared to participants who thought their own ability was likely superior to that of the simulated system. Finally, we computed a difference score between the participant’s estimates (as percentages) of their own accuracy on the task and that of the AFRS, such that positive values indicated that they thought the AFRS was better at the task than they were. This index (which is conceptually similar to Lee and Moray’s trust/self-confidence scale discussed below in H4) was positively – and significantly – correlated with improvement from baseline; again, such that participants who thought that the AFRS was more accurate than they were experienced a greater increase when using it as a decision-aid (suggesting greater reliance) than participants who thought their own abilities were better than those of the system. Taken together, these findings suggest that participants who were more open to the idea of AFRS being highly capable/accurate benefited most when given the opportunity to use the system as a decision aid. We intend for this re-analysis to be presented as “Experiment 1” in any resulting manuscript, while the current study will be presented as “Experiment 2”. The aim of the current study is to confirm that we can replicate these findings in a pre-registered experiment that is specifically designed to measure trust in the simulated AFRS, and to show that these findings generalise to a new face matching task.
