title_r: Measuring ethnic discrimination using Investment Games
abstract_r: Over the past decades social scientists have increasingly started to use behavioral games to measure actual trust (Bader and Keuschnigg 2020; Gereke, Schaub, and Baldassarri 2018), cooperation (Keuschnigg and Schikora 2014; Koopmans and Rebers 2009), or discrimination (Enos and Gidron 2016; Fershtman and Gneezy 2001) in an experimental setting. Although artificial, behavioral games are often regarded as more valid because they are incentivized and measure actual decisions rather than attitudes or hypothetical decisions. Based on this assumption, some scholars have investigated, how reflective survey questions are of the decisions take in behavioral games. We follow these studies and test how well several new and established survey constructs predict equivalent measures based on decisions taken in trust games. We replicate earlier studies that investigate how well generalized trust and risk taking predict respective behaviors in trust games. We also investigate the predictive power of new items that hypothetically ask about behavior in a trust game. Most importantly, however, we present new tests of how well three different types of survey measures of perceived discrimination reflect both expected discrimination and actual discrimination in trust games. Moreover, we also investigate whether anti-immigration attitudes predict ethnic discrimination in trust games. That is, in the current study we aim to answer the question how behaviorally relevant the survey questions are, and how good they are as a proxy for actual discrimination. Vice verso, we investigate to what extent measures of perceived discrimination can be used to measure perceived discrimination in individuals’ day-to-day life.

title_r: Investigating the effect of switch probability on the size of the CSE effect in task switching between Simon and Flanker tasks.
abstract_r: Previous research finding the size of the congruency sequence effect (CSE) in repetition trials is greater in dual task blocks than single task blocks suggests that the greater control required for a dual task block leads to increased conflict adaptation. However, another potential explanation in this context could be that the greater working memory load of dual task blocks leads to a magnification of the CSE effect. To distinguish between these accounts, the planned experiment manipulates the level of control required between sessions while keeping the working memory load constant by manipulating the probability of a switch in a task switching setting. Our first experiment investigating this question (see https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/8BNGF) asked participants to switch between two Erikson Flanker tasks (one with number words and one with colour words). However, we also want to investigate whether this effect would be present (and perhaps even larger) when switching between more dissimilar tasks. Therefore, we will carry out a conceptual replication of that experiment, with the one key difference being the use of one Flanker task and one Simon task in the current experiment. Note: as the data collection for this experiment was carried out as part of two Bachelor thesis projects, there are two additional pre-registrations for this experiment available on OSF (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ZBJND, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/EY3BT). These were created for educational purposes and the current pre-registration is the definitive version for this experiment.

title_r: Predicting early vocabulary development from infant prelinguistic communication and caregiver responses
abstract_r: Language development is argued to be built on a foundation of infant-caregiver interactions. While there is robust evidence that infant prelinguistic acts and caregiver talk separately predict later child vocabulary, recent exploratory work suggests that, around children’s first birthdays, the strongest predictor of vocabulary growth over the second year is the dyadic combination of intentional infant communication (vocal and gestural) with relevant caregiver responses (Donnellan et al., 2020). The goal of the current study is to build on this exploratory work in two ways. First, we propose to create a single count measure of infant communicative behaviours that were observed by Donnellan et al to be more or less valuable positive predictors of later language (namely gaze-coordinated vocalisations, index finger points and give and show gestures). This measure is relatively quick-to-code by observing interactions collected remotely via mobile phone and should, in a conceptual replication of Donnellan’s exploratory study, be a positive predictor of later language. Second, we propose to test theoretical proposals regarding the roles of different socially contingent interactions in driving early language learning. In particular, we would like to differentiate the value of vocally responding to infants’ communicative acts in any way (including ‘content light’ responses such as imitating the child’s babble or making minimal remarks like ‘oh’, for example) versus responding in a way that provides linguistic content that is semantically contingent on the infant’s focus of interest. The former should reinforce infants’ communication whereas the latter should additionally provide linguistic content to learn from. Therefore, the primary aims of the current study are to 1) produce a conceptual replication of key elements of Donnellan et al.’s exploratory work to confirm the specific predictive value of infants’ intentional, prelinguistic communicative acts and caregivers’ responses to them for predicting later vocabulary outcomes and 2) compare the predictive value of different types of caregiver response (no responses, any vocal response, ‘content light’ response, specifically semantically contingent response for later vocabulary). Secondary aims include examining whether caregiver education influences the relation between early interactions and later language development. Background Donnellan et al. (2020) reported a novel procedure for predicting vocabulary development in the second year of life via multi-model inference over a comprehensive set of infant behaviours produced at 11 and 12 months. This established the relative predictive value of different infant communicative acts that were hierarchically organised by level of granularity. (The set of infant communicative acts (vocalisations and gestures) considered is reproduced from their paper in the attached PDF preregistration). Also measured was how often infants combined one of these acts with a gaze to their caregiver (a proxy measure for communicative intent that was almost always present for infants’ gestural communication but only sometimes present for vocalisations). Finally, in addition to counting infant communicative acts, Donnellan et al. counted how often caregivers replied to them with a response that was related to what the infant appeared to be attending to and thus likely communicating about. Of all the communicative acts infants produced, the frequency with which infants produced gaze-coordinated vocalisations (where the infant vocalised and looked to the caregiver within one second of doing so) was identified as the most valuable predictor of expressive vocabulary. Other positive predictors included the infants’ production of give and show gestures and index-finger points. These four types of infant communicative act were assumed to be especially predictive because they were likely to have been produced intentionally (as opposed to non-gaze-coordinated vocalisations that may be produced purely for vocal play with no intention of having an effect on a communicative partner). When caregiver responses to infants’ prelinguistic communicative acts were also considered, the dyadic combination of infant gaze-coordinated vocalisations with caregivers’ prompt and semantically contingent responses was revealed to be an even more valuable predictor. It was assumed that this was the case because this measure reflected how often an infant intended to communicate with their caregiver and received a prompt response that contained linguistic content that was semantically relevant to what they had been trying to convey. Finally, the dyadic combination of infant vocalisations of any type (gaze-coordinated or not) and caregiver responses was also among the best predictors. For this count measure, it was not assumed that the infant necessarily had any communicative intent since they were not necessarily looking to the caregiver when producing the vocalisations and it is known that infants often babble to themselves without appearing to want to communicate ostensively by doing so. Nonetheless, it would appear that this sequence of vocalisation and contingent response was a valuable predictor of infant language learning (albeit not as strong as the count restricted to only those vocalisation that were gaze-coordinated and responded to contingently). This perhaps suggests that even when infants vocalisations are not necessarily produced ‘for’ a caregiver (to initiate or continue communication with them), responding contingently may nonetheless be helpful for language learning (a simpler instance of reinforcement and associative learning). On the theoretical front, this exploratory study suggested that specific, socially-contingent sequences of behaviour are important for driving language learning. On the practical front, it suggested that if one sought to predict vocabulary growth over from 12 to 24 months, one could observe a child interacting with their caregiver at 11-12 months and count specific infant acts and infant-caregiver behavioural sequences. While some infant behaviours are incredibly time consuming to code (e.g., all infant vocalisations, which are produced at very high frequency), the most valuable positive predictors observed in this study are relatively quick to count from a 5-minute video. To recap, these behaviours and sequences are as follows: Infant Prelinguistic Communicative Acts (PCAs) that positively predict language outcomes: - Gaze-coordinated vocalisations - Index finger points - Give gestures - Show gestures Infant-caregiver dyad sequences that positively predict language outcomes: - Gaze-coordinated vocalisations + semantically contingent response - Any vocalisation + semantically contingent response This study seeks to build on Donnellan et al.’s exploratory study to test whether we can usefully predict variance in expressive vocabulary size at 17 months by coding 5-minute home videos of 12-month-old infants playing with their caregivers for infant prelinguistic communicative acts and caregiver-infant dyadic sequences of interaction. Importantly, this is a confirmatory test of the claims that arose out of Donnellan et al’s exploratory study. To test theoretical accounts, we seek to establish whether semantically contingent caregiver responses to communicative acts were especially valuable. We also seek to explore the relative value of “content-light”caregiver responses, which includes those that were prompt but not semantically contingent. To address these questions, we will analyse a new dataset with participants from socially diverse areas of the four nations of the UK (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). For these infants and their caregivers, we have measured: - the frequency of infants’ Prelinguistic Communicative Acts (PCAs: gaze-coordinated vocalisations + index-finger pointing gestures + give gestures + show gestures) - the frequency of PCAs that elicited a caregiver response that was either a) semantically contingent or b) “content-light” (i.e., not semantically contingent). - the frequency of PCAs and infants’ non-gaze-coordinated vocalisations that elicited a caregiver response that was either a) semantically contingent or b) “content-light” (i.e., not semantically contingent). By testing the predictive value of these 12-month measures, we will verify the conclusions of the exploratory Donnellan et al. study and theoretical proposals regarding the role of different types of social contingency in early language learning. On a practical level, we will also test whether a relatively quick-to-code measurement of socially contingent interactions during naturalistic play derived from home videos collected remotely is useful in predicting early child language development. The new cohort of 125 families (whose data we will analyses here) took part in a larger Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT) which tested the effects of an early language intervention (see clincialtrials.gov and https://osf.io/kme68/ for pre-registration). Approximately half of the participants in the current study (N = 61) took part in the intervention with the other half (N = 64) taking part in an active control condition. Condition did not have an impact on caregiver reported vocabulary (the outcome variable here). Nonetheless, we control for intervention condition in all analyses. We will also explore the relation between caregiver education (undergraduate degree/no degree) and predictor variables. This document will refer to the pre-registration for the larger RCT where the details are identical.

title_r: Examining the processes underlying implicit impression revision: IAT Data
abstract_r: The present study is a follow-up to a previous study we conducted: https://osf.io/bg38d. This program of research is based on unpublished data from Mann, Ferguson, and Axt in which they examined the effectiveness of two interventions: 1) information that prompts a reinterpretation of information and 2) information that produces a joint negation and affirmation (without reinterpretation). To examine the interventions, participants initially learned negative information about a target, then completed an initial Affect Misattribution Procedure (AMP: Payne et al., 2005), then employed the two interventions and a control condition, followed by a second AMP. The previous researchers applied the AMP model (Payne et al., 2010) to participants’ data and found that the Associations parameter was equivalent between experimental conditions (i.e., reinterpretation, negate + affirm), and reliably different from the Associations parameters from the control condition. We re-analyzed those data using a different parameter estimation method, as well as different models. We replicated Mann, Ferguson, and Axt’s initial findings: both the Reinterpretation and Negate+Affirm manipulations influenced the Associations parameters of the AMP model. Additionally, we found that both Reinterpretation and Negate+Affirm affected the Application (but not the Activation) parameter of the SMT model (Krieglmeyer & Sherman, 2012). This pattern of results suggests that the two experimental manipulations induce a degree of intentional control that cannot be detected by the AMP model. The present research intends to follow up on these findings by applying the same implicit revisions paradigms (reinterpretation and negate+affirm) to the Implicit Association Test (IAT) to investigate whether the same patterns of results replicate across different implicit bias measures.

title_r: Social Priming and Perseverative Errors
abstract_r: This project is a replication study of a pilot study (N = 91) wherein participants were primed with either a close other, neutral other, or neutral object before performing the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (WCST). Following the WCST participants filled out self report measures (Attachment style - ECR, Personality - BFI, and shared reality - SR-G). We observed a statistically significant cross-over interaction effect between conscientiousness and experimental condition. Specifically, we found that participants who received the close other prime made more perseverative errors than those who had received neutral primes (pooled), but this differences was only significant for participants who were at least 1 standard deviation above the mean on conscientiousness. The current study is a direct replication in a larger sample. The only difference is whereas the pilot study used Qualtrics for self-report measures and Inquizit for the WCST, the current study is entirely hosted in Gorilla

title_r: Signaling Dehumanization
abstract_r: In a prior study that was not pre-registered, we found that people view an immoral target as less capable than neutral targets of experiencing hunger and memory--two items we viewed as relatively neutral and not morally valenced. This was the case despite the fact we attempted to mask our hypotheses by including a variety of targets. In this follow-up study, we seek to replicate our original finding that immoral targets are rated as less capable than neutral targets even of neutral, non-valenced capacities. We are including our original items (hunger and memory) as well as two additional items (sickness and pain) which we have pre-test data to suggest are also viewed as non-positive. We predict an overall effect whereby, for all four items, immoral targets will be viewed as less capable than neutral targets.

title_r: Expectation and memory encoding II : How object-location expectancy in visual scenes influences memory formation
abstract_r: This study investigates how schemas influence the formation of new memories. Previous research has shown that information congruent or incongruent with schemas are better remembered than unrelated information. The SLIMM framework predicts a U-shaped memory function based on schema congruency, and recent studies have supported this prediction using experimentally trained rules and immersive virtual reality stimuli (Greve et al., 2019; Quent et al., 2022). SLIMM also suggests that different memory types are associated with each end of the curve, supported by distinct brain systems: the medial temporal lobe (MTL) system and the ventral medial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC). This study is a replication of our previously preregistered study (see: https://osf.io/9py2j), which used static images instead of immersive virtual reality. In line with Quent et al. (2022), our previous results confirmed the predicted u-shape function that shows information congruent and incongruent with schemas is better remembered than unrelated information. However, to ensure a more accurate assessment of participant-specific expectancy levels, a small procedural change is introduced in this replication study. Expectancy ratings are now collected at the time of encoding rather than after retrieval, as participants' ratings may have been influenced by the prior encoding and retrieval of all object-location scenes. title_r: Prioritization of effort cues in a Cued Reward Difficulty paradigm with Random Dot Motion task
abstract_r: Recent literature suggests that preparatory cues predicting the level of trial difficulty and reward influence task performance (Krebs et al., 2012; Schevernels et al., 2014). Participants specifically improve performance on hard trials when a high reward is prospected as compared to a low reward. Vassena et al. (2019) have further investigated how reward and difficulty information is integrated in time. In an arithmetic task, participants showed the expected performance benefit for high reward trials compared to low reward, either when the difficulty and the reward cue dimensions were presented simultaneously or when the reward dimension was prioritized, but not when the difficulty dimension was prioritized (by temporal segregation). In a recent online study, we observed a similar prioritization effect based on the spatial position of the cues. As shown in Figure 1 (https://osf.io/ay3wm/), each cue was composed by two centrally presented vertical sliders, and the slider track (placed at the bottom or at the top) anticipated trial difficulty (easy or hard) and reward (low or high). Crucially, we observed a response time benefit on hard trials when a high reward was prospected as compared to a low reward, but only when the reward information was spatially prioritized (i.e., the reward slider was the left one). The prioritization effect in our pilot data (i.e., modulation of reward x difficulty interaction) is an extension of the prioritization effect observed by Vassena and colleagues (2019) (i.e., modulation of reward effect), possibly because the RDM task used in our study allowed more subtle manipulations of task difficulty. In the current experiment, we want to replicate the spatial prioritization effect of reward vs. difficulty cues with the RDM task. Moreover, in contrast to our previous study, in which all the trials were correctly cued, we will add an intermediate difficulty condition on 1/3 of the trials (incorrectly cued by easy and hard cues). This addition will allow to test how difficulty cues influence task preparation/effort allocation, and how this is affected by spatial prioritization of cues.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Montez & Hayward (2014), from Demography
abstract_r: The claim selected from Montez & Hayward (2014) is that early-life SES independently predicts transitions across degrees of functional ability. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "Within levels of educational attainment, adults from disadvantaged childhoods lived fewer total and active years, and spent a greater portion of life impaired compared with adults from advantaged childhoods." The dependent variable captured the transition from healthy to reporting difficulty with (including inability to do) at least one of six activities of daily living (ADL)—walking across a room, dressing, bathing, eating, getting in and out of bed, and toileting. The transition rates are estimated from multivariate hazard models using PROCLIFEREG in SAS 9.3, which assume that the variation in transition times between states within an exposure interval can be described by an exponential survival distribution (i.e., the risk was constant within the age interval). The focal test result is reported in the “Healthy to ADL” panel in figure 1 (capture in the dark gray error bars). The dark gray bars show that multiple SES adversities predicted unfavorable transitions—particularly functional deterioration. SES adversities and deterioration exhibited a dose–response relationship (ancillary analyses did not find significant nonlinearities), with three or more adversities consistently predicting an elevated risk of decline (p < .05) compared with zero adversities.

title_r: Agreeableness and Theory of Mind Correlates Replication 2
abstract_r: This study aims to replicate an effect found in the original "Agreeableness and Theory of Mind Correlates" study (linked here: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/Z2TND). In that study we aimed to find correlations between the personality trait agreeableness and some theory of mind measures. We used the HEXACO personality inventory to assess agreeableness, and three tasks to assess theory of mind: the Reading the Mind in the Eyes task, the Strange Stories task, and the Sandbox task. We found no significant correlations between agreeableness scores and any theory of mind scores but did, however, find a significant correlation between scores on the personality trait honesty-humility and Strange Stories scores. We then successfully replicated this correlation in a subsequent study and now want to run another replication study, addressing some limitations in these first two studies: 1. Poor reliability was observed for HEXACO personality traits (Cronbach’s α ranged from .232 - .555). 2. No control stories were used in the Strange Stories task Addressing the first limitation, we will use the 60-item version of the HEXACO personality inventory rather than the 24-item version we had used previously. Using the 60-item measure should significantly improve the its reliability, giving us a more robust measure of honesty-humility. Addressing the second limitation, we will add control stories to the Strange Stories measure. This helps us ensure the correlation we observed involves the perspective taking abilities assessed by the Strange Stories task, not just the ability to remember details from the stories. Besides these changes, this new replication study will mirror the design of our previous study. We will keep the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Task in this replication to mirror the procedure of the original study, as participants in that study completed the Reading the Mind in the Eyes task before completing the Strange Stories task. The order in which the Reading the Mind in the Eyes task and the Strange Stories task appear will be randomized to control for order effects. The last change to this new study is that the order of the Strange Stories and control stories will be randomized to control for order effects.

title_r: Comparative Priming - Human replication with pigeon methods
abstract_r: We are studying perceptual priming (hereafter, priming), a type of unconscious visual memory. This study is based on Brodbeck (1997), which found human-like priming in pigeons, and Basile and Hampton (2013), which did not find human-like priming in rhesus monkeys, despite using similar testing conditions to those employed with pigeons. Because priming is expected to be a basic feature of the visual system, this discontinuity is surprising. As part of an overarching research project to resolve this discrepancy, we are systematically comparing priming between humans and pigeons. In pilot testing, we found that humans did not show priming when tested with the methods that had been used with pigeons. In the previous preregistered experiment, we confirmed that this failure to find priming was not due to experimenter incompetence by demonstrating that we can successfully measure priming effects in humans under the conditions in which humans are typically tested. In this experiment, we will evaluate whether our pilot finding, that humans do not show priming when tested with pigeon-like methods, was a fluke; we will run a direct replication.

title_r: Individual Motivations and Psychosocial Resources Predict Change in the Level and Appraisal of Domain-Specific Perceived Expectations for Active Aging: Analyses of the Jena Study on Social Change and Human Development
abstract_r: Recent evidence suggests that certain socioeconomic and health resources are associated with perceived expectations for active aging (PEAA) in a domain-specific or domain-general way (Pavlova et al., in press). Moreover, individual motivations and other psychological variables appeared to contribute to PEAA more than objective or external factors such as SES or characteristics of household members (Radoš et al., in preparation). However, it is unclear whether individual motivations and psychological resources can also predict change in domain-specific PEAA over time and what is the role of motivations and resources in appraising overall (i.e., not domain-specific) PEAA as a threat or a challenge (secondary appraisals). The objectives of the current study are to investigate (a) whether individual motivations and personal and social resources predict change in domain-specific (i.e., physical and mental health, social engagement) PEAA over one year, and (b) whether the combination of motivation and different types of individual resources (socioeconomic, health, personal, and social) predict change in the appraisal of overall PEAA (i.e., as a threat or a challenge) over one year. This study will also serve as a conceptual replication of parts of our parallel study on a different sample (https://osf.io/24pw8). To these ends, we will utilize two waves of survey data from the Jena Study on Social Change and Human Development from a sample of young-old Germans (aged 56-75 at baseline).

title_r: Re-examining the role of eye contact within online disinhibition on the behavioural effects of swearing
abstract_r: This study is looking to replicate and extend previous research (Dobson & Haffey, in prep.) which had investigated the role of researcher presence in counteracting online disinhibition, a psychological construct thought to block the behavioural effects of swearing in unsupervised online testing environments. Repeated monotonous vocalisation of single swearwords has been found to increase pain tolerance to aversive stimuli (Stephens et al., 2009), increase physical strength (Stephens et al., 2018), and increase the undertaking of risky behaviour (tested via a simple, computerised task; Dobson & Haffey, in prep.; Stephens et al., 2022). These findings were robustly obtained using ‘face-to-face’ testing methods in laboratory-based studies, but did not replicate using unsupervised online testing methods due to the Covid-19 pandemic’s enforced lockdowns. This was thought to be because unsupervised online environments can result in behaviours consistent with being in a disinhibited state (Lapidot-Lefler & Barak, 2012; Stephens et al., 2022): the anonymity and lack of eye-contact pre-empting any subsequent effect of swearing, blocking the expected effect. Adjusting the online testing methodology to use ‘researcher-guided’ testing, in which an online ‘video call’ allowed the researcher to supervise each participant undertaking the study, and ensuring the participant made eye-contact with the researcher whilst vocalising each word (swearword/control) within that study, regenerated the expected effects of swearing on both physical strength and risky behaviour (Stephens et al., 2022). Dobson and Haffey (in prep.) successfully replicated the ability to regenerate the expected behavioural effect of vocalised swearing in online testing environments using enforced eye-contact and researcher supervision via ‘video calling’ software. However, as part of that study they also tested whether requiring participants make eye-contact whilst vocalising a swearword with a researcher displayed on screen in a pre-recorded video, i.e, the researcher was not even virtually “live”, would also generate the expected behavioural effects of swearing on risky behaviour. Their results found that requiring eye-contact with a non-live researcher in a pre-recorded video could generate behavioural effects of vocalised swearing. The current study aims to: 1. replicate the finding that eye-contact made to a researcher in a pre-recorded video whilst swearing can generate subsequent increased in risk-taking behaviour, strengthening Dobson and Haffey’s (in prep.) original finding. 2. extend that finding to see whether (i) a pre-recorded video has to show the researcher’s entire face/upper body (as originally used by Dobson and Haffey) or whether a video of just the researcher’s eyes would be enough to counteract any online disinhibition and allow swearing to generate the expected effect; and (ii) whether the same increase in risky behaviour after vocalised swearing can be generated without a video, using just a static image of the researcher’s eyes instead. The study will be a direct replication of Dobson and Haffey (in prep.) ‘video’ testing condition. The only alterations will be that, along with the original pre-recorded video of the researcher, a new video of just the researcher’s eyes will be created, as well as a static image of the researcher’s eyes. These will then be used in a multi-session, repeated measures study.

title_r: Testing the dual representation account of memory for trauma: Experiment 2
abstract_r: In our previous experiment (pre-registered at this link: https://osf.io/fxj9n), we aimed to test the dual representation account (DRA) of traumatic memory (Brewin et al., 2010), by applying a visuospatial interference procedure (Reminders+Tetris) which previous trauma film paradigm studies have found to reduce involuntary memories (Holmes et al., 2009), while leaving voluntary recall and recognition unaltered (Lau Zhu et al., 2019; 2021), supporting the notion of separate trauma memory traces. Using a between-participants design with three factors – intentionality of retrieval (voluntary or involuntary), content of films (negative or neutral) and intervention (Reminders+Tetris or Reminders+Podcast control) – we aimed to test three predictions derived from the DRA. First, we aimed to replicate the functional dissociation between voluntary and involuntary memory after the visuospatial interference intervention, even when we match the retrieval conditions more closely than in the original reports. Second, we aimed to test the prediction that the effect of the intervention will be greater in the negative condition than the neutral condition. Finally, we aimed to test the prediction that voluntary memory would decrease in the negative compared to neutral condition. We used a Bayesian sequential design and stopped when evidence for the first two hypotheses reached a threshold of BF₀₁>3, ending with a total sample size of N=240. However, the two hypotheses that we used to decide on stopping relied on a particular effect being observed in the data. Specifically, both assumed that employing the visuospatial intervention (Reminders+Tetris), compared with our podcast control condition, would significantly decrease involuntary memory for the negative film. Crucially, the data from our initial experiment did not support this assumption. Contrary to previous literature, there was no indication that involuntary memories were reduced in the Tetris group relative to the verbal control condition (Podcast). Specifically, regarding lab-based (trauma film) involuntary memory counts within a vigilance task, the Tetris group had marginally higher intrusion counts (M = 12.5, SD = 5.3) than the Podcast group (M = 10.0, SD = 5.6), although the evidence level was inconclusive (BF₁₀ = 0.98). Similarly, unique details within lab-based (trauma film) involuntary memories were marginally higher in the Tetris group (M = 15.6, SD = 9.2) compared to the Podcast group (M = 13.7, SD = 8.1), with anecdotal evidence favouring the null (BF₁₀ = 0.35). This failure to replicate a reduction in lab-based trauma intrusions following visuospatial interference means that the evidence for the null in our interaction-based hypotheses, which led to stopping data collection, no longer provide a valid test of the DRA. Put simply, these DRA-derived hypotheses can no longer be tested using the data from this initial experiment. The present study (Experiment 2) is therefore an attempt to robustly replicate the previously observed effects of visuospatial interference on lab-based intrusions using a refined methodological approach, which is more closely matched with previous protocols that have produced this effect, using both lab-based and diary-based measures of involuntary memory (i.e. Lau-Zhu et al., 2019). To do so, Experiment 2 will differ from Experiment 1 in the following ways. First, the verbal control task employed in Experiment 1 (listening to a political podcast) has been replaced with a passive rest period, to more closely align with Lau Zhu et al. (2019). This change addresses the possibility that our previous control task was not sufficiently neutral in topic and may have unintentionally elicited visuospatial cognition. Second, while in Experiment 1 Visuospatial task instructions and a practice took place after the reminder cues, all participants will now complete a practice session of Tetris with instructions emphasising mental rotation, before film viewing. This reduces the interval between delivering reminder cues and beginning the intervention and is more aligned with Lau Zhu et al. (2019). Third, the structured filler period between the film and the reminder cues will be increased from 5min in Experiment 1 to 30min here, replicating the 30min filler period in Lau Zhu et al. (2019). Fourth, the experimenter will now be fully blinded to participants' allocation to the intervention or control condition, with post-reminder task instructions administered without the experimenter present. This is in contrast with both Experiment 1 and Lau Zhu et al. (2019), in which the experimenter directly administered the intervention, creating the potential for experimenter-related bias in subsequent memory measures. Fifth, given the restricted aim of replicating the previously observed effects of visuospatial interference on intrusive memories, in Experiment 2 we will only examine involuntary memories (i.e. no voluntary memory test) of the trauma film (i.e. no neutral film). Finally, unlike the prior study which involved only a brief period of experimenter training, more extensive experimenter training was employed prior to this experiment, across several sessions, covering the delivery of trauma film viewing instructions, mental rotation instructions and involuntary memory measurement instructions.

title_r: Neural correlates and subjective assessments of multimodal training on perception of foreign language prosody
abstract_r: This is a follow-up to a previous pre-registration: https://osf.io/rbkuh Japanese pitch accent is crucial for L2 learners to master in order to communicate effectively with native speakers. Pitch accent in Japanese is phonemic, meaning that it varies by word and can mark the difference between otherwise alike words. For example, /kami/ means ‘god’ with a high-low (HL) pitch pattern, while it means ‘hair’ with a LH pitch pattern. Although pitch accent is highly important in Japanese, it can be very difficult for many L2 learners to perceive and acquire, especially native English speakers, as English does not make distinctions based on pitch. Our previous research evaluated Japanese naive participants using a pre/post test design and one of three training conditions: (1) audio and a flat written notation, (2) audio and a visual spatial written notation, and (3) audio with visual spatial written notation and left hand gestures that trace the pitch accent pattern of the words (Friedman, Shiner, Kaicher, Kelly, & Hirata 2021). Results indicate that the audio and visual spatial notation training (2) was most robust in its learning benefits, as participants improved significantly on both trained and novel words. Such results suggest that gestures may distract from useful visual input, and may not benefit learning on tasks in which phonological demands are high. The present study is a follow up experiment which explores the neural mechanism behind the observed behavior. Using the Emotiv EPOC+ EEG system will allow us to measure oscillations within the frequency band and assess alpha (8-12 Hz) and theta (4-7 Hz) activity during training sessions. Previous studies have shown that changes in the alpha and theta bands of EEG oscillations reflect task difficulty and cognitive load (Antonenko et al. 2010). Specifically, decreased alpha activity indicates an increased cognitive load, whereas increased theta activity reflects greater cognitive load. As per previous research, alpha power will be measured from occipital electrodes (O1, O2) and theta power will be measured from prefrontal electrodes (AF3, AF4). Power values as measured by the Emotiv software will be averaged for each trial and then averaged across trials for one alpha average and one theta average for each condition per participant. No baseline will be used, as we are interested in comparing absolute power values across conditions. Additionally, a time-locked baseline would not be possible due to the nature of our stimuli; namely, the participants will be hearing sentences without long pauses in between, resulting in a baseline that may not accurately differentiate a true resting state from an attentive state. Gesture perception has been found to reduce cognitive load as measured by alpha and theta oscillations, but it is not known how gesture production affects cognitive load (Pi et al. 2020). In the proposed study, we aim to replicate the results from our previous research (Friedman et al. 2021), this time using EEG and subjective measures to investigate demands on cognitive load during Japanese pitch accent learning. Rather than a between-subjects training design, we will use a within-subjects design and add a fourth training condition in which participants gesture with their right hand rather than left. We plan to measure EEG oscillations during the third repetition of the training sentence, which will have no spatial notation or gesture, reflecting the priming effect of the first two repetitions (which will have the multimodal features corresponding to that condition) on cognitive load as the word is processed. In addition, we plan to conduct exploratory analyses on neural synchrony measures during these training sessions, as studies indicate it may provide a mechanism for multisensory integration of information that matches across sensory signals (Pouw et al. 2021).

title_r: Revisiting reduced audiovisual benefit for nonnative-accented speech
abstract_r: This experiment builds on the direct replication of Yi et al. (2013), in which we found reduced audiovisual benefit for nonnative (Korean-accented English) speakers compared to native speakers. Notably, in both our replication study and Yi and colleagues’ original study, both native and nonnative speech was presented at the same signal-to-noise ratio (-4 dB SNR), resulting in overall poorer performance in the nonnative compared to native conditions. Thus, one alternative explanation for the findings is that there is a smaller AV benefit for nonnative speech than native speech because the overall difficulty of that condition was greater. In this experiment, we aim to test whether there will still be a reduced AV benefit for nonnative speech if the difficulties of the two accent conditions were reversed. In other words, we seek to confirm that the observed difference in AV benefit is due to the accent of the speakers, not the difficulty of the task.

title_r: Fall memories of the spring pandemic: Effects of age
abstract_r: The COVID-19 pandemic has had far reaching effects on all of us, and we are only beginning to grasp the full extent of its impact. The novelty and disruptions to daily life that arose with the pandemic provide a unique opportunity to understand how individuals of different ages remember portions of the pandemic. Although many prior studies have looked at “Flashbulb”-type memories for stressful events, never before has there been such a sustained, shared event such as this one. We previously collected memory data from our participants in early June, with a particular interest in how age affects the way that adults remember the spring phase of the pandemic. We found that age was associated with a greater focus on the positive aspects of the pandemic and with increased vividness and reexperiencing of the participant’s most positive pandemic memory. These findings were consistent with an earlier finding from the study of the 2013 Marathon bombing (Ford et al., 2018) that demonstrated that older age was associated with an increased tendency to focus on positive aspects or “silver linings” of the event (e.g., the city coming together). We aim to determine whether we will replicate these findings in the current study with memory data collected four months after our initial memory assessment. In addition, we will look at the effects of age on the change in these memory ratings and narratives over time. Prior work from our lab has revealed that age is associated with a tendency for memories to become less negative over time (Ford et al., 2018). However, this will be the first time multiple memory assessments will be collected for a public event that has not yet resolved. This will be the first assessment of older adults’ resilience to a sustained negative stressor, determining whether their ability to focus on the positive persists even as it extends into its seventh and eighth months. On the one hand, we may replicate the same patterns as seen previously when examining memory for a time-delimited event like the 2013 bombing. On the other hand, it is plausible that we may not replicate the same patterns given the sustained nature of the current pandemic; in other words, participants are still directly experiencing the effects of the pandemic during this second memory assessment, and that may lead to different patterns with regard to the associations with age, time. In the present study, we recruited and regularly assessed a large sample of adults ages 18 to 90. For the present study, we will include the subset of these participants who completed at least the memory portion of the questionnaires that were sent out in fall 2020. As there is a heavy skew toward North American participants, we will restrict analyses to that sample to improve the homogeneity of the timeline of the experienced spring pandemic. For analyses examining change over time, the sample will be restricted to those participants who completed memory surveys in both summer and fall.

title_r: Textbook maps and homeland attachments in Ecuador
abstract_r: We explore the effects of maps on national identity formation, territorial identity formation and norms of willingness to sacrifice for the homeland. Following on earlier research on the effects of maps in Bolivia, Argentina, Thailand, Colombia and Chile, we replicate and extend our analyses in Ecuador. Ecuador offers a rare opportunity to examine and test for the enduring effects of maps taught in school years. Until 1995 -- and since the mid 1940s -- maps of Ecuador used in geography textbooks, school atlases and wall maps all included a very large area in the East, where the protocol of Rio de Janeiro was declared inoperative. This area was often but not always highlighted as disputed with Peru. After the Cenepa War of 1995, a peace settlement was finally reached and subsequent maps no longer include that area as part of Ecuador. Ecuador thus offers a unique opportunity to compare the effects of two different maps of the same country, by age cohort. Using an original survey experiment, we examine whether exposure to the national map inspires willingness to sacrifice for homeland defense, and whether the pre-1995 map and the post-1998 map have differential effects depending on the age of the respondent. We expect that both the old and new maps will increase willingness to sacrifice among older respondents, who would be familiar with both maps. Younger respondents, however, who were educated only with the new map should respond more strongly to the new map than the old one.

title_r: Overcoming Algorithm Aversion with Transparency: Can Transparent Predictions Change User Behavior?
abstract_r: Previous work has shown that allowing users to adjust a machine learning (ML) model's predictions can reduce aversion to imperfect algorithmic decisions. However, these results were obtained in situations where users had no information about the model's reasoning. Thus, it remains unclear whether interpretable ML models could further reduce algorithm aversion or even render adjustability obsolete. In this paper, we replicate a well-known study that examines the effect of adjustable predictions on algorithm aversion and extend it by introducing an interpretable ML model that visually reveals its decision logic. Through a pre-registered user study with 280 participants, we investigate how transparency interacts with adjustability in reducing aversion to algorithmic decision-making. Our results replicate the adjustability effect, showing that allowing users to modify algorithmic predictions mitigates aversion. Transparency's impact appears smaller than expected and was not significant for our sample. Furthermore, the effects of transparency and adjustability appear to be more independent than expected.

title_r: Experiment 1A: Replication of the head nodding and shaking effect in a web-based experiment
abstract_r: Given that nodding and shaking head motions are used as communicative signals, such as signals of approval (and denial), these motions might be expected to modulate perceived trait impressions of model faces. We used movie clips of nodding and shaking head motions of computer-generated figures and examined the modulation effects of these motions on perceived trait impressions. Results showed that the nodding head motion significantly increased ratings of subjective likeability and approachability compared to the shaking or control conditions, whereas the shaking motion did not affect ratings. However, previous studies have primarily examined this effect using laboratory-based experiments with Japanese university students, which limits the generalizability and replicability of the results. Therefore, the present study examined whether this effect can be observed in a web-based experiment and for crowdsourcing service workers. In this experiment (Experiment 1A), we re-examined the effects of nodding and shaking motions on perceived likeability.

title_r: Active Learning about the Self (ALaS) study II
abstract_r: In this study, we investigate whether 4- to 8- year-old children and adults make effective training choices depending on the task characteristics, with the final goal of maximizing their performance at test. In particular, we study whether participants tailor their learning strategies to boost their strengths (i.e., maximizing wins) or compensate for their weaknesses (i.e., minimizing losses). We aim to replicate the results of a prior study and address some of its shortcomings. Participants play three different game blocks presented to them on a tablet screen. On each block, participants are presented with two sets of eight cards each. Each set of cards belongs to a different game: In the animal picture game, they have to guess the animal illustrated on the picture, whereas in the object picture game, they have to guess the object illustrated on the picture. In both games, we presented participants with pictures of familiar animals or objects (e.g., a cat or a soccer ball). However, we mask varying proportions of the pictures, making it easy to recognize the object or animal at hand in the easy game but masking large parts of the pictures in the difficult game, making it almost impossible to identify the objects or animals. During the familiarization phase, participants play 4 cards of each game and receive feedback for their performance. Participants are expected to correctly identify 3 out of 4 cards in the easy game and 0 out of 4 cards in the difficult game. Participants are not given the correct answers for the cards they guess wrong or do not know. After the familiarization phase, we tell participants that eventually, they will be tested on all the 8 cards of one of the two games. We incentivize children by promising them to get one sticker for each correct answer and losing one sticker for each incorrect answer. We incentivize adults by telling them that those participants who answered all items correctly will eventually participate in the lottery of a 50€ amazon voucher. Critically, we will manipulate whether we tell participants that eventually they will be tested on the easy game (easy game condition), the difficult game (difficult game condition), or a randomly chosen game (random game condition). Participants then decide which game they want to practice with all cards of one of the two games. This choice is our dependent measure. In this practice phase, we tell participants the correct answers for all the cards in the game they choose. After this, participants enter the testing phase, where they are tested either on the easy game (easy game condition) or on the difficult game (difficult game condition/ random condition). After the test is over, participants move on to the second and third game blocks. These blocks are designed precisely as the first block, but we always present participants with a condition they have not yet encountered in the previous block in a within-subjects design. Our aim is to see how participants adapt their practice decisions compared to the first round. The order of games, assignment to difficulty level, and assignment of animal and object stimuli to the two games are pseudorandomized.

title_r: Visual Transposed word serial processing
abstract_r: Evidence has supported the idea that readers lexically process words serially (one at a time), but evidence by Mirault et al. (2018) has demonstrated a transposed word effect. This effect is where readers have difficulty deciding that sentences such as “do love you me? “are ungrammatical, in which the transposition of two adjacent words (i.e., love you) would form a grammatical sentence, compared to sentences in which the transposition of two words does not result in grammaticality (e.g. the cat white was slowly). This has been taken as evidence for the parallel lexical processing of multiple words simultaneously. Evidence has also shown that the transposed word effect can be attributed to a combination of noisy bottom-up word position coding and top-down syntactic constraints. This effect can be interpreted within serial, as opposed to parallel, reading models. The present study will examine the transposed word effect by varying modality input and type of processing for which each of the two transposed words will be presented. In the previous experiment, we observed the transposed word effect in visual grammatical decision task. However, we aim to replicate the previous findings and assess this pattern of findings with different input modalities (auditory and crossmodal) and different processing strategies (visual transposed word parallel, crossmodal transposed word serial and crossmodal transposed word parallel). In this experiment, we manipulate sequence type and later on modality. Thus, we expected that the transposed word effect in visual serial paradigm to be replicated such that transposed words are responded to more slowly and are more error prone than control words. However, the main focus is on accuracy.

title_r: Black Women's Perceptions of Social Comparison Perceptions in Organizations
abstract_r: Black Americans are severely underrepresented in organizational settings. Inadequate representation is consequential because it can activate concerns about fit and belonging, subsequently reducing intentions to remain in such settings. Although the relationship between low numerical representation and worse outcomes has been well-established in prior research, limited work has examined the mechanisms through which this relationship emerges. The current work focuses on the role of social comparison perceptions (i.e., beliefs that others are making direct comparisons between oneself and another ingroup member) as a mechanism that can undermine Black Americans’ outcomes (e.g., sense of belonging) in organizational contexts. Previous studies conducted by the research team show that when Black adults are placed in a hypothetical organization where they are one of two (token status) or several (non-token status) Black employees, they report stronger social comparison perceptions, which subsequently predicts decreases in belonging, willingness to participate in the organization, and motivation to perform well in the organization. In a follow-up experiment, we replicated and extended these findings by showing that when Black women were placed in a hypothetical situation where they had token status based on their racial or gender identity (e.g., when they were one of two Black employees or one of two women in the organization, respectively) relative to when they had non-token status, they were more likely to report social comparison perceptions. Of note, the demographic representation of the organization impacted social comparison perceptions regardless of whether Black women perceived that they were being compared to a Black man or a White woman. Furthermore, another significant main effect showed that Black women reported stronger social comparison perceptions in response to a Black man (versus a White woman), regardless of the demographic representation of the organization. In the current experiment, we aim to replicate and extend our previous work by testing whether perceived social comparison perceptions (observed when Black women have token status) are mitigated in response to a multi-pronged intervention (e.g., when employees at the organization make individualizing statements about Black individuals/women and organizational policies promote employee individuation). Black women will be randomized to one of six conditions in a 2 (target: Black man, White woman) x 3 (demographic composition: non-token status, token status, token status with intervention). We hypothesize that, consistent with our previous study, Black women who are in the token (versus non-token) condition will report stronger social comparison perceptions and experience worse outcomes (e.g., lower belonging, willingness to participate, and intentions to the remain at the organization) than participants in the non-token condition. Moreover, we expect that these results will emerge regardless of whether Black women see a Black male target or White female target. Additionally, we expect that Black women in the token + intervention condition (e.g., who see organizational policies and employees who individualize Black individuals or women) will exhibit significantly better outcomes than Black women in the token condition who are not exposed to such statements. As in the previous studies, we also expect that the relationship between the demographic composition manipulation and Black women’s outcomes (e.g., belonging, willingness to participate, motivation, and intentions to remain in the organization) will emerge via social comparison perceptions. Therefore, this online experiment will test a multi-pronged intervention to reduce social comparison perceptions (e.g., concerns about being compared to other ingroup members) and improve organizational outcomes for Black women.

title_r: Cognitive and social foundations of competency judgments in DEI contexts (Initiative Replication)
abstract_r: How do people perceive successful candidates from marginalized groups? Across a series of studies, we investigate how people evaluate successful candidates differently when they are from a marginalized social group (Hibble; “DEI'' condition) versus a dominant one (Glerk; “perpetuating inequality” condition). In previous studies, we found that selection process did not significantly impact participants' judgments of the chosen candidate. However, judgments were shaped by the perceived initiative behind the selection ("DEI" versus "perpetuate inequality"). Overall, participants rated candidates more positively if they were selected through the “DEI” initiative. Our data suggest that this effect is moderated by causal attribution and participant priors. Across conditions, participants who attributed the selected candidate’s success solely to their quality (instead of social group membership) rated the candidate more favorably. Conservatism also predicted lower ratings of candidates selected under a “DEI” initiative. In the present study, we aim to replicate these effects and further explore how political ideology shapes evaluations of successful candidates.

title_r: Re-examination of temporal dynamics of action-induced memory enhancement: online replication
abstract_r: Yebra et al. (2019, Nat. Commun.) demonstrated that the items presented with the action executions were better memorized than the items presented with the action inhibitions (i.e., action-induced memory enhancement: AIME). However, what factors drive the enhance effect remains poorly understood. We have investigated whether the AIME is modulated by the temporal relationship between the item presentation and the actions. Our previous work showed that action execution enhanced memories only for the items presented after the action execution. On the other hand, the memories for items presented before the action executions and inhibitions were not significantly different. However, Kinder and Buss (2021, Mem. Cogn.) reported that even items presented during the action inhibition were better memorized compared to those presented in motor-neutral task like a counting task. Thus, it remains inconclusive whether there is no enhancement before the action. In this study, we aim to replicate our previous finding (i.e., more prominent memory enhancement after the action) and investigate whether the memory before the action is enhanced compared with that during the motor neutral task.

title_r: A psychometric review and conceptual replication study of the Five Facets of Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) latent structure
abstract_r: The Five Facets of Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) is a popular tool in mindfulness research. However, some controversies are being upheld regarding its psychometric qualities and its replicability This study introduces novel evidence regarding two main issues: Firstly, questionable psychometric practices in validation studies confirmed previous concerns about the FFMQ’s properties. Secondly, a replication study using frequentist and bayesian techniques tested the structure of the FFMQ. The original structure did not provide a good fit with both techniques, while a proposed alternative provided mixed results. Systematic fit improvements were found in both techniques regarding the exclusion of the Observe facet and the inclusion of method factors. Therefore, a failed replication of the structure of the FFMQ was concluded. Alternatively, a new provisional FFMQ model was proposed. Future research proposals on improving techniques and models towards mindfulness assessment are presented and discussed.

title_r: Individual Differences In Second-Order False-Belief Understanding and Executive Processes: A Further Investigation Into the Specificity of the Associations
abstract_r: In a previous pre-registered study (osf.io/vf7dn), our group was among the first to examine how individual differences in three foundational executive functions (i.e., inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility and working memory) relate to the extent of adults’ Second-Order False-Belief (SOFB) performance. Our analysis revealed moderate-to-high associations between SOFB and both working memory (WM) and cognitive flexibility (CF), but no presence of significant associations between SOFB and inhibitory control. In this planned follow up research we aim to replicate and build on these findings by conducting an in-depth assessment of the specific contribution of both WM and CF to SOFB reasoning in adulthood. According to dominant frameworks (e.g., Mayr & Kliegl, 2000; Unsworth & Engle, 2007), WM and CF can be decomposed into finer-grained components. We thus proceed to increase the specificity of our prior findings by examining whether the different processes that compose WM and CF differentially relate to SOFB.

title_r: Societal Relevance of Humanities Research: Follow-up replication
abstract_r: This study investigates 150 documents for 5 fields of research in the humanities (History, Philosophy, Religion, Linguistics, Literature), i.e. 20 journal papers and 10 books per field. For each of these documents, the associated abstracts will be rated for a) whether they are societally relevant or not; and b) for their relevance-rank compared to that of abstracts from each of the other disciplines. The rating will be done by two groups of raters: one of at least 5 (and at most 10) PhD students or recent PhD holders (2018 or later) from humanities fields (at least one for each of the five fields listed above); and one of at least 5 (and at most 10) PhD students or recent PhD holders (2018 or later) from non-humanities fields. We will then use these two measures to 1) evaluate the extent to which rater characteristics (such as chauvinism and strictness) and the abstract field influence ratings, and 2) evaluate the societal relevance of research in the humanities, and each of the subfields separately. The study was approved by the KU Leuven Social and Societal Ethics Committee (File G-2023-6847-R5(MIN) (v.1.3)) NOTE: Due the funding running out, we have to start data-collection before the full analysis plan is ready. We will therefore start collecting the data without accessing it. title_r: Representation of dynamic and static materials in the human brain
abstract_r: We encounter a variety of different materials in our environment: rigid objects, deformable objects, as well as liquid and granular ‘stuff’. Yet, fMRI research has largely focused only on rigid objects. Several studies have investigated the role of the lateral occipital complex (LOC) in extracting the 3D shape of rigid objects (e.g., Kourtzi & Kanwisher, 2000) or the role of the ‘physics network’ in judging the physical properties and relations of rigid things (Fischer, Mikhael, Tenenbaum, & Kanwisher, 2016; Schwettmann, Tenenbaum, & Kanwisher, 2019; Pramod, Cohen, Tenenbaum, & Kanwisher, 2022). In a previous experiment (in the following referred to as Experiment 1; preregistered under: Paulun, V. C. (2023, January 17). Representation of dynamic materials in the human brain. Retrieved from osf.io/36bva) we found that both LOC and the physics system respond to dynamic materials more than scrambled or intact control conditions albeit the physics system responds more strongly to ‘Stuff’ than ‘Things’, whereas LOC responds at least as strongly (or more strongly) to deformable materials than to rigid things. We further found evidence for two bilateral regions, one ventral and one dorsal, that respond more strongly to ‘Stuff” > ‘Things’. The purpose of the current experiment (in the following referred to as Experiment 2) is threefold: 1) We want to replicate our previous findings while controlling for eye movements, i.e., subjects have to maintain fixation throughout the experiment. 2) We want to test whether the results depend on the dynamic nature of the stimuli or whether we will find the same pattern of results if we present static snapshots of the movies used in Experiment 1. 3) In case that we replicate the finding of a ventral region that responds more strongly to ‘Stuff’>’Things’, we want to better characterize the function of that region and relate it to previous work by adding additional functional localizers for color- and food-selective regions in the ventral stream.

title_r: Using adaptive presentation times to explore subjectively unaware EC
abstract_r: Here is a short sketch of the study, all further details can be found in the experimental script (osexp). ## Aim In previous studies, our lab has found evaluative conditioning when the subjective visibility of the CSs was high (subjects perceived at least one letter of a nonword), but not when it was low (they did not perceive a letter). In this study, we want to replicate these results with these two main changes: First, the nonwords (CSs) of the two valences do not share any letter, so that CS_pos and CS_neg can be discriminated when subjects can identify at least one letter. Second, the CS durations were adapted so that inter-individual variance is reduced and so that group effects are not biased by single subjects with extreme data points. ## Methods Subjective visibility is measured with an adapted Perceptual Awareness Scale from 1 to 6: 1. PAS1: "I could not perceive anything of the nonword" 2. PAS2: "I perceived a brief glimpse of the nonword in between the two pattern masks" 3. PAS3: "I perceived single lines of the nonword (but no letters)" 4. PAS4: "I perceived one letter quite clearly" 5. PAS5: "I perceived more than one letter clearly" 6. PAS6: "I perceived the entire nonword clearly" Half of the nonwords were paired with pleasant and the other half with unpleasant OASIS pictures. Because CS_pos and CS_neg were selected so that they did not share any letter, a PAS rating of 4 is sufficient to discriminate the CS_pos and CS_neg. The CS durations are adapted during a pre-phase with other nonwords than in the learning phase and with neutral pictures. Also during the learning phase, CS durations are still adapted to account for learning and fatigue effects. All manipulations are within-subjects. ## Stopping rule and statistical analysis Participants who respond to briefly-presented (i.e., adaption target PAS 2.5) CSs with PAS ratings $\geq 5$ on more than 5% of learning trials will be excluded from analyses of EC effects. Sample size will be determined using a sequential Bayesian procedure: Data will be collected in batches of 30 participants, where after each batch, we will test for the presence or absence of EC effects for both adaptation-target conditions (i.e., PAS 2.5 or PAS 5) with Bayesian *t* tests using the **Bayesfactor** package in R, with a scaled Cauchy prior on the standardized effect size for the alternative hypothesis with scale sqrt{2}/2. If the BF in favor of an EC effect in the PAS-5 condition exceeds 10 *and* the BF in favor of either the presence or absence of an effect in the PAS-2.5 condition exceeds 3, we will stop collecting data. If these conditions are not met, we will continue collecting data in batches of 30 participants up to a maximum of 120 participants.

title_r: Do Apologies Play a Different Role in Helping Male and Female Social Rejectors Achieve Two Interpersonal Goals?
abstract_r: This research will test whether apologies differ in their success when used by men and women to achieve the two goals that social rejectors most commonly have when faced with rejecting someone’s request for social inclusion. Previous research has identified two prevalent interpersonal goals of social rejectors: to protect their reputation (Baumeister et al., 1993; Besson et al., 1998; Folkes, 1982; Freedman et al., 2016), and to protect the feelings of the individual they are rejecting (Baumeister et al., 1993; Besson et al., 1998; Folkes, 1982; Tong and Walther, 2011). Social rejectors often apologize while voicing their rejection (Freedman et al., 2017), but do apologies have a different effect for male and female rejectors trying to achieve their goals of sparing the rejectee’s feelings and protecting their reputation? Research on apologies suggest that apologies conform to social norms around how someone should act when committing a social transgression (Darby & Schlenker, 1982; Hodgins & Liebeskind, 2003) and often lead to favorable outcomes in conflict resolution (Fehr, Gelfand, & Nag, 2010; Hodgins & Liebeskind, 2003). Furthermore, observers of a social transgression look more favorably on perpetrators who apologize and show remorse (in comparison to those who do not: Darby & Schlenker, 1982; Risen & Gilovich, 2007; Ungar, 1981). However, previous research suggests that apologies may not protect the feelings of the rejectee and, in fact, can even make the rejectee feel worse than if there was no apology at all (Freedman, Williams, & Beer, 2016; Freedman et al., 2017; Risen & Gilovich, 2007). Preliminary research in our lab suggests that the gender of the social rejector plays a role in the effect of apologies on hurt feelings of the rejectee: although rejectees were perceived as having less hurt feelings when a male rejector apologized (compared to them not apologizing), an apology from a female rejector made no significant difference in the perceived hurt feelings that the rejectee might feel (Okland & Beer, 2021). The current research will test the previous apology x gender interaction on rejectee feelings using a conceptual replication study (i.e., gender of rejector will be experimentally manipulated). Additionally, previous research on likability of social rejectors has found conflicting results related to male and female rejectors. One study found that women rejectors were perceived to be less likable than male rejectors (Freedman, Fetterolf, & Beer, 2019), while a preliminary study in our lab found that women were more likable than men when they were rejecting someone (Okland & Beer, 2021). The current study will build on previous research by measuring effects of rejector gender on likability.

title_r: Reactive Spiral: A replication
abstract_r: The current study seeks to replicate a recent investigation that assessed whether already being in a state of reactance (or not in a state of reactance) when a message is received will moderate the influence of a message that is either highly threatening or mildly threatening to people’s freedom. This is our third study in this sequence. The first one was not pre-registered. The second study was pre-registered, but we were unable to get the necessary college student sample, making it vastly underpowered. As such, we are conducting the current study on Amazon’s MTurk, and we are switching the topic from students’ ability to choose their own courses to mask-wearing. Further, while the prior studies compared a message that was highly threatening (e.g., “all of your classes will be chosen for you”) to one that was less threatening (e.g., “some classes will be chosen for you”), the current study will compare a highly controlling message (e.g., “you must wear a mask”) to an autonomy-supportive message (e.g., “the choice to wear a mask is yours”). This change led us to remove the hypothesis of the prior study that predicted a main effect of the reactance prime. As noted by the research question we now ask, we are unsure as to the influence of receiving an autonomy-supportive message after a reactance prime. N.B.: As we describe below, any participants who write about COVID-relevant topics in response to the writing tasks will not be included in the central analysis. We will remove these participants because the central goal of this study is to assess what happens when someone in (or not in) a state of reactance receives a message that is focused on a behavioral freedom that was not the cause of the initial reactance.

title_r: PM Reminder Fail - Single Cue Specificity
abstract_r: Under high load (8 PM targets), reminders reduce study durations and improve PM performance across the first three blocks. Critically, expecting a reminder on the fourth block reduces PM performance, whereas knowing that a reminder will not be available results in longer study durations and improved memory performance. This suggests that strategic encoding processes benefit PM performance. Notably, high memory load places demand on the retrospective component of PM. We therefore sought to replicate our previous findings when participants learn only a single PM target (thereby reducing the retrospective load). A second purpose of the current study was to examine how intention (and reminder) specificity influences performance. Previous research suggests that a single specific PM target can be noticed relatively automatically (i.e., spontaneous retrieval), whereas a single nonspecific PM target requires attention to notice (i.e., monitoring). By manipulating intention specificity, we can further specify the mechanisms underlying intention fulfillment. One possibility is that we replicate the previous findings that participants in the expecting reminder condition will study for less duration in block 4 and have worse target detection, for both specific and nonspecific PM intentions, consistent with the encoding effort hypothesis. Alternatively, because discrepant processing from repeated specific PM targets is more likely to stimulate retrieval automatically, it is possible that PM performance between expecting and non-expecting conditions will be similar with specific intentions regardless of any differences in study durations, consistent with the perfunctory view. However, for attentionally demanding (nonspecific) intentions, study duration may still be diagnostic of performance, such that those in the expecting condition study for less amount of time and show worse PM performance, consistent with an effortful encoding view. Finally, it is possible that performance with both specific and nonspecific intentions with be similar between expecting and non-expecting conditions regardless of any differences in study durations, consistent with the perfunctory view. If this were the case, it would suggest that the benefits from offloading and encoding effort from previous experiments may derive largely from improving the retrospective component of PM (i.e., under high load).

title_r: Does assigning intentions to others involve visual motion processing?
abstract_r: We use others’ gaze to identify their object of attention. Guterstam and colleagues suggested that the capability to link the gaze of observed persons to their object of interest is mediated by an imaginary “gaze beam” that emanates from the others’ eyes and moves through space. The central tenet of this hypothesis is that the gaze beam recruits the visual motion processing system. Görner et al. argued that the experimental evidence supports not only this “gaze beam hypothesis” but also a different interpretation, namely the beholder´s understanding that the other displays a particular object-related intention. We refer to this as “intentional binding hypothesis”. This assignment of an intention may involve the prediction of an upcoming movement of the observed person engaging the same system. To critically compare the explanatory power of the two hypotheses, we aim to replicate and extend the original psychophysical study by Guterstam et al. to test the alternative hypothesis.

title_r: Experiment 1C: Replication of the head nodding and shaking effect in a web-based experiment
abstract_r: Given that nodding and shaking head motions are used as communicative signals, such as signals of approval (and denial), these motions might be expected to modulate perceived trait impressions of model faces. We used movie clips of nodding and shaking head motions of computer-generated figures and examined the modulation effects of these motions on perceived trait impressions. Results showed that the nodding head motion significantly increased ratings of subjective likeability and approachability compared to the shaking or control conditions, whereas the shaking motion did not affect ratings. However, previous studies have primarily examined this effect using laboratory-based experiments with Japanese university students, which limits the generalizability and replicability of the results. Therefore, the present study examined whether this effect can be observed in a web-based experiment and for crowdsourcing service workers. In this experiment (Experiment 1C), we re-examined the effects of nodding and shaking motions on perceived attractiveness.
