title_r: Group Based Pain Perception
abstract_r: The current study is a replication study that tests the accuracy of pain tolerance estimates across Black and White men and women targets. Notably, in our previous study, we included participants from outside the United States. Because attitudes about race and gender can differ across nationalities, and because we are primarily interested in Black-White race and gender pain care disparities in the United States, we plan to recruit only participants from the United States in this replication study. We previously recruited phase 1 participants to undergo a pain task in which we measured their pain threshold and pain tolerance. Neutral pictures were taken of phase 1 participants (hereafter referred to as targets) and will serve as target stimuli in the current work. The goal of the current work is to investigate pain perception accuracy across target race and target gender. To this end, naïve participants will view the neutral pictures of targets and estimate their pain threshold and pain tolerance. Participants will also estimate each target’s pain sensitivity to eighteen general injuries (Trawalter Hoffman, & Waytz, 2012). This multi-phase method will enable us to examine actual group differences in pain sensitivity and tolerance (by examining target sensitivity and tolerance), perceived group differences in pain sensitivity and tolerance (by examining perceiver judgments of sensitivity and tolerance), as well as the accuracy of perceiver sensitivity and tolerance judgments (i.e., by examining the difference between perceiver ratings and targets’ actual sensitivity and tolerance).

title_r: Accumulated Loss Binding: A Replication
abstract_r: This experiment seeks to replicate the conditions of the experiment titled 'Prisoners of the Past', which was preregistered on OSF on 7th July 2024: https://osf.io/hg6u3. Abstract of previous experiment: Intentional binding, a perceptual compression of time between action and outcome, is routinely operationalised as an implicit measure for sense of agency. Whilst preceding research has shown that time perception can be influenced by negative outcomes, no previous study has explored whether the intra-event combination of multiple, continuing outcomes might carry an aggregating effect. We hypothesised that negative events would demonstrate a noticeable impact on time perception, and furthermore, that this impact would increase progressively when incorporated within a continuous sequence (i.e. a losing streak). Our novel experiment presented 30 participants with an ecologically aspirant gambling game: using a standard deck of 52 French-suited playing cards, participants guessed whether the next card in a sequence would be ‘higher’ or ‘lower’, with each guess being succeeded with an immediate financial reward or punishment. The results found statistical significance in showing that binding was stronger following losses, and that an unbroken and concurrent sequence of negative outcomes had an accumulative influence on time perception. To our knowledge, this is the first time that this effect, ‘Accumulated Loss Binding’, has been reported: the longer a losing streak, the stronger the binding. This boost in agency may help explain why problem gamblers are attracted to financially destructive activities with similar gamification features and could be clinically implemented to provide a coping mechanism for patients with agentic deficiencies.

title_r: Decomposing the role of alpha oscillations during brain maturation
abstract_r: During childhood and adolescence, the human brain undergoes various micro- and macroscopic changes. Understanding the neurophysiological changes within this reorganizational process is crucial, as many major psychiatric disorders emerge during this critical phase of life. In electroencephalography (EEG), a widely studied signal component are alpha oscillations (~8-13 Hz), which have been linked to developmental changes throughout the lifespan. Previous neurophysiological studies have demonstrated an increase of the alpha peak frequency and a decrease of total alpha power to be related to brain maturation. The latter results have been questioned by recent developments in EEG signal processing techniques, as it could be demonstrated that aperiodic (non-oscillatory) components in the EEG signal conflate findings on periodic (oscillatory) changes, and thus need to be decomposed accordingly. In previous analyses, using an openly available pediatric dataset of 1766 children and adolescents in the age range of 5 to 21 years, we could replicate the finding of decreased total individualized alpha power with increasing age. However, when controlling for the aperiodic signal component, this effect inverted such as the aperiodic adjusted individualized alpha power increased with advanced brain maturation, while the aperiodic signal component flattened and its offset decreased. Furthermore, relative individualized alpha power also showed a positive association with age. The here investigated sample consisted to a large proportion of children with psychiatric disorder, thus, diagnoses and ADHD scores were accounted for in the statistical models. These models provided no evidence for an association of ADHD and alpha power or the aperiodic signal parameters. Additionally, a subsample of subjects without any given diagnose was examined, showing consistent results to the larger analysis. To produce more generalizable results, we will investigate a second, independent EEG dataset of 369 children and adolescents. Before analyzing any of these data, all steps are preregistered here, based on the analyses which were performed on the openly available dataset. This additional dataset consists of healthy children and children with diagnosed ADHD. The full sample will be analyzed while controlling for the ADHD diagnoses. As an additional control analysis, the subsample of healthy children will be investigated.

summary: According to the metaphorical framing model, the use of metaphors in discussing an issue influences recipients’ understanding and assessment of that issue. In a recent study, participants read a text referring to a city´s crime problem either as a beast or a virus and then proposed counter-measures for that problem. The participants´ suggestions differed depending on the metaphor used in the text they had read. This replication matched the original procedure in terms of the content of the rhetorical figures (beast vs. virus), the topic under focus (crime), and the measurement of the dependent variable, using an open-end format to ask participants for their proposals. The procedure differed from the original with respect to language (German instead of English) and by including the formal type of rhetorical figure (metaphor or simile) as a factor. The influence of the content of the figure on the types of measure suggested was observed to be systematic. Presenting the rhetorical figure as a metaphor or a simile had no effect. Overall, we were able to replicate the main effect of the original study. Metaphors do indeed frame reasoning.

title_r: Talking Heads and Cueing in Educational Videos
abstract_r: In this online experiment, we investigate the design tool 'talking head' (i.e. the talking face of the instructor) and its interplay with cueing elements in educational videos. With this study, we want to extend the results of a first study (Talking Heads in Educational Videos) in which we investigated the design tool talking head and its interplay with graphic and text slides in educational videos. We varied whether a talking head was presented in addition to the actual learning videos or not. As a within-subject factor, we varied whether the contents of the slides in the videos were text-based or graphic-based. We designed the graphic slides in such a way that they contain relevant information that does not appear in the audio track. There were no learning-inhibiting effects of the talking head, neither for videos with graphic slides nor for those with text slides. We assume that cueing elements on the slides repeatedly drew the attention of the learners to the slides (and thus away from the talking head), so that no learning-inhibiting effect of the talking head on graphic slides could occur. Therefore, in a new study, we want to replicate the previous study and additionally vary as between factor whether the slides in the videos contain cueing elements or not. With these variations, it is possible to determine which constellations of the instructor's presence and cueing elements lead to better (or worse) learning results and which version participants prefer. We assume that the talking head attracts learners' attention. The instructor’s presence should have a learning-inhibiting effect for graphic slides that do not contain cueing elements, because they contain relevant information that does not appear in the audio track and the lack of cueing does not draw the learners’ attention to the relevant information on the slides (away from the talking head).

title_r: Pre-registration of Study 2a & 2b on Mental Health Messaging
abstract_r: This study is a part of a research project on drivers of diffusion in political communication online and a continuation of previously done studies. Study 1a and 1b of the project looked at the relationship between the level of certain linguistic features in tweets by US and UK politicians, respectively, and the number of times the post was reshared. The linguistic and control features for the statistical models were selected based on a systematic review of the previous work in the field. In the experimental work we wish to replicate the findings from the archival data and add the potential moderating effect of the source of the social media post (ingroup vs. outgroup member vs. no information about the message source), which has so far been overlooked in the literature. The experimental material for the studies is created by adopting the tweets from the archival dataset. To avoid potential confounding effects of a topic, which in itself can induce polarization, we will use tweets on a neutral topic (“mental health”) and the content of tweets will not in itself be polarizing. Using stratified sampling we selected tweets that fall into one of two experimental conditions: encourage retweet condition (in which we hypothesize higher participant willingness to share the message) and inhibit retweet condition (in which we hypothesize lower participant willingness to share the message). Tweets in encourage vs inhibit condition are significantly higher on scores of “we” and negative agency and lower in positive sentiment and communal words, and vice versa. Other variables that we measured in Study 1a and 1b (concreteness, presence of exclamation points, analytical language, words pertaining to power, positive agency and word count) are kept at similar levels across both conditions.

title_r: Replicability of gene-environment interactions on gray matter brain structure in the context of major depression
abstract_r: Gene environment interactions are at the heart of pathogenic models of depression. Childhood maltreatment is the most prominent environmental risk factor, putatively influencing brain development and exerting a long-lasting impact on mental health trajectories. The genetic predisposition has been suggested to moderate the neural effects of childhood maltreatment. A variety of candidate genotypes have been reported to play a role in this regard. This project aims to conduct a series of replication studies in order to examine the evidence for these gene-environment interactions on brain structure. To this end three different large deep-phenotyping cohorts, entailing genotyping, clinical characterization and cerebral neuroimaging of participants with and without major depressive disorder are used to replicate previous findings involving childhood maltreatment interaction effects with 5HTTLPR, FKBP5, OXTR and BDNF candidate genotypes. Further, an interaction between childhood maltreatment and polygenic risk for depression on brain structure is novelly tested (not a replication). The analysis plans and hypotheses of all individual replication projects and the novel polygenic analysis are preregistered as 'secondary preregistrations' (for already existing data sets). Each individual project is linked in this overarching OSF project. All analyses will be conducted at the Institute for Translational Psychiatry at the University of Münster, Germany.

title_r: Social and Affective Impacts of the COVID-19 Pandemic on University Students
abstract_r: The current study is a follow-up to a survey study conducted in April and May of 2020 by the same laboratory. The current study will closely follow the design of this previous study. This line of research is investigating the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on the affective health and regulation of university students. Some of the key questions of this line of research include how the pandemic has influenced students’ social interactions, their use of reappraisal to regulate emotion, and how their mental health has been affected by these changes. At the beginning of the pandemic, students were subjected to a full lockdown, affecting their social interactions and mental health. However, as pandemic restrictions have been lifted, students have been able to engage in more social interactions, potentially aiding in social forms of affect regulation, and alleviating mental health symptoms. title_r: Understanding Uncertainty in Perceptual Decision-Making - Experiment 2: Neural Correlates
abstract_r: To accurately detect, recognise, discriminate and classify visual stimuli, our brains combine inherently noisy sensory data with prior knowledge about the environment (Brascamp & Shevell, 2021; de Lange et al., 2018). In a previous experiment (https://osf.io/s7d59), we demonstrated that human participants estimated the direction of noisy motion signals more precisely after learning which directions were more likely. Behavioural estimates were also biased toward the most likely directions, with the strongest biases emerging when sensory signals were most noisy and learned expectations were very strong. These findings fit with the idea that participants engage in precision-weighting, a probabilistic process by which the influence of prior expectations on decision-making depends on the relative uncertainty associated with those priors and the current sensory input (Knill & Pouget, 2004; Weiss et al., 2002). Precision-weighting is a key component of dominant theoretical frameworks such as predictive coding that aim to understand perceptual decision-making through the lens of Bayesian inference. While this view is dominant in the literature (de Lange et al., 2018; Press et al., 2020), relatively little is known about how these inferential computations are performed by the brain. In the present study, we aim to replicate our behavioural experiment while additionally recording functional brain activity as they perform the task using electroencephalography (EEG). We will use multivariate decoding methods to explore patterns of stimulus-specific brain activity as they unfold during a trial. If stimulus representations decoded from EEG show evidence of bias toward a prior, the time course of such biases may yield insights into how neural representations support precision-weighted perceptual behaviour. One possibility is that representations of stimuli that are likely on the basis of a prior might be ‘sharpened’ relative to unlikely or neutral (neither unlikely nor likely) stimuli (Bell et al., 2016; Kok et al., 2012) via increased gain of sensory neurons tuned to likely stimulus values. Such sharpening would lead to better decoding of more probable stimulus values and might also contribute to the observed behavioural biases. Other work has suggested that ‘sensory templates’ for expected stimulus values might be activated ahead of stimulus onset, reducing the threshold for activation of neurons (or populations of neurons) selectively tuned to the expected stimulus value (Aitken et al., 2020; Kok et al., 2017).

title_r: The illusion of multitasking and its effect on working memory and attention
abstract_r: Across several studies employing various experimental tasks, Srna, Schrift and Zauberman (2018) demonstrated that manipulating people’s perception of a task by presenting it as either a single task or multiple tasks impacted their performance on said task. Remarkably, those in the multiple tasks conditions, who believed they were multitasking, performed better than those who perceived the task as a single task. Moreover, in Study 3, Srna and colleagues (2018) found that participants who believed they were multitasking showed greater pupil dilation and overall task-switching relative to their “single-task” counterparts. The researchers thus concluded that the performance benefits observed among participants who believed they were multitasking were driven by increased task engagement. In a recent study, we investigated how framing a task as constituting a single versus multiple tasks influenced people’s working memory and level of engagement. Participants performed a working memory (2-back) task containing two types of thought probes measuring participants’ levels of engagement. These appeared together on 19 occasions throughout and assessed (a) their level of concentration on the 2-back as well as (b) the amount of control they were exerting over their thoughts while completing the task. Importantly, prior to completing the 2-back, participants were told that they would be performing either a single task or multiple tasks. Performance on the 2-back did not vary as a function of task framing, however we found a significant main effect of task framing on responses to the concentration probes such that those in the multitasking condition reported higher levels of concentration than those in the single task condition. We also found a significant interaction between task framing and probe responses over time for both probe types. Specifically, the multitasking and single task framing groups diverged in their responses to both probe types within a few minutes of beginning the task, with deeper concentration and greater control reported by those in the multitasking condition relative to those in the single task condition. This pattern remained relatively consistent through to the completion of the task. Due to certain concerns arising from this initial study, namely the difference in group size between the multitasking (N = 64) and the single tasking (N=53) conditions as well as the possibility of our results being under-powered, we are motivated to conduct a high-powered replication using a participant pool that extends beyond that of the undergraduate population (Amazon’s Mechanical Turk). In the present study we are primarily interested in replicating the interaction found in our original study between task framing and probe occurrence for both probe types.

title_r: ALAS Move (Active Learning About the Self - Move) - Training Decisions in Motor Sequence Learning
abstract_r: In previous experiments, we found that children (ages 4-8) make effective decisions about what to practice in light of distinct goals. However, it is unclear whether young children can make adaptive training choices in motor skill learning. In this study, we investigate whether 4- to 8- year-old children make effective training choices depending on the task characteristics, with the final goal of maximizing their performance at a final test phase. In particular, we study whether participants tailor their learning strategies to boost their strengths (i.e., maximizing wins) or compensate for their weaknesses (i.e., minimizing losses). We aim to replicate the results of a prior study. DESCRIPTION OF THE METHODS Participants play three different game blocks (=conditions) presented to them on a tablet screen. In each block, participants are presented with two frog-catching games (SRT tasks). Children see a frog jump between the cells of a 4x4 grid on the screen, and they are instructed to tap on the frog at each jump with their index finger as quickly as they can. Crucially, in each block, one frog jumps in a fully predictable spatial sequence (e.g., jumping from one grid cell to the next) in what we call an Easy game, while the other frog jumps in a partially random manner, which we call the Difficult game, as it is not trivial to predict where the frog will jump next (every second jump happens to a random grid cell). The temporal sequence - i.e., the inter-stimulus interval between the frogs' appearances - is fixed across game difficulty levels. During an initial familiarization phase, participants try to play the Easy or the Difficult frog game first (order counterbalanced across conditions and participants), in which they try to catch the frog 16 times and receive feedback about their performance defined as the number of hits. After this, we ask participants to indicate how difficult they found the game on a 4-point Likert scale (absolute difficulty rating). Then participants proceed to play the other frog game and are asked to indicate its absolute subjective difficulty level on the same 4-point Likert scale. Additionally, we ask participants to indicate which of the two games they just played was easier, and which one was more difficult than the other (binary difficulty rating). To visualize this and provide memory aid throughout the task, we ask participants to place the image of a person lifting small and heavy weights next to a picture of the frog game they found easy or difficult, respectively. After the familiarization phase, we tell participants that eventually, they will be tested on one of the two games they just played (the Easy or Difficult game). We incentivize children by promising them to get one small goodie item if they catch the frog at least 15 out of 16 times. Critically, we manipulate whether we tell participants that eventually they will be tested on the Easy game (Easy game condition), the Difficult game (Difficult game condition), or a randomly chosen game (Random game condition). Participants then decide which game they want to practice for one round before the test. This choice is our dependent variable. In this practice phase, participants have to catch the frog of their choice, who jumps in the same spatial sequence as it jumped during the familiarization phase (i.e., the Easy game is exactly the same sequence as before, as is the Difficult game). After this, participants enter the testing phase, where they are tested either on the Easy game (in the Easy game condition/Random game condition) or on the Difficult game (in the Difficult game condition/Random game condition). After the test phase is over, participants move on to the second and third game blocks presenting the rest of the three experimental conditions. The order of conditions, games within a condition (i.e., whether the Easy or Difficult game is presented first), and the colors of the frogs assigned to each difficulty level are randomized.

title_r: Experiment 3 - Testing limits of recall in numerical estimation in an applied setting
abstract_r: We are interested to research how memory abilities contribute to numerical estimation tasks. Recall is an ability that is essential to many of our daily tasks, of which most require memory of some kind. A common finding when researching free recall of sequentially presented items are effects of recency and primacy, i.e. easier recall for the first and last items presented in a sequence (e.g. Murdock, 1962). Primacy and recency effects have also been shown to influence human decision making. For instance, candidates who perform on the first or last position are typically evaluated more favourably. It is, however, unclear how much primacy and recency effects in decision making can be explained by memory recall. In two previous experiments, we investigated how participants estimated the average of sequences of only numbers and found that the serial position weight of an item in this averaging task correlated higher with the recall probability of an item on this position in the free recall task when participants did not know which task lie ahead (randomly interpersed; r=0.6, Exp. 1) than when they did know which task lies ahead (blocked such that the first half of sequences were averaging tasks, and the second half were free recall tasks; r=0.38, Exp. 2). These correlations were mainly due to recency effects. Differences arising from such knowing or not knowing were investigated in recall tasks by Oberauer (2003) who called these procedures "pre-cueing" and "post-cueing", respectively. For a third experiment, we aim to generalize our findings to a cued recall task in which participants are presented not solely by a number, but a number associated to an object. As objects, we use shopping carts filled with six random products, each from a different product category. We aim to replicate our findings of numerical averaging from our first two experiments. Further, we try to get a more general understanding on contribution of memory to numerical estimation and thus include a further task in our experiment: summation. Interestingly, Scheibehenne (2019) found that participants especially rely on the middle items of a sequence when summing numbers up. This would suggest an opposite contribution of memory to this task. More likely, however, participants use different strategies when averaging and summing (possibly even adjusting for a bias in recency and primacy).

title_r: The Bioscope: two replications
abstract_r: Bioscope is a sensor that, according to developers, is able to perceive a physiological state of biological organisms. The sensor is based on measuring the intensity of light scattered from a thin opaque material. In this paper we describe two replications of this sensor, performed by two independent laboratories located in different countries. Measurements are curried out with biological (plants) and organic objects, and different rotational, entropic, fiber-optic and hydrodynamic devices. Additional high resolution sensors of temperature and humidity are utilized in over a hundred of measurements. The obtained results do not allow making unambiguous conclusions and require revising the design of reflection-scattering elements. Some measurements demonstrate uncharacteristic dependencies between temperature, humidity and sensor output, which indicate a necessity of further research with this device.

title_r: The comparison between the evaluation of future-oriented people and present-oriented people
abstract_r: Today, achieving a sustainable society is becoming a more important problem. In light of this, researchers start to investigate whether people have the future-orientation, which is a tendency to behave beneficially to future generations in exchange for the cost to the present generation. Some studies revealed that people show future-orientation at least in some specific situations. However, it is still unknown how future-oriented people are evaluated by others. In the previous study, we revealed that people who displayed future-oriented behavior were evaluated better than people who displayed present-oriented behavior, i.e., beneficial for the present generation but costly for future generations. However, this positive evaluation was shown only when the target’s altruistic tendency toward contemporaries was unknown: when the target’s altruistic tendency toward contemporaries was obvious, the positive evaluation was disappeared. Therefore, we suppose that the reason for the good evaluation of future-oriented people comes from the high estimated altruistic tendency toward contemporaries. We are planning to conduct a study to confirm this hypothesis. The aim of this preregistered study is to examine the following two points. First, we aim to replicate the result of the previous study. Second, we aim to test the hypothesis that people tend to evaluate a future-oriented person better than a present-oriented person because a future-oriented person is estimated more highly altruistic toward contemporaries.

title_r: Do adults use counterfactual reasoning to decide which person to thank for preventing a negative outcome?
abstract_r: We ask whether adults use counterfactual reasoning when making judgments in cases where different outcomes are prevented from occurring. In a previous experiment, we presented participants with scenarios in which the main character, Granny, dropped two different items on the same surface, with one outcome being worse than the other. The outcomes were prevented from occurring by two different people. We asked participants to determine which person deserved to receive the thank-you sticker. In this experiment, we replicate the previous setup, but with Granny dropping two identical items on different surfaces, each caught again by a different individual. We will ask participants to determine which person deserved to receive the thank-you sticker. title_r: COVID-19 Climate Change Norms
abstract_r: Behavior essential to reducing risks from COVID-19 have become highly politicized in the U.S., despite ever increasing COVID-19 cases and fatalities. Due to this politicization, the social norms of partisan groups drive people’s reaction to highly visible risk reduction behavior (e.g., Republicans feel masks are a threat to their symbolic values; Axios, 2020; Bruine de Bruin et al., 2020; Garadian et al., 2020). Thus, for successful COVID-19 health promotion, communication about relevant behaviors must somehow displace the conflict of political social norms. However, the current social norms that are used for promoting behavior are often unilateral, and thus not equipped to displace conflicts arising from subordinate norms (e.g., Haidt, 2012). To combat this, our study draws from previous literature to craft several iterations of a new class of social norms, called conflict-displacing norms. We predict that these new conflict-displacing norms will increase masking intentions across party lines, compared to current messaging strategies. Preliminary results from a previous pilot study show that the conflict-displacing messages do increase Republican masking intentions in a student sample, but non-significantly due to small cell sizes. Furthermore, depending on the specific conflict-displacing norm involved, there may be trade-offs that come in the form of decrease in intentions among Democrats, or in the form of dependency on certain environments. Thus, this preregistration outlines a replication study meant to corroborate previous findings and further examine the issue of trade-offs in conflict-displacing norms.

title_r: Preregistration
abstract_r: Cognitive costs of emotion regulation strategies Relatively little is known about cognitive costs of emotion regulation (ER) strategies. Two studies examined the relationship between use of ER strategies and memory. Richards and Gross (2000) could show that “Expressive Suppression” led to poorer memory, but not “Reappraisal”. The authors argued that “Expressive Suppression”, a form of response-focused emotion regulation, should have not only higher, but also chronic expenditure demands on cognitive control processes. Further studies observed a dilation of the pupil during use of ER strategies. This pupil dilation reflects mental effort (Johnstone, van Reekum, Urry, Kalin, &amp; Davidson, 2007; Kinner et al., 2017; Urry, van Reekum, Johnstone, &amp; Davidson, 2009; van Reekum et al., 2007). To address cognitive costs of emotion regulation, the present study will examine the question whether different ER strategies (“Expressive Suppression” and “Detachment”) require different amounts of mental effort. Therefore, the aim of the present study is to compare the aforementioned strategies not only subjectively, but also using objective measurements, e.g., skin conductance rate (SCR), electrocardiography (ECG) and Pupillometry. Recently, a study has been conducted, to investigate mental effort of emotion regulation and the influence of individual differences, as well as situational factors, comprehensively (Scheffel, Gärtner, Graupner, Strobel, &amp; Dörfel, in prep.; preregistered at https://osf.io/9wjyp). The current project aims to replicate these findings. In the previous mentioned project, emotional pictures were grey-scaled due to technical reasons. This has now been changed and colored pictures are used. However, almost all studies that investigated emotion regulation used colored pictures (Dörfel, Gärtner, &amp; Scheffel, 2020; Gärtner et al., 2019; Scheffel et al., 2019). We therefore want to replicate our findings to find out, whether previous results are also applicable with influential studies in the field. Research Questions: 1 Can we replicate typical effects of emotion regulation on subjective and objective measurements? 2 Can we replicate previous findings on the mental effort of two emotion regulation strategies (detachment and suppression in comparison to viewing)?

title_r: CDDS (Change Detection During Saccades) Experiment 1A (Calibration Phase)
abstract_r: 3.1. John Grimes’ (1996) early work on the effects of saccades upon perceptual abilities revealed unexpected results: subjects failed to detect retrospectively obvious scene changes that occurred during saccades, despite having fixated before and after on the changed stimulus. In that study, Grimes selected images from magazines and used Adobe Photoshop to make changes in the identity, color, size, rotation, position, and presence of an object (or objects) in the image. Using advanced eye tracking, Grimes had participants view the images while performing a memory cover task, and he paired image changes to the moment when a specific saccade was made; subjects were required to report when they noticed anything change in the image. Results showed that for many images, fixations upon changed visual stimuli failed to yield detection of those changes. Since its publication, no attempt has been made to replicate the original work by Grimes. Given the current concerns about replication in the sciences generally and psychology in particular, this stands in need of remedy. Here, in our proposed experiment, we will replicate Grimes’ work and include a post-experiment questionnaire of subjective reports of participants’ experiences.

title_r: Are we more cruel towards people with different political opinions? A replication of Milgram's Obedience Study
abstract_r: In this study we want to replicate the well known Milgram study on obedience to authority figures. The original study wanted to look at how far humans are willing to go to obey orders, the experiment involved the participants delivering high-voltage electric shock to an actor in another room. The actor would scream and beg for the shock to stop, and eventually go silent making the participant believe the other person is in pain. The shocks were not real, but it was implied to the participant that they were. Majority of the participants did obey the orders and ignored the screaming. Findings of these experiments showed us that humans are susceptible to obeying orders, and how we can do unthinkable things to other humans under certain circumstances. Milgram used this finding to explain how historically we can go along with genocide and other atrocities. It may be a stretch to compare a controlled experiment and complex social behaviour, but it still gives us some insight in how social psychological factors leads us to do cruel and unpredictable things. This study has been replicated many times and in many ways. It is important to research and to find out how the human brain functions in terms of how we behave towards people who are different from us, where we might not see the consequences for our actions immediately. To understand how humans can be so cruel under the ruse of authority. We want to believe that we would never give another human electric shock, but the original experiment and several replications come to almost the same conclusion. In this replication we are adding a twist to the hypothesis, we want to see if political beliefs play a role in how far the participants are willing to go in giving shock. The sample group will either be a Republican or a Democrat and will be told that the person receiving shock belongs to the opposite political party. The political landscape in the United States is very polarised and makes an interesting setting to replicate this study. As humans we want to belong to a group and identify with many characterics of said group. They define us and are a part of our self actualization. In USA there are two main political parties, and who you vote for is a part of the whole identity of someone. It can give insight into what your social background and standing is, like race, colour, education, where you live and income. The social aspect of this replication is interesting because at this moment in time there is a lot of tension between the two political parties and it reflects over to the general population. During the last few years with Donald Trump being the president, the global pandemic and social differences being even more visible, it is compelling to see how political differences can influence the willingness of the participant to obey orders. Our prediction is that it is a big possibility that knowing someone's political standing will make their decision to give shock easier than not knowing anything about them.

abstract_r: Previous research has examined possible types and indicators of embarrassment, though the research on this topic is somewhat limited. abstract_r: Research in cognitive science has shown that visual manipulations to the presentation of mathematical problems influence the way that students perceive and solve problems (e.g., altering the spacing between, coloring, or arrangement of symbols). While there is a consistent impact of perceptual cues on students’ problem-solving, other cognitive skills such as inhibitory control may interact with perceptual cues to impact students’ arithmetic problem-solving performance. In previous work, we investigated this relation among college students; here, we plan to replicate the study with middle and high school students. title_r: Understanding the visual constraints on lexical processing: New empirical and simulation results (Experiment 4)
abstract_r: It is well known that visual acuity is not uniform across the visual field. Acuity instead decreases precipitously from the center of vision. The region of maximum acuity, called the fovea, is comprised of the central 2º of the visual field, with a region of rapidly decreasing acuity called the parafovea extending an additional 5º of visual angle to either side of this. Although the photoreceptors required for perceiving fine detail are largely limited to these two regions of the visual field, it remains unclear precisely how the rapid drop off in visual acuity that results from the distribution of these photoreceptors affects our capacity to rapidly and accurately identify printed words. This project aims to investigate the physical constraints imposed by our visual system on reading by conducting a conceptual replication of a highly cited study by Rayner and Morrison (1981). The original study compared lexical-decision and naming performance at central fixation (0 degrees), or between 1 and 5 degrees to the left or right of central fixation. Participants were either instructed to maintain central fixation (no eye-movement condition) or move their eyes to the location of the stimulus (eye-movement condition). The proposed study improves on several features of the original study by (i) testing a much larger sample of participants; (ii) using a larger number of more highly controlled items that are not repeated during the experiment and that vary in both word length and frequency; (iii) ensuring participants maintain central fixation by tracking eye movements and terminating trials on which the participant moves their eyes. Previous experiments in this project measured lexical-decision performance for words and one-letter-different nonwords. This experiment tests naming performance for the same word stimuli at central fixation and at 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 degrees to the right of fixation.

title_r: Cross-cultural examination of violence justification: the role precarity and law enforcement (Studies 2a, 2b, 3a, 3b)
abstract_r: Anthropologists and social psychologists have described honor as a fundamental concern in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, Latin American, South Asian, and Southern US contexts, reflecting one's self-worth and the worth assigned to them by others in the society (Uskul & Cross, 2019, 2020). In these contexts, honor is perceived as "a right to respect," difficult to earn but easy to lose. Consequently, individuals engage in various behaviors to gain or maintain respect while fiercely defending their honor against threats. Previous research has shown that individuals endorsing honor values exhibit more positive judgments toward those who confront provocations compared to those who ignore them (Cross et al., 2014). In cultures of honor, intolerance towards provocations is expected, potentially leading to a higher prevalence of certain types of violence. Honor cultures tend to emerge in regions characterized by two ecological factors: scarce resources and inadequate law enforcement. However, empirical studies on these factors remain limited. In our initial study, we examined the contextual and individual drivers of honor norms in relation to the justification of interpersonal violence using data from the World Values Survey across 57 countries (n = 73,838). We found that greater precarity (which speaks to more scarce resources) and higher crime frequency (which speaks to inadequate las enforcement) predicted a greater justification of violence. Notably, in stable, affluent, and less corrupt countries, perceived precarity and crime frequency strongly predicted the justification of violence. In contrast, in countries with uncertain political/legal systems and scarce/unequally distributed resources, the justification of violence was less strongly predicted by perceived precarity and crime frequency. In other words, in countries with stronger honor orientation, the justification of violence is higher when precarity and inadequate law enforcement are at lower levels. However, for higher levels of precarity and inadequate law enforcement, the justification of violence is higher in countries with weaker honor orientation compared to those with stronger honor orientation. In the studies preregistered here, we aim to replicate these previous findings using primary data collected in the UK, US, and Turkey. Additionally, we seek to extend our understanding by testing the causal relationship between ecological characteristics of honor and the justification of violence through cross-cultural experiments. We plan to conduct 2x2 between-subject experiments, manipulating scarcity and inadequate law enforcement, in two non-honor contexts (the UK and the northern US) and two honor contexts (Turkey and the southern US). Based on power analyses using effect sizes from the initial study, our target sample size is 880 participants per cultural context.

title_r: Experiment 1B: Replication of the head nodding and shaking effect in a web-based experiment
abstract_r: Given that nodding and shaking head motions are used as communicative signals, such as signals of approval (and denial), these motions might be expected to modulate perceived trait impressions of model faces. We used movie clips of nodding and shaking head motions of computer-generated figures and examined the modulation effects of these motions on perceived trait impressions. Results showed that the nodding head motion significantly increased ratings of subjective likeability and approachability compared to the shaking or control conditions, whereas the shaking motion did not affect ratings. However, previous studies have primarily examined this effect using laboratory-based experiments with Japanese university students, which limits the generalizability and replicability of the results. Therefore, the present study examined whether this effect can be observed in a web-based experiment and for crowdsourcing service workers. In this experiment (Experiment 1B), we re-examined the effects of nodding and shaking motions on perceived approachability.

title_r: The Role of Lexical and Phonological Processing during Recognition and Learning of Spoken Word and Pseudoword (Exp5a & b)
abstract_r: Previously, we conducted four online behavioural experiments (Exp1, 3, 4a & b) and one MEG experiment (Exp2) manipulating the process of spoken word recognition and learning through the competitor priming effect (Monsell & Hirsh, 1998). The competitor priming effect shows that a spoken word prime (e.g. captain) delays subsequent recognition of a neighbouring target spoken word sharing the same initial segments (e.g. captive). We replicated this effect in Exp1&2 by presenting interleaved prime and target items in a lexical decision task (LDT). In Exp3, we replaced the LDT with the pause detection task (PDT; Mattys & Clark, 2002; Gaskell & Dumay, 2003) and found that a pseudoword prime, but not a word prime, delayed word recognition. This unexpected result made us wonder at what stage competitor priming was triggered. Was it during the encoding phase in which the prime was presented or the phase in which the target was presented? In order to answer this question, we then pre-registered and conducted Exp4a (osf.io/9453v) and b (https://osf.io/jcuar) which respectively used PDT and LDT in the prime phase (when the prime is presented) but LDT in the target phase (when the target is presented). We found that despite the different tasks in the prime phase in the two experiment versions, our bayes factor analysis did not provide evidence in favour of a main effect or interaction caused by the different prime tasks in the target phase. Furthermore, with an informative prior based on our previous experiments, we found supporting evidence showing competitor primed words recognised more slowly than unprimed and pseudoword primed words regardless the task adopted during the prime phase. These results indicated that the competitor priming effect was probably triggered by lexical processing in the target phase. In order to learn more about the pseudoword priming effect found in Exp3, we plan to conduct two further experiment Exp5a&b, also using PDT and LDT respectively in the prime phase, but PDT in the target phase. These two experiments will help us further investigate the role of sublexical processing in competitor priming.

title_r: Neural Mechanisms and Efficacy of Imagery Rescripting for Fear of Failure: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract_r: Introduction Imagery techniques have been reported to be effective in reducing mental problems. One of the Imagery techniques is Imagery Rescripting (IR) which has been shown to be efficient in clinical studies (Arntz, 2012), however, is still under research and its neuronal foundations are yet to be discovered. Further, it seems promising to combine IR along with our knowledge about the memory reconsolidation mechanisms. Imagery rescripting Imagery rescripting is a technique, in which patients are recalling traumatic memories in imagery as if they were happening in the present. During this recall, the therapist is guiding the patients so that they change the content of their memory into a more positive outcome, e.g. by preventing the traumatic experience from happening and satisfying the emotional needs of the patient. Memory reconsolidation One of the hypotheses regarding the effectiveness of IR is that it is based on disrupting the memory reconsolidation - a biological process happening in the brain. During this process the neuronal trace underlying the memory of a recalled event becomes unstable and ready to be changed. These changes have been shown to be more effective when they are introduced ca. 10 minutes following recall (Schiller et al. 2013). Merging imagery rescripting with these findings seems a promising perspective for providing more effective interventions. Previous study Our previous research included analysis of the efficacy of various imagery techniques for reducing fear of failure and related mental problems, as measured with treatment-related changes in skin conductance level, alpha-amylase, and several behavioral variables, including emotion rating. We invited participants aged 18-35 with high fear of failure and no severe mental disorders (affective disorders, psychotic episodes, suicidal tendencies, substance abuse, personality disorders). Each subject had an assigned therapist, who ensured that the subject was eligible for participation and conducted imagery sessions to extract necessary information about participants`s memories of various neutral events and aversive events, u.a. situations of being criticized. Based on that standardized recordings of the extracted events and a recording of rescription have been prepared and presented to the participants. Results show that IR is effective in terms of reducing fear of failure and related problems, as measured with treatment-related changes in skin conductance level, alpha-amylase, and several behavioral variables, including emotion rating. Current study We aim to investigate how brain reactions to memories of being criticized change after standardized treatment with IR. We want to replicate the previous effect, with fMRI measurements of reaction to the above mentioned memories. We want to conduct the study, in which healthy subjects with high fear of failure will participate in either Imagery rescripting intervention or a control condition. To study the underlying mechanisms of IR, we will conduct two fMRI experiments, before and after the intervention.

summary: According to the metaphorical framing model, the use of metaphors in discussing an issue influences recipients’ understanding and assessment of that issue. In a recent study, participants read a text referring to a city´s crime problem either as a beast or a virus and then proposed counter-measures for that problem. Participants´ suggestions differed depending on the metaphor they had read. This replication matched the original procedure regarding the content of the rhetorical figures (beast vs. virus), the topic under focus (crime) and the measurement of the dependent variable (open-end format to collect participants’ proposals). The procedure differed from the original with respect to language (German instead of English) and by including the formal type of rhetorical figure (metaphor or simile) as a factor. Taken together, we were able to replicate the main effect of the original study. Metaphors do indeed frame reasoning.

title_r: Information Diversity, Zero-Sum Beliefs, and Political Polarization
abstract_r: Political polarization is a major societal issue in the United States. Research has produced mixed findings regarding the effect of information diversity on polarization. We argue that one factor that political psychological research has largely omitted is individual differences in the belief in a zero-sum game (BZSG), which is likely to affect how people interpret information from political outgroups. In an initial study with 301 participants, we found that individuals with stronger BZSG are more likely to exhibit stronger ideological and affective polarization. Additionally, for individuals with stronger BZSG, more political outgroups in one’s personal networks and greater media diet diversity had stronger facilitating effects on ideological polarization but weaker mitigating effects on affective polarization. Nevertheless, these initial findings, although encouraging, came from a rather small sample. Therefore, the current study serves as a high-powered replication of the initial study. We plan to recruit 1,000 US adult citizens from the Amazon Mechanic Turk platform. Participants will complete a questionnaire that contains measures of their political alignment, diversity of personal network and media usage, BZSG, ideological and affective polarization, and some other measures (e.g., belief in anomie, perception of political leaders). A series of linear multiple regression models with multiplicative interaction terms will be used to test the moderation effects of BZSG on the association between information diversity (including network diversity and media usage diversity) and political polarization (including ideological and affective polarization).

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Kim et al. (2016), from Social Science & Medicine
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Kim & Radoias (2012) is that, for the specific case of asymptomatic disease detection, education should have a clear positive effect for individuals in poor health status (and at the aggregate level), and a smaller (possibly zero or negative) effect for individuals in good health status; the positive effect for individuals in poor health status is the portion of this claim selected for the SCORE program. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "In terms of disease detection, more educated respondents have a higher probability of being diagnosed, but only conditional on being in poor general health." Evidence in support of the claim is found in Table 2, which contains the probit regression results for the determinants of hypertension under-diagnosis. The dependent variable is a dummy equal to one for those respondents who were found to be hypertensive during the IFLS [Indonesian Family Life Survey] screenings, but were not previously diagnosed by a doctor. The three separate columns represent, in order, the results for the entire sample, the results for the subsample consisting of respondents in good general health, and the results for the subsample consisting of respondents in poor general health. For the SCORE program, the analysis of the subsample consisting of respondents in poor general health is selected. The predictor of interest is Years of Education (see the right column of Table 2 for details of the model). Education matters for these people, as more educated persons generally have higher opportunity costs of feeling sick and hence value their health higher, which pushes them harder to look for a cure in a doctor’s office (marginal effect for Years of Education = -0.00867, SE = 0.00420, significant at 5% level).

title_r: In search of experimental evidence for secondary antisemitism - A file drawer report - version 1
abstract_r: In 1955, Adorno attributed antisemitic sentiments voiced by Germans to a paradox projection: The only latently experienced feeling of guilt were warded off by antisemitic defense mechanisms. Similar predictions of increases in antisemitic prejudiced in response to increased Holocaust salience could also be based on other theoretical apparatuses from social identity theory as well as just world theory. Based on the – to our best knowledge –only experimental evidence for such an effect (published in Psychological Science in 2009), the present research reports a series of studies originally conducted to better understand the contribution of the different assumed mechanisms. In light of a failure to replicate the basic effect, however, the studies shifted to an effort to demonstrate the basic process. We report all studies our lab has conducted on the issue. Overall, the data did not provide any evidence for the original effect. In addition to the obvious possibility of an original false positive, we speculate what might be responsible for this conceptual replication failure.

title_r: New Online Tools to Assess Children’s Implicit Social Cognition: Replication and Generalization of In-Person Research
abstract_r: Reported is the development of new self-administered online tools for testing implicit social cognition in children. These tools adapt adult Implicit Association Tests (IATs) so they can be used for remote testing of children without a trained experimenter. Four studies are proposed. The first two studies with elementary school children (Grades 2–5) will use text-based IAT methodology suitable for this age group. As an initial test of the validity of the new online IAT procedures, Study 1 will investigate a well-replicated “known groups” effect (gender identity) using both the standard in-person procedure (N=48) and the online procedure (N=72). Study 2 will investigate math–gender stereotypes using the online procedure (N=76). The second two studies with preschoolers will use a pictorial IAT methodology suitable for 5-year-olds. As an initial test of the validity of the new online procedure for preschoolers, Study 3 will investigate strongly polarized affective categories (flower–insect attitudes) using both the standard in-person procedure (N=64) and the new online procedure (N=64). Study 4 will investigate in-group bias using the online procedure (N=64). We will evaluate the data for potential method effects and assess the reliability of both the in-person and the online tools. The new online child IAT procedures can: (a) contribute to efforts to reach populations not easily tested in person thereby increasing demographic diversity in child data, and (b) pave the way for large-scale studies investigating developmental continuity and change in important psychological/educational topics such as implicit stereotypes and bias.

title_r: Symbolic and Nonsymbolic Ratio Congruity Effect
abstract_r: Fractions knowledge is critical for mathematical development, with multiple studies showing a link between fractions knowledge and algebraic competence (e.g., Barbieri et al., 2021, Hurst & Cordes, 2018a; Siegler et al., 2012). Unfortunately, many studies have reported on difficulties children and adults have understanding fractions (e.g., Hansen et al., 2017; Namkung & Fuchs, 2019; Siegler & Lortie-Forgues, 2015; Tirosh, 2000). Some have surmised that these difficulties result because fractions are not “naturally compatible” with human cognitive architectures (unlike whole numbers). However, a growing body of evidence suggests that this is not true, demonstrating that humans and other animals have the capacity to represent fractions magnitudes when presented in non-symbolic ratio form (e.g., Jacob et al., 2012; Lewis et al., 2015; Park et al., 2021). Moreover, work has shown that this ability to process nonsymbolic ratios interfaces with symbolic fractions competence (e.g., Matthews & Chesney, 2015; Kalra et al., 2020). Indeed, Matthews and Lewis (2017) demonstrated that nonsymbolic ratio magnitudes automatically interfere with symbolic fraction processing using a Stroop-like task. This automaticity where irrelevant nonsymbolic dimensions influencing symbolic fraction judgments (i.e., a nonsymbolic ratio congruity effect or nRCE) highlights that foundational non-symbolic cognitive systems may be compatible for processing symbolic rational numbers. Building on this, we aim to replicate Matthews and Lewis (2017) with a new sample (Experiment 1) and further to extend the study with new stimuli (Experiment 2). The key distinction will be making the bounding boxes associated with the non-symbolic ratios in the original experiment visible, thus enabling conscious decisions about their magnitude in future experiments. The current study will then examine if this congruity effect is also present in the reverse direction – with the magnitude of symbolic fractions automatically interfering with the processing of non-symbolic ratios (Experiment 3).

title_r: Values, Psychological Distance, and Climate Engagement Intentions
abstract_r: One of the widely believed reasons for low public engagement with climate change is that people perceive climate change as a distant threat. However, studies that attempt to provide information about proximal impacts of climate change revealed mixed results on their effectiveness of increasing climate concerns and intentions to act. Schoenefeld and McCauley (2016) found that individuals holding higher self-enhancement values expressed less concern and intention to act on climate change after reading about local climate change impacts. title_r: Undergraduate COVID-19 Anxiety, Learning, and Emotion Regulation (Fall 2020/Winter 2021)
abstract_r: The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic has had far-reaching academic consequences, one being for undergraduates who have rapidly modified their social and learning contexts away from in-person supports. Compared to prior academic terms, undergraduates reported stark increases in anxiety following the pandemic’s onset (Huckins et al., 2020). High levels of anxiety can hinder academic performance and engagement (Beilock, 2008), underscoring the urgency of addressing these emotional consequences of the pandemic. A critical question is precisely how COVID-19 anxieties may impact learning and performance – information that would provide key insights for interventions to facilitate academic success despite the continuing crisis. This study tests mind wandering as a mechanism underlying the concerning impact of COVID-19 anxieties on students' learning potential. We test undergraduates’ learning from short-term, controlled videotaped instruction. Specifically, we asked if students’ performance on recall and higher-order processing questions following an asynchronous neuroscience lesson was hindered by individual differences in COVID-19 anxiety. If so, we probed whether this relationship was explained by increased mind wandering, akin to how math anxiety and stereotype threat can compromise performance by inducing task-irrelevant worries that overload cognitive resources (Schmader et al., 2008). We also tested the efficacy of brief emotion regulation interventions prior to learning. Some students received positive reappraisal instruction encouraging them to reframe anxious arousal as beneficial for performance (Jamieson et al., 2010). Others received mindfulness instruction describing how anxiety can overload cognitive resources, and how mindful redirection of attention can promote performance under high states of anxiety (Schuster et al., 2015). This study is a follow up to a prior study conducted in Spring 2020. Those data highlight the important mediating role of mind wandering on the relationship between COVID-19 anxieties and undergraduates' learning from the lesson, particularly on the higher-order thinking items. We found some evidence to suggest that the emotion regulation strategies benefited lower anxious students' learning, though we were underpowered to detect interactions. This study builds on the Spring 2020 data collection: 1) we hope to replicate the findings with a larger sample, and 2) we added a mindfulness intervention aimed at redirecting attention due to the important role of mind wandering.

title_r: How Economic Conditions Changed the Number of U.S. Farms, 1960-88: A Replication and Extension of Gale (1990) to Midsize Farms in the U.S. and Abroad
abstract_r: We replicate and extend the analysis of Gale (1990) to find that economic factors like population pressure, financial stress, and infrastructure play an important role in explaining the growth rate in the number of farms by farm size. We do not find support for the disappearing middle hypothesis, despite a declining trend in the number of midsize farms in the U.S. over time. Economic factors are also important to explain the increase in small and midsize farm numbers in Brazil, and the decreasing small farm numbers in the Eurozone, showing opposite trends in farm numbers globally.

title_r: NASCO: A new method and program to generate dot arrays for non-symbolic number comparison tasks
abstract_r: Basic numerical abilities are generally assumed to influence more complex cognitive processes involving numbers, such as mathematics. Yet measuring non-symbolic number abilities remains challenging due to the intrinsic correlation between numerical and non-numerical dimensions of any visual scene. Several methods have been developed to generate non-symbolic stimuli controlling for the latter aspects but they tend to be difficult to replicate or implement. In this study, we describe the NASCO method, which is an extension to the method popularized by Dehaene, Izard, and Piazza (2005). Their procedure originally controlled for two visual dimensions that are mediated by Number: Total Area and Item Size (i.e., N = TA/IS). Here, we additionally propose to control for another twofold dimension related to the array extent, which is also mediated by Number: Convex Hull Area and Mean Occupancy (i.e., N = CH/MO). We illustrate the NASCO method with a MATLAB app—NASCO app—that allows easy generation of dot arrays for a visually controlled assessment of non-symbolic numerical abilities. Results from a numerical comparison task revealed that the introduction of this twofold dimension manipulation substantially affected young adults’ performance. In particular, we did not replicate the relation between non-symbolic number abilities and arithmetic skills. Our findings open the debate about the reliability of previous results that did not take into account visual features related to the array extent. We then discuss the strengths of NASCO method to assess numerical ability, as well as the benefits of its straightforward implementation in NASCO app for researchers.

title_r: The role of individual variability in tests of functional hearing
abstract_r: This dissertation explores the role of individual variability in real-world (functional) hearing ability and how this ability is assessed in the clinic. It principally concerns two domains that play a role in overcoming the noisy environments in which speech regularly occurs: the ability to use acoustic structure inherent in noise to overcome its deleterious effects and the ability to use one's learned linguistic regularities to aid in reception of the target speech. The properties of each ability and the cognitive mechanisms that underlie them are probed and subsequently discussed in the chapters contained herein. Chapter 2 probes the use of temporal regularity present in noises to overcome their masking effects. Chapter 3 further delineates the properties of the noises found in chapter 2 and explores their relationship to canonical maskers. Chapter 4 explores the ability to use one's internal language model to improve in the reception of masked speech. Their individual abstracts are as follows: ? Chapter 2. In the real world, speech perception frequently occurs under adverse listening conditions. Laboratory studies have identified distinct phenomena associated with more or less constant sources of noise (energetic masking), and competing verbal information (informational masking). One issue complicating direct comparisons between them is that common paradigms for studying energetic and informational masking differ along many dimensions. We have developed a paradigm that uses temporally patterned noise, with the goal of comparing energetic and informational masking under more comparable conditions. We hypothesized that listeners would be able to take advantage of the structure in the masking noise, providing a processing advantage over energetic masking. The initial experiment provides strong evidence for this hypothesis, but conceptual replications did not produce the same pattern of results?at least with respect to measures of central tendency. A direct replication of the first experiment did not replicate the large differences in the means. Interestingly, however, analyses across all four experiments reveal robust evidence that patterned noise conditions produce increased individual variability. Further, we observed strong correlations, specifically between the patterned conditions. We attribute these findings to as yet unidentified cognitive ability differences allowing some participants to benefit from the use of additional temporal information while others are hurt by the addition of unusable distracting information. Hypothesized predictive measures of task performance, such as working memory, inhibitory control, and musical experience did not correlate with performance, however. ? Chapter 3. This work serves as a companion to our previous work in Courtland et al. (2019). Here, we undertake several follow-ups to delineate the properties of the temporally regular masking patterns introduced in that work?particularly where the new maskers are situated vis-a-vis canonical energetic and informational masking. In this paper, we perform experiments using a dynamic spectral profile for the maskers, manipulating their global SNR, and increasing the number of patterns presented prior to the target word. The findings support much of the conclusions of the previous work with respect to the role of offline information (the recurrence of a pattern across trials) and its importance in moderating task performance. While much of the support comes from negative results, the increased number of repetitions replicates our initial finding that shows a significant difference in task performance between a recurring condition and a baseline control. This experiment also replicates the initial finding of a significant difference between an online, repeating masker and its offline counterpart that controls for glimpsing windows. We also observe replications of variance effects seen in the previous paper, supporting the conclusion that offline information plays an important role in individual variability. ? Chapter 4. Cognitive tests used to measure individual differences have traditionally resorted to standardizing testing materials because of the onerous nature of creating test items. These tests are generally designed with equality in mind: the same ?broadly acceptable? items are used for all participants. This approach ignores participants' diverse language experiences that potentially significantly affect testing outcomes. This has unknown consequences for equity, particularly when a single set of linguistic stimuli are used for a diverse population of language users. We hypothesized that differences in language variety would result in disparities in psycholinguistically meaningful properties of test items in two widely-used cognitive tasks (reading span and SPiN), resulting in large differences in performance. As a proxy for individuals' language use, we administered a self-report survey of media consumption. We identified two substantial clusters from the survey data, roughly orthogonal to a priori groups recruited into the study (university students and members of the surrounding community). We found effects of both population and cluster membership. We then sought to explain this finding of significant performance differences between clusters on the tests based on their media consumption. To this end, we modeled the language contained in these media sources using an LSTM trained on corpora of each cluster's media sources to predict each test item's target words. We also modeled semantic similarity of test items with each cluster's corpus using skip-thought vectors. We found robust, significant correlations between performance on the SPiN test and the LSTMs and skip-thought models, but not the reading span test.

title_r: Effects of violence by Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) against Palestinian civilians on attitudes towards anti-Semitic protest behavior among people in Germany: Results of two survey experiments conducted before and after October 7th 2023. Paper presented at the 82nd Annual Conference of the Midwest Political Science Association, Chicago (IL), April 5th, 2025.
abstract_r: To assess the potential impact of international developments on public attitudes in Germany, we regularly conduct survey experiments. These experiments are embedded in the representative Survey „Menschen in Deutschland International“ („People in Germany: International) which is conducted bimonthly since November 2022. One important issue are effects of the ongoing military conflict in the Middle East on political attitudes and protest behavior among people living in Germany. At present increases of the prevalence of anti-Semitic prejudice as well as an increase of violence against jewish people and jewish institution are a heavily debated social and political Problem in Germany. In an initial survey experiment conducted in May 2023 we examined the impact of reports on the use of armed force against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank on antisemitic and anti-Israel protest behavior in Germany. In this experiment, we systematically varied whether the violence described in the scenarios was perpetrated by the Israeli military or by Jewish settlers. We found that violence committed by the Israeli military significantly increased acceptance of antisemitic protest behavior. However, this effect was almost exclusively observed among individuals who already exhibited traditional antisemitic prejudices. No effects were observed for identical violence carried out by Jewish settlers. In a follow-up study conducted in September 2024, we replicated and expanded this experiment. The new study aimed to examine 1) whether the effects observed in May 2023 were still present in 2024, following Hamas' attack on Israel, 2) whether these findings were region-specific or applicable to attacks by the Israeli military in the West Bank, Gaza Strip, and southern Lebanon, and 3) whether the moderating effect of traditional antisemitic prejudices could also be observed for pre-existing Israel-related antisemitic attitudes.
