title_r: Cone of Direct Gaze - Perceived Pupil Dilation
abstract_r: When an observer watches someone else (the ‘gazer’) who is looking near them, does the observer’s perception of the gazer’s pupil size influence whether the observer sees the gazer to be looking toward or away from them? We will explore this by quantifying percepts of directed gaze as the Cone of Direct Gaze (CoDG; Gamer and Hecht, 2007), i.e. the range of eye gaze deviations that are perceived as looking at the observer as opposed to away from the observer. We have pilot data from an initial study suggesting that dilated pupils may lead to a wider CoDG compared to normal pupils; in addition, there was a trending difference between constricted and normal pupils -- suggesting that any deviation from average may widen the CoDG. The current experiment is a high-powered replication of those pilot data.

title_r: Effects of Fixation Location and Orientation on the neural processing of Face and House images
abstract_r: Using a gaze contingent paradigm and a within-subject design, the goal of the study is to investigate the neural correlates of the effects of fixation location and plane inversion on the processing of face and house stimuli using robust mass-univariate analyses (MUA). We intend to replicate and extend our previous MUA findings (Siklos-Whillans and Itier, in prep.) obtained in different participant samples (one experiment on house stimuli and one experiment on face stimuli). Participants will fixate on a fixation cross until an eye tracker registers their fixation, hereby triggering the presentation of a stimulus (a face or a house) which will be presented in such a way that the participant's fixation will be situated on particular areas of the stimulus (left eye, right eye, nasion -in between the eyes-, tip of the nose and mouth for faces, with the equivalent in house stimuli: left window, right window, between windows etc..). Participants will view faces and houses and will be required to press a button when they see a stimulus upright and another button when stimuli are inverted. This study will further our knowledge on the similarities and differences in the neural processing of faces and objects.

title_r: Experiment 3
abstract_r: This project explores whether event-omissions differences in the outcome of a causal scenario interact with action-inaction differences as potential causes in disjunctive causal scenarios. This is a conceptual replication of recent work (https://osf.io/preprints/osf/pcvfd_v1) that attempts to avoid potential confounds. This experiment varies whether the potential cause is an action or an inaction and whether the outcome is an event or an omission in a disjunctive causal scenario. The prediction is that there should be an interaction between the event type of the outcome (event|omission) and the action type of the potential cause (action|inaction) such that people have stronger causal judgments for actions when the outcome is an event rather than an omission and people have stronger causal judgments for inactions when the outcome is an omission rather than an event. Like Experiment 2, this experiment is just like Experiment 1—only this is a disjunctive causal scenario. When I ran the replication study in this project I realized, that I had included the word 'only' in the vignette when describing the necessary and sufficient conditions. I changed this wording in the replication vignette in order to be consistent with previous work. I realized, however, that this slight change in wording could have made a difference to the results in Experiment 2. Participants might have been confused about necessary and sufficient conditions in those cases. As such, this experiment is exactly like Experiment 2—only with the word 'only' removed from the vignette. I am doubtful that this slight change will make a difference, and even if I find the predicted effects here, they would be small and inconsistent. This experiment is primarily aimed at prospectively understanding the extent to which participants judgments will be affected by such changes in materials like these.

title_r: Methods and Measures
abstract_r: Participants Participants will be recruited by convenience sampling using Amazon MTurk. They will be 18 years old or older in order to be able to provide informed consent. Since the present study is an exact replication of Powell et al. (2005), our sample was limited to White participants only. All participants will be given $1 as compensation for their participation. Demographic Questions Participants will be asked to report their race, gender, age, and income. Measures Study One Framing Inequality Participants will be given a set of 24 statements that have to do with racial inequality between Whites and African Americans. There are two versions of these statements (See Appendix B). In the first version, participants will receive a set of statements that frames racial inequality in terms of White Privilege (condition 1). These statements include, "The national media encourages White Americans to feel proud of their race." Responses to these statements will be given using a 7 point-scale with (1) indicating Strongly Disagree and (7) indicating Strongly Agree. Collective Guilt Index Participants will be given a five item measure that includes statements such as, "I feel guilty about White Americans' harmful actions toward African Americans." Participants will respond using a 7 point-scale where (1) indicates Strongly Disagree and (7) indicates Strongly Agree. Responses to these 5 items will be averaged to create a collective guilt index. Higher ratings indicate higher collective guilt (See Appendix D). Racism Scale Participants will be given a five item measure that includes statements such as, "On average, people in our society treat White Americans and Black Americans equally." Participants will respond using a 7 point-scale where (1) indicates Strongly Disagree and (7) indicates Strongly Agree. Responses to these five items will be averaged to create a racism index. Higher scores indicate more racism (See Appendix E). Study Two Framing Inequality Participants will be asked to create their own statements. Instructions for this task will vary by condition. Participants in the White Privilege condition were asked to write down the many ways in which they have benefited or been advantaged because of their race. Participants in the Black Disadvantage condition were asked to write down the many ways in which African Americans have not benefited or have been disadvantaged because of their race (See Appendix C). Collective Guilt Participants will be given a seven item measure, the five items from study one plus two more. Participants will respond using a 7 point-scale where (1) indicates Strongly Disagree and (7) indicates Strongly Agree. Responses to these 7 items will be averaged to create a collective guilt index. Higher ratings indicate higher collective guilt (See Appendix D). Racism Scale Participants will be given a five item measure that includes statements such as, "Discrimination against Blacks is no longer a problem in the United States." Participants will respond using a 7 point-scale where (1) indicates Strongly Disagree and (7) indicates Strongly Agree. Responses to these five items will be averaged to create a racism index. Higher scores indicate more racism (See Appendix E). Beliefs in White Privilege and White Identification Participants will be asked to respond to two statements that have to do with their perception of the prevalence of White privilege. Additionally, they will be asked to respond to seven statements that will be used to measure White identification (See Appendix F). Responses to these seven items will be averaged to create a White identification index. Higher scores indicate greater White identification.

title_r: Sanctions Support and Effectiveness – US sample – Unexpected Event
abstract_r: This pre-analysis plan describes the hypothesis, research design, and sampling procedures for a survey experiment about public support for economic sanctions in the US. The planned study is a follow-up study, which builds upon a previous study conducted on 10 January 2022. Using a vignette web-survey experiment with 1.005 participants from the US, the first study found that multilateral sanctions – specifically those with US government and United Nations Security Council (UNSC) approval – receive substantially more public support relative to unilateral sanctions issued by the US without the UNSC. Moreover, the results indicate that public support is higher for sanctions that respond to an international crisis than for sanctions that are issued in response to domestic events in a foreign country. Finally, the results also suggest that public support is substantially changed when sanctions are further described as effective or ineffective. Respondents substantially increased their support when sanctions were described as effective, and strongly decreased their support when sanctions were considered ineffective. We seek to replicate and extend these findings by surveying the same participants again shortly after the event of the full Russian invasion of the Ukraine on 24 February 2022. To analyze how this event affected public support for sanctions, the follow-up survey will provide the same participants with the same scenario and again ask them about the same outcome measures of public support for the described sanctions as the original study did.

title_r: The Influence of Norm Feedback on Conservation Behavior: Replicating the Boomerang Effect
abstract_r: Research shows that social norms can be tools to encourage positive behaviors, but recent studies are also asking the question of whether the powerful draw toward the norm can also have negative implications. When individuals are provided with normative information, specifically descriptive norms which denote the behavior engaged in by members of the group, they use this knowledge to gauge and often adjust their own behavior (Schultz et al., 2007). Whether it be above or below the norm, being made aware of deviation from the norm, even in positive ways such as lower energy consumption, can cause individuals to change their behavior in the direction of the norm (Schultz et al., 2007). Further studies have shown the potential to combat this boomerang effect by acknowledging compliance with injunctive norms, in the form of a smiley face signifying social approval, when revealing to people that their behavior falls below the norm in a positive way (such as lower levels of water consumption) (Schultz et al., 2019). The proposed study is designed to replicate the 2007 study discussing the theory of this boomerang effect and the potential for injunctive norms to moderate it.

title_r: Prejudice in Contrast 2
abstract_r: In this study we test whether people show more bias in a standard Black-White IAT than in two consecutively implemented Black and White SC-IATs (not contrasting the two groups directly). title_r: Visual cues to racial prototypicality shape racial bias in pain perception (Replication with female targets)
abstract_r: Individuals rapidly extract category-level information about other people, such as race gender, and age (e.g., Mason, Cloutier, & Macrae, 2006; Ito & Urland, 2003), which may activate group-based stereotypes and bias subsequent person perception (Macrae & Bodenhausen, 2001; Freeman & Johnson, 2016). As such, the degree to which a person perceives an individual to be prototypic of a given category can influence recruitment of stereotype content and affective evaluations. While race is not biologically supported, the consequences of racial categorization, prototypes, and stereotypes are real. Through racism, this social construct has important influences on how we navigate the world and interact with others. For example, lighter-skinned Black individuals are afforded greater access to opportunities in terms of hiring, pay, housing, and healthcare, compared to their darker-skinned counterparts (Goldsmith, Hamilton, & Darrity, 2007; Keith & Herring, 1991; Stewart, Cobb, & Keith, 2020). In turn, work in social psychology has focused on the causes and consequences of how others perceive Black individuals based on their proximity to prototypes of Blackness (Maddox & Perry, 2018). A growing body of evidence demonstrates that racially prototypic features are associated with differences in health outcomes, as well. For example, darker (versus lighter) skin tones are associated with higher blood pressure (Armstead, Hébert, Griffin, & Prince, 2014; Dressler, 1991; Monk, 2015; Sweet, McDade, Kiefe, & Liu, 2007), worse self-reported physical and mental health (Dent, Hagiwara, Stepanova, & Green, 2020; Monk, 2015), and higher all-cause mortality rates (Stewart, Cobb, & Keith, 2020) in Black individuals. Further, Black racial prototypicality shapes judgments of social pain in experimental settings (Deska, Kunstman, Bernstein, Ogungbadero, & Hugenberg, 2020b). In our own work (e.g., Drain et al., in prep; https://psyarxiv.com/6gu8j/), we’ve observed evidence of the effects of racial prototypicality on the visual perception of facial expressions associated with physical pain. Overall, darker skin tones were associated with more stringent pain perception (e.g., collapsing across race), and dark-skinned Black targets’ pain was least readily perceived and received the lowest treatment recommendations. On the other hand, racially prototypic structural features exacerbated racial bias in pain perception. Specifically, this perceptual bias was largest when Black targets had Afrocentric features versus either Eurocentric or racially neutral structural features. That said, while this prior work systematically manipulated skin tone and structure (either independently or interactively), this work did not allow for the consideration of the influence of target-level variations in holistic perceptions of prototypicality on pain outcomes. Perhaps more importantly, this work in our lab did not involve any actual measurement of prototypicality judgments or assessment of the relation between subjective judgments of prototypicality and either pain thresholds or treatment. In more recent work that addressed these issues, we observed that perceivers’ own assessments of target racial prototypicality predict their perceptual thresholds for seeing painful expressions: pain was seen less readily on Black faces as they were judged by participants to look more prototypically Black, while pain was seen *more* readily on White faces as they were judged to look more prototypically White. However, this work used only male faces. In the present work, we will replicate this previous protocol using female faces instead.

title_r: Practitioner Knowledge and Implementation of the Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS) in UK Schools
abstract_r: It is estimated that up to 25% of children with an autism spectrum conditions (ASC) never acquire speech, and therefore rely on augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) systems as their primary mode of communication (Lord et al., 2004). The Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS™) is one such AAC system. Individuals learning to use PECS are initially taught to communicate simple requests for items and activities through the exchange of pictures and icons. Once the initial phases are mastered, the picture system is later expanded to enable the learner to use more elaborate language (e.g., making comments, responding to questions). There is some evidence in support of the use of PECS for learners with minimal verbal repertoires (e.g., Brignell et al., 2018; Lamb et al., 2018; Preston & Carter, 2009). The intervention is also widely used; in an international survey of over 500 parents of children with ASD, Green et al. (2006) reported that PECS was being used by 28% of respondents, with a further 31% reporting having used it in the past. Finally, in a survey of 160 parents of children with ASD focusing exclusively on the United Kingdom, Denne et al. (2017) reported that PECS was currently used by 19% of respondents, with 23% having used it previously. While the available evidence suggests that PECS is widely employed in special education settings in the UK, the level of training of those tasked with implementation is often very limited (Howlin, Gordon, Pasco, Wade, & Charman, 2007). Consequently, the intervention is at risk of not being implemented as intended (Bondy, 2012). May et al. (under review), evaluated how well PECS is understood and implemented in special education schools in the UK. The study revealed a high degree of variability in teachers’ knowledge and implementation of PECS. Notably, we identified gaps in knowledge and implementation in particular aspects which could serve to weaken its effectiveness. Importantly, the paper found that staff who have received PECS-specific training were more accurate in their understanding and consistent in their implementation than those who had not received such support. These are important findings; the consequences of compromised treatment integrity can range from reductions in the effectiveness of an intervention (Arkoosh et al., 2007) through to the outright rejection of evidence-based treatment programs (Moncher & Prinz, 1991). The present research aims to refine, replicate, and extend existing research (May et al.,) in two ways. First, the study will serve as a preregistered replication of the original study by May et al., (under review) in order to test the robustness of those findings. Second, we will explore the impact of controlling for additional factors than those in the initial modelling. Specifically, we will look to estimate the impact of type of PECS training (the estimand of interest) on knowledge and implementation survey scores (outcomes), adjusting for job role and supportive environment (covariates) in the model.

title_r: Resilience on Job Stress and Temporal Discounting
abstract_r: Objective: This study aims to further explore the relationship between job stress and temporal discounting, with a focus on how resilience might moderate this relationship. Background: Our previous study indicated that job stress itself unexpectedly reduces temporal discounting, contrary to existing literature on general stress. New Study Design: 1. Job Stress Induction: To address the moderate job stress levels observed in our previous sample, we will use techniques such as active memory recall or imaginative scenarios to induce higher job stress levels. 2. General Stress Measurement: We will include a baseline measurement of general stress to compare its effects on temporal discounting with those of job stress. 3. Resilience as a Moderator: We will examine whether resilience moderates the relationship between job stress and temporal discounting. We hypothesize that higher resilience will weaken the impact of job stress on temporal discounting, potentially preventing the shift toward more temporal discounting, and in the case of low resilience, reversing the effects observed in our first study. Anticipated Outcomes: We expect to replicate previous findings where general stress leads to increased temporal discounting and job stress leads to reduced temporal discounting. Additionally, we anticipate that depending on the resilience level the effects of job stress on temporal discounting will vary, potentially explaining the unexpected results from study 1. This study aims to provide deeper insights into how resilience influences decision-making under job stress and enhance our understanding of the stress-temporal discounting dynamics.

title_r: Replication: psychometric curves analysis of an online vigilance task
abstract_r: Fitting psychometric curves to vigilance data using hierarchical Bayesian modeling, McCarley and Yamani (in press) found that the vigilance decrement was driven by a sensitivity loss, conservative bias shift, and increase in attentional lapse rate. The present study is an attempt to replicate these results in an online sample. Pilot data gave evidence of a conservative bias shift and very large increase in lapse rate, but no evidence for or against a change in sensitivity. Differences between the pilot results and McCarley and Yamani's results could be due, in part, to participants not fully attending to the task when completing it in an uncontrolled setting. title_r: Effect of spatial divider on flanker task (attention orienting and executive attention)
abstract_r: Target identification is interfered with by a distractor even if the distractor is task-irrelevant. This interference could be modulated when the target and the distractor are presented in different objects (e.g., target is presented within Object A, and distractor is presented within Object B). Our previous experiments replicated this modulation effect, especially in a low load task. But we also showed that the interference effect could not be modulated when the target and the distractor are presented in different areas which are separated by spatial dividers. Therefore, we suggested that people can inhibit the interference by the distractor embedded in other object from the target, but they cannot inhibit this effect when the distractor is presented in the different area with spatial dividers. That is, the presentation of the spatial divider could not influence executive attention. In this experiment, we aim to replicate this effect. In addition, we examine the presentation of the spatial divider influences attention orienting.

title_r: The temporal gradient of retroactive interference in the laboratory
abstract_r: In a prior online study, we used a multinomial processing tree (MPT) storage-retrieval model to show that the temporal gradient of retroactive interference (TGRI) is driven by retrieval rather than storage processes. The respective preregistration can be found here: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/YB7SX This result pattern suggests that the TGRI can best be explained in terms of temporal distinctiveness (Ecker et al., 2015) rather than opportunistic consolidation (Mednick et al., 2011). In the present study, we aim to critically test this interpretation. To this end, we will replicate both conditions from our previous study in a controlled laboratory setting to make sure that cognitive effort during the distractor task is indeed minimized. Additionally, we will test whether the retrieval effect found in our previous study is sensitive to the similarity of original L1 and interpolated L2 items, as suggested by the distinctiveness theory but not the opportunistic consolidation hypothesis.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Powell (2009) in Comparative Political Studies.
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Powell (2009) is that government congruence under SMD [single member district] is usually determined by the distance between the median voter and the plurality vote winner (Hypothesis 2a). This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: "The association between election rules and congruence has declined in the past decade, as shown by all three major approaches, due primarily to convergence toward the median of plurality parties in the SMD elections." Table 2 shows regression analyses of the distance between the median voter and the government in SMD systems, using the manifesto method in the two left columns and the cit-ex method in the two right columns. The selected analysis uses the manifesto method. The independent variables are simple dummy variables for each of the 10-year periods (the 1945-1955 period is omitted as a reference baseline), as well as a variable for the distance between the median voter and the plurality vote winner. As part of the evidence in support of H2a, this latter term (‘Plurality party distance to median voter’) is selected (see Model 2 under ‘Manifesto Method’ in Table 2 for details). In that specification, only the plurality vote winner distance is (very strongly) statistically significant, whereas the time dummies are reduced, most to insignificance (‘Plurality party distance to median voter’ term: estimate = 0.84; panel-corrected SE = 0.05; significant at .01).

title_r: Pupillometric signatures of representing multiple possibilities in 14-month-old infants
abstract_r: Contrasting possibilities has a fundamental adaptive value for prediction and learning. Developmental research, however, yielded controversial findings. Some data suggest that preschoolers might have trouble in planning actions that take into account mutually exclusive possibilities, while other studies revealed an early understanding of alternative future outcomes based on infants' looking behavior. To better understand the origin of such abilities, we suggest using pupil dilation as a potential indicator of infants' representation of possibilities. In our two previous experiments, ten- and fourteen-month-olds were engaged in an object identification task watching video animations where three different objects with identical top parts moved behind two screens. Importantly, a target object emerged from one of the screens but remained in partial occlusion, revealing only its top part, which was compatible with a varying number of possible identities. We found that pupil diameter increased with the object's potential identities in fourteen- but not in ten-month-olds. In this experiment, we aim to replicate and extend our previous results by showing 14-month-old infants similar object identification tasks as in our previous studies, but here, the identity of the displayed objects will be compatible with not 1 or 2, but with 2 or 3 mutually exclusive possibilities. Just as adults' pupil diameter grows monotonically with the amount of information held in memory, we expect that infants' pupil size will increase with the number of alternatives sustained in memory as candidate identities for the partially-occluded object.

title_r: Underlying Mechanisms of Nature’s Effect on State Authenticity
abstract_r: In our previous studies, we showed that nature can enhance individuals’ state authenticity, across various nature manipulation, such as exposure to both real nature settings and digital nature pictures (vs. urban nature and digital ones) and engagement with nature-related activities (vs. control ones). We also found in our previous studies that this effect is mediated by need for autonomy, positive affect, self-esteem, and mindfulness, independently. In the current experiment, we ask participants to view a 5-minute video depicting non-threatening nature scenes (vs. an urban ones) and to immerse themselves into the scenes. Subsequently, we ask participants to fill out scales measuring—at the state level—the four plausible mediators (need for autonomy, positive affect, self-esteem, mindfulness) and the dependent measure (i.e., authenticity). We aimed to replicate and extend the prior findings by testing these four mediators (i.e., need for autonomy, positive affect, self-esteem, mindfulness) both independently and in parallel. We provide all stimulus materials in the Appendix.

title_r: The impact of threat to personal control on trust in experts and non-experts communicating about risk
abstract_r: In this project, we aim at understanding potential processes underlying trust in experts communicating risks associated with an emerging technology. To achieve this, we plan to replicate previous findings from our initial experiment (i.e., Study 1). In Study 1, we first manipulated participants’ sense of personal control (high vs low). Subsequently, participants read an article discussing risks associated with nanotechnology in food. We manipulated expertise of the article source (high vs low) and the extent to which the source communicated with certainty or uncertainty. We measured perceived trust in experts (ability, integrity, benevolence, and overall trust) as well as attitudes towards nanotechnology in food. Partially supporting our hypotheses, we found that participants perceived the source to be of higher ability when it was an expert (vs. non-expert) and it communicated with certainty (vs. uncertainty). When participants’ personal sense of control was threatened or affirmed and the source communicated with certainty, perceived ability trust towards the source was higher for the expert as opposed to non-expert source. The same tendency, although marginal, was true for perceptions of overall trust. Interestingly, we found that participants had more positive attitudes towards nanotechnology when the source was an expert (vs. non-expert), communicated with certainty (vs. uncertainty), and participants’ sense of control was threatened (vs. affirmed). To further support these results, we will conduct a follow-up experiment using the same design, but with slightly modified materials. We will reframe the main article to precisely manipulate certainty, such that the article will strongly emphasise certainties and uncertainties associated with nanotechnology. This will be done to reduce the possibility of manipulating valence in combination with certainty. However, as it might not be possible to disentangle valence and certainty entirely (i.e., an article communicating with certainty might appear to be more positive than an article communicating with uncertainty), we will additionally measure participants’ perception of the article valence.

title_r: Who speaks what (Study 2: 8-11mo)
abstract_r: In a previous study, we investigated 8- to 11-month-old infants' visual preferences for speakers of a native vs. foreign language. We presented infants with two conditions: (1) a static condition, in which two pair of faces was presented side by side, and (2) an action condition, in which the two individuals appeared side by side reaching for, grasping, and lifting an object. Exploratory analysis found that, during the goal of the action (i.e., when the experimenters grasped and lifted the toy), infants preferred to look at the speaker of a native language. However, in the same time window during the static condition, participants showed the opposite pattern -- they preferred to look at the foreign language speaker. Here, we aim to replicate these findings to provide further evidence that infants attend differently to native and foreign language speakers depending on the context and content of information.

title_r: The Relation between Uncertainty-Guided Exploration in Decision Making, Autism and Other Traits
abstract_r: This study is part of a larger correlational study, see a general preregistration for the overarching project at https://osf.io/9u8gd. In that project, we hypothesize that autism is related to the context-sensitivity of cognitive flexibility, such that participants with autism or more autistic traits show a lower context effect on cognitive flexibility. Additionally, we explore correlations with other personality traits. The overall study consists of five computer tasks measuring cognitive flexibility, self-report questionnaires measuring autistic symptoms and other personality traits, a cognitive abilities test and demographic questions. The experiment will be conducted online, in three sessions all completed within one week. Participants will consist of a neurotypical group (n = 500) and an autism group (n = 100) and will be recruited through the recruiting platform Prolific. This allows us to do (1) correlational analyses between effects of interest and questionnaire scores, and (2) between-group analyses comparing the autism group with a matched subset of neurotypical participants for the effects of interest. This preregistration will discuss the paradigm aimed to investigate whether there is a relation between autistic traits and the exploration strategy in value-based decision making in vast decision spaces. We use the spatially correlated multi-armed bandit paradigm (Wu et al., 2018) to study the strength with which participants generalize observed rewards over unexplored options, exploit from prior experience, and explore in random and uncertainty-guided manners. In this paradigm, participants have to accumulate the highest possible reward by sampling tiles on a square grid. Previous studies (e.g., Wu et al., 2018) showed that participants use generalization (computationally modelled by Gaussian Process Regression with a Radial-Basis-Function kernel) to extrapolate prior experiences to unexplored tiles on the grid. The length scale of the Radial-Basis-Function, i.e. the generalization parameter, determines the strength with which participants ‘smooth out’ the observed rewards. To inform where to sample next, participants balance exploitation (of tiles for which they are certain to yield high rewards) with exploration (of more uncertain tiles to learn more about the reward distribution of the grid). The weight with which participants consider the uncertainty of a tile is governed by the exploration parameter. First, we expect to replicate these findings of Wu and others for our population. Second, we want to investigate whether there is a relation between autistic traits and the generalization parameter and/or the exploration parameter.

title_r: Replication of Turri et al. (2015) at Franklin and Marshall College
abstract_r: According to the Justified True Belief (JTB) account of knowledge, a person’s ability to know something is defined by having a belief that is both justified and true (i.e., knowledge is justified true belief). However, this account fails to consider the role of luck. In 1963, Gettier argued that JTB is insufficient because it does not account for certain situations, called Gettier cases, wherein a person is justified for believing something true but only because of luck. It is unclear whether lay people’s intuitions about knowledge lead them to agree with Gettier, such that lay people believe that individuals in these cases lack knowledge (referred to as Gettier intuitions). We attempt to provide a robust estimate of the Gettier intuition effect size by replicating Turri and colleagues’ (2015) Experiment 1. The Collaborative Replications and Education Project (CREP) selected this study for replication based on its undergraduate appeal, feasibility, and pedagogical value. However, in light of some inconsistent results, suboptimal designs, and inconsistent evidence for cultural variation (e.g., Machery et al., 2015; Nagel, et al., 2013; Seyedsayamdost et al., 2015; Starman & Friedman, 2012; Weinberg et al., 2001), the improved methodology of Turri et al. (2015) make it an important study to replicate cross-culturally. Therefore, we propose a multisite collaborative preregistered replication of Turri and colleague's (2015) Experiment 1 (35 labs from 14 countries across 4 continents signed up at time of submission; expected minimum N = 1,500). Results of this study are expected to provide a clearer picture of the Gettier intuition effect size, lay people’s theory and practice of knowledge, and potentially cross-cultural similarities and differences. PSA lab USA_173 will collect data from Franklin and Marshall students online.

title_r: Does assigning intentions to others involve visual motion processing?
abstract_r: We use others’ gaze to identify their object of attention. Guterstam and colleagues suggested that the capability to link the gaze of observed persons to their object of interest is mediated by an imaginary “gaze beam” that emanates from the others’ eyes and moves through space. The central tenet of this hypothesis is that the gaze beam recruits the visual motion processing system. Görner et al. argued that the experimental evidence supports not only this “gaze beam hypothesis” but also a different interpretation, namely the beholder´s understanding that the other displays a particular object-related intention. We refer to this as “intentional binding hypothesis”. This assignment of an intention may involve the prediction of an upcoming movement of the observed person engaging the same system. To critically compare the explanatory power of the two hypotheses, we aim to replicate and extend the original psychophysical study by Guterstam et al. to test the alternative hypothesis.

title_r: Eyewitness Description Quality Varies with Face Recognition Ability
abstract_r: Witness statements provided by eyewitnesses are frequently used to help identify possible perpetrators of a crime (Meissner et al., 2007). Thus, improving the quality of a witness’s description of a perpetrator may also improve police’s ability to locate the perpetrator. One proposal aimed at improving eyewitness description is the Person Description Interview (PDI), which seeks to obtain a more complete description of the perpetrator, as compared to existing interview-techniques (Demarchi & Py, 2009). The PDI consists of two consecutive free recall tests that is inspired by the apparent human inclination to first describe someone generally and then to describe their specific features (Demarchi & Py, 2009). The PDI has been compared to standard verbal instructions and the standard French police interview for person description (SFPIPD) and was found to yield more complete descriptions that were not associated with an accompanying increase in incorrect details (Demarchi, 2003; Demarchi & Py, 2009). Further evaluation found that PDI descriptions were also more accurately matched to the target they described by a naive individual, although accuracy rates for both SFPIPD and PDI descriptions were low (Demarchi & Py, 2009). We further examined the quality of descriptions generated from either PDI or standard instructions in an unpublished study. Stimuli for this study were collected from a prior, published study where participants saw a video of a robbery and then were given either the PDI instructions or standard instructions to generate a description of the perpetrator (Dodson et al., 2024). Participants in Dodson and colleagues’ (2024) sample varied in face recognition ability, which was assessed with the Cambridge Face Memory Test (CFMT). In this prior unpublished study, we only included descriptions that came from participants with average to strong face recognition ability in order to increase the likelihood that our evaluators would perform above-chance at identifying the described face, as this is a notoriously difficult task (Demarchi & Py, 2009). We measured the quality of the descriptions that were generated from either the PDI or the standard instructions by examining the rate at which a new set of participants can use the description to identify the target face from a pair of faces. The target face in each pair was the culprit in the video who was the focus of the description by the Dodson et al. participants. When evaluators were given a description elicited from PDI instructions, they were better able to identify the target face when the description had been generated by a stronger face recognizer (CFMT scores from 68-72, Mean =78%) than an average face recognizer (CFMT scores from 56-60, Mean =63%). By contrast, the face recognition ability of the describer did not affect evaluators’ performance when standard instructions were used (i.e. evaluators showed identification rates of 68% and 68% when they used descriptions that had been generated by average and strong face recognizers, respectively). In a generalized linear model (GLM) we observed that the accuracy of identifying the target face was predicted by an interaction between the description instructions (standard verbal or PDI) and the face recognition ability of the describer (χ2(1) =12.83, p<.001). In the current study, we aim to replicate and extend the findings of the prior study by examining PDI and Standard Verbal descriptions that were generated from individuals across a wider range of face recognition ability (e.g., from weak to very strong). We will also extend the former study by investigating whether the quality of the description is worse when it had been generated by a describer who subsequently misidentified vs. correctly identified the target face from a lineup. Extant research shows little association between an evaluator’s ability to use an eyewitness’s description to accurately identify a perpetrator and whether the description was followed by a correct or incorrect eyewitness identification (Meissner et al., 2007). The few studies that do find an association between utility of description and accuracy of the eyewitness theorize that a heavy reliance on using featural descriptions contribute to this effect (Rhodes et al., 1989; Sporer, 2001a). Because a feature of the PDI is a focus on featural justifications (i.e. Try to describe the face of the person you saw. Begin with the lower part of his face – such as his chin – and then go up to the top), it is possible that descriptions garnered from PDI instructions may be more useful in situations in which an eyewitness is correct. This could explain some of its instructional utility when compared with standard verbal instructions.

title_r: Perceptions of moral decoupling: Independent voter (December 2024)
abstract_r: This study is conceptual replication of a study we have already conducted. In that study, we presented participants with a scenario about an election in which a target was deciding whether to vote for her inparty candidate (who was described as having committed a moral transgression) or her outparty candidate (who was not described as such). Whether the target (and the problematic candidate) belonged to the participant's inparty (versus outparty) was manipulated between subjects, and we measured the extent to which participants believed the target was engaging in moral rationalization and decoupling, as well as participants' liking for the target. We found that attributions of decoupling negatively influenced participants’ liking for the outparty target (who voted for the participant’s outparty candidate) but did not affect liking for the inparty target (who voted for the participant’s inparty candidate). Evaluations of decoupling in this initial study therefore appeared to depend on whether decoupling was used to support a politically congenial decision. By contrast, attributions of rationalization negatively influenced liking for the target regardless of her party identity, such that even when she voted for the problematic ingroup candidate, they liked her less to the extent that they thought she was rationalizing away the candidate's transgression. The design and materials for the present study are modeled after those of our initial study, with some modifications. Participants will again read a scenario in which a target considers two political candidates, one of whom is described as having committed a moral transgression (we refer to this candidate as the "dirty" candidate and the othe as the "clean" candidate as shorthand). In this study, we will hold the target’s party identification constant (by specifying that she is an Independent, thus belonging to neither party) and orthogonally manipulating two factors: 1) whether she votes for the clean (vs. dirty) candidate, and 2) whether that candidate belongs to the participant’s inparty versus outparty. The result is therefore a 2 (Candidate moral status: Clean vs. Dirty) x 2 (Candidate alignment: Inparty vs. Outparty) between-subjects design.

title_r: Perceived economic inequality, affective polarization, and support for redistribution and collective actions (UNDPOLAR)
abstract_r: In this study, we seek to replicate previous findings from our research about the positive association between perceived economic inequality and affective polarization toward class-based groups. Furthermore, we argue that affective polarization toward class-based groups can be a predictor of supporting actions to redress inequality, such as support for redistribution and collective actions. However, it is highly likely that these associations will be conditional on people's system-justifying ideologies, such as social dominance orientation and other system-justification beliefs. Therefore, this study seeks to contribute to the literature by examining the side effects of perceived economic inequality in exacerbating both positive and negative feelings toward class-based groups, which in turn might motivate people to engage in strategies aimed at reducing inequality.

title_r: MPT Reliability
abstract_r: The Implicit Association Test (IAT; Greenwald et al., 1998) was long thought to capture stable individual differences in implicit cognition (i.e., implicit biases). Though evidence suggests that person-level factors influence IAT scores (Rae &amp; Greenwald, 2017), the perspective of the IAT as a measure of stable individuals differences is difficult to reconcile with studies suggesting that the IAT demonstrates good internal reliability but low test-retest reliability (Gawronski et al., 2017; Wilson &amp; Lai, 2021). Payne and colleagues (2017) sought to resolve this theoretical puzzle with a new perspective on implicit bias reflecting context-dependent concept accessibility rather than stable individual differences. Context dependence necessarily implies that implicit biases should fluctuate as people move between contexts, which would seem to explain observed low IAT retest reliability. The present research seeks to investigate these two competing perspectives on implicit bias: as a person-based vs. a context-based construct. To the extent that implicit bias reflects something stable about individuals, a measure of implicit bias should demonstrate high retest reliability, but to the extent that implicit bias reflects something that varies according to individuals’ contexts, a measure of implicit bias should not necessarily demonstrate high retest reliability. Evidence to date indicates that the IAT (and all other implicit bias measures) do not demonstrate high retest reliability (Gawronski et al., 2017; Wilson &amp; Lai, 2021). However, existing evidence overlooks the possibility that some of the processes that contribute to responses on implicit measures are stable, but others are context-dependent. Implicit bias is typically operationalized in terms of summary statistics; in the context of the IAT, this is the d-score (Greenwald et al., 2003), which reflects mean differences in response latency between blocks of trials. Summary statistics reflect the contributions of all processes that influence responses on implicit measures, but cannot distinguish among the contributions of distinct processes. Consequently, in the present research we will use formal mathematical modeling to decompose IAT responses into estimates of multiple cognitive processes. In doing so, we will gain a greater understanding of the extent to which the various processes underlying implicit bias change over time. In a previous pre-registered analysis, we relied on the Quad process model (Conrey et al., 2005) to disentangle the influence of multiple distinct cognitive processes on IAT performance. Building on these findings, we will apply the process dissociation procedure (PDP; Payne, 2001) to the same data in order to observe whether the pattern of results observed from the Quad model generalizes to another model. Not only do these analyses reflect a conceptual replication of our initial analyses, but they also prevent us from drawing strong conclusions based on this single operationalization of the cognitive processes underlying IAT performance (i.e., Quad vs PDP). In the current analysis, we plan to apply the PDP to six samples of race IAT data, each reflecting two measurement occasions. The PDP model estimates parameters for Automatic and Controlled responding, which vary by trial type. The most commonly-used specification of the PDP includes 2 different Automatic responding parameters, one for White faces and another for Black faces; and 4 different Controlled responding parameters, one for White faces, one for Black faces, one for pleasant words, and one for unpleasant words. As exploratory analyses, we will also estimate an alternative specification of the PDP that includes 2 different Automatic responding parameters, one for White faces and another for Black faces; and 2 different Controlled responding parameters, one for target stimuli and one for attribute stimuli. After estimating the PDP parameters, we will compute ICC values for each specified parameter, from which we will infer the extent to which each parameter is stable over time. We interpret ICC values of &lt;0.40 as poor, 0.4-0.6 as fair, 0.6-0.75 as good, and &gt;0.75 as excellent reliability. A high ICC value provides relatively straightforward evidence that a parameter captures a relatively stable, person-level, trait-like process. However, a low ICC value could reflect multiple possibilities. One possibility is that a parameter with a low ICC captures a relatively state-like, contextually-determined process. Another possibility is that a parameter with a low ICC captures a process that is temporally-variable, that is, a process that is not consistent across measurement occasions even if the context is stable.

title_r: Intentions Implementation and COVID19 preventive measures
abstract_r: This experiment is a direct replication of a pilot study conducted in France which showed that a paper pencil implementation of intentions exercise could lead in increased intentions to enact COVID-19 preventive measures. Results from the pilot study are available in the corresponding folder. The procedure is attached. After reading a short visual poster containing CDC recommended health behavior to limit the spread of COVID19, participants are asked once to rate the effectiveness of the proposed measures. They are then split between a control (deliberation) condition or an implementation of intentions exercise. After this part, both groups are asked to rate again the perceived effectiveness of the measures and proceed with the DV. The pilot study contained measures of conspiracy beliefs, supposed to mediate the effect, but these were not affected by the intervention, thus removed from the US replication study. Similarly, perceived effectiveness of measures are not affected by the procedure, and this measure is thus considered part of the intervention protocol (i.e. not theorized as a mediator). The effect was observed across all items averaged, but worked better when not considering the item related to vaccination. Vaccines in France were not available to our target sample (students) at the time of the study, and vaccine hesitancy in France is one of the highest of all OECD countries. One goal of this replication study is thus to establish, beyond replicability of the effect, its potential for increasing vaccination intentions too.

title_r: Capturing, Clarifying, and Consolidating the Curiosity-Creativity Connection (Study 2, Preregistered)
abstract_r: Study aims: This study is a preregistered follow-up and conceptual replication of an earlier experiment (referred to here as Study 1). The primary aim of the current study is to examine the association between curiosity and creativity when: (a) both curiosity and creativity are measured using behaviorally observed outcomes (rather than only self-report), and (b) both curiosity and creativity are assessed using behavioral measures that assess two core aspects of each construct. For curiosity the two core aspects involve: (i) internally generated exploration and identification of what an individual does not know or desires to know, here operationally assessed through the formulation and posing of questions ("question asking") regarding experimentally presented factual information; (ii) externally supported exploratory information seeking, here operationally assessed through an individual's choosing to look at the answers to visually provided questions ("information foraging"). For creativity the two core aspects involve: (i) divergent thinking, the generation of multiple, varied, and original ideas in response to an open-ended problem, for which a large number of possible responses are acceptable and may be deemed correct; (ii) convergent thinking, the generation of the single best (or correct) answer to a clearly defined problem or question.

title_r: Toenemende wiskundeangst bij toenemende wiskundekennis: een replicatie- en uitbreidingsstudie rond natural number bias
abstract_r: Heel wat leerlingen hebben moeite met het begrijpen van rationale getallen, en breuken in het bijzonder. Een belangrijke verklaringsbron is de natural number bias (NNB): het fenomeen waarbij leerlingen onterecht de eigenschappen van natuurlijke getallen toepassen op rationale getallen (bijv. denken dat 1/3 + 1/4 = 2/7). Recent werd aangetoond dat het oplossen van opgaven met breuken bij leerlingen een gevoel van angst kan teweegbrengen. Inmiddels werd het verband tussen het oplossen van breukopgaven en wiskundeangst ook longitudinaal aangetoond in de Finse studie van Van Hoof et al. (in press): Leerlingen in de bovenbouw van het lager onderwijs losten opgaven rond breukrekenen op. In het begin van het schooljaar werden twee groepen leerlingen opgespoord: leerlingen met een uitgesproken NNB en leerlingen die laag scoorden maar geen NNB hadden. Bij hen werd ook het gevoel van wiskundeangst gemeten bij het oplossen van de taken. Op het eind van het schooljaar werd dezelfde breukrekentaak opnieuw afgenomen, en werd de wiskundeangst opnieuw gemeten. De resultaten toonden dat leerlingen bij wie de NNB doorheen het schooljaar sterk afnam (en die dus beter presteerden) aanzienlijk meer wiskundeangst vertoonden. Dat was niet het geval voor de leerlingen die aanvankelijk laag presteerden en doorheen het schooljaar beter gingen presteren. In deze masterproef zullen we de Finse studie repliceren, door dezelfde studie met dezelfde instrumenten in Vlaanderen af te nemen bij leerlingen in het 5de leerjaar. Verder breiden we deze studie ook uit. Zo nemen we naast de breukrekentaak ook taken af rond het rekenen met natuurlijke getallen, breuken en kommagetallen. Na elke taak volgt één wiskundeangstmeting. De taken worden klassikaal afgenomen op papier op 2 momenten. Elk testmoment zal ongeveer 30 minuten duren.

title_r: Replication on Closeness Regulation in Couples
abstract_r: All information including tables and illustrations can be found in the preregistration file in the project. The present study will be a conceptual replication and extension of a study on dissociations in the regulation of closeness discrepancies (i.e., deviations of experienced closeness from the desired amount of closeness with a romantic partner) by Hilligloh and Hagemeyer (in revision). In the original study, the authors conducted continuous time structural equation models on daily-diary data (n = 240 individuals, t = 12) of mixed-gender couples. Based on a set-point perspective and the Intimacy Process Model (Reis & Shaver, 1988), the authors hypothesized that the regulation of closeness frustration (i.e., a desire for more closeness with the partner) is slower and more dependent on the partner than the regulation of closeness surfeit (i.e., a desire for less closeness with the partner). Additionally, effects of personal and situational conditions on closeness regulation were explored. As personal conditions, implicit and explicit motivational orientations (IMO; EMO) were examined, constructs that reflect whether communal or agentic motive dispositions were predominant in the individual. The couple’s daily contact duration was analyzed as a situational condition. Continuous time models approach an estimation of effects that are independent of the measurement interval. In the continuous time framework, the rate of change in a criterion is estimated instead of the absolute change. In the present case, the rate of change can be interpreted as regulatory speed. A greater rate of change denotes a faster regulation and a smaller rate of change denotes a slower regulation. Additionally, the great flexibility of the models allows a separate estimation and comparison of the processes of closeness frustration and closeness surfeit in the same model. The results indicated that the regulation of closeness frustration was slower and more dependent on partner contact than the regulation of closeness surfeit. However, more partner contact than usual was associated with a faster regulation of closeness discrepancies in general. IMO and EMO moderated the effect of partner contact on closeness regulation. Regardless of the kind of the closeness discrepancy, communally oriented individuals regulated faster on days with more partner contact than usual compared to agentically oriented individuals. Conversely, agentically oriented individuals regulated faster on days with less partner contact than usual. Only for EMO of the male partner did the interaction not become significant. Nevertheless, we will test the moderation hypothesis in the replication study for this case as well. In the present study, continuous time structural equation models of experience sampling data (n = approx. 510 individuals, 140 measurements over 28 days on two levels) will be used to conceptually replicate the findings of this study. The data allows us to: a) replicate the findings from Hilligloh and Hagemeyer (in revision) on the day-to-day level, and b) extend the replication to the finer-grained momentary level. On the day-to-day level, closeness discrepancies were assessed with the same instrument as in Hilligloh and Hagemeyer (in revision). On the momentary level, closeness discrepancies were assessed by a different instrument. Please note that the original study is still undergoing review, and changes in methods and results may occur. We preregister the expected hypotheses and methods (as they appear in the current version of the manuscript at the time of preregistration). In case of changes in the original study, we will deviate from the preregistration and follow the original study. To ensure that preliminary analyses for the replication study do not influence the review process of the original study, such analyses will be conducted with scrambled data up until the acceptance of the original manuscript.

title_r: Impact of consideration of future consequences on environmental intentions
abstract_r: In the current study, we will aim to examine the effect of future thinking on Consideration of Future Consequences (Strathman et al., 1994) and pro-environmental intention and investigate whether this effect is mediated by facets of consideration of future consequences. Specifically, we use prospect-concept priming (Arnocky et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012) to manipulate future thinking. Literature shows a small to moderate positive association between consideration of future consequences (CFC, Strathman et al., 1994; or similar constructs such as ZTPI, Zimbardo & Boyd, 1999) and pro-environmental intention or behavior (see e.g., Bruderer Enzler, 2015; Joireman et al., 2001; Milfont et al., 2012; Milfont & Gouveia, 2006). Previous studies failed to show a causal effect of CFC on pro-environmental intention or behavior. Consideration of future and immediate consequences (CFC-F, CFC-I) is a relatively stable personality trait (Strathman et al., 1994; Toepoel, 2010). However, priming-based interventions have been used previously to manipulate CFC in experiments (Arnocky et al., 2014). In the current study, we will use prospect-concept priming (Arnocky et al., 2014; Cheng et al., 2012) to manipulate CFC and we will test whether this manipulation increases pro-environmental intention. Arnocky and colleagues (2014) discovered that participants in the future condition scored significantly lower in consideration of immediate consequences (CFC-I) than participants in the present condition; this manipulation did not affect consideration of future consequences (CFC-F) though. Participants in the future condition scored also higher in environmental concern and pro-environmental intention. The effect of future-priming on environmental concern and pro-environmental behavior motivation was partially mediated by CFC-I. This study is a conceptual replication of Arnocky et al.'s Study 2 (2014). Unlike the original study, we implemented prospect-concept priming in an online setting, eliminating the direct supervision by an experimenter. We have revised the guided imagery task duration, changing it from 3 minutes to a minimum of 30 seconds, before respondents can continue to the next question. title_r: SecEUrity Project: Replication of Solidarity Experiment
abstract_r: The project is a partial replication of a project previously registered at OSF. There, experiments were embedded in a 2020 Pan-European survey to test whether European solidarity is driven by norm-based and self-interest based motives. The experiments used hypothetical crisis scenarios in the foreign and security domain. One experiment used a scenario in which Russia attempts to destabilize Latvia through paramilitary actions and create a situation similar to the one in Ukraine in 2014. For details, see the registration of the previous project (https://osf.io/kur5h). We will conduct the exact same experiment with European citizens in the post-invasion context and compare the findings to the pre-invasion findings. We approach the research question of context-sensitivity in an exploratory fashion. Below, we preregister research questions about differences in the distribution of the outcome variables and the experimental effects. We abstain from proposing hypotheses about these differences. Hence, the purpose of this preregistration is tying our hands not to move from an exploratory to a confirmatory approach after data analysis. The experiment will be embedded in surveys conducted in 9 EU member states and the UK. Data will be collected through an additional wave of an existing panel survey in France, Germany, and the United Kingdom and a cross-sectional survey using fresh samples in Estonia, Finland, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Hungary. title_r: A Multiverse Analysis on Frontal Alpha Asymmetry in Depression in Adolescences
abstract_r: The replication crisis in research and especially in psychology has brought forward different approaches aimed at forstering the robustness and transperancy and reducing the researches degree of freedom in research practice. title_r: Super-recognising kernels of truth? Exploring the relationship between personality, person judgment accuracy and face recognition.
abstract_r: Research has shown that individuals can recognise personality traits from photographs of others’ faces. It is suggested that this is possible as faces contain a biometric ‘kernel of truth’ for personality traits. If biometric facial features facilitate person judgments, then those adept at face memory (super-recognisers) could show heightened ability at recognising personality traits. This study evaluates the links between face memory accuracy and trait judgment accuracy. We investigated the relationship between participants’ face memory, Big Five personality traits and their accuracy in judging the Big Five personality traits (from 50 self-selected photographs of unknown individuals) in a sample of 792 individuals. We replicated previous findings that participant extraversion relates to face memory ability. We find no relationship between other personality traits, personality judgment accuracy and face memory. Individual differences in detecting personality traits do not relate to their face memory abilities. We do replicate the relationship between extraversion and face memory ability in the largest sample to date. This suggests that super-recognising faces and traits are domain-specific abilities. If surveillance operators are expected to detect impending incidents, then our findings would suggest that this is something that super-recognisers would need training in.

title_r: Replication of a Research Claim from Einstein & Glick (2017), from The American Journal of Political Science
abstract_r: The claim selected for replication from Einstein & Glick (2017) is that, all else equal, bureaucrats will be less friendly to Hispanics than they are to whites. This reflects the following statement from the paper's abstract: “Moreover, we observe substantial differences in email tone. Hispanic housing applicants were 20 percentage points less likely to be greeted by name than were their black and white counterparts.” The claim is tested by e-mailing public housing authorities at their publicly available e-mail addresses (or online contact forms) using an audit study design. Each housing authority received an e-mail on one of two days in the same week during 2014. The authors e-mailed all public housing authorities that could plausibly be matched with a core city in a metropolitan or micropolitan area. Each housing authority was randomly assigned (via random number generator) to receive an e-mail from one of six different accounts with putatively white, Hispanic, and black names. For each racial/ethnic group, the authors chose one male and one female name. The dependent variable, Friendliness, is measured as whether the e-mailer is addressed by proper name, and it is regressed in a logit model on indicators for black name and Hispanic Name (base category is white, and males and females are pooled together), with controls for percent black and percent Hispanic in the community, poverty rate, logged population, and a variable that indicates that a housing authority’s online contact address was difficult to obtain. The coefficient of interest for testing the claim is on the Hispanic name indicator. The Hispanic name indicator variable is substantial, negative, and highly significant (coefficient = -0.82, SE = 0.22, p < .01).

title_r: People combine multisensory cues based on subjective confidence rather than objective signal reliability
abstract_r: Summary Previous studies found that in a multisensory scenario, people make decisions by weighing the objective reliability of signals from each modality. However, an alternative possibility is that people don't actually have direct access to the reliability of the signals of each modality but only to a subjective estimate of their confidence. An unexamined alternative is that we may base our perceptual judgments on the subjective confidence of each modality. Here we will address this issue with an accuracy-confidence dissociation paradigm where the accuracy in each task is comparable but there is a difference in confidence. In a multisensory motion direction discrimination task, the confidence for the visual task will be high in the high intensity condition and low in the intensity condition. We aim to determine whether the discrimination performance and confidence in the multisensory condition is predicted by the confidence or the discrimination accuracy in the unisensory condition. Participants will be asked to judge the direction of visual motion in the visual-only condition and judge the direction of auditory motion in the auditory-only condition. In addition, we will include a multisensory condition where congruent or incongruent visual and auditory motion will be presented at the same time. Participants will be asked to report the auditory motion in the multisensory condition. After each trial, the confidence of their judgements will also be collected. By investigating whether the influence of visual motion on auditory motion judgement is determined by the accuracy or the confidence of the visual motion judgement, we expect that the study will provide insights on how decisions are made in a multisensory environment. We have already run a version of the study proposed here with 14 participants; the current preregistration is for a direct replication of that initial exploratory study. Relevant background In everyday life, it is not uncommon when multiple sources provide information to the same stimulus feature, and we need to make our decisions combining many pieces of information. Cue combination has been extensively studied in multisensory scenarios where different information is available from different sensory modalities (Ernst & Banks, 2002; Alais & Burr, 2004; Gao et al, 2021). It has been shown that people are able to make decisions based on information from more than one modality by weighing the reliability of signals from each modality (Ernst & Banks, 2002). However, it is unclear if people have direct access to the reliability of the cues and some studies have found that cue reliabilities are sometimes inaccurately estimated (Battaglia et al, 2003; Knill & Saunders 2003; Rosas et al. 2005). An unexamined assumption is that we may base our judgement on the accessible part of our knowledge, which is the confidence judgement of the signals. In the current study, we will test this assumption using a confidence-accuracy dissociation paradigm used previously in Odegaard et al. (2018).

title_r: Mentalizing in children's and parents' interpretation of quotative ‘be like’
abstract_r: Quotative ‘be like’ (QBL) is a recently emerged quotative that uses ‘like’ to quote a wide range of contents, such as thoughts and utterances. For example, QBL: I was like “that’s so weird!” QBL does not by itself signal whether the quoted content was said out loud or just thought. This raises a specific interpretation challenge. In some instances of QBL use, interpreters have to decide whether QBL is used to invoke an overt utterance or a hidden thought. Recent work with adult interpreters shows that English speaking adults agree significantly more on the interpretation of QBL in contexts that contain implicit information about goals and social norms (Overmark et al. In preparation). Because goals and social norms are central to everyday social cognition and mentalizing specifically (Apperly, 2010; Dennett, 1989; Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Spaulding, 2018; Zawidzki, 2013), the authors interpret these findings to suggest that QBL raises specific mentalizing requirements. This study investigates interpretation of QBL in children aged 6-9 years and their parents or another primary caregiver. Concretely, the study 1) attempts a conceptual replication of Overmark et al (In preparation) with adult English speakers using an adapted version of the original QBL interpretation task which has been changed to be suitable for child participants too, 2) investigates children’s interpretation of QBL using this newly adapted child-friendly task, and 3) investigates possible relations between child and caregiver interpretation. By testing child and caregiver interpretation of QBL, the study will shed light on the role of mentalizing in pragmatic interpretation, and QBL interpretation specifically, adapting an existing design to a new population, but the study can also shed light on how individual differences in pragmatic interpretation can arise, by comparing child interpretation to the interpretations of caregivers.

title_r: Preferential Differences for Transactional vs. Transformational Leadership - A Laboratory Study
abstract_r: Transformational leadership, which is said to raise the level of motivation and morality of followers by engaging with them and creating a connection, has been the most researched leadership style of the last 30 years and despite new leadership theories emerging, the relative amount of research on this leadership style remains the largest (Gardner, Lowe, Meuser, Noghani, Gullifor, & Cogliser, 2020). Transformational leadership is often associated with and compared to transactional leadership, which recognizes followers’ needs and wants but focuses on exchanges between leader and follower in order to achieve outcomes. According to the process-view of leadership an individual’s ability to lead is dependent on followers’ responses to leadership behaviors and styles (Northouse, 2015). Following this view, it is interesting to examine which of the described leadership styles followers prefer: The arguably more satisfactory transformational leadership style or the transactional leadership style, which is more concerned with the clarifaction of roles and task-requirements? In a previous study, we set out to examine preference distributions for transactional and transformational leadership in two different samples: University students and a working population. Examining a sample of N = 127 participants we expected the student population (n = 64) to strive for ideals, teamwork and self-actualization and thus prefer the transformational leader, while expecting the working population (n = 63) to strive for clarity regarding requirements and goals and thus prefer the transactional leader. Contrary to our expectations and in contrast with what research on transformational leadership would postulate, we found conclusive evidence that preferences for transformational and transactional leadership are equally distributed in both the student and the working population. In the proposed study we attempt to replicate these findings with in a laboratory setting. In an exploratory analysis will further investigate whether leader preferences can be predicted by Big-5 Personality, personal needs as well as Implicit Leadership Theories.
