title_r: Belief change in response to evidence: Predictors and persistence over time (Study 2)
abstract_r: Research Questions: Does belief change in response to empirical evidence persist over time? What variables are associated with belief change in response to empirical evidence? Study Overview/Design: This study is a conceptual replication of Study 1 on a different stimulus study topic (gun control). In Study 2, participants will read about a real study examining the relationship between state gun control laws and murder rates. Participants will be randomly assigned to read evidence suggesting that gun control is associated with lower or higher murder rates. Participants will only read one stimulus study in this experiment. Beliefs will be measured before and after the presentation of the evidence, along with at a follow-up 24 hours later. Possible individual difference variables associated with belief change in response to empirical evidence will be measured. In this design, the primary factors of interest are the stimulus study findings (gun control associated with lower or higher murder rates) and time of belief assessment (T1, T2, T3). Procedure: Participants will be recruited from Amazon’s Mechanical Turk for a two-part study. Session 1. Participants will first report their position on gun control (1=strongly oppose, 7=strongly support; position T1), belief about how background checks on gun sales are associated with gun-related murder rates (1=much lower, 7=much higher; correlational belief T1), belief about how background checks on gun sales affect gun-related murder rates (1=strongly decrease, 7=strongly increase; causal belief T1), and the certainty of their (causal) belief (1=very uncertain, 7=very certain; certainty T1). Participants will also answer a few distractor questions and complete a scale assessing their current emotions. Next, participants will be presented with a summary of a recent study examining the relationship between state gun control policies and gun-related murder rates. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two conditions, in which the study suggests that gun control is associated with lower or higher murder rates. In both conditions, the evidence presented is summarized from a real study, so there is no deception. Following the study summary, participants will evaluate the study in a closed (2 items, 7-point scales; “How well was the study conducted?” and “How convincing was this study?”, which will be averaged) and open-ended manner (i.e., “Why do you think the study you just read does or does not support the argument that gun control [decreases/increases] gun-related murder rates?”). Then, participants will again report their emotions, position on gun control (position T2), belief about how background checks on gun sales are associated with gun-related murder rates (correlational belief T2), belief about how background checks on gun sales affect gun-related murder rates (causal belief T2), and the certainty of their (causal) belief (certainty T2). They will also be asked to recall the study findings (included as an attention check). In the second part of Session 1, participants will complete several individual difference measures: social desirability (Crowne & Marlowe, 1960), actively open-minded thinking (Haran, Ritov, & Mellers 2013), perceptions of scientific (un)certainty, a measure of commitment to one’s beliefs about gun control, and scientific reasoning ability (Drummond & Fischhoff, 2017). These measures will be presented in randomized order, with the exception of the scientific reasoning scale, which will be presented last (due to the difference in its formatting). Because two factors emerged from the scientific (un)certainty scale developed in Study 1, but only 2 items loaded on the second factor (and thus had low reliability), an additional 4 items were added to further assess this component of the scale. At the end of Session 1, participants will answer several demographic questions. Participants will be paid $2 for completing Session 1. Session 2. Approximately 24 hours after completing the first session, participants will be sent a link to complete a brief additional survey. In this survey, they will again be asked to report their position on gun control, beliefs about how background checks on gun sales are associated with and affect gun-related murder rates, and the certainty of their (causal) belief. Participants will be paid an additional $1 for completing Session 2. Copies of the Qualtrics surveys for each session (with exact question wording) are available on OSF. Power Analysis: For a 2 (research findings: gun control associated with lower vs. higher gun-related murder rates) x 3 (time: T1, T2, T3) mixed-model ANOVA, a sample size of N=116 is necessary to obtain small-medium effects (f=0.15) at power of .95, alpha=.05. The power was set high (.95) to ensure the quality of the replication (Funder et al., 2014). Because it was anticipated that many participants would fail to return to complete Session 2 of the study (administered 24 hours after Session 1), an initial sample of N=300 was targeted for Session 1. Planned Analyses: Exclusions. The main analyses will be performed with and without those who fail the attention checks and provide nonsensical/off-topic responses to the open-ended questions. Any discrepancies in the findings based on whether participants are excluded will be reported. If no discrepancies exist, all participants will be retained in the results reported. Belief, Position, and Certainty Change. 2x3 mixed-model ANOVAs, with research findings as a between-subjects factor and time of belief/position assessment as a within-subjects factor, will be performed to examine whether participants change their beliefs (or position) in response to each study and maintain this shift 24 hours after the presentation of evidence. Although the primary test of the hypothesis is the analysis for beliefs, position will also be examined as it has shown change in previous studies, though to a lesser degree (Anglin, 2019). Planned contrasts will be performed comparing T1 to each subsequent time point (T1 vs. T2, T2 vs. T3). To control for multiple comparisons, the significance level for all planned contrasts will be set to p < .01. Hypotheses. Based on the results of Anglin (2019) and Study 1, an interaction between research findings and time of assessment is expected, with participants shifting their beliefs (and position) in response to the evidence presented and maintaining this shift 24 hours later. Note: The evidence presented is correlational rather than causal, and some participants may not shift their beliefs about whether gun control decreases or increases gun-related murder in response to the evidence for this reason. Therefore, in Study 2, an additional belief question was added at each time point to assess participants’ (correlational) belief about the association between gun control and gun-related murder rates. This question will be examined in an exploratory fashion, as it is unknown how strongly correlated responses to the correlational and causal belief questions will be. Belief and position change based on the (in)consistency of the evidence with prior views. Beliefs at T1 will be recoded so that higher scores indicate a stronger belief in the direction of the evidence presented, and belief change scores will be calculated (from T1 to T2 and T1 to T3) so that higher scores indicate more belief change in the direction of the evidence. Then, regression analyses will be performed, with the recoded belief at T1, research findings, and their interaction as predictors of belief change, to examine whether participants exhibit more or less belief and position change based on the consistency of the evidence with their initial belief (or position). Hypotheses. Based on the findings of Study 1, participants are expected to show the most belief and position change when the evidence conflicts with their prior views (presumably because these individuals have more room with which to move). Study evaluation ratings. A regression analysis will be performed, with belief at T1, research findings, and their interaction as predictors, to examine whether participants evaluate the evidence more favorably when it is more consistent (vs. inconsistent) with their beliefs. Hypotheses. An interaction between belief at T1 and research findings is expected, such that participants are expected to evaluate each study more favorably when it is more consistent with their initial belief. Open-ended evaluations. Participants’ open-ended evaluations will be examined in an exploratory fashion. Correlates of belief change. If the items from each individual difference measure have good internal consistency (i.e., α ≥ .70) and all items load ≥ .40 on a single factor, they will be averaged to create a composite measures. If not, items with low item-total correlations will be dropped and/or multiple factors (as determined by a factor analysis) will be examined separately. Correlates of belief change in response to the evidence (from T1 to T2 and T1 to T3) will be examined. If the two belief items correlate strongly (i.e., r > .70), they will be averaged; otherwise, they will be analyzed separately. Correlations will be conducted between each belief change and individual difference measure (study evaluations, social desirability, positive and negative emotion at T1 and T2, actively open-minded thinking, scientific reasoning, belief commitment, and perceptions of scientific uncertainty). Exploratory analyses will also be performed to examine whether belief (in)consistency moderates these relationships. Hypotheses. Based on the findings from Study 1, study evaluations are predicted to correlate positively and perceptions of scientific uncertainty negatively with belief change for the causal item.

title_r: Diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance in the Norwegian population. A replication of Darley and Latanés bystander study in Lillehammer, Norway.
abstract_r: In the 1960s, the two psychologists John Darley and Bibb Latané were one of the first to conduct a study on the phenomenon of the bystander effect. They first became intrigued by the violent murder of a young woman, called Kitty Genovese which was witnessed by many people who didn’t act to the emergency. They conceptualized the bystander effect which states that the number of people who are present in an emergency, influences how quickly if, at all, any individual responds. They believed that if people were together with others when they experience an emergency, they may feel that their own responsibility for their actions is being diminished. Therefore, they did an experiment that focused on the concept of diffusion of responsibility, which is called the White Smoke Experiment. Darley and Latané asked a group of students at Columbia University to share their views in a study about the problems of living and being a college student in New York City. They were then taken to a waiting room to fill out a survey before they were supposed to get interviewed. This was just a cover story, and the real experiment started when the participants were left alone in the room. Harmless, but visible smoke would then start to seep in under the door after a short amount of time. The aim of the experiment was to see whether people left the room to report about the smoke, and how long it would take before they did so. It was done in two different conditions; alone or in a group with two or three others who either were naïve participants or confederates who had been told to ignore the smoke and to remain passive throughout the time. If the participants still didn't raise an alarm after six minutes, the experiment was terminated. The researchers noted that the presence of the students in the room affected their reaction to the smoke. For instance, when the study participants were alone, 75% immediately left the room after seeing the smoke. However, when other people were in the same room, only 38% raised an alarm. In addition, the participants responded much more quickly to the former condition. Around 55% of the participants alone in the room reported the smoke after two minutes, while only 12% of the three-member groups did so. After four minutes, 75% of the participants alone in the room reported it. However, the reporting rate for the other groups of four was 12%. Furthermore, when the other people were confederates, the others were more likely to remain quiet and only 10% raised the alarm. This shows how huge the power of group pressure really is. It is important to replicate the study to see if the same results from the experiment taking place in the US can be generalized to other countries (as Norway) when it comes to the likelihood of people helping in emergencies when other people are present. In the original study, the participants were also very homogeneous, so it is worth examining the influence of sociodemographic factors (such as age and gender) on the results. Would the diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance still be the same in another country and decades later?

title_r: When “Sometimes” Means “Often”: How Stereotypes Affect Interpretations of Quantitative Expressions
abstract_r: Two studies investigated whether interpretations of quantitative expressions about described actors’ behaviors are influenced by stereotypic expectancies. In two online experiments (one in Dutch language, and a direct replication in English language), participants were presented with sentences containing frequency adverbs describing either stereotype-consistent or stereotype-inconsistent behaviors. They rated perceived frequency of the described behaviors. Results showed that recipients inferred a higher numerical frequency when behaviors were stereotype consistent (vs inconsistent) for the described actors. These effects of stereotype consistency were stronger for high (vs low) degree frequency adverbs. The findings show how neutral statements about a person can be interpreted as stereotype-confirming information, which, in turn, may contribute to stereotype use and maintenance. Keywords: linguistic bias, frequency adverbs, stereotypes, prejudice, language

title_r: Many-analyst Project
abstract_r: Many-Analysts: Gender-Inclusive Language Project Description & Theoretical Background Project synopsis In this project, we will use a many-analysts approach (see e.g., Silberzahn et al., 2018) to investigate the effects of gender-inclusive language forms compared to generic masculine forms on the cognitive retrieval of female exemplars. This means that multiple analysis teams will analyze the same dataset to answer the same research questions. This many-analyst approach enables us to evaluate whether previous findings on gender-inclusive language are robust to choices in data preprocessing and analysis as well as implications for the practical and theoretical relevance of these findings. Specifically, we will evaluate (1) how much the results (i.e., effect sizes) of the different analysis teams vary, (2) whether analysis teams arrive at different conclusions (i.e., the presence or absence of the effects, theoretical and practical relevance), and (3) whether analysis outcomes and conclusions are influenced by characteristics of the analysis teams (e.g., knowledge on statistics). Project procedure The project is divided into two stages. In the first stage, we will provide you with the questionnaire, a clean dataset and documentation of the dataset. You will be asked to pre-register your analyses and take part in a brief pre-analysis survey. In the second stage, you will execute your analyses and be asked to submit a short report summarizing the results in a post-analysis survey. Theoretical background The generic masculine describes the phenomenon where people are described with the masculine word form regardless of their gender. For example, before the term firefighter was popularized, the term fireman was used for firefighters of all genders. The generic masculine is the standard way of speaking in many European languages, such as German or Italian. Since the 1970s, the use of such masculine generics have been seen as perpetuating “sexist” language (e.g., Miller & Swift, 1977). Research has shown that the use of the generic masculine biases cognitive associations. For example, when asking people to name four “Politiker” (generic masculine form for politicians in German), they are more likely to name four male politicians than when asked to name four “Politiker und Politikerinnen” (male and female politicians). These cognitive biases may cause down-stream discrimination that perpetuates gender inequity. For example, if only men come to mind when looking for new “Ingenieure” (male form of “engineers”), a man will be more likely to be hired for the position. Indeed, research showed that when the generic masculine (compared to the feminine-masculine form) was used for job titles, female applicants were perceived to be less suitable for a high-status position than male applicants (Horvath & Sczesny, 2016). As such, several institutions have taken formal measures to discourage the use of masculine generic language (e.g., APA, 2020; APA Publication Manual Task Force, 1978; Bailey et al., 2022). Despite the societal importance of such linguistic conventions, few studies have empirically tested the robustness of the generic masculine effect. Stahlberg and colleagues (2001) argued that in gendered languages, such as German or Italian, the use of the generic masculine leads to a higher frequency of masculine markings in a text, because differently gendered nouns get absorbed and represented by the generic masculine. This could potentially intensify male associations and result in a stronger male bias compared to English. They conducted an experiment that was ostensibly about media consumption to demonstrate the generic masculine effect. 90 German speaking participants were randomly prompted with the generic masculine (e.g., “Sportler”), feminine-masculine (e.g., “Sportlerinnen und Sportler”) or internal-I form (e.g., “SportlerInnen”) of three occupations: athletes, singers, politicians, and TV hosts. They were then asked to list three names they know from the category that they were shown. They found that participants reported more women across the categories when gender-inclusive forms were used compared to the generic masculine (d = 0.59, 95% CI [0.14, 1.04]). The present research constitutes a many-analyst investigation of a many-labs replication led by Brohmer of this original study by Stahlberg and colleagues (2001). The many-labs replication project is still in progress. In addition to replicating the original experiment by Stahlberg and colleagues (2001), the many-lab replication by Brohmer and colleagues (https://osf.io/kbynp/?view_only=) expanded the original experiment by including the now frequently used gender-star form (e.g., “Sportler*innen”) and a neutral, genderless form (e.g., “Personen aus dem Bereich Sport”) as a control condition. Second, they also measured the perceived base rate of each occupation (i.e., the proportion women to men in any given occupation prior to treatment) and other possible moderators such as political orientation, attitudes toward gender-inclusive language, social dominance orientation, and preference for socio-economic equality. Third, they added two more categories of popular occupations - writers and actors. They tested the following hypotheses: H1: Compared to the generic masculine form, the internal-I and feminine-masculine form will yield a higher number of women mentioned. H2: Compared to the generic masculine and the control form, the internal-I, feminine-masculine, and gender-star form will yield a higher number of women mentioned. H3: Higher scores on the perceived base rate (perceived higher proportion of women) are associated with a higher number of women mentioned, when it is controlled for the form effect. The present study follows Brohmer and colleagues’ replication to investigate who comes to mind (i.e., cognitive accessibility), when different generic terms are used in the German language. Similarly, we ask the following research questions: Do gender-inclusive forms increase the cognitive retrieval of female exemplars compared to generic masculine forms? Does the perceived base rate (perceived proportion of women) increase the cognitive retrieval of female exemplars? Our primary goal is to seek to establish the robustness of the generic masculine effect by conducting a many-analyst approach of testing the hypotheses of Brohmer’s study. This many-analyst approach further enables us to evaluate whether previous findings on gender-inclusive language are robust to choices in data preprocessing and analysis as well as implications for the practical and theoretical relevance of these findings. title_r: Influence of noninvasive brain stimulation on connectivity and local activation: a combined tDCS and fMRI study
abstract_r: The effect of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) on neurobiological mechanisms underlying executive function in the human brain remains elusive. This study aims at examining the effect of anodal and cathodal tDCS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) in comparison with sham stimulation on resting-state connectivity as well as functional activation and working memory performance. We hypothesized perturbed fronto-parietal resting-state connectivity during stimulation and altered working memory performance combined with modified functional working memory-related activation. We applied tDCS with 1 mA for 21 min over the DLPFC inside an fMRI scanner. During stimulation, resting-state fMRI was acquired and task-dependent fMRI during working memory task performance was acquired directly after stimulation. Seed-based functional connectivity analyses and dynamic causal modeling were conducted for the resting-state fMRI data. We found a significant stimulation by region interaction in the seed-based ROI-to-ROI resting-state connectivity, but no effect on effective connectivity. We also did not find an effect of stimulation on task-dependent signal alterations in working memory activation in our regions of interest and no effect on working memory performance parameters. We found effects on measures of seed-based resting-state connectivity, while measures of effective connectivity and task-based connectivity did not show any stimulation effect. We could not replicate previous findings of tDCS stimulation effects on behavioral outcomes. We critically discuss possible methodological limitations and implications for future studies.

title_r: People have an extrinsic motivation to share money fairly but an intrinsic motivation to share effort fairly - Experiment 2
abstract_r: As a further test of the resource-specific hypothesis, Experiment 2 manipulated time pressure. Our rationale was as follows: if the resource-specific hypothesis is true, then we should expect people to exhibit a more pronounced preference for equal distributions of effort compared to money when there is time pressure, and when people therefore do not have the cognitive capacity to deliberate or to think strategically. This line of reasoning draws upon previous work by Rand and Nowak (2013), showing that people tend to make more cooperative decisions about resource distribution when under time pressure. Thus, Experiment 2 was designed to provide a conceptual replication of Rand & Nowak’s (2014) studies, extending it to contexts in which decisions are made about effort distribution as well as contexts in which decisions are made about money distributions. We predicted that participants would distribute effort more closely to an equal distribution than money. Moreover, we also predicted that when under time pressure, participants would exhibit a stronger preference for equal distributions both for effort and for money. Finally, we predicted that time pressure should have a larger effect on decisions about money than on decisions about effort - namely, because the intuitive preference for fairness is more robust in the context of decision-making about effort than in the context of decision-making about money.

title_r: How Does Moral Reframing Affect Environmental Attitudes: A Replication in a Turkish Sample
abstract_r: There is a difference in endorsement of moral foundations between individuals from the political right and left. This difference is used for studying attitudinal and behavioral differences between political poles in varying issues, such as climate change. However, most of this literature consists of correlational studies and experimental uses of moral foundations are limited. Moral foundations are also used to create framed messages, a technique called moral reframing. Some studies morally frame climate change messages in terms of individualizing vs. binding foundations or care vs. sanctity foundation to investigate the effectiveness of morally framed messages on conservatives and liberals. However, most of these studies are not pre-registered, and have small sample sizes. In addition, they are conducted on WEIRD samples. In this study, we aim to eliminate these methodological limitations and replicate an effect of moral foundations based frames on an under-represented sample. We will apply the procedure of Feinberg & Willer (2013; Study 3). Participants will receive either care or sanctity framed text or a control text. Then, they will indicate how much they felt five emotions including disgust, and fill out a scale about environmental attitudes. Afterward, we will give participants some additional measures in contrast to the original experiment (Feinberg & Willer, 2013): Moral Foundations Questionnaire as a manipulation check, an actual donation question as an indicator of environmental behavior, and a Psychological Distance Scale and Comprehensive Thinking Scale as potential moderators.

title_r: Multiple cues in the learning of non-adjacent dependencies: the effect of sequential vs simultaneous presentation
abstract_r: Language learners must acquire multiple cues to meaning and structure within natural languages. Although in naturalistic situations these cues are experienced simultaneously, previous work suggests that some cues are prioritised over others, and that the salience and availability of specific cues can influence the learning of grammatical categories (Bates & MacWhinney, 1989; Culbertson et al., 2017). In the current experiment, we use an artificial language paradigm to control which cues learners are exposed to, and when: we will examine whether exposing participants to cues sequentially rather than simultaneously can enhance learning. Participants will be trained on a set of novel word-stems paired with affixes: a co-occurring prefix and suffix which are associated with the salient semantic category of animacy (e.g. tib Xeem words paired with pictures of animals; ked Xool words with artefacts). Participants will then be assessed on their learning of word forms and meanings, as well as the grammatical regularities in the language: the determiner and suffix mapping to semantics, and the co-occurrence of the determiner + suffix. In previous experiments using this paradigm we have found that learners prioritise a) semantics and b) the early-available cue (i.e. the determiner; Mirkovic et al, 2021; Vogliqi et al., unpublished). We have found robust evidence of learning of the determiner-semantics mapping, but poor learning of the suffix-semantics mapping, and particularly the determiner-suffix co-occurrence. We have also found that training participants without the determiner initially can enhance learning of the suffix. With the current study, we aim to replicate and extend this finding, to examine whether initially training word-forms with the suffix but without the determiner or semantics, and introducing these cues subsequently, can improve learning of the suffix and the determiner-suffix co-occurrence.

title_r: Three factors in explaining scalar diversity
abstract_r: Rates of scalar inference, whereby the utterance of a weaker term (e.g., some) leads hearers to infer the negation of a stronger term (all), have been found to vary substantially across lexical scales. For instance, the some but not all scalar inference arises much more robustly than good but not excellent. This finding has been termed scalar diversity. In this paper, we first replicate scalar diversity on 60 different pairs of scalar expressions, which represent a better balance across grammatical categories than has been tested in previous work. We then turn to the open question of what can explain scalar diversity, proposing three factors: 1) a language production-based metric of how accessible the stronger alternative (all) is; 2) the distinctness of the two scalar terms (some vs. all), as measured by posterior degree estimates; and 3) the meaning of the negated strong scalar term (not all), again measured by degree estimates. We report on three experiments showing that these factors can indeed explain some of the observed variation in scalar inference rates.

title_r: Replicating the effects of egocentric ignorance
abstract_r: This experiment is a direct replication of a prior experiment, preregistered under the title 'Testing the effects of egocentric ignorance'. This experiment investigates the effects of egocentric knowledge or ignorance when making predictions about the actions of others. To this end, participants are asked to make predictions about the behavior of a character, as he searches for a ball. Participants are presented with a simple scene, consisting of a table, with three baskets placed on top of the table. A character stands behind the table, facing it. In each trial, occluders are placed to obscure the participants, or characters, visual access to some of the baskets, and a red ball is placed in one of the three baskets. Participants are then asked to select the basket in which the character is most likely to search for the ball. In some trials, the occluders are placed such that the participant can see the ball. In other trials, the participant cannot see the ball, but can infer its location. And in some trials, the participant can neither see, nor infer, the location of the ball. Occluders also obscure the perspective of the character such that he can see the ball, not see the ball but infer its location, or not infer infer the ball's location, depending upon the trial. In cases in which both the participant and the character can see or infer the location of the ball, it is expected that the participants will respond that the character will search for the ball in the actual location (expecting the character to search for the ball in its mutually known location). However, when either the participant or the character cannot see the ball, or cannot infer its location, the predicted outcome is more complicated. The present hypothesis is that, when participants do not know the ball's location, they will expect the character to search in locations to which they have visual access (that is, they will exhibit a bias toward expecting the character to search for the ball in locations that they already know about, even if the participants has no reason to believe the ball is actually there). This effect will not be observed when participants do know the location of the ball. This effect will be reflective of a broader trend: our behaviors concerning the knowledge states of others will changed depending upon our own knowledge states. That is, what we know will ground our considerations of what others know.

title_r: Revisiting the false consensus bias
abstract_r: Through this experiment, we aim to answer: to what extent do individuals agree on the interpretation of contractual language featuring vague/underspecified terms (e.g. 'sudden and unforeseen', 'perceived emergency'), and can individuals accurately predict population-level agreement? Solan et al. (2008) demonstrate experimentally that lay participants are roughly evenly split in their opinions as to whether edge cases of 'earth movement' and 'pollution' indeed fall within the boundaries of those respective terms; however, participants in their study tended to believe that a majority of other respondents would agree with their individual judgments. Our study is a conceptual replication of Solan et al.'s original 2-item experiment. We investigate the interpretation of 25 common insurance terms in 138 hypothetical scenarios to see whether Solan et al.'s observed 'false consensus bias' effect replicates in a broader linguistic domain.

title_r: Need for uniqueness and belief in conspiracies about ingroup vs. outgroup: The moderating role of mortality salience.
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that those who have a higher need for uniqueness tend to be attracted to holding conspiratorial worldviews because conspiracy beliefs are seen as secret, special, and scarce information about the world that the majority of the “regular” people are unaware of. Hence, holding such beliefs might allow those who have higher need for uniqueness to feel special and unique. Decades of research emerging from Terror Management Theory has shown that following reminders of mortality (as compared to control): a) people defend and reaffirm their pre-existing belief systems, and b) are more likely to derogate a perceived outgroup. One of the potential ways in which outgroup derogation can take place is by holding conspiratorial beliefs about them. No study to date has tested whether or not mortality salience will lead those who are higher on need for uniqueness to more likely to believe in conspiracies about one’s outgroup as comapred to control. A previously conducted (as of yet unpublished) study by the current authors found that mortality salience (vs. a control) lead people with a higher need for uniqueness to endorse increased conspiracy beliefs about an outgroup. However, since those analyses were exploratory in nature, the present study is pre-registered replication of those findings.

abstract_r: Public perceptions of protests tend to be negative (Teixeira et al., 2020). This is especially true if protestors engage in extreme or non-normative protest actions that are disruptive and harmful. Perceptions of extreme acts from protesters of a movement are associated with decreased support for the movement, less identification with the issue at hand, and less likelihood for others to join the movement (Feinberg et al., 2020). Research demonstrates that in movements where protesters and police interact, police tend to dehumanize protesters which contributes to greater feelings of hostility and legitimization of violence against protesters (Ziobina & Anduja, 2021). However, not much is known about how police actions shape perceptions of protesters in addition to perceptions of the police. title_r: “Up is not always good” A fieldwork study for examining body-specificity hypothesis in Guangxi and Chongqing, China.
abstract_r: According to the body-specificity hypothesis (BSH), people associate upside and downside with positive and negative emotions (space–valence metaphor: e.g., Meier & Robinson, 2004). This metaphor has been observed in many countries around the world (Marmolejo-Ramos et al, 2013). However, based on our previous survey, compared with Zhuang people in Guangxi, China, the Yao people in mountainous areas in Guangxi, China, have no evident tendency of the space–valence metaphor. We assume that their unique geographical environment, a particular culture, and living habits have attenuated their space–valence metaphor. The present study will make a direct replication on these two groups, to the robustness of the findings. At the same time, we will make a conceptual replication between two groups of Han people, the ethnic majority in China. The experimental group consists of manual workers "Bangbang" in Chongqing, whose life and work environment are similar with that of Yao people. The control group are recruited from Han college students. We will compare the two groups to find whether geographical environment and living habits affect space–valence metaphor.

title_r: Eye-tracking evidence for the reinstatement for emotionally negative and neutral memories
abstract_r: The main goal of this experiment is to see if we can find evidence of emotional memory biases in the way that people reinstate gaze patterns at retrieval. This work is inspired by recent eye-tracking studies that have linked gaze reinstatement—when eye movements from encoding are reinstated during retrieval—with memory performance. Here, we aim to replicate and extend these studies using the emotional memory trade-off paradigm. Importantly, we use scenes that are composed of negative or neutral objects on the left or right of neutral backgrounds, which allows us to measure gaze reinstatement in terms of whether people looked at the side of the screen that had the object during scene memory tests. We ran an initial exploratory experiment in Spring 2022 and presented our results at the Annual Psychonomics Meeting in November 2022. title_r: Evidence for Indirect Retrieval effects for an associated stimulus in a prime-probe paradigm
abstract_r: This experiment investigates whether stimulus-response bindings can be indirectly transferred to a stimulus that has prior associations with prime stimulus. Two stimuli are paired together and learnt in the first phase of the study by means of contingency learning – 100% contingent presentations of a stimulus (name) followed by another stimulus (adjective) (S-S association formation phase). The order is also balanced within each participant so that for half the presentations, the name precedes the adjective and for the other half the names follow after an adjective. Both trial orders are presented randomly. Following this association phase, there will be a prime-probe sequence with a colour classification forced choice task. Here the stimuli from the association phase are presented as prime and probes in 4 different colours – 2 colours mapped to one response key, and participants press the relevant key based on the colour. For each prime-probe sequence, the probe will either be the identical stimulus, the associated stimulus from the previous S-S association phase or a different/unassociated stimulus from the other pairs in the association phase. We investigate whether associated stimuli can access and retrieve bindings from the prime trial. This experiment is intended as a direct replication of a previous study which was also preregistered.

title_r: Perceived Likelihood of Fulfilling Belonging and Interpersonal Behavior Following Social Rejection
abstract_r: One of the biggest paradoxes in the rejection literature was that rejected people sometimes behaved antisocially and at other times prosocially. Researchers responded to this paradox by demonstrating that the prospect of fulfilling belonging predicted these varied responses. A close inspection of the foundational studies, however, revealed small sample sizes relative to today’s standards. Hence, we conducted a conceptual replication of the prospect of fulfilling belonging hypothesis using a high-powered 2-day preregistered study. On Day 1, we manipulated the prospect of fulfilling belonging through a profile exchange with a confederate. On Day 2, we manipulated rejection using a recall paradigm and then measured prosocial and antisocial responses toward the confederate. Rejected participants who expected the confederate to fulfill belonging showed similar levels of prosocial and antisocial responses compared with those who did not. These results suggest that the prospect of fulfilling belonging hypothesis needs further refinement.

title_r: Extension of Marks (1987; Exp.3)
abstract_r: Both humans and animals routinely pool information from more than one sensory modality to guide perceptual decision making and go about their business in the physical world more effectively (Gibson, 1966). For example, interaural time differences in sound pickup between the left and right ear hint at the loci of distal auditory stimuli. These hints can be complemented by fixing one’s line of vision roughly towards the direction of the sound to aid source localization. In this toy example, the streams of energy impending on the eyes and the ears contain convergent information about the state of the observer's immediate environment, and his/her perceptions thereof can advantageously be stabilized by making use of both sources of information simultaneously. Formal theories of multisensory integration work from the idea that humans and animals are able to weigh the unimodal signal components of multimodal sensory input in a statistically optimal fashion according to the relative evidential strength of each component (ideal observer theory; see Nopponey, 2020). But a more elusive class of multisensory phenomena termed crossmodal correspondences has hitherto evaded analysis in such terms. A prime example of a crossmodal correspondence is people's inability to selectively attend to and process acoustic frequency and visuospatial elevation independent of one another (Miller, 1991; Patching & Quinlan, 2002). This correspondence between pitch and elevation is reflected in everyday language, for instance when people label rapidly oscillating acoustic frequencies as “high pitched” and slower frequencies as “low pitched”. Importantly, this pitch-elevation association does not seem to reflect any natural correlation between how pitch and elevation tend to co-occur in the physical world. Indeed, a general hallmark of the crossmodal correspondence is that it does not necessitate overlap in terms of informational content between the unimodal signal components, yet the components are seemingly processed conjointly (Spence, 2011). The present preregistration concerns the possibility of a crossmodal correspondence between our perceptions of psychophysical stimulus intensity in the visual (brightness) and auditory (loudness) modalities. Chronometric evidence for a crossmodal correspondence between loudness and brightness was first reported by Marks (1987; Experiment 3) who tasked people to categorize visual targets as either dim or bright (brightness categorization task), or dark or light (lightness categorization task) in a speeded fashion. On any given trial, the visual stimuli were accompanied by a concurrent auditory tone that was either soft or loud. Marks found that people were faster and more accurate in their brightness judgments on those trials when the auditory-visual signal pair was concordantly mapped in terms of intensity (soft-dim and loud-bright stimulus pairs) as compared to when this mapping was inverted (soft-bright and loud-dim stimulus pairs). In the lightness categorization task the accessory auditory stimulus had no facilitating effects on people's lightness judgments when the auditory-visual mapping was intensity congruent (soft-dark and loud-light stimulus pairs) as compared to when it was incongruent (soft-light and loud-dark stimulus pairs). We previously replicated these results (https://osf.io/knzvy/) and now seek to test a possible hypothesis of why perceived brightness and perceived loudness exhibit a crossmodal correspondence, whereas colorimetric lightness and perceived loudness does not. We argue that an important but overlooked pattern of results in Marks' original study was how average choice response time in the lightness categorization task was some 80 milliseconds shorter than in the brightness classification task. This tendency of people to make faster lightness judgments also held true for the outcome of our replication study. Marks arrived at the conclusion that two different representational formats must underlie our impressions of visual magnitude in the two (brightness and lightness) categorization tasks. Moreover, he claimed that only the representational format belonging to brightness perception shows a crossmodal correspondence with loudness, whereas the representational format of lightness does not. We, in contrast, hold the opinions that 1) faster responses in the lightness categorization task relative to the brightness categorization task is due to differential task demands inherent to the two types of classification, and 2) that differential crossmodal interaction effects in lightness and brightness categorization is best understood by considering how different information is conveyed by the visual stimuli in the two types of tasks. Before we present our critique of Marks' theoretical account, we briefly review some key concepts from the field of brightness and lightness perception. We then turn to the topic of how information was conveyed by visual stimuli in the two tasks. The apparent brightness of an astronomical object such as a star denotes the intensity of the light source as directly registered by a measuring apparatus (e.g. a photometer or the human eye). In this regard, the notion of the perceived brightness of a surface has a rather straightforward interpretation as it clearly stands in correspondence to a measurable physical attribute. Colorimetric lightness in turn maps on to the physical attribute of surface reflectance, yet nonetheless evades a strictly physicalist interpretation. To illustrate how confusion can arise in this matter, we consider how the total luminance L of light reflected from a surface equates to the product of the intensity of the illuminant source I and the reflectance coefficient R of the illuminated surface, such that L = I × R. Our ability to perceive differences in lightness ranging from black to white must therefore attest to how the visual system is able to reverse engineer an estimate of R solely on the basis of the more directly accessible quantity L (Kingdom, 2011). Importantly, the resulting reflectance estimate is an interpretation imposed on the world by the visual system, and is therefore highly dependent on the contextual circumstances of the visual scene which is being inspected. For instance, perceived objects seem to retain roughly the same lightness value throughout the day despite variations in illumination associated with the diurnal sun cycle, or indoor versus outdoor lighting conditions. This is truly remarkable when we consider how the reflectance of surfaces belonging to everyday objects most usually varies by no more than two to three orders of magnitude, whereas the dynamic range of vision covers ten orders of magnitude luminous flux. As noted by Gilchrist and colleagues (1999) this context-dependency leads to the conclusion that pretty much any intensity of light can be associated with any value of perceived colorimetric lightness. On the basis of the above sketched theoretical issues, we find Marks’ (1987) distinction between brightness and lightness categorization to be untenable in the context of the present research. First, the primary stimulus manipulation that separated the two tasks was the change in background luminance from 8 candelas (brightness classification) to 80 candelas (lightness categorization), but perceived surface lightness is known to be strikingly independent of background luminance (Heller, 2006; Gilchrist et al., 1999). Secondly, little to no contextual information such as referent surfaces or illumination cues are available to the observer in either (brightness or lightness) categorization task. Instead, all visual stimulus materials employed in Marks’ experiment were unambiguously self-luminous, and did not reflect any light in the strict sense of the term. Therefore, we hardly find it reasonable to assume that people were making their visual intensity judgments on the basis of qualitatively different perceptual substrates (perceived brightness and perceived lightness) in the two types of tasks. This opinion is in concordance with the more general idea that brightness perception has precedence in most common vision science laboratory settings, whereas the contribution of lightness perception is limited (a view championed by Kingdom, 2011). Our candidate explanation of why lightness judgments were faster than brightness judgments underscores procedural differences in task demands associated with brightness and lightness categorization. It draws inspiration from a distinction recently made by Hubbard (2021) between “first order” and “second order” psychophysics. In a first order psychophysical task, all the task-relevant information necessary to provide a response is embodied in external referents in the physical world, and is therefore directly available to the observer's sensorium. In this regard, Mark’s (1987) lightness categorization task must be considered a first-order task, because the background luminance of the monitor here serves as a useful external referent to the observer, against which the target stimuli can be probed to aid performance (“is the target less or more intense, relative to the mid-grey background?”). title_r: Cost-benefit trade-off in deliberate reasoning and the role of need for cognition
abstract_r: Masterproject on deliberate reasoning (14 items from heuristic and problem-solving literature) taken unlimited, time-limited and incentivized. To disentangle the role of motivation and analytical ability we also measure Need for Cognition, numeracy and verbal intelligence. I) We expect that a person’s Need for Cognition, as a propensity for motivation to engage in cognitively demanding tasks, is positively correlated with performance in the rational task battery. II) We expect that a person’s intelligence correlates with the person’s deliberate reasoning ability, i.e. the higher the analytical abilities, as measured with the Berlin numeracy test (numerical intelligence) and Word sum test (verbal intelligence), the higher the deliberate reasoning score (here also abbreviated with RQ for Rationality Quotient, the sum sore from the rational task battery). III) We expect, as a corollary from I) that perceived / subjective effort of performing the rational task battery is lower among person’s high in NFC. This is measured with the NASA task load index (Hart, 2006). IV) We expect that a person’s curiosity for science and research is positively correlated with their NFC. Curiosity is measured with the subscale from the 5-Dimensional curiosity scale (Kashdan et al., 2018) Research question 1 – effect of incentives of deliberate reasoning (conceptual replication of Sandra and Otto, 2018): 1A) Will persons with low need for cognition perform better on deliberate reasoning tasks when incentivized compared to their performance at baseline where no incentives are provided? 1A adjunct) Will this also be seen as spending more time on the items? 1B) Will persons with high need for cognition perform similar on deliberate reasoning tasks when incentivized compared to their performance at baseline with no incentive? Research question 2 – effect of time pressure / limits of algorithmic ability: 2A) Will persons with high algorithmic ability perform similar on deliberate reasoning tasks when time pressured compared to performance at baseline with no time pressure? 2B) Will persons with low algorithmic ability perform similar or worse on deliberate reasoning tasks when time pressured compared to performance at baseline with no time pressure? Research question 3 – perceived effort 3A) Will perceived effort at baseline correlate with performance and need for cognition? 3B) Will perceived effort and temporal effort be higher in the time-pressure condition than in the baseline condition? 3C) For those for whom the time-pressure condition is not more effortful, is this due to them having fast response times in the baseline condition? Assumptions (need to be met to continue with testing hypotheses) 1) Participants high in NFC have higher RQ scores at baseline than participants low in NFC, i.e. in accordance with previous studies we expect a positive correlation between NFC and RQ of at least .4 2) Our sample varies in their algorithmic ability, here assessed with Berlin numeracy test and Wordsum test 3) Perceived effort is higher in time-pressure than baseline condition. title_r: The role of emotion type and attention to emotion in emotional cue evaluation
abstract_r: Attention to emotion measures the degree to which one notices, values, and is guided by one’s own emotions (Salovey, Mayer, Goldman, Turvey, & Palfai, 1995), yet it is less known how higher levels of attention to emotion impact the evaluation of emotional cues expressed by other people. In our research, preregistered exploratory analyses suggested that individual differences in attention to emotion may be related to less differentiation between the intensity of emotions (angry, happy, and sad) for individuals higher on attention on emotion. This effect was driven by elevated perceptions of emotional intensity for angry and sad expressions by individuals higher in attention to emotion when compared to individuals with lower degrees of attention to emotion. Evaluations of happy expressions were not significantly associated with individual differences in attention to emotion. The purpose of the present study is to test emotion category effects as a priori hypotheses in a replication study. In our previous study, happy faces were rated by our participants as significantly more intense, and this follow up study uses a modified stimuli set which considers standardized intensity ratings with the aim of happy faces reflecting equivalent average intensity ratings as the angry and sad faces. Based on the pre-registered yet exploratory findings in our previous study, we hypothesize that higher levels of attention to emotion will relate to higher ratings of emotional intensity for angry and sad facial expressions, but will not show a significant relation to intensity ratings for happy expressions.

title_r: TOPP Replication Study
abstract_r: Mathematica will conduct a replication study of Teen Options to Prevent Pregnancy (T.O.P.P.), a multicomponent intervention to delay repeat pregnancy among adolescent mothers. Mathematica conducted an earlier evaluation of T.O.P.P. with a sample of 598 adolescent mothers in Columbus, Ohio, as part of a larger federal study. To test the potential for T.O.P.P. to have similar benefits when implemented on a larger scale and in a different context, we will conduct a replication study with a sample of about 1,000 adolescents recruited from up to 11 hospitals in New York City. The study will be a randomized control trial, with mothers in the treatment group being offered the T.O.P.P. intervention for 18 months, and mothers in the control group accessing the existing standard-of-care reproductive health services. About 18 months after enrollment, we will conduct a follow-up survey to examine whether T.O.P.P. has reduced repeat pregnancies. We also plan to access administrative data to determine whether T.O.P.P. has reduced repeat births. Exploratory analyses will explore program implementation and fidelity, the resources required to implement the program, and the impacts of T.O.P.P. on additional mediating and downstream outcomes as well as potential adverse outcomes

title_r: The Effect of Meaningful Choice on Sense of Agency (II)
abstract_r: Consistent research has shown how the Sense of Agency (SoA: the feeling of control that we attribute to our actions and their subsequent consequences) can be influenced by both predictive and postdictive factors (processes that occur prior to and succeeding an action, respectively). This has been shown in studies that manipulate the choice we have over our actions, and the nature of the outcome that follows (such as a positive, or negative outcome). In our initial work, we explored the possibility that both choice (choice or no-choice) and outcome valence (positive or negative) would interact. Here, our findings only provided strong evidence for a postdictive effect of outcome (greater intentional binding for positive outcomes) on SoA. Studies have also revealed that increasing the amount of choice, influences the SoA. From this, we decided to explore whether increasing choice (from 1-7 choices), would increase the agency we feel over our actions. Though we replicated our finding of a postdictive effect of outcome on SoA, we showed that increasing choice had no effect on SoA. One reason for a lack of a predictive effect of choice in both studies, may be that the ‘choice’ was meaningless. Whichever choice the participant made, the outcome was 50% positive, 50% negative. Research has shown that the SoA for our action-outcomes, is influenced when the outcome is more predictable. As such, we explored whether a choice that has a predictable outcome (more likely to produce a specific outcome 75% of the time), influences our SoA. Interestingly, we replicated the same postdictive effect of outcome, yet, showed that even a meaningful choice still had no effect on SoA. Something to consider, is that our previous studies measure ‘outcome-binding’ (reflecting a shift in perceived time of the outcome (tone) backward towards the action which initiated it (key press)). This may explain why we found a consistent postdictive effect of outcome, and not a predictive effect of choice. Research has proposed that ‘action-binding’ (a shift in perceived time of the action (key press) towards the outcome (tone) which it produces) may instead be a more reliable measure of SoA for our actions. For this reason, this current project aims to replicate our latest study where our choice has a predictable outcome (The Effect of Meaningful Choice on Sense of Agency), with a focus on measuring action-binding instead. By measuring action-binding, we aim to assess whether a choice with a predictable outcome, does increase the SoA and/or interact with the effect of outcome, compared to having no-choice.

title_r: Is racial bias in pain perception evident under minimal exposure conditions? (Replication)
abstract_r: Recent work demonstrates that racial bias in pain care stems, at least in part, from a perceptual source (Mende-Siedlecki et al., 2019). Racial bias in pain perception arises from disruptions in configural face processing, cannot be explained by low-level stimulus features, persists even when identical expressions of pain are rendered on computer-generated targets, and predicts biases in treatment above and beyond explicit stereotypes and prejudice. That said, the speed with which painful expressions are processed is somewhat unclear, and further, the automaticity of this bias is as of yet uncertain. Are differences in evaluations of Black and White facial expressions of pain evident under minimal presentation conditions, or does this bias require more time (and deliberation) to emerge? One initial experiment (https://osf.io/jz5kw) designed to address these questions demonstrated that a) pain judgments made at 33ms were correlated with unconstrained judgments (though the strength of this correlation increased with presentation time) and b) racial bias in pain judgments was evident as early as 33ms and was correlated with bias in unconstrained judgments. Here, we wish to replicate these findings in a separate sample with additional power (in terms of observations per participant) to demonstrate the robustness of these effects.

title_r: Conscientiousness, students’ goal orientation, and reasoning ability: significance for educational standards
abstract_r: Previous studies show that students’ goal orientation and conscientiousness are related to academic performance. Few studies, however, allow conclusions to be drawn about the factor structure of goal orientation and its distinctions from conscientiousness. In a study with N = 145 secondary school students (M = 13.9, SD = 0.85; 41% male), we investigated if the residuals of latent factors of goal orientation are still meaningfully correlated with academic performance and reasoning. Based on structural equation models, we have replicated the theoretically derived four-factor structure and showed that conscientiousness explains 29% of the variance in learning goals and 40% of the variance in work avoidance. Furthermore, we show that the residuals of goal orientation are mainly not significantly related to reasoning or educational standards (only work avoidance correlated with reasoning, and performance goals correlated with educational standards). Educational standards were highly correlated with reasoning. Implications for school practice and possible interventions are discussed.

title_r: Bullying Victimization and Mental Health Among Canadian Gender and Sexually Diverse Youth: A Replication and Expansion of Previous Studies
abstract_r: Gender and sexually diverse youth disproportionately experience bullying and emotional problems. However, small samples and limited intersectional research have hindered our understanding of this vulnerable population. In the present study, the moderating role of gender identity and sexual orientation in the relation between bullying victimization and emotional problems was examined in a large sample of Grade 7–12 Canadian students drawn from the Health and Peer Relations Study (N = 6,824; racial/ethnic minority = 38.7%; sexually diverse = 29.8%; gender diverse = 5.3%). Controlling for race/ethnicity and grade, there was no three-way interaction among bullying, gender identity, and sexual orientation, nor a two-way interaction between bullying and gender identity. However, a significant bullying by sexual orientation interaction emerged, wherein bullied sexually diverse youth reported more emotional problems than their non-bullied sexually diverse peers and bullied straight youth. A gender identity by sexual orientation interaction was also found where sexually diverse girls had worse mental health compared to sexually diverse boys and sexually-gender diverse youth endorsed more emotional problems than sexually diverse girls and boys. Overall, sexually diverse youth who were bullied by their peers and gender diverse youth, particularly those identifying as sexually diverse, reported significant mental health challenges. These results support minority stress and intersectionality models and highlight the need for anti-bullying and mental health initiatives. Future research should further explore intersectional variations and contextual factors contributing to these disparities.

title_r: Personal Values and Vaccination against Covid Preregistration Analysis
abstract_r: A1 Background Vaccine hesitancy, the decision to reject or delay accepting vaccines despite the availability of vaccine services (MacDonald, 2015), is an urgent problem in combating the Covid-19 pandemic because in countries with sufficiently available doses, vaccine uptake is slowing. Coming closer to herd immunity (Anderson & May, 1985) will be a prerequisite of reducing non-pharmaceutical interventions such as social distancing, school closures, or mask wearing. The moral dimensions of liberty, purity, authority, and possibly harm have been found to correlate with vaccination hesitancy measured as parents’ and caregivers’ attitudes and intentions towards vaccina-tion against child’s diseases (Amin et al., 2017; Rossen et al., 2019). Further predictors of vaccine hesitancy have been demonstrated to be vaccine attitudes, political atti-tudes, conspiracy beliefs, faith in science, and cognitive thinking style. All these predictors are known to be interrelated and have never been investigated together in a single study. A2 Objectives and Research questions The present study aims at investigating the relationship between moral values with psychological pre-cursors to adults’ decisions to be vaccinated against Covid-19, a decision directly concerning the de-ciders themselves. First, from the perspective of applied research, vaccination programs need to be informed about psy-chological factors beyond beliefs in safety and efficacy of vaccines in order to tailor messaging di-rected especially at vaccine hesitant subpopulations. The objective of the present study is to identify subpopulations in vaccine hesitant persons and their moral signatures. The moral signatures of vac-cine programs have been demonstrated to have an effect on vaccine uptake (Heine & Wolters, 2021). Second, from the perspective of basic research, the present study investigates the relationship be-tween vaccine beliefs, vaccination decisions, and moral values. The current pandemic situation allows to differentiate vaccine attitudes and mere intentions from the factual decision to become vaccinated or not. This allows to answer the research question: Do moral values predict the decision to vaccinate against Covid-19 over and above vaccination beliefs and attitudes? Third, the study aims at a direct replication of a previously unpublished finding of the relationship between moral foundations and the decision to vaccinate against Covid-19. A3 Participants A sample of German adults is aimed to be drawn with 50% participants already vaccinated against Covid-19 at least once and 50% who do not intend to be vaccinated. A4 Study method Participants are asked to complete an online survey using the moral foundations questionnaire (J. Graham et al., 2011), psychological antecedents of vaccination in general and against Covid-19 spe-cifically („5C model“ Betsch et al., 2020), conspiracy mentality (Stojanov & Halberstadt, 2019), faith in science (Farias et al., 2013), propensity to think rationally (Thomson & Oppenheimer, 2016), open-minded thinking style about evidence , and political attitudes (Akkerman et al., 2014; Decker et al., 2013). First, data-driven clustering methods will be used to model groups of vaccination hesitancy and their relationship to the endorsement of moral domains. A5 Open Science The analysis is pre-registered in this file. Study materials are available in the second file of this pre-registration. Data and executable analysis code will be made publicly available.

title_r: Open-label placebo effects on psychological and physical well-being: A conceptual replication study
abstract_r: Background: Contrary to traditional placebos, open-label placebos (OLP) abstain from deception, i.e., participants are openly informed to receive an inert substance. Studies in clinical and healthy samples evidence the efficacy of OLPs. This study aims to conceptually replicate and expand findings of a recent OLP study in healthy participants while implementing a within-subject design and daily instead of retrospective assessments. Additionally, the effect of a brand name on the medicine container is tested and possible predictors of the OLP effects are explored. Method: Healthy participants (N = 75) received OLP and no placebo for 5 days each (randomized sequence) and answered daily questionnaires on sleep quality, bodily symptoms, mental well-being, and psychological distress. The medicine container of half the participants had a brand name, the remaining did not. Different personality traits and situational factors were assessed. Results: Mental and physical well-being did not differ between OLP and control phase, i.e., overall, no OLP effect emerged. Contrast analysis indicated that an OLP effect emerged for sleep quality and psychological distress when no brand name was present. Further, an OLP effect emerged in persons with higher expectations for bodily symptoms (r = .23, p = .046) and psychological distress (r = .24, p = .037). Conclusions: Methodological differences to the original study are discussed as an explanation for the failure to induce overall OLP effects. Future studies should continue to replicate previous findings and determine the exact conditions of successful implementation of OLP effects in healthy as well as clinical samples.

title_r: Stata Syntax for: Pedestrians’ alertness and perceived environmental safety under non-uniform urban lighting
abstract_r: The influence of urban lighting on the visual tasks of pedestrians is well known and, in line with this, numerous studies have explored the relationship between urban lighting and pedestrians’ feelings of safety. This earlier research has traditionally focused on minimal required illuminance for various visual performance tasks (e.g., obstacle detection and face recognition). However, this focus may have been too narrow, as other light-moderated factors, such as pedestrians’ general attentiveness to the environment, may also be important for safety. Despite this, the psychological concepts related to the individuals’ attention, such as alertness, arousal and anxiety, have only rarely been considered in street lighting research to date. The current manuscript takes a first step in this direction, by testing the sensitivity and direction of response of relevant metrics in a pilot study. We decided for a conceptual replication of a field experiment from 1916 and managed to partly replicate the findings. Limitations of the present study, as well as implications for future research in this domain are discussed.

title_r: Profit motives, environmental motives, and perceived corporate greenwashing revisited: A replication and extension of de Vries et al. (2015)
abstract_r: As the climate change crisis has become more evident, a growing number of businesses and organizations have gotten involved in sustainability efforts. But not all corporate sustainability efforts are applauded: sometimes the public accuses companies of greenwashing, i.e., overstating the extent to which the company is environmentally friendly. There is little research on the factors that influence perceived greenwashing amongst the public. Here, we report a replication and extension of one of the few studies of this topic, Experiment 2 in de Vries et al. (2015, https://doi.org/10.1002/csr.1327). The original study found that people perceived more greenwashing when an oil company communicated an environmental motive for a sustainability investment (carbon capture and storage), as opposed to a profit motive, d = 0.98 [0.37, 1.59]. The present pre-registered replication (n = 516) did not find support for this effect, with very little difference in perceived greenwashing depending on communicated motive, d = -0.09 [-0.38, 0.21]. As extensions, we included a condition where a mixed motive (both environment and profits) was communicated, tested the effect using a different type of company than the original, included a measure of general attitudes to the company in addition to perceived greenwashing, and included measures of individual differences in attitudes towards corporate social responsibility and belief in climate change. The most noteworthy exploratory finding was that attitudes were more positive when an environmental or a mixed motive was communicated rather than a profit motive.

title_r: Effects of Transition Metal Dopants on the Mechanosensitivity of Lanthanide-Based Upconverting Nanoparticles in Polymers
abstract_r: Biomechanical forces are critical to our understanding of physiological and pathological phenomena. However, current methods of quantifying biophysical forces, such as traction force microscopy, colonic stents, and more are often limited in scope and/or reliability. To remedy this, we need less invasive, biocompatible force sensors with high spatial resolution and stable readout signal that changes with applied force. In this thesis, we address this issue by designing probes based on upconverting nanoparticles (UCNPs) embedded in polymer matrices for use as biophysical force sensors. Using an AFM-confocal microscope assembly, we characterize the emissions of five spin-coated thin film samples of UCNP-polymer probes, varying Mn2+ dopant concentration, UCNP core-shell structure, and host polymer type. We replicate the linear increase in the percent change of the integrated red:green ratio of UCNP emitted light with increasing Mn2+ concentration seen in previous studies with UCNPs embedded in PDMS and alginate gels. We additionally identify that Mn2+ co-doping increases UCNP-PDMS mechanosensitivity up to a certain limit within 4.2% Mn concentration. Finally, we find that Mn2+ as a crosslinking agent in a less rigid alginate matrix similarly increases the colorimetric optical response of core-double-shell UCNPs, suggesting that UCNP structures with dopants moved to shell layers or the external polymer host are still effective. By demonstrating our ability to adapt and optimize force-sensitive UCNPs in different polymer hosts, we take preliminary steps toward implementing them in target biological systems to develop them further as biophysical force probes.

title_r: Perceived Causal Strength in Chains vs. Common Causes
abstract_r: Recent work highlighted a cause’s scope, the number of distinct effects it generates, as important for changing perceived causal strength. The findings, however, have been inconsistent, with researchers offering effect valence and domain knowledge as mutually exclusive explanations for the presence of scope effects. Our pre-registered experiment (N=322) simultaneously controlled or manipulated the links between scope and causal strength to adjudicate between the two accounts. We also examined another structural feature as a potential moderator of a cause’s perceived strength: while prior work has focused on causal power in common cause networks, we compared them with causal chains, where mechanistic clarity may lead to higher causal power ratings. We found that causal strength is robustly higher in chains regardless of valence and domain (p=.009). However, we failed to replicate the prior findings on the scope effect. Our experiment casts doubt on previous authors’ interpretation of scope's impact on causal judgments.

title_r: Revisiting Dependency Length and Intervener Complexity Minimisation on a Parallel Corpus in 35 Languages
abstract_r: In this replication study of previous research into dependency length minimisation (DLM), we pilot a new parallel multilingual parsed corpus to examine whether previous findings are upheld when controlling for variation in domain and sentence content between languages. We follow the approach of previous research in comparing the dependency lengths of observed sentences in a multilingual corpus to a variety of baselines: permutations of the sentences, either random or according to some fixed schema. We go on to compare DLM with intervener complexity measure (ICM), an alternative measure of syntactic complexity. Our findings uphold both dependency length and intervener complexity minimisation in all languages under investigation. We also find a markedly lesser extent of dependency length minimisation in verb-final languages, and the same for intervener complexity measure. We conclude that dependency length and intervener complexity minimisation as universals are upheld when controlling for domain and content variation, but that further research is needed into the asymmetry between verb-final and other languages in this regard.

title_r: Scaling Up: Revisiting Mining Android Sandboxes at Scale for Malware Classification
abstract_r: The widespread use of smartphones in daily life has raised concerns about privacy and security among researchers and practitioners. Privacy issues are generally highly prevalent in mobile applications, particularly targeting the Android platform, the most popular mobile operating system. For this reason, several techniques have been proposed to identify malicious behavior in Android applications, including the Mining Android Sandbox approach (MAS approach), which aims to identify malicious behavior in repackaged Android applications (apps). However, previous empirical studies evaluated the MAS approach using a small dataset consisting of only 102 pairs of original and repackaged apps. This limitation raises questions about the external validity of their findings and whether the MAS approach can be generalized to larger datasets. To address these concerns, this paper presents the results of a replication study focused on evaluating the performance of the MAS approach regarding its capabilities of correctly classifying malware from different families. Unlike previous studies, our research employs a dataset that is an order of magnitude larger, comprising 4,076 pairs of apps covering a more diverse range of Android malware families. Surprisingly, our findings indicate a poor performance of the MAS approach for identifying malware, with the F1-score decreasing from 0.90 for the small dataset used in the previous studies to 0.54 in our more extensive dataset. Upon closer examination, we discovered that certain malware families partially account for the low accuracy of the MAS approach, which fails to classify a repackaged version of an app as malware correctly. Our findings highlight the limitations of the MAS approach, particularly when scaled, and underscore the importance of complementing it with other techniques to detect a broader range of malware effectively.

title_r: Conceptual replication that the general evaluability theory predicts the cheerleader effect
abstract_r: A recent article demonstrated that a change in evaluation mode predicts the cheerleader effect. The present article is a conceptual replication, and it provides additional evidence with morphed faces. Again, faces of low attractiveness appear as more attractive when they are flanked by equally low attractive faces than they do in isolation. This is in line with the predictions of the change in evaluation mode, but not with other theoretical explanations of the cheerleader effect. This article is documentation of this additional study, the data and material. There is no additional theoretical gain, except the evidence that the results could be replicated with morphed faces. For a review of the theoretical explanations of the cheerleader effect, see Messner, Carnelli and Höhener, 2020.

title_r: Fiscal expenditure and the exchange rate: A sticky -price, rational -expectations approach
abstract_r: This dissertation presents, solves, and estimates two sticky-price monetary models under rational expectations, to investigate the relationship between fiscal expenditure and the exchange rate. The first project extends the Driskill and Sheffrin (1981) (DS) model by adopting a detailed aggregate demand specification which includes a specific government purchases variable. We estimate the extended DS model for the DM/US$ exchange rate. As background to our extension, we also present an attempted replication, correction, and update of the DS results. Our replication and update are an improvement on the DS results. Most of our estimates are significant, correctly signed, and plausible; however, the restrictions imposed by the structural model and rational expectations are rejected. Our extended DS model estimation finds evidence for a negative, but insignificant, relationship between fiscal expenditure and the exchange rate. The second project adapts the Wickens (1985) model to a secular inflationary environment. We also modify the Wickens aggregate demand specification to capture dependence on real interest rate, and to specifically include a government purchases variable. In this model a permanent shock to the money supply could lead to either overshooting or undershooting of the exchange rate. However, our attempts at estimating the extended Wickens model for the Can$/US$ exchange rate, proved to be unsuccessful. An unconstrained version of the model finds some evidence for a link between fiscal expenditure and the exchange rate.
