title_r: Counter-attitudinal behavior without attitude change: A Novel Understanding of Cognitive Dissonance in Environmental Research
abstract_r: In this study we examine the proclaimed attitude change in induced-compliance paradigm. In classic induced-compliance research participants are pushed to show a behavior that is supposedly attitude-contrary, hence discrepant with respect to a preexisting attitude. This is said to evoke an affective state referred to as cognitive dissonance. The alleged dissonance effect in induced-compliance paradigm is most often derived from between-group comparisons of a single rating of an opinion item and interpreted as substantial attitude change. We want to question this assumption by 1. looking at the behavioral relevance of this attitude change, 2. investigating the attitude change given a reliable and validated measure of attitude is applied and 3. exploring alternative explanations for the difference in said single opinion item. We assume that: 1. The opinion change after counter-attitudinal behavior is not behavior relevant; 2. There is no substantial change in attitude after performing a counter-attitudinal behavior. 3. The difference in the single opinion item is partly due to a self-selection of participants, as the choice to write a counter-attitudinal statement is influenced by the level of environmental attitude. To test these assumptions, we seek to replicate results from a previous study (preregistered by Nicolas Neef) and to further consolidate our explanatory model. In the previous study, counter-attitudinal behavior showed no effect on manifest behavior or on attitude (post-hoc measured). Unfortunately, pre-intervention attitude and opinion differences were not considered. Actual attitude change was therefore not examined.

title_r: Modes of Morality: Investigating moral decisions in response to 2D videos
abstract_r: Moral judgments are typically studied using text-based vignettes that describe hypothetical moral dilemmas that involve a trade-off between sacrificing a few lives and saving many more lives. In attempts to increase the contextual saliency/richness of these experimental materials, several studies have incorporated Virtual Reality (VR) reconstructions of these moral dilemmas. Across studies, researchers have found a discrepancy between moral judgments given in response to text-based moral dilemmas and simulated moral actions in VR counterparts (e.g., Francis et al., 2016; 2017; 2018; McDonald et al., 2020; Patil et al., 2014). While there are suggestions that these findings support a judgment-behaviour discrepancy in the domain of morality of harm, research has yet to systematically investigate whether it is differences in the mode of presentation that drives this discrepancy. Following from studies investigating responses to moral dilemmas presented with images and sounds, we conducted a study in German using a 2D video version of a moral dilemma. In this study (n = 235) we did not find evidence that mode of presentation influenced moral decision-making. To build on this work and in this pre-registered replication, we will present moral dilemmas as 2D videos to incorporate the movement and real-time features of VR across both a UK sample in English and a German sample in German.

title_r: Individual differences in global/local processing and the transfer of global/local processing modes
abstract_r: In a previous study (De Luca, Verschoor & Hommel, in press), we tested whether particular processing modes show transfer between different tasks. The hypothetical modes were derived from Förster and Dannenberg’s (2010) GLOMOsys theory, which claims that people process perceived events and internal information in either a more global or a more local processing mode, thus facilitating the processing of global or local stimulus aspects, respectively. We tried to induce a global or local processing mode by having participants respond to either the global or the local letter(s) of Navon stimuli (where a large, global letter is composed of many smaller, local letters). The key questions were whether this mode would transfer to another task and whether this transfer would be observed with very similar tasks only (near transfer) or also with very different tasks (far transfer). We created conditions that were thought to be optimal for transfer. We reduced the temporal distance between prime and probe trials by integrating them into a dual-task paradigm and used probe tasks that were either almost identical with the prime task, or at least shared the relevant modality and attentional demands. We obtained significant transfer effects between almost identical visual global/local tasks, irrespective of the degree of cognitive conflict that these tasks generated, but did not find any evidence for somewhat farer transfer to other visual tasks, like a flanker task and an attentional blink task. That is, any substantial change in the probe task’s characteristics compared to the prime task eliminated almost any signs of transfer. Altogether, we concluded that either global/local processing modes as envisioned by GLOMOsys do not exist or they normally do not transfer from global/local tasks to other, unrelated tasks. In the present study, we aimed to replicate the near transfer with very similar tasks, but we were also interested in possible interindividual differences in the amount of transfer. Processing modes like those postulated by GLOMOsys can be considered metacontrol modes (Hommel & Colzato, 2017) that are regulating the processing style of individuals. There is strong evidence for particular metacontrol biases and considerable interindividual differences therein (Hommel & Colzato, 2017). For instance, some people tend to be more focused, persistent, and affected by the current goal, while others tend to be more open, flexible, but also more distractible on average or per default. Here we asked what to make of such differences and how to assess them. The recent years have seen increasing support for the Big-5 approach to personality. This approach holds that people differ with respect to five basic traits called agreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, neuroticism, and openness. More interesting for our purposes, there is increasing evidence that these five traits converge onto two metatraits, stability and plasticity, which are semantically almost identical with the metacontrol concepts of persistence and flexibility (Hommel, 2022). In particular, stability is assumed to be related to agreeableness, conscientiousness, and (negative) neuroticism (or positive emotional stability), whereas plasticity is assumed to be related to extraversion and openness (DeYoung et al., 2008). Along these lines, two sets of predictions can be tested. The first set, which we will test in Experiment 2 of our study, refers to the transfer between tasks, as reported by De Luca et al. with very similar tasks. Transfer can be considered as a kind of control (over-) generalization, suggesting that this transfer would be less pronounced if stability is high (and plasticity low) and more pronounced if plasticity is high (and stability low). Accordingly, participants high on traits related to stability (i.e., high in agreeableness and conscientiousness, low neuroticism) should show less transfer than participants high on traits related to plasticity (i.e., high in extraversion and openness). The second set of predictions, which we will test in Experiment 1 of our study, relates to the global-local effect proper. Navon stimuli typically generate the global-precedence effect: participants perform faster and more accurately if they are to report the global stimulus letter than the local stimulus letter (Navon, 1977). This global-precedence effect has been attributed to the natural tendency to focus on global aspects, at least under some circumstances. Accordingly, people can be assumed to have a preference for global processing, which they need to overcome is being required to report the local stimulus. Interestingly for our purposes, participant groups that are assumed to have a strong persistence bias have been found to show a stronger precedence effect (XXXX), suggesting that persistence makes it more difficult to switch to the less preferred stimulus level. If so, we would expect participants high on traits related to stability to show a larger precedence effect (i.e., a stronger advantage if responding to global levels than to local levels) then participants high on traits related to plasticity.

title_r: Women's Confrontation of Ambivalent Sexism and The Role of Perpetrator's Age Study 2
abstract_r: This experiment is a follow-up study of a previous study that investigated women's confrontation of sexism and the role of the perpetrator's age. I look at the effect of two kinds of sexism (hostile sexism: negative evaluation/stereotypes against women, and benevolent sexism: prejudice against women that appears positive) on women's willingness to confront. I will also investigate how sexist perpetrators' age can play a role in women's willingness to confront benevolent and hostile sexism. The study is a 2 (perpetrator age) x 2 (types of sexism) between-subjects experimental design. My research goal is to explore the complex interplay between sexism and age-based stereotypes on women's willingness to confront sex-based discrimination. In this follow-up study we seek to replicate our previous study and also find factors that can explain some of the results we have found before (age x type of sexism interaction in affecting womens' confrontation of sexism).

title_r: Effects of bodily movements on language comprehension
abstract_r: The action-sentence compatibility effect (ACE) paradigm originally reported in Glenberg and Kaschak (2002) has been widely employed to test language-motor coupling at the behavioral level. In the classical version of this paradigm, participants are asked to judge the sensibility of written or auditory sentences implicating a direction toward or away from them by moving their hand towards or away from their body. Response times are typically shorter when sentence and response movements are in the same direction. Despite various conceptual replications the reliability and robustness of this effect has been questioned by a recent failed multi-lab replication (Morey et al., 2022). In the present study we aim to test whether changes in bodily movements linked to new technologies – e.g., swiping on a touchscreen instead of using a computer mouse – might have played a role in these 2022 failed replications when younger generations, who likely have more experience with swiping than using a mouse, are concerned. To this aim, we implemented the same paradigm used by Morey and colleagues with two different response devices: a computer mouse and a tablet allowing for swiping movements as responses. We tested a total of 64 German participants (aged 18-25) with the same English stimuli employed by Morey et al. (2022). In line with our reasoning on previous results, we expect to replicate the ACE effect using the tablet, but not the computer mouse, condition as the matching between sentence and movement may be affected by participants' bodily expertise and their increasing familiarity with swiping movements. This would suggest that language-motor coupling is flexibly adapted as a function of everyday bodily movements.

title_r: Experiment 1E: Replication of the head nodding and shaking effect in a web-based experiment
abstract_r: Given that nodding and shaking head motions are used as communicative signals, such as signals of approval (and denial), these motions might be expected to modulate perceived trait impressions of model faces. We used movie clips of nodding and shaking head motions of computer-generated figures and examined the modulation effects of these motions on perceived trait impressions. Results showed that the nodding head motion significantly increased ratings of subjective likeability and approachability compared to the shaking or control conditions, whereas the shaking motion did not affect ratings. However, previous studies have primarily examined this effect using laboratory-based experiments with Japanese university students, which limits the generalizability and replicability of the results. Therefore, the present study examined whether this effect can be observed in a web-based experiment and for crowdsourcing service workers. In this experiment (Experiment 1E), we re-examined the effects of nodding and shaking motions on perceived likeability about personality.

title_r: Actions at a Glance - Colour
abstract_r: The experiment aims to reveal the temporal gradient in which actions, objects, scene context, and sensory information are perceived in a free recall paradigm (Fei-Fei et al., 2007), when coloured images are used as stimuli. In another study (Preregistration: Vrabie et al., 2022, September 18), we investigated the time course in which different action scene components of grayscale images are perceived in a free-recall paradigm similar to Fei-Fei et al. (2007). We found that actions could be perceived significantly faster than objects or scene context, and that objects could be perceived significantly faster than scene context. However, previous work suggests that colour information can affect the recognition of scenes (e.g., Castelhano & Henderson, 2008) and objects (e.g., Witzel & Gegenfurtner, 2018). To our knowledge, no such effects have been investigated for action recognition with human observers yet. Thus, it might be that the absence of colour information selectively impaired scene- and object recognition while sparing action recognition. In the experiment pre-registered here, we want to replicate our findings using coloured images as stimuli in order to exclude image colouration as a confounding factor. The experiment will be separated into two stages: In stage 1, a free recall paradigm is used to collect descriptions from coloured pictures containing actions embedded in naturalistic scenes at 6 different, very short presentation times. In stage 2, participants will rate the picture descriptions gathered in stage 1. The rating scheme will be similar to the scheme used by Fei-Fei et al. (2007). Participants will rate if different features of the image (action, scene context, objects, sensory information, key action, key scene, manipulated object) have been described correctly. References: Castelhano, M. S., & Henderson, J. M. (2008). The influence of color on the perception of scene gist. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human perception and performance, 34(3), 660. Fei-Fei, L., Iyer, A., Koch, C., & Perona, P. (2007). What do we perceive in a glance of a real-world scene? Journal of Vision, 7(1):10, 1–29, http://journalofvision.org/7/1/10/, doi:10.1167/7.1.10. title_r: Elliott et al.’s (2010) “Red, Rank, and Romance” Effect: A Meta-Analysis of Collaborative Replications and Education Project (CREP) Replications
abstract_r: The present article reports the results of a meta-analysis of eight student replication projects of Elliot et al.’s (2010) Experiment 3. The eight student projects were part of the Collaborative Replication and Education Project (CREP; https://osf,io/wfc6u/), a research crowdsourcing project for undergraduate students. Studies to be replicated were identified by the CREP advisory board, after which student teams (under the supervision of a local faculty supervisor) selected a study to replicate. Following this choice, student teams created a project page on the Open Science Framework, uploaded their materials, and pre-registered their replication prior to data collection. All replications were reviewed by experts to ensure high quality data, and were pre-registered prior to data collection. Results of this meta-analysis showed no effect of red on attractiveness ratings; this null result held with and without Elliot et al.’s (2010) data included in analyses. Exploratory analyses examining whether being in a relationship or not moderated the effect of color on attractiveness ratings also produced null results.

title_r: Study 2: Does shifting demographics impact the (counter-)empathy of White Americans? Testing a new shifting demographics manipulation.
abstract_r: This study is the second study in the SDO, empathy, and shifting demographics line. In previous studies (Hudson, Cikara, & Sidanius, 2019) we’ve found that SDO correlates with reduced empathy and increased counter-empathy towards others in general. However, when group dynamics and group competition is primed, (White) participants feel even less empathy and even more schadenfreude towards racial out-groups. In a separate line of work, researchers (Craig, Richeson, 2014a/2014b) have shown that reminding White Americans about the impending shift in racial dynamics causes threat and increases levels of fear. Thus, we are interested in assessing whether exposure to shifting demographics can also cause group based empathic reductions, and counter-empathic increases, on the part of White Americans. Overall this study assesses the impact that hierarchy-related ideology has on emotional responses to changing racial dynamics. Future studies will assess other ideologies as well as psychological mediators. We ran an initial study exposing White participants to shifting demographic information and assessing their levels of empathy and counter-empathy towards racial in-group and racial-outgroups. We replicated past work on the relationship between SDO and (counter-) empathy; as SDO increased participants felt less empathy and more counter-empathy. Furthermore, there was an interaction between SDO, prime, and emotions such that SDO’s negative relationship between empathy and positive relationship with schadenfreude became stronger for all targets when participants were exposed to shifting demographics compared to control. However, the anticipated four-way interaction was not significant. In other words, the shifting demographics prime did not relate to reduced empathy and increased counter-empathy specifically for Black and Latino out-group targets compared to White in-group targets. Purpose of Study: In this study we replicate this paradigm but with a new manipulation that focuses more on the consequences of shifting demographics compared to just exposure. Furthermore, we include new stories that are more related to hierarchy than the mild ones used previously.

title_r: Individual differences in masked-perpetrators face recognition under low cognitive load
abstract_r: Perpetrators often wear masks to avoid being recognized. Previous studies have suggested that contextual congruency can facilitate recognition performance for masked perpetrators. Here we aim to replicate and extend this finding with a reduced number of studied targets to address the potential influence of cognitive and memory load. Additionally, we aim to explore whether individual differences in face recognition influence the relationship between contextual congruence and recognition accuracy for masked perpetrators. Also, to be consistent with previous findings, we expect high-ability face recognizers to maintain this advantage across both congruent and incongruent sets as opposed to participants with low face recognition ability under low memory load.

title_r: Replication: Between bravery and brutality: impact of media presentation on implicit and explicit attitudes toward police
abstract_r: To validate results of the first study and a dissociative effects of our experimental manipulation on implicit and explicit attitudes we decided to lead an exact replication of our study using the prolific platform. In accordance to our power analysis, we will do the best to achieve the required sample size, depending on the resources available to conduct this research (with an effect size of d = .285, a statistical power of 95% and α = .05, the required sample size estimated a priori is 252 participants in each condition). Description of our research: The aim of this research is to study impacts of media police presentation on explicit and implicit attitudes towards this social category. This study is original in this field as it is the first to implicitly measure people attitudes towards police. Moreover, even if numerous studies have shown that media exposure can have different influences on perception of the police depending on information valency, only few studies attempted to experimentally manipulate this media exposure. In this experiment, we are interested in how positive (such as the arrest of a terrorist) or negative (such as police brutality) media events involving the police can have direct effects on people's attitudes towards the police. The extant literature suggests that positive or negative media portrayals of the police has a direct effect on the population's self-reported attitudes towards this social category. However, since much of the research in this area has only used longitudinal or correlational studies, we decided to investigate the impact of a single video presentation involving the police on attitudes towards this category. We hypothesized that the mere presentation of an event involving the police could positively or negatively affect people's attitudes towards the police, depending on the positive or negative valence of the event. Therefore, we randomly assigned participants to three experimental conditions that differed only in the video they were presented with and the description of their historical context. In the first condition (police brutality condition), participants watched a video of police violence against an activist during the Yellow Vests movement of December 2018. In the second (police heroism condition), the video showed a crowd acclaiming police officers because of the arrest of a terrorist perpetrator in December 2018. Finally, the third video (control condition) was a road safety video without direct reference to the police. These videos were intended to depict positive, negative or neutral content. Following the presentation of this video, participants were asked to indicate the emotions they felt after watching this video on a scale ranging from 0 = very negative to 100 = very positive. This question was intended to test the effectiveness of our experimental induction. A contrast analysis showed that participants who had seen the brutality video reported more negative emotions (M = 11.3, SD = 16.1) than those who had seen the control video (M = 36.8, SD = 30.8), who in turn reported more negative emotions than those who had seen the heroism video (M = 52.6, SD = 30.6), β = 20.64, p < .001, η² = .29. After this short video, participants completed a French version of the Attitude towards Police Legitimacy Scale– a scale of behavioral intentions to cooperate or to compete with police, and an implicit measure of attitudes towards police (Single Category Implicit Association Test : SC-IAT) based on Karpinski and Steinman’s article (2006). This task was used to assess the behavioral tendency to associate pictures of police with positive and negative words. Finally, we collected additional demographic variables: personal and media exposure to police brutality, protest involvement during last months, gender and age. This study took place in France during the social protest of the Yellow Vests (« Gilets Jaunes »). A link to the survey was sent by email to students at the University of Poitiers and posted on social networks, asking participants to forward the study to others with a snowball sampling. In compliance with our required sample size estimated a priori (according to the average effect size in psychology f = 0.195 and a power of 0.80) we collected 267 complete responses. Before analyzing the effect of our manipulation, we wanted to assess correlations between this new implicit measure with self-reported attitudes towards the police and with factors that influence them, but also to study its predictive validity on self-reported behavioral intention to help or confront the police. Consistent with our preregistration, our analyses showed a significant positive correlation between explicit and implicit attitudes (r = .41, p < .001). In addition, both of these constructs are predicted by self-reported personal exposure and self-reported media exposure to events of police violence. These results suggest that predictors of explicit attitudes also have a significant influence on the population's implicit attitudes towards the police. Furthermore, as explicit attitudes significantly predict willingness to help or oppose to the police, implicit attitudes in isolation were also found to be significant in predicting these same self-reported behavioral intentions. Taken together these results reveal that this new implicit measure of associations of police images with positive or negative words appear to measure constructs similar to those of explicit attitudes. The aim of this research was to study the impact of positive or negative presentation of the police on explicit but also implicit attitudes towards the police. Indeed, implicit measures are generally used to overcome problems related to the experimental demand because of their uncontrollable specificity. This measure should allow us to limit the effect of demand on an issue as sensitive as attitudes towards the police. Thus, we hypothesized that the priming of the police concept negatively (by presentation of a video showing police violence) would decrease positive attitudes towards the police compared to a control video unrelated to the police. On the contrary, the priming of the police concept positively (by presentation of a video showing police officers being applauded) should increase positive attitudes towards them compared to the same control video. Furthermore, we hypothesized that this experimental manipulation would have an effect on both explicit and implicit measures of attitudes. However, our contrast analysis (brutality = -1, control = 0 ; heroism = 1) showed no significant effect of experimental condition on explicit attitudes (p = .84) and an equivalence test revealed that our brutality and heroism conditions were equivalent using a SESOI (smallest effect size of interest) of d = 0.29 based on the mean effect size in the experiment of Intravia et al. (Intravia, Thompson, & Pickett, 2020) which study the effect of media exposure on police attitudes (t(168.89) = -1.703, p = 0.045, ΔL = -0.29, ΔU = 0.29). Regarding the implicit measure of attitudes towards police, our contrast analysis reveals only a marginal effect of our experimental conditions (β = 0.07, p = .057, η² = .14). Although means of our experimental conditions are in line with our hypotheses (brutality condition: M = -0.42, SD = 0.48 ; control condition: M = -0.33, SD = 0.46 ; heroism condition: M = -0.29, SD = 0.43), we cannot conclude that there is a significant difference between our experimental conditions. Furthermore, a test of equivalence between the heroism and brutality experimental conditions does not allow us to conclude that these two conditions are equivalent using a SESOI of d = 0.45 based on the maximum effect size we could detect with 80% statistical power given the samples in each of experimental conditions (t(174.84) = -1.097, p = 0.137, ΔL = -0.45, ΔU = 0.45). Although more data are needed to conclude whether or not our manipulation had an effect on implicit attitudes (effect size calculated a posteriori: d = .285; 1 - β = .596), taken together, these results may suggest a dissociation of the effect of our experimental conditions on implicit and explicit attitudes towards the police. Thus, on the basis of dual processing theories that often show differential effects on implicit and explicit attitudes, it is possible that simply showing a video that positively or negatively primes the concept of police may influence implicit attitudes towards the police, but not explicit attitudes. Thus, although previous findings have shown that explicit attitudes towards the police may decrease (increase) following the presentation of information that portrays the police negatively (positively), previous studies have mainly used correlational studies that show that the more people have access to valenced information about the police, the more their attitudes towards this category change. Thus, it is possible that it is merely the repetition of information that deeply change explicit attitudes, whereas the presentation of a single video is not able to change these explicit attitudes. This hypothesis seems related to some results in the literature which show that changing the viewpoint of a police arrest video (or the accompanying speeches) is not likely to change individuals' self-reported attitudes towards the police. Also, it is possible that implicitly measured attitudes (through the association between "police" and positively or negatively valued words) are more influenced by the presentation of a single video than are explicit measures. This is consistent with findings that implicit measures can be easily modified by contextual cues, contrary to a commonly accepted idea that implicit attitudes are only modified by repeated occurrences. title_r: A low-cost Morris Water Maze for undergraduate research: Construction and demonstration in a rat model of obesity-induced diabetes
abstract_r: The Morris Water Maze (MWM) is a standard task for assessing hippocampal-dependent learning and memory, but the cost of commercial versions of the task may be prohibitive for some undergraduate research projects. We describe the construction of a low-cost MWM for use with rats, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the MWM in a study of the effect of diet-induced obesity on cognitive function in rats. Previous studies have described an impairment in MWM performance in rats fed a high-fat diet combined with streptozotocin injection (to model Type 2 diabetes). We attempted to replicate this finding, and to test the ability of a novel anti-inflammatory treatment to reduce cognitive deficits in the diabetic model. Across five days of hidden-platform training, rats in all groups (normal pellet diet vs. high-fat diet, vehicle vs. treatment) improved on the water maze at similar rates. On a 30-second probe trial, each group showed a preference for the target quadrant used during training. On the probe trial, rats in the high-fat diet group receiving vehicle injections performed significantly better than rats on a normal pellet diet receiving vehicle injections, or on a high-fat diet receiving treatment. These results did not replicate previous findings that a high-fat diet combined with streptozotocin injections produces deficits in the water maze. However, the results did validate the effectiveness of a low-cost water maze constructed from commonly available materials for hidden platform water maze training, which we expect may be of use to other undergraduate researchers interested in learning and memory.

title_r: Charisma Replication
abstract_r: Charisma is a personality trait characterized by influence, affability, and charm (Welsh and Lenzenweger, 2021). Despite its common usage in language and media, little research has been conducted investigating charisma’s relation to other personality traits. In addition, despite the fact that charisma is a fundamentally interpersonal phenomenon, almost no research has yet explored what factors predict charisma as rated by observers (as compared to self-reported charisma). One personality trait that is frequently associated with charisma is psychopathy. However, whether psychopathy is associated with observers’ perceptions of charisma is not known. Previous research has indicated that observers can accurately assess others’ personality after a brief interaction of only a couple of minutes (Carney et al., 2007). In a preliminary study, we conducted 5-minute interviews with participants asking them conversational questions. These interviews were recorded and rated by observers for charisma as well as psychopathy, narcissism, dominance, potency, energy, warmth, attractiveness, and expressiveness. We found that individuals overestimated their charisma, in that their reported charisma scores were, on average, higher than observed charisma ratings. Additionally, though reported and observed charisma were predicted by some similar variables (observed energy, potency, warmth, and reported extraversion), they also had different relationships with other variables (reported agreeableness, conscientiousness, narcissism, charismatic leadership, and observed dominance and psychopathy). This discrepancy informed us that current report charisma measures may not accurately capture observers’ perceptions of charisma. We sought to construct a self-report measure of charisma that emphasizes behavioral data. This study aims to test a new measure, The Charisma Quotient (CQ), that includes reported behaviors, to determine if a behavior-based measure would be more consistent with observer ratings of charisma. In this measure, we included items with factor loadings >0.65 and utilized reverse coding and neutral language to strengthen our measure. Another goal of this study is to replicate the results of a previous study. This study found that charisma is a moderating variable between antisocial behavior and psychopathy. For individuals high in psychopathy, those who are charismatic are less likely to participate in antisocial behavior. We hope to replicate this result to further establish this relationship.

title_r: Perception of emotions based on facial expressions among Arab cultures: A replication effort.
abstract_r: A highly cited study by Masuda and colleagues (2008) showed that the way we interpret facial expressions on faces can be influenced by our cultural background. The researchers in that study compared how American and East Asian participants interpreted emotional expressions. This type of comparison (Western vs East Asian) is by far the most common in cross-cultural research on emotion. Arab populations, however, are rarely included in this type of work. In the original study, the authors hypothesized that when judging the emotions of an individual, people from a collectivistic culture would be more sensitive to the social context than their counterparts from individualistic cultures. This stems from the difference in cognition observed between the cultures, where collectivistic cultures tend to prioritize context and background elements in visual scenes, adopting a holistic approach whereas individualistic cultures adopt a more analytical approach where they disentangle objects from the context in which they are embedded. In order to test their hypothesis, the researchers created a facial judgment task where the participants are presented with a set of cartoon illustrations of a group, where a central figure is surrounded by four other individuals. In line with the reasoning above, the authors predicted that the participants from individualistic cultures will focus on the central person’s emotions and disregard the surrounding characters, hence exhibiting analytical cognition while their counterparts would take the emotions of the surrounding figures into consideration when making their judgment, hence exhibiting holistic cognition. For this project, we propose to replicate and extend this original study with an Arab sample. Arabs have been observed to have characteristics from both collectivistic and individualistic cultures. They diverge from collectivistic cultures such as Japan insofar they recruit the emotion of anger in service of self-assertion, just like members of individualistic cultures. This gives us reason to believe that a replication of the original study in this context will produce collectivistic effects for the perception of emotions underlying universal facial expressions of sadness and happiness, and deviate in the case of anger, where Arabs will demonstrate analytical cognition usually associated with individualistic cultures. Similar to the original study, this research study will be conducted through two within-subject experiments. Participants will be presented with a facial judgment task in the form of cartoon illustrations adapted to the cultural context where a central figure is surrounded by four other individuals in a group, all depicting Arab facial features. They will be told that the cartoon illustrations are used in the study to test the realism of stimuli for future use in an educational television show for children. In both experiments, the participant will be presented with 28 illustrations in random order, and be instructed to judge the middle person’s emotion from their facial expressions on a ten-point scale, through rating their degree of either sadness, anger or happiness. Experiment 1: Administered through Qualtrics software 1a: Participants will be university students aged between 18-25 from the American University of Sharjah. They will be awarded 0.4 credits upon the completion of the study. Participants will be presented with three trial questions before they begin the experimental block of the study. After going through the illustrations, the participants will be presented with a survey based on the “Culture Orientation Scale” (Triandis & Gelfand, 1998). 1b: To avoid fatigue effects, participants will be asked to complete a survey based on an honor scale as a follow-up study. Experiment 2: Administered to through tobii eye-tracking system Participants will be university students aged between 18-25 from the American University of Sharjah. They will be awarded 30 AED upon completion of the study through gift vouchers. This experiment is conducted to investigate the role of analytical and holistic cognition in the evaluations of emotions Arab participants make from facial expressions. The survey will be administered through laptop-mounted eye trackers. These will measure the direction of the eye movements and the duration for which the participants focus on the central figure, and the surrounding figures. Participants will then complete scales similar to Experiment 1 (Culture Orientation Scale and Honor Scale).

title_r: Why does the darkness promote cheating II: The effect of the ambiguity in task outcomes
abstract_r: A previous study showed that darkness environment could increase cheating by creating a sense of “illusory anonymity” that let individuals expect that they would be difficult to be perceived by others (Zhong et al., 2010). We have successfully replicated the phenomena reported by Zhong et al. (2010) in an early study (https://osf.io/nkjq5). However, the perceived anonymity of participants in our results did not support the explanation by Zhong et al. (2010). According to our results, we proposed another hypothesis that the outcomes of the task in a dark environment could present a kind of “ambiguity”. It means that it was difficult for participants (and also for experimenters) to visually confirm the outcome because of the dark illumination conditions. We considered participants tended to believe that the outcome was in their favor and reported it without a closer check of the true outcome in this situation. Thus, we designed a non-visual task to ensure that participants could know the outcomes, then used the task to check participants’ cheating indicators in different illumination conditions (See more details in https://osf.io/p6j4t). In contrast to the earlier study, we found that in terms of illumination, there was no significant difference in the cheating indicators, and the effect size was considerably smaller (d = 0.1) than in the study using a visual task (https://osf.io/nkjq5, d = 0.37). To further confirm the effect of ambiguity of the task outcomes on cheating, we decided to conduct an experiment by directly manipulating this factor (https://osf.io/ju9ah). In this experiment (https://osf.io/ju9ah), we found the limitations of the experimental method made us fail to analyze whether the participants in the “ambiguity group” cheated. Therefore, in the present study, we improved the experimental method to test the hypotheses again (See more details in the “Hypotheses” part).

title_r: Public Support for the Use of Force in Authoritarian Regimes
abstract_r: Using an original, pre-registered survey experiment conducted in June 2022 with 4,008 respondents in China, we find that the Russian invasion of Ukraine significantly increases public support for the Chinese government's use of military force primarily through non-instrumental considerations. However, the effects we found above might have been influenced by the timing of the original survey. The survey was conducted during a period when the Ukraine War received extensive coverage in Chinese news media. Consequently, the observed effects could be temporary and contingent upon the prevailing context at that specific time. This is particularly important for this study as the situation and the narrative surrounding the Ukraine War have undergone significant changes in China since the survey was conducted almost a year ago. Thus, we propose to replicate most parts of the previous study and test whether the findings in the original survey still hold one year later.

title_r: Replication of a research claim from Dumas et al, 2018, in Academy of Management Journal
abstract_r: We selected the claim that there is a significant relationship between family structure and work absorption, such that single, childless employees report lower work absorption than employees with other family structures (Hypothesis 1 in the original paper). This reflects the following statement from the paper’s abstract: “A survey of business school alumni (Study 1) revealed that single, childless workers reported lower absorption than workers with other family structures.” The work absorption construct captures the extent to which individuals become engrossed in their work. Hypothesis 1 predicted that single, childless respondents would report lower levels of absorption. The authors tested this hypothesis via ordinary least squares regression. As the authors expected, the effect of being single and childless on work absorption was negative and significant (b = -.31, SE = 0.13, p < .05).

title_r: Analyzing socially acceptable human-robot interaction holistically - a social-psychological multi-level approach
abstract_r: The successful implementation of new robotic technology in contexts with human users requires a socially acceptable human-robot interaction and needs to consider the socio-technical system holistically. Human-robot interaction is embedded in a social system and shapes but also is shaped by this social context. Research in human-robot interaction thus needs to take into consideration the social matrix in which the interaction is embedded on multiple levels of analysis. One scientific field that can enhance human-robot interaction research in achieving socially acceptable designs of systems is social psychology. Based on these assumptions, this dissertation has three major contributions: First, it is conceptually shown how socially acceptable human-robot interaction can be studied holistically by applying social-psychological theories, methods, and research practices on multiple levels of analysis. In doing so, a framework with two layers is proposed, a layer of phenomena, on which the human-robot interaction as a social phenomenon is analyzed, and a meta-scientific layer, on which philosophical foundations, theories, methods, and research practices of human-robot interaction as a discipline are critically reflected. Furthermore, on the layer of phenomena, human-robot interaction is analyzed on three different levels, an individual level focusing on social thinking, a situational level focusing on social relations and contextual effects, and a higher system level describing social impact emerging from social system dynamics.Second, in order to contribute to a better understanding of human-robot interaction on each level of analysis, four empirical studies are presented addressing research gaps on different topics of human-robot interaction. Social thinking is analyzed in a laboratory experiment on the social desirability bias with N = 107 participants. This experiment is a conceptual replication of a classic study by Nass, Moon, and Carney (1999) stating that technological devices are perceived as social actors. However, the results failed to show such an effect indicating that the social desirability effect is overestimated. Social relations are analyzed by studying personal space in human robot interaction. A systematic literature review and meta-analysis including k = 27 studies with N = 1299 participants, as well as theoretical considerations, show that knowledge on personal space in human-robot interaction is limited due to mixed effects and many problems in theory, methods, and research practices. An additional laboratory experiment with N = 72 participants on the effect of contextual factors on personal space is presented to address a research gap. However, neither room size nor working memory load had significant effect on users’ comfort distance toward an approaching manufacturing robot. In order to understand the social impact of robots, attitudes toward the implementation of a new cooperative industrial robot were analyzed based on data of N = 556 workers from manufacturing companies using factor and network analysis. In doing so, a new, context-specific 12-item questionnaire (ACIR-Q) had been developed. This study shows how workers’ attitudes toward robots are influenced by organizational variables and differ between organizations.A third contribution of this dissertation is based on meta-scientific conclusions. Throughout the dissertation, it is demonstrated how human-robot interaction research can be improved in terms of theory, methods, and scientific practices. Human-robot interaction is facing the same problems that have been discussed in context of social psychology’s replicability crisis. Therefore, the reforms in social psychology are also recommended for human-robot interaction research.Human-robot interaction is still in its infancy and the results in this dissertation show that it is facing many challenges. Social-psychology can not only help to design social-acceptable human-robot interaction on different levels of analysis, but also enhance the human-robot interaction discipline’s research methods and theory.

title_r: The Stereotype Content Model and Appraisal Theories of Emotion
abstract_r: The current study will examine the role of appraisals in generating differing perceptions and emotions in response to social groups. This study builds on several previous studies in which we have found support for the idea that appraisals likely play a role in generating specific emotions towards social groups. In order to build on our previous work, this particular study was designed with three goals in mind. First, we will conduct this study as a direct replication of a previous study. Direct replications are underutilized in psychology and in many other disciplines as well. Yet, replications have clear value in reinforcing the importance of the research - a successful direct replication indicates that the relevant research is more likely to be successfully replicated in the future. A second research goal, also related to potentially improved replicability, was to firmly ground our research in the principles of Open Science. To accomplish this second goal, we are pre-registering this project at the Open Science Framework. Moreover, we plan to publish our data files at the Open Science Framework. A third goal was to ensure that the current study had sufficient statistical power.

title_r: Predictive Learning and Accuracy in Faces Perception Study 2
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that lower reinforcement rates between an event (e.g., circle) and outcome (e.g., appearance of a lightning bolt) lead to greater generalization of that learned association (higher predictions of the outcome for generalization stimuli that are similar to the learning stimulus) than with higher reinforcement rate. We believe this learning strategy has important implications for understanding social judgments (including stereotyping) and social memory (including eyewitness accuracy). We recently replicated the previous findings with social stimuli (faces). In the current project we aim to explore how reinforcement rate affects generalization by using a memory test. Specifically, we will pair faces with an outcome (lightning bolt) at varying rates of partial reinforcement and test the extent to which participants recognize more dissimilar faces as the original, paired face.

title_r: A Homeostatic Relationship Between Emotions and Spontaneous Thoughts
abstract_r: Emotions and thoughts are deeply intertwined, with each influencing the other. While emotions shape the content and structure of spontaneous thoughts, the way thoughts unfold over time—thought dynamics—may in turn regulate emotions. This study investigates the role of thought dynamics in emotion regulation across a three-week period while also examining how emotional states influence the content and structure of spontaneous thoughts. Each day, participants will rate their emotions before and after completing a 5-minute think-aloud exercise, narrating their thoughts out loud. On four occasions, the think-aloud exercise will be preceded by a negative mood induction (i.e., recalling a negative memory). On day 0, before beginning the 3 weeks of daily exercises, participants will complete a survey that includes a 9-minute think-aloud task and questionnaires assessing mood, emotion regulation abilities, creativity, memory, and other constructs. In our prior work, we found an interesting dissociation between thought content and thought dynamics. Content refers to what people think about, such as the topic, valence, temporal orientation, and more. Dynamics refers to how people move from thought to thought. To quantify thought dynamics, we used spatially embedded networks where each node represents a thought and edges reflect semantic similarity between them. Streams of thought can have more expansive dynamics—characterized by larger diameters, lower clustering coefficients, longer path lengths, and greater momentum (thoughts that quickly become more dissimilar from each other and distance themselves from negative content)—or less expansive dynamics. In this previous study, participants were induced into a negative mood through the recall of a negative memory. They then completed a 10-minute think-aloud task. Their valence was measured before and after the think-aloud. Initial valence predicted the content of spontaneous thought such that more negative valence preceding a think-aloud exercise predicted having more negative, past-focused, and distanced thoughts. Initial valence did not predict thought dynamics. Instead, the dynamics of spontaneous thought were related to changes in valence–specifically, how well people recovered from their negative mood–over the course of the think-aloud task. Streams of thought with more expansive dynamics were associated with the greatest mood improvements after the think-aloud task. While changes in valence were linked to thought contents becoming more positive more quickly over time, we found that measures of thought dynamics were related to valence changes even after controlling for changes in thought content. These results suggest that how people move through thought space may matter more for emotion regulation than what people think about. Primary Research Questions: How Do Thought Dynamics Shape Emotion Regulation? Our primary aim is to replicate and extend the findings from the preliminary study that suggest expansive thought dynamics facilitate emotion regulation. To that aim, we will investigate two questions: Do expansive thought dynamics facilitate emotion regulation? Specifically, do more expansive thought dynamics predict greater mood improvement following a think-aloud task? This question is a replication of our prior finding–observed in a single-study design–to a longitudinal context where participants experience both experimentally induced and naturally occurring fluctuations in emotional states. What mechanisms underlie expansive thought dynamics? Individuals tend to revisit a subset of their thoughts, influenced by factors such as current concerns, environment, and personality. These recurring thoughts define a person’s "thought space." Expansive thought dynamics may emerge from two non-mutually exclusive factors: 1. Representation: The structure of one’s thought space, which shapes the connections between thoughts, might support expansiveness. 2. Process: The way individuals navigate their thought space when confronted with negative emotion. We will explore how these two factors, alone or in combination facilitate emotion regulation by supporting expansive thought dynamics. Specifically, we will test if more expansive thoughts are driven by the structure of a person's thought space (representation), the way they navigate thoughts in real time (process), or both. Secondary Research Question: How Does Emotion Shape Thought? While our primary focus is on how thought dynamics may support the regulation of emotions, we will also investigate how emotional states influence spontaneous thought content and dynamics. Our prior study found that initial negative valence predicted future thought content but not dynamics. Here, we aim to replicate and extend these findings by investigating the following questions: 3. How does initial emotion influence the content of spontaneous thought? 4. How does initial emotion influence the dynamics of spontaneous thought? 5. How does thought content influence changes in valence? In doing so, we aim to clarify the distinct roles of thought content and dynamics in shaping emotional experiences and fluctuations in emotional states.

title_r: Replication of Grauepner & Comin (2017), Part 2
abstract_r: In our initial replication attempt, we observed the relationships that Grauepner and Coman reported, but we also observed surprising relationships that were inconsistent with their theoretical argument. For example, whereas social exclusion was associated with conspiracy beliefs, many other emotions (as measured by the PANAS) were also associated with conspiracy beliefs. In fact, both negative AND positive emotions were associated with conspiracy beliefs. This runs counter to the theoretical arguments put forth in the original paper. To explore this issue further, this cross-sectional study will seek to test the hypothesis that intense emotions generally (regardless of valence) are associated with conspiracy beliefs. Thus, conspiracy beliefs may be associated with high arousal, rather than a particular negatively-valenced emotion of social exclusion.

title_r: Look over there! Lower social class predicts spontaneous gaze sharing
abstract_r: Inequality undergirds the formation of distinct social class cultures that shape social cognition in critical ways. Lower social class contexts promote interdependence and the deployment of attentional resources to others, whereas higher social class contexts promote independence and inhibit the deployment of attentional resources to others (Dietze & Knowles, 2016). However, the degree to which social class guides intersubjective attention—perceivers’ spontaneous attempts to share another person’s perspective—to social targets has yet to be adequately explored. In a behavioral pilot, we recruited 129 undergraduates (US nationals) at New York University to complete a visual attention task. Participants were instructed to detect a dot that either appeared on the right or left side of their screen as quickly and as accurately as they could. Critically, a face looking either to the left or right side of the screen appeared just prior to the dot. Although participants were instructed that the faces should be ignored while detecting the dots, we surmised that if people spontaneously adopted the visual gaze of the face, they would be faster at detecting dots that appeared on the side of the screen toward which the face was looking. We did not find evidence that participants spontaneously gaze-shared (b = -5.58, p = 0.171). However, this was qualified by a significant interaction with social class. Consistent with theories of class-as-culture, we found that lower social class individuals were more likely to spontaneously gaze share relative to their upper class counterparts (b = 7.31, p = .05). In the present study, we seek to replicate our initial findings and pre-register our analyses and methods here.

title_r: Are different placeholders for essences important for different domains? An extension and replication with low frequency items.
abstract_r: An important idea about essences is that they are represented by placeholders: we can treat a kind as having an essence without knowing what that essence is. Though most work on essentialism has assumed there is only one kind of placeholder for essences, one that is causal and can be elaborated with the acquisition of scientific knowledge, a different view is that placeholders might sometimes be teleological. On this view, we might represent essences in terms of a telos (i.e., a purpose or function) though we may not know what the telos is. In addition to thinking there might be different kinds of placeholders for essences, it may be that kinds can be represented in terms of multiple types of essence placeholders. And it may be that while some kinds can be represented in terms of multiple essence placeholders, other kinds might privilege some placeholders over others. Our question is whether some kinds might be represented in terms of both teleological and causal-scientific placeholders and whether one of these placeholders is privileged for some kinds (e.g., artifacts). Here we are following up on our third experiment (see: https://osf.io/yqg5p) with low frequency items from Castro et al, 2021. We aim to replicate our findings using “true purpose” in place of “what it is for” and “true nature” in place of “true essence”.

title_r: Experiment 2
abstract_r: This project explores whether event-omissions differences in the outcome of a causal scenario interact with action-inaction differences as potential causes in disjunctive causal scenarios. This is a conceptual replication of recent work (https://osf.io/preprints/osf/pcvfd_v1) that attempts to avoid potential confounds. This experiment varies whether the potential cause is an action or an inaction and whether the outcome is an event or an omission in a disjunctive causal scenario. The prediction is that there should be an interaction between the event type of the outcome (event|omission) and the action type of the potential cause (action|inaction) such that people have stronger causal judgments for actions when the outcome is an event rather than an omission and people have stronger causal judgments for inactions when the outcome is an omission rather than an event. This experiment is just like Experiment 1—only this is a disjunctive causal scenario.

title_r: Replication of processing of task-irrelevant food information in oddball fast periodic visual stimulation
abstract_r: Food information has a high reward value for human beings, and may be more so for those who are overweight or obese. Stimuli with high reward value may be particularly conspicuous, demanding our attention even when we are attending to something else. Yet, the nature and neural signals of potential biased processing of food information remains unclear. Moreover, despite decades of research, a reliable measure of food information processing remains elusive, making it a methodological bottleneck in obesity and disordered eating research. To address the nature of biased attention processing, we ask 1) how attention is biased toward two cardinal properties of food information, namely, healthfulness and tastiness, even though the food information is irrelevant to the task at hand; and 2) whether and how such processing might be dependent on the demandingness of the central task (i.e., perceptual load). In our previous study which has been preregistered, we recruited 32 participants and measured their responses to infrequent visual food information embedded in streams of other visual objects in EEG, specifically, by using a variant of steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP), oddball fast periodic visual stimulation (FPVS). The infrequent food objects (i.e., oddballs) are one of four different combinations in different trials based on healthfulness and tastiness: 1) high healthfulness and high tastiness; 1) high healthfulness and low tastiness; 3) low healthfulness and high tastiness; and 4) low healthfulness and low tastiness. The perceptual load of the central task is either low (detection of a certain color of letters) or high (detection of certain combinations of color and identity of letters). In this study, the results demonstrated robust and reliable implicit categorization of food information at the individual level for all 32 participants, with the effect not modulated by perceptual load or tastiness (but might be by healthfulness). Since oddball FPVS is a novel paradigm applied to studying food information processing, it would be critical to replicate the findings in order to develop FPVS as a reliable measure of food information processing as well as apply this tool to obesity or other clinical sample with eating disorders. In particular, the modulating effect of healthfulness observed was not salient and requires further evidence. Furthermore, the lack of modulation by tastiness and perceptual load also warrants replication. Therefore, we plan to conduct a replication study with the same paradigm and sample size to validate our previous findings.

title_r: Testing different question formats for assessing participants’ race
abstract_r: When collecting information about research participants’ racial identity, researchers often rely on question formats that use traditional taxonomies (e.g., White, Black, Asian, etc.), such as the one provided by the National Institute of Health (NIH), following the 1997 Revisions to the Office for Management and Budget (OMB) directive 15. However, considering the complexity of racial identities in an increasingly diverse society, this practice may be sub-optimal. In two previous studies we found that some participants who do not identify with a race category commonly used in the US (e.g., Black, Asian, White) felt that the racial categories they had to settle for when answering closed-ended questions did not accurately capture their racial identity, and felt negatively about being referred to by the category they chose. Furthermore, the racial composition of the same sample of undergraduate students significantly varied depending on the question format used to collect such information. The study described below is a pre-registered replication of these studies, using university undergraduate participants.

title_r: Examining the Effects of Organizational Solidarity Statements on Black Adults
abstract_r: In response to recent social events (e.g., the murder of George Floyd), many organizations released statements of solidarity to signal support of Black Americans and cultivate trust among current and prospective Black employees. Although some of these statements were well-received by Black Americans (e.g., due to beliefs that companies were genuinely motivated to support Black Americans), other statements were criticized due to beliefs that these statements were disingenuous. This work focuses on the (in)effectiveness of organizational efforts to signal inclusion to Black individuals by examining how various features of organizational solidarity statements impact Black Americans’ sense of identity-safety in these settings. Furthermore, we examine the role of two mechanisms (beliefs about performative allyship and beliefs about procedural fairness) that may underlie Black Americans' feelings of identity-safety. In our previous experiments, we examined Black adults’ evaluations of statements that were released by a hypothetical organization in response to a mega-threat (e.g., George Floyd’s murder). Findings showed that solidarity statements which acknowledged systemic racism or actions that the organization is taking to address racism increased identity-safety for Black individuals due to reduced perceptions that the organization was engaging in performative allyship and increased perceptions that the organization was procedurally fair for Black employees. However, statements which acknowledged organizational practices that perpetuate racism for Black employees reduced identity-safety for Black individuals due to decreased perceptions of procedural fairness. In the current experiment, we aim to replicate and extend our previous work by examining Black Americans’ responses to organizational statements when the statement is released in response to an event at the organizational-level (e.g., recently acquiring a company that has racial inequities in employee pay). Black adults will be randomized to see one of four statements: control, acknowledges systemic racism, acknowledges organizational racism, acknowledges systemic and organizational racism. Consistent with the previous studies, we predict that when a hypothetical organization acquires a company that has racial inequities in employee pay and releases a statement in response to this event, Black adults who see a statement that acknowledges systemic racism (versus not) will report greater identity-safety at the organization, and Black adults who see a statement that acknowledges organizational racism (versus not) will report decreased identity-safety at the company. As in the previous studies, we also expect that the relationship between the statement manipulations and identity-safety will emerge via perceptions of performative allyship and procedural fairness. Therefore, this online experiment will test whether the pattern of results that emerged that in our previous studies emerged due to a matching effect (e.g., acknowledging systemic racism is beneficial only in response to mega-threats) or if the pattern of results generalize to different types of events (e.g., events at the organizational level).

title_r: Decision making under uncertainty and source credibility
abstract_r: Previous research has shown that people are more averse to uncertainty caused by conflicting but precise information (conflictive uncertainty) than uncertainty caused by consistent but imprecise information (ambiguous uncertainty), which is termed conflict aversion (Cabantous 2007; Cabantous et al, 2011; Smithson, 1999). A pilot study showed that source credibility was likely to be the mediator between information conflict and aversion to conflictive uncertainty. In this first study (https://archive.org/details/osf-registrations-83ker-v1), we found evidence about the effect of source credibility on people's aversion to uncertainty. However, we didn't find evidence for conflict aversion. We suspect that this absence of evidence of conflict aversion can be due to sampling error. Thus, this is a direct replication of the first study.

title_r: The impact of Need for Cognition on the relation between self-control and non-clinical depression and anxiety
abstract_r: Need for cognition (NFC) describes a person's tendency to invest cognitive effort and to perceive this effort as satisfying (Cacioppo et al., 1996). NFC correlates positively not only with academic success, but also with life satisfaction, emotional balance and mental health (Bertrams & Dickhäuser, 2012; Bye & Pushkar, 2009; Strobel et al., 2021). The underlying cognitive motivation to face and overcome cognitive challenges could also help people to regulate their emotional states, improve depressive or anxious symptoms or even prevent them from developing mental disorders (for an overview of the relation between NFC and well-being, see Zerna and colleagues (2023)). The aim of the present study is the conceptual replication and extension of research findings on the influence of NFC on the relationship between self-control and psychological symptoms (non-clinical depression and anxiety). In addition, further potentially influencing variables will be included in the investigation of the present study. The focus of the study is on understanding the relationship between cognitive and self-regulatory mechanisms and non-clinical symptoms of anxiety and depression.

title_r: Enhancing sensorimotor adaptation of speech using tDCS over motor cortex and cerebellum: a replication study
abstract_r: Sensorimotor adaptation of speech plays an essential role in speech production. Specifically, speech processing relies on a dynamic interaction between the auditory and motor systems of the brain. Previous studies have indicated that the primary motor cortex (M1) and the cerebellum contribute to speech-motor adaptation. Anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) was used to increase excitability over the left M1 and the right cerebellum during a speech adaptation task in which participants compensated for a shift in the formant frequency fed back to them in real-time by altering the frequency in their speech production (Lametti, Smith, Freidin, et al., 2018). Stimulation over the left M1 drove participants to compensate for the shift in the first formant by adapting both the first and the second formant in their production, thereby producing speech closer to an existing vowel category. The shifts produced in both formants exceeded those produced by participants who received only sham stimulation. In contrast, anodal tDCS over the right cerebellum drove significantly greater adaptation in the first formant, but the second formant was unchanged. Here, we aim to replicate these findings. We will use software to provide the formant shift rather than the hardware setup used previously. We will also use a different location for the cathode electrode placement in the cerebellar stimulation since attaching it to the face may have impeded speech production in the original study. We also propose a revised experimental design by introducing the speech-shaped noise feedback masking to limit unlearning when the perturbation to feedback is removed. Finally, we will test categorical perception with identification and discrimination tasks before and after the adaptation to examine the effect of individual variability in perception on adaptation and the effect of adaptation on perception.

title_r: Ideological Differences in Harm-Based Moral Judgments of Toxic Speech
abstract_r: Surges in outgroup derogatory online content can be observed around significant social and political events (e.g., the 2021 U.S. Capitol attack, the 2015 Paris attacks). People’s political ideology plays an unequivocally central role in how people react to social and political events and how (un)favorable they regard certain outgroups. It is yet unclear if and how progressive and conservative people differ in their moral judgments of toxic online comments. Drawing on the prejudice literature, we test two competing hypotheses. On the one hand, conservatives and progressives might equally condemn toxic comments when it targets ideologically favored vs unfavored outgroups – the ideological symmetry hypothesis. On the other hand, conservatives compared to progressives might be generally less condemning of toxic comments irrespective of the target – the ideological asymmetry hypothesis. To pit these hypotheses against one another, we invited a representative sample of German citizens (N = 903) to an online study and experimentally varied the target of toxic comments. Our findings showed that conservatives and progressives are sensitive to the target of online hate, yet conservatives exhibit overall lower levels of condemnation and perceived harmfulness. Here, we preregister a replication attempt of the first study using a U.S. sample (N = 450). We test whether our observed main and interaction effects from study 1 (German sample) replicate in study 2 (US sample).

title_r: Why replication is not enough: Insights from a cross-cultural study of social discounting
abstract_r: The social and behavioral sciences are undergoing a revolution spurred by mounting evidence that many published findings do not replicate. As a consequence, there is growing interest in scientific reform. One such reform, direct replication, has emerged as a leading solution. Despite its importance, the focus on direct replication may divert attention from another problem plaguing the social sciences: lack of generalizability to the full range of human contexts. Here, we use our lab’s recent cross-cultural study of social discounting to illustrate why developing broadly-applicable theories of human nature requires a complementary investment in generalizability. Social discounting is a repeatedly-documented and purportedly fundamental human tendency to sacrifice more for socially-close individuals. In our lab, we consistently document social discounting in U.S., MTurk, and college-student samples. However, when adapting a typical social discounting protocol to low-literacy and resource-scarce settings in Bangladesh and Indonesia, we find no independent effect of social distance on generosity, despite still documenting this effect among typical U.S. participants. Additionally, we document high-levels of “inconsistent” responding in Bangladesh and Indonesia. This finding strongly contrasts with current models of choice in various discounting literatures (e.g. social, probability, temporal, risk). These results highlight the need to complement current replication efforts with investment in strong checks on generalizability. By failing to do so, we risk developing theories of human nature that reliably explain behavior among only a thin slice of humanity.

title_r: Who to defend, who to blame? Framing rejection shapes dual identification and political participation of Turkish postmigrants in Germany
abstract_r: The perception of rejection (e.g., perceived discrimination), as well as its experience, is a crucial factor for minorities’ feelings of belonging toward their ethnonational identities (Branscombe et al., 1999; Jasinskaja-Lahti et al., 2009) which can be more critical for the form and level of political participation of minorities than the legal frameworks of naturalisation (i.e., become a citizen) or opportunity structures in the broader society (De Rooij, 2012; Herzog-Punzenberge et al. 2012). In social psychology, however, researchers mainly examine perceived discrimination by quantifying its subjective level, as if it is a unidimensional phenomenon (André & Dronker, 2016; Major et al., 2002). On the other hand, recent theoretical and empirical research postulates that both the source and causal attribution to rejection matter for intergroup relations (Amemiya et al., 2021; Costerolli, 2007; Greenaway & Cruwys, 2018). In a pre-registered pilot study (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/7U5R4) based on an experimental vignette manipulation, we elaborated the rejection concept with two sub-factors, namely the appraisal of threat and causal attribution. Our initial results show that apart from the quantity, the quality of rejection is essential for the sense of belonging, and political participation of minorities. In this preregistered report, we aim to replicate our initial findings in a broader sample using correlational design via a survey with better measurements

title_r: Exploring a Cascade Model of Urgency: Momentary Dynamics of Stress, Affect, and Impulsivity and their Correlates
abstract_r: Negative urgency, as part of the four-factor model of impulsivity, refers to rash action taken in response to negative emotions (Whiteside & Lynam, 2001). Positive urgency or action taken in response to strong positive affect, has been suggested as a potential fifth factor contributing to impulsivity (Cyders et al., 2007). Sperry and colleagues (2018) have strongly argued against considering positive urgency as a distinct entity and instead suggest that all manifestations of impulsivity in the context of strong emotions be subsumed under a single factor of urgency (without valence modifier). However, we believe further research on these constructs is warranted, especially when directly assessed as dynamic processes. Urgency refers to an if… then process (“If I experience strong negative (or positive) emotion, then I will engage in risky behaviors.”) which dispositional scales can, at best, only approximate. Following this, we considered a cascade model from which stressful experiences lead to affective reactions, which in turn lead to both impulsive actions and impulsive urges in the absence of discrete risk behavior engagement (in individuals with personality disorders; Sharpe, Simms, & Wright, under review). At the daily level, our results were consistent with the hypothesized links between affect, stress, and impulsivity. Stress enhanced impulsivity both directly and through negative and positive affect. Parts of this process (namely the connections between stress and impulsivity and negative affect and impulsivity) are amplified in individuals who report stronger impulsive traits. The presence of independent effects for both regression pathways in the same model, as well as a lack of association among within-person links in PA, NA, and impulsivity suggest that the cascade of negative urgency and positive urgency operate as separate processes. In the present study, we will use multilevel structural equation modeling to examine within- and between-person predictors of momentary impulsivity with a particular focus on testing a cascade model of affect and momentary stress in a 10-day ambulatory assessment study of non-undergraduate community members. We seek to replicate our previous results from analyses at the daily level by modeling a cascade from stress to impulsivity through both positive and negative affect at the momentary level by regressing momentary impulsivity on the severity of lagged stress, positive affect, and negative affect. At level 2 (i.e., between-person) we will include trait impulsivity as measured by Impulsivity facet scores at baseline on the Personality Inventory for DSM-5 (PID-5; Krueger, Derringer, Markon, Watson, & Skodol, 2012) as a between-person predictor. Additionally, we will extend the nomological network of the urgency cascade by examining associations of individual differences in within-person paths with other pathological traits (Negative Affect, Detachment, Antagonism, Disinhibition, and Psychoticism) and externalizing behaviors (alcohol consumption and drug use).
