title_r: Spatial cueing of attention by rotational motion — Floors and ceilings, with different SOAs and rotation speedsUntitled
abstract_r: In a previous experiment, we found that viewing a rotating object oriented observers’ spatial attention, and that the nature of this spatial cueing depended on how the object was touching another surface (a horizontal line drawn above or below it). For example: if an object is touching a surface below it, then clockwise rotation would normally cause the object to move rightward — and, accordingly, in the floor-touching condition, clockwise rotation produced faster response times to targets presented on the right than on the left (and counterclockwise rotation vice versa). Conversely, if an object is touching a surface above it, then clockwise rotation would normally cause the object to move leftward — and, accordingly, in the ceiling-touching condition, clockwise rotation now produced faster response times to targets presented on the left than on the right (and counterclockwise rotation vice versa). In this experiment, we aim to replicate and extend the previous results. To allow other factors to be studied with greater power, the present experiment will replicate only the previous study’s floor-touching and ceiling-touching conditions, and not include trials in which the object does not touch the line. Most importantly, the present study will introduce two new between-subjects factors to study how the ceiling-touching cueing effect and floor-touching cueing effect depend on (1) object rotation speed (using rotation speeds of 120°/sec, 240°/sec, and 360°/sec) and (2) duration of stimulus exposure (using object-target SOAs of 100ms, 200ms, and 300ms).

title_r: Working memory (within-subjects) and shift to habitual behaviour
abstract_r: Goal-directed behavior is mediated by the anticipation of a desirable outcome. According to certain two-process theories, extensive behavioral repetition leads to a shift from flexible, goal-directed control over instrumental actions to inflexible, outcome-insensitive habits (de Wit & Dickinson, 2009; Dickinson & Balleine, 1994; Heyes & Dickinson, 1990). Outcome-devaluation procedures assess the ability to adjust one’s behavior to a sudden decrease in outcome desirability (Adams & Dickinson, 1981; Balleine & O’Doherty, 2010; Dickinson, 1985). In a previous study we found that individuals placed under WM-load at test showed increased reliance on habits in an outcome devaluation paradigm, relative to participants not under WM-load. We aim to replicate the pattern of findings with a within-subject WM-load manipulation.

title_r: A Pre-registered Falsification Test of the Decision by Sampling Model and Rank-order Effect
abstract_r: Many social scienctists have assumed that people’s preferences can be described by stable and coherent “utility” functions. This notion of stable utility functions has been challenged by cognitive psychologists who suggest that preferences are malleable and constructed in the moment, but neither camp has explained how the perceived utilities themselves arise. One influential attempt to do so is the Decision by Sampling (DbS) model which suggests that a quantity’s subjective value is its rank-order in a momentarily activated memory sample. DbS thus implies that manipulating the recently experienced stimulus distribution should change people’s valuations, for example from the typically assumed concave shape of the utility function to a convex shape. However, recent studies have pointed out methodological errors in the evidence previously thought to support this prediction (and thus DbS). In this pre-registered study, we replicate the previous paradigm but correct the methodological errors to test if such a “rank-order” manipulation does change valuations. We derive qualitative predictions from DbS to verify that our conditions yield distinct predictions. Confirming the predicted effect would vindicate DbS and suggests that the phenomenon is not an artefact of methodological limitations of the previous studies.

title_r: Materials
abstract_r: This is a replication study as part of the CREP project. Background of Original Study Previous research has identified two predictors of well-being, economic prosperity and psycho-social prosperity (Diener et al., 2010). In this large scale study, economic prosperity and psychological prosperity were found to predict different indices of well-being. Greater economic prosperity, assessed via raw income, predicted greater positive life evaluations. Whereas, greater socio-psychological prosperity, indexed by greater fulfillment of psychological needs (such as learning, autonomy, ability to count on others) was more predictive of negative and positive emotions. Previous research has found strong associations between financial wealth and higher levels of well-being, but not always. Furthermore, individuals from poorer economic areas, who have little material goods, often report high levels of of happiness and wellbeing; this has been found in populations such as the Amish community (Biswas-Diener, Vitterso, & Diener, 2005) and people living in the slums of Calcutta (Biswas-Diener & Diener, 2001). Indeed, the study by Diener et al. (2010) demonstrated that different types of wealth (financial or psychological resources) predict different constructs of wealth being. This current study aims to replicate a study by Diener et al. (2010) which showed that income predicted perceptions of life satisfaction, and psycho-social resources predicted frequency of negative and positive emotions. Replication Aim We wish to replicate this study using both a student sample and a non-student sample as these groups may differ in terms of material wealth and income. It may be the case that the predictive value of income may differ between groups. This study will examine predictors of well-being (life evaluations, negative emotions, and positive emotions). There is considerable interest in the relationship between wealth and happiness. We wish to examine the different factors that are associated with happiness and wealth, including: income basic needs the fulfilment of psychological needs the standard of living material goods Specifically, it will examine the predictive value of wealth on well-being, and psycho-social resources on well-being. This study aims to test this relationship in members of the Irish public (students and non-students). As part of this study participants will also complete an additional three scales, as part of another study. These are the Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (ERQ; Gross & John, 2002), the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (DERS; Gratz & Diener, 2004) and the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS; Cohen, 1983). These scales are presented at the end of the questionnaire and unrelated to the current replication study.

title_r: Contextual preference reversals in ethical decisions (Study 2)
abstract_r: Contextual preference reversals occur when choices between two multi-attribute options change as a function of unchosen decoys. Preference reversals have been observed in many decision domains including buying consumer products, choosing a gamble to play, and judging the area of rectangles (Huber et al., 1982; Wedell, 1991; Trueblood et al., 2013). We have shown that contextual preference reversals can be observed in ethical dilemmas imitating Wedell (1991)‘s gambles. In those dilemmas, the two attributes are the probability of saving lives and the number of lives to save. In our previous experiment, we have found evidence that contextual preference reversal can be shown in ethical dilemmas that contain attributes consisting of not only probability and numeric value. In this experiment, we include a follow-up study to our previous study where we aim to replicate the results showing contextual preference reversals in ethical decision making with improved materials. We have also added filler items. We have also added a new experimental manipulations to the study to invesitigate whether learning about the dominance relationship between target and decoy option changes contextual preference reversals.

title_r: Indirect attitudes towards (in)visible disability: a replication using the Incident VAAST
abstract_r: Previous research by Granjon et al. (in process) has shown that individuals with invisible disabilities (i.e., hemophilia) elicit different attitudes compared to those with visible disabilities (i.e., hemiplegia). title_r: Can very small font size enhance memory?: Replication
abstract_r: The impact of font size on memory has been studied multiple times over the past ten years, however the results of each study are inconsistent, leaving the question still unanswered. The first study to test the effect of font size on memory was done by Rhodes and Castel in 2008. In this study, the participants were tested using 18 pt and 48 pt font size and were asked to memorize words and determine a judgement of learning which measures “how confident they were that they would later be able to recall that word.” The researchers predicted immediate recall would not be affected by font size but the judgement of learning would be impacted. Rhodes and Castel found that participants predicted that the larger font sizes would be more memorable. There are several studies that support this theory including a study done by Diemand-Yauman et al which shows that memory is improved when a difficult to read font is used instead of an easy to read font. A common theory of why this may be can be derived from the fact that degraded formats engage more cognitive resources, or just simply force the reader to concentrate more to parse and understand the words being read, hence giving a feeling of ‘enhanced’ learning. However there have been studies that show the opposite effect or little to no effect. For example, One study done by Mulligan in 1996 found that the benefits of perceptual degradation only occurred when the study time, or how long a participant read words was relatively short. In this study, we will attempt to replicate the research presented by Halamish. More specifically, we will be focusing on Study 8, which tested participants' recognition with short study time and no JOLs. We will do so by running an online replication where participants will be shown words in different font sizes, and will be asked to recognize which words were shown from a list provided to them afterwards. We want to test the hypothesis that words shown in smaller font size will be more memorable to the participants.

title_r: Preferential Differences for Transactional vs. Transformational Leadership - An Exploratory Study with Adapted Vignettes
abstract_r: Transformational leadership, which is said to raise the level of motivation and morality of followers by engaging with them and creating a connection, has been the most researched leadership style of the last 30 years and despite new leadership theories emerging, the relative amount of research on this leadership style remains the largest (Gardner, Lowe, Meuser, Noghani, Gullifor, & Cogliser, 2020). Transformational leadership is often associated with and compared to transactional leadership, which recognizes followers’ needs and wants but focuses on exchanges between leader and follower in order to achieve outcomes. According to the process-view of leadership an individual’s ability to lead is dependent on followers’ responses to leadership behaviors and styles (Northouse, 2015). Following this view, it is interesting to examine which of the described leadership styles followers prefer: The arguably more satisfactory transformational leadership style or the transactional leadership style, which is more concerned with the clarifaction of roles and task-requirements? In a previous study, we set out to examine preference distributions for transactional and transformational leadership in two different samples: University students and a working population. Examining a sample of N = 127 participants we expected the student population (n = 64) to strive for ideals, teamwork and self-actualization and thus prefer the transformational leader, while expecting the working population (n = 63) to strive for clarity regarding requirements and goals and thus prefer the transactional leader. Contrary to our expectations and in contrast with what research on transformational leadership would postulate, we found conclusive evidence that preferences for transfomrational and transactional leadership are equally distribute in both the student and the working population. In the proposed study we attempt to replicate these findings with two new leader vignettes, which are to be validated in the present study. In an exploratory analysis will further investigate whether leader preferences can be predicted by Big-5 Personality as well as personal needs.

title_r: Do Infants Expect Imitators to be More Prosocial? Replication
abstract_r: Imitation & Helping: Previous studies have suggested that infants are sensitive to imitation at an early age, and are able to use their observations of imitative actions to generate inferences about the imitator and their affiliation to others. For example, 4 and 5-month-old infants expect those who imitate to be more likely, compared to non-imitators, to affiliate with the target of their imitation (Powell & Spelke, 2018a), and preferentially attend to imitators, compared to non-imitators (Powell & Spelke, 2018b). 7-month-old infants expect that individuals will act in a manner that is consistent with their group (Powell & Spelke, 2013), and 12-month-old infants preferentially reach for a character that imitated another, compared to another that failed to imitate (Powell & Spelke, 2018b). Other research has provided evidence that infants prefer individuals who act in a way that is helpful, compared to another who hinders others’ goals (Hamlin, et al., 2007; Hamlin, et al., 2011). Adopted utility: Jara-Ettinger, et al., (2016), proposed that human social cognition is grounded in a common sense framework, or naïve utility calculus, in which humans, starting in infancy, expect agents to behave rationally, minimizing the costs of their actions, while maximizing their rewards. This “naïve utility calculus” enables infants to generate inferences about hidden mental states (e.g. preferences, beliefs, and/or knowledge) based on behavior, as well as predict future behavior based on known states of an actor (Gweon, 2021). For example, 10-month-old infants are able to infer which of two objects a character values more highly, based on the effort that character is willing to exert to obtain each item (i.e., the cost they have previously incurred for each reward) (Liu et al., 2017). Moreover, older children, between 5-7 years of age, appear to weigh the value of what to teach others based on the information the learner is unlikely to acquire without their assistance, thus maximizing the learner’s expected utility of learning from instruction and exploring (i.e., prioritizing what the learner is unlikely to acquire by exploration alone) (Bridgers et al., 2020). In sum, this common sense manner in which humans make sense of others’ behavior, seems to be early emerging, and expressed in a variety of contexts. Powell, (2021), has proposed that, from infancy, human ability to reason about social affiliation is based within the naïve utility calculus model, with the earliest beliefs regarding peoples’ affiliative stances towards others emerging from the apparent weight one person places on the rewards of another, in a model of adopted utility. Imitation, in this context, can be conceptualized as one individual adopting their social partner’s goal into a shared utility function, illustrating an affiliative stance to the target. Such an affiliative stance should provide a salient cue that the imitator is more likely to act prosocially (i.e., place a certain amount of value on the rewards/goals) towards the character they affiliated with (i.e., the target of their imitation) in subsequent interactions. An initial experiment found evidence for this expectation in 8- and 9-month-old infants. Infants first saw a protagonist interact with two social partners, one who imitated the protagonist and one who did not. Subsequently, infants looked longer when the non-imitator helped the protagonist than when the imitator helped the protagonist, suggesting the former event was more surprising (Pepe & Powell, unpublished). This initial finding is consistent with two possibilities. Infants may have inferred from the initial interactions that the imitator had an affiliative stance toward the target, in particular, while the non-imitator did not. Alternatively, infants may have inferred that the imitator was more likely to affiliate with, or adopt the utility of, any social partner, not just the protagonist. A second experiment tested both of these possibilities: Asking whether 8- and 9-month-old infants expected an imitator, compared to a non-imitator, to be more likely to act in a prosocial manner exclusively towards the target of imitation, or if such expectations extend to helping directed at novel characters. Infants looked longer when the non-imitator helped the target of imitation, as compared to when the imitator helped, but did not show a significant difference in looking behavior during the events in which helping was directed towards the novel social agent (Pepe & Powell, unpublished). A third experiment assessed whether initial evidence more consistent with a disposition-based motivation to imitate would elicit expectations that imitators are likely to possess a prosocial disposition. In this study, 8- and 9-month-old infants observed a social agent imitate the actions of four different social partners, compared to another who chose not to imitate the same social partners. At test, infants watched as either the imitator or non-imitator helped a novel social agent. We did not find evidence that infants expected the imitator or non-imitator to be more likely to help a novel social agent during the test trials, even when given evidence that is more consistent with a dispositional inference.. This study: This study will attempt to replicate the second experiment described previously, while addressing some important limitations. First, the previous sample may have been underpowered to detect an interaction between trial type and help recipient. Second, infants may have had difficulty differentiating the original and novel target agents during the test trials, as the two characters only differed in color. Third, infants' difference in looking time may have resulted from expectations that the imitator was more likely to be in closer physical proximity to the target of their imitation, compared to a non-imitator. To address these limitations, infants will see events identical to the second experiment, except for the following changes. First, we will include 64 participants in this experiment to increase our power to detect a significant interaction of trial type and help recipient. Second, the novel target will differ in both shape and color from the target of imitation to bolster infants’ ability to represent the two characters as distinct social agents. Third, the helper and target will remain further apart throughout the test trials (see methods) to diminish the likelihood infants could use the proximity of the characters to reason about the test trials.

The original paper focused on images presented on conservative and liberal news web sites of Donald Trump; this study will focus on images of Joe Biden. The same web sites utilized by Lin & Oyserman will be utilized in this study.

The procedure described by Lin and Oyserman will be closely followed. Only pictures of Joe Biden presented alone will be downloaded. In addition, cartoons and collages will be excluded. One adjustment to the procedure will be that for a given news source during a given time frame, we will select eligible photos only from the first 400 images yielded by the search.

As in the Lin & Oyserman paper, our search will cover one year--in this case, 2021. We will also record whether the image appeared from January through August or from September through December of that year. It was at the end of August that surveys revealed that Biden's unfavorable ratings by members of the public started to exceed his favorable ratings. See--

https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/biden-approval-rating/

All searches will conform to the following template (this is just one example):

site:townhall.com "president biden" after:2020-12-31 before:2022-09-01

If a given image appears more than once, it will be counted multiple times as long as each appearance is from a different news story.

Pictures will be coded for locations in which a significant portion of the President's face/head appears, as described by Lin & Oyserman.

We hypothesize that liberal outlets will present Biden's face in up-right parts of the image significantly more frequently than conservative outlets, and that liberal outlets will present Biden's face in down-left parts of the image significantly less frequently than conservative outlets.

In addition, we hypothesize that this difference will be more pronounced in the January-August time period than in the September-December time period,

title_r: Confirmation bias: Snyder & Swann (1978) 40 years later
abstract_r: Building on the seminal work of Snyder and Swann (1978), the aim of the present study is to provide new evidence for the hypothesis-confirming bias. In Snyder and Swann’s article (Study 2, 1978), participants had to investigate if another participant was extraverted or introverted. For that purpose, participants were paired and each was assigned either the role of “interviewer” or the role of “target”. Half of the interviewer-participants were instructed to assess to what extent the target was extraverted and the other half were instructed to assess to what extend the target was introverted. After receiving the instructions, they had to select a limited number of questions to ask to the target out of a large set of questions biased either in favor of extraversion or in favor of introversion (plus unrelated questions). After this question-selection phase, target-participants were tape recorded while answering the questions selected by the interviewer. Then, interviewer-participants and external judges had to rate the target-participants on personality traits related to extraversion-introversion. The authors showed that interviewer-participants appear to have formulated confirmatory hypothesis-testing strategies (i.e. they selected extraverted questions when they were instructed to investigate whether the target was extraverted and similarly for introversion). Moreover, in the second stage of the experiment, they demonstrated that target participants tended to present themselves in a way to confirm the strategies initially formulated by the interviewers. An initial study was conducted to replicate Snyder and Swann (1978) effects on confirmatory hypothesis-testing with a few differences: a) all participants were assigned the interviewer role and the target was fictitious and b) participants received feedback (ambiguous on the dimensions of extraversion/introversion) regardless of their experimental condition. In this initial study, we replicated the effect of hypothesis confirmation in the "choice of questions" task. However, on the evaluation of the target, the results were unexpected. Participants in the extravert condition judged the target as more introverted than participants in the introvert condition. In this study we aim to replicate this latter result and explore possible mechanisms at play. A possible explanation is that the effect on Task 1 is an effect of experimental demand and that participants had no expectations/hypothesis regarding the level of introversion/extraversion of the target. Without a clear hypothesis in mind, participants may have intended to remain as neutral as possible leading to a counter-regulation effect (Rothermund, 2011). In other words, participants exposed to positive information (i.e., extraverted condition) or negative ones (i.e., introverted condition) may have focused more on information of opposite valence to regulate their affective-motivational sate which impacted target evaluation. To test this possibility, we will conduct another study similar to the initial study with a several differences. As in Study 1, participants will be randomly assigned to test whether the target is introverted (vs. extraverted). The only difference is that for half of participants we will add that "the majority of psychology students are introverted (vs. extraverted)" in order to make sure that participants have clear expectations regarding the level of introversion/extraversion of the target. We will then have a high vs. low expectations conditions. The second part of the experiment will remain unchanged. For the first task, we expect participants to show confirmatory hypothesis-testing strategies regardless of the level of expectation (high vs. low). However, in the second task, we expect different outcomes. The hypothesis is that participants in the high-expectations condition will form impressions consistent with the experimental condition (i.e. the target should be seen as introvert in the introvert condition and extravert in the extravert condition). In the low-expectations condition, we hypothesize that participants will form impressions opposed to their experimental condition, replicating results of Study 1.

title_r: Do lonely people anthropomorphize non-human agents more while being less attached to them?
abstract_r: Anthropomorphism is a phenomenon where non-human agents are attributed with human-like characteristics, motivations, intentions, or emotions (Epley et al., 2007). Epley et al. (2007) identified the desire for social contact and affiliation as one of the three psychological determinants of anthropomorphism. This suggests that lonely individuals may anthropomorphize more frequently in order to satisfy their need for social connection. Furthermore, it is possible that lonely individuals may develop stronger attachments to non-human agents they anthropomorphize with. However, in a previous pilot study, we found a contradictory relationship. Specifically, we found that while loneliness was positively associated with anthropomorphism, it was negatively associated with attachment to the non-human agent. In this study, we aim to replicate these findings using a larger and more diverse sample. We will explore the association between loneliness and both anthropomorphism and attachment to non-human agents. We will recruit participants using Prolific, an online platform, and collect data on trait-level measures of loneliness, anthropomorphism toward a plant product (with a provided picture), and attachment to the same plant product. Correlational analyses will be performed to explore these relationships.

title_r: List-Strength Effect in Recognition Memory: Massed Repetition
abstract_r: Ratcliff et al. (1990), Experiment 1 and our replication and extensions of that experiment found an inverted list-strength effect: a bigger effect of stimulus-duration in pure lists than in mixed lists. Our current theoretical explanation (our hypothesis) of the inversion invokes the assumption that participants encode shallow stimulus features, but then disregard those features following pure-strong (long-duration) lists only. To our knowledge, inverted list-strength effects are never (or at least rarely) found with spaced repetition. We test the idea that strengthening items by repetition is different than using stimulus-duration because each onset obliges participants to re-process shallow features. With multiple onsets, these shallow features may become more important for making old/new judgements, so disregarding them is not useful for pure-strong lists. If so, the inversion of the list-strength effect might be weakened with massed repetition, even if total study time per item is equated between the long duration and mass-repetition conditions. One group is a replication of conditions we already found an inverted list-strength effect, where stimuli are displayed for 500 ms, the entire duration, with no subsequent ISI (short condition) or followed by a1500-ms mask. The second group controls for the stimulus-onset pattern of group 3; the long condition is followed by mask-1 for 250 ms, mask-2 for 500 ms, mask-1 again for 250 ms and mask-2 for 500 ms. The third group is like the second but the word itself is repeated in place of mask-2 (for a total of three "massed" repetitions).

title_r: Income and gratitude towards essential workers
abstract_r: This project is a follow-up from a previous study designed to test a social-cognitive model of gratitude towards different kinds of workers. According to Wood et al.'s (2008) social-cognitive model of trait and state gratitude, people experience gratitude depending upon their perceptions of three aspects of a situation: (1) the value of the aid they have received, (2) the cost to the benefactor and (3) the intention of the benefactor, specifically whether they appear to be acting altruistically. Gratitude should be elicited if the action is perceived to be of high cost to the benefactor, to bestow high value benefits and if implemented out of a genuine desire to help. Individuals who are high in trait gratitude are more likely to make such valuations and to experience state gratitude accordingly. Study 1 has now been completed and the data analysis supports all key hypotheses: the social-cognitive model of gratitude predicted gratitude towards essential workers and in turn desired absolute pay for absolute workers. The data also indicate that one of the factors associated with high gratitude towards essential workers, particularly nurses, is the perception of relatively low pay. This study is designed to provide a conceptual replication of the main findings as well as directly test the hypothesis that the strength of gratitude felt towards an essential worker is in part contingent on how well they are thought to be paid. This will be explicitly tested by directly manipulation what participants are told about the current earnings of essential workers (either high or low). If gratitude is in part determined by perceptions of income then it is predicted that participants will be more likely to indicate that they feel more gratitude towards workers receiving relatively low pay. This will be examined for four different job domains: health care, education, food distribution and local government in order to examine whether any relationship between income and gratitude is stable across different job domains. Finally, in light of evidence which indicates that people systematically underestimate the positive impact of receiving thank you letters (Kumar & Epley, 2018), participants will be asked to indicate how happy they think the key worker would be to receive the thank you letter, a pay rise, see lots of people engage in the clap for carers and see lots of people sign a petition for a pay rise. This will allow for explorative examination of perceptions of the relative impact of different prosocial rewards and how these relate to trait gratitude.

title_r: The effect of unlimited preparation on gender differences in willingness to compete
abstract_r: Motivation Although women have surpassed men in education outcomes such as college attendance and graduation rates1, they are still underrepresented in top management positions in nearly all sectors2 and a gender wage gap still persists3. Traditional economic variables account for some, but not all, of these disparities3. As such, additional explanations have been proposed, including gender differences in willingness to compete4,5. Previous research suggests that women are less willing to compete than men, even when they are equally, if not more, qualified6. A few factors, including women’s relatively lower levels of confidence in their performance, were shown to partly explain this gender difference7. Since prior research has shown that confidence can improve with preparation and training8-10, providing potential competitors with opportunity to prepare before entering a competition may alleviate the gender gap in willingness to compete. The proposed study extends previous work where we replicated the gender difference in willingness to compete but did not find evidence that manipulating opportunities to prepare (i.e., with a restricted number of problems) affected the willingness to compete. In the current study, we plan to assess whether unlimited preparation reduces the gender difference in competitiveness. In prior work, we also found that while women were still less willing to compete they were more likely to prepare for the task compared to men. This finding also aligned with participants’ perceptions of gender differences in preparation – that is, both men and women believed that women would prepare more for the task. Thus, we will assess whether the previously observed gender difference in preparation and lay beliefs about gender differences in preparation are replicable.

title_r: Abrams and Weidler (2014) Exp. 1 Replication
abstract_r: Recent literature has indicated that visual information processing can be biased towards either the magnocellular pathway or the parvocellular pathway using hand positioning (Abrams & Weidler, 2014; Kelly & Brockmole, 2014). These pathways are better suited to process certain types of visual information. For example, the magnocellular pathway is better at processing action information with little detail while the parvocellular pathway is better at processing detail-oriented information. Additionally, other published literature has found that the body’s posture may also impact performance on visual cognitive tasks (Chen et al., 2018; Fraizer & Mitra, 2008; Smith et al., 2019). We will run a replication of Abrams & Weidler (2014) to test the size of this effect in our testing population with the intent to use this visual processing bias theory in a subsequent postural control study.

title_r: Forking a Way Through the Replication Crisis in Psychology: A Conceptual Replication of a Multiverse Analysis on Frontal Alpha Asymmetry in Depression on a Sample of Children and Adolescents
abstract_r: The replication crisis in psychology has sparked many different initiatives to promote robustness and transparency, and to reduce researcher degrees of freedom in research practice. The present work utilizes a complementary approach, named multiverse analysis. It follows the idea of showing not just one, but all alternative analysis options, thus making the robustness of a single pathway and its dependence on specific choices transparent. The present master thesis is a conceptual replication study of the multiverse analysis by Kolodziej et al. (2021) testing the validity of the EEG-based frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA) in depression. Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide, leading to tremendous personal and social burdens and substantial economic costs. Over 322 million people are living with depression, and the proportion of individuals affected in the younger age group is increasing alarmingly, associated with a more severe course and greater burden of disease. The urgency for standardized and objective methods for early detection and the need for novel treatment options for depression has spawned the discussion of FAA as a potential biomarker, irrespective of age. However, inconsistencies in the findings of both assessing FAA in depressed individuals and neurofeedback therapies based on alpha asymmetry have led to questioning this assumption. The present study applied a multiverse analysis on a dataset of 258 children and adolescents from the Healthy Brain Network (HBN) biobank, consisting of both healthy and diagnosed subjects. In total, 2’700 analyses were performed, and only 7 were consistent with the theory behind FAA as a potential biomarker for depression. These results point in the same direction as the findings from Kolodziej et al., highlight the methodological dependency of the outcome, and offer a transparent basis to move the theoretical discussions forward.

title_r: Beneficial and adverse consequences of aggression: Replication
abstract_r: Aggression is argued to have addictive properties (see Golden et al., 2017). Retaliatory aggression is often reinforcing as indicated by heightened activity in brain regions associated with reward processing (Brune et al., 2013; Chester & DeWall, 2016). Provoked individuals reap hedonistic rewards when retaliating (e.g., Chester & DeWall, 2017; de Quervain et al., 2004). Moreover, revenge-related feelings of pleasure, satisfaction, and gratification motivate some individuals to compulsively seek revenge (Dyduch-Hazar et al., 2022). Engagement in behavior despite adverse consequences is one of the features of addictive behavior (e.g., Potenza, 2008). Thus, the question arises: would individuals still retaliate out of desire to improve their affective state, if retaliating brings them adverse consequences? This research aims to address this issue.

title_r: Identities to Traits - Study 2
abstract_r: This is a confirmatory, pre-registered replication of the exploratory Study 1 of this series of studies. We examine people’s beliefs about how identities idiosyncratically relate to one another, how identities relate to normative trait structure, and how this identity and trait structure shapes beliefs about their identities and their self-views on the traits. There has been much prior theorizing on multiple identities, identity networks, etc. but few quantitative implementations of these ideas. Moreover, plenty of research has described the influence of identities on self-views and behaviors (e.g., Stereotype Threat, Identity-Based Motivation Theory, Self-Categorization Theory), but here we attempt to provide insight into this psychological structure and how it varies between individuals, and how the structuring of identities on identities and identities on traits shapes self-beliefs.

title_r: The effects of visual repetition on the trade-off between visual sampling and memory
abstract_r: This preregistration describes a replication study building on two previous experiments (Experiments 1 and 2) exploring visual repetition effects on the trade-off between visual sampling and memory. In both experiments, observers performed a copying task where they tasked with reconstructing a Model; a 4x4 grid with a configuration of 8 items (colored polygons). To view the Model grid that is otherwise concealed, participants have to move the mouse cursor toward the location of the Model. To reconstruct the Model, participants need to select items from a Resource grid (containing items that are used in the Model, as well as distractor items) and place them in an originally empty Workspace grid. Experiments 1 and 2 found that when all items (Experiment 1) or half of the items (Experiment 2) occurred at the exact same locations across consecutive trials, observers sampled (i.e., viewed) the Model less frequently compared to when items were not repeated. This suggests that participants increasingly rely on visual memory (rather than external sampling) as items in the Model repeat across trials. Specifically, we concluded that upon repetition of the same items in the same locations, participants build up a (long-term) memory of the repeated items in the display, allowing these items to be placed with less external sampling. However, a potential confound exists in the original design: We not only repeated certain items in the Model grid but also kept their location repeated in the Resource grid. The repetition of the Resource grid could have facilitated the placement of repeated items, by (1) building up a memory for the layout of the Resource grid, and/or (2) building up a memory for the motor actions required to place the repeated items. The reduced sampling observed for repeated items could thus be caused by repetition of the Resource grid, on top of (or instead of) increased memory for the Model grid. To isolate the effect of Model repetition on sampling behavior, and exclude the confounding effect of repeating the Resource grid, we conduct the present preregistered replication. Here, we aim to replicate the key finding—reduced reliance on external sampling when items in the Model are repeated—using the design of Experiment 2 (i.e., repeating 50% versus 0% of items in the Model across trials), while excluding the confound of Resource grid repetition. To this end, we use the same 16 items in the Resource grid (i.e., the combination of 4 unique hues and 4 unique shapes) in all trials, for both experimental conditions (i.e., blocks where 50% of items is repeated across trials, and blocks where no item is repeated) throughout the whole experiment. Additionally, on every trial of both experimental conditions, we randomize item locations within the Resource grid by independently shuffling: (a) row order (keeping items within rows unchanged), and (b) column order (keeping items within columns unchanged), to ensure that participants cannot learn the location of (repeated) items in the resources grid, while preserving the organization of color/shape features along rows and columns. By doing so, there will be no systematic difference in the Resource grid between different experimental conditions (50% versus no repeat conditions), and there will be no way to learn motor responses associated with repeated items. The only manipulation of repetitions, then, pertains to items in the Model grid: In the so-called ‘repeat block’, we randomly select 4 items from the Resource grid to be positioned in the exact same location of the Model grid across consecutive trials, and we randomly (re-)select the remaining 4 non-repeated items from the Resource grid (with the only restriction that no item appears more than twice in a Model) and randomly assign them to different locations in the Model grid on each consecutive trial. In the so-called ‘non-repeat block’, all Model items are randomly selected from the Resource grid and randomly assigned to a location in the Model grid on every trial.

abstract_r: The study aims to investigate whether famous names lead to higher frequency estimates than non-famous names due to their retrieval availability. Additionally, it examines whether male names are estimated more frequently than female names and whether famous male names are more overestimated in frequency judgments compared to famous female names. Participants then listen to four randomized lists of names, which include famous male names, famous female names, non-famous male names and non-famous female names. title_r: Evaluating the evaluation methods for co-speech motion in embodied conversational agents
abstract_r: Many studies that evaluate gesture generation in embodied conversational agents (ECAs) make use of either the pairwise comparison or rating scale approaches. With the pairwise comparison approach, participants are typically presented with two stimuli at once and asked to select which of the two they prefer (e.g., find more naturalistic, appealing, or appropriate). With the rating scale approach, participants are typically presented one stimulus at a time and asked to rate its quality (e.g., “How natural is the motion in this video?”) on a numerical rating scale (often an ordinal scale ranging from 1-to-7). After experimenting with both ways to evaluate virtual agents, we have an intuition that Likert scales are able to detect only a major difference, while preference tests would also detect a subtle difference. We set up this study to verify and examine this opinion. In this study, we will compare and contrast the pairwise comparison and rating scale approaches to evaluating the quality of ECA stimuli. Our primary aim is to determine the pros and cons of each approach, e.g., in terms of time-efficiency, participant experience, statistical assumptions and reliability, and the type and amount of information provided. Will there be one style of evaluating that is preferred over the other? And how do participants view this? As an application scenario we consider evaluating virtual agent’s gesticulation models. We replicate a previous study by Kucherenko et al. of the paper “Gesticulator”. As an example of a strong difference between models we consider “No Text” and “Full” models, we refer to this comparison as “StrongDiff”. As an example of a minor difference we consider “No Audio” and “Full” models , we refer to this comparison as “WeakDiff”.

title_r: Attractiveness Halo effect in a pairing-Halo design with attractiveness made salient
abstract_r: This experiment aims at replicating the attractiveness Halo effect (e.g., Dion et al., 1972; Eagly et al., 1991) when using a pairing design similar to the ones used in evaluative conditioning (EC) effects, hereafter called "pairing-halo design". We will use similar instructions as Dion et al. (1972) but instead of asking participant to evaluate faces varying on attractiveness (low vs. medium vs. high), we will pair these faces with other faces relatively average on attractiveness. This procedure thus ressembles EC procedure where unconditioned stimuli (US) on attractiveness are paired with conditioned stimuli (CS). We expect the US-CS pairing procedure to influence participant's responses on the CS in a way that is consistent with what we previously observed in the Halo effect. Specifically, we expect the attractiveness of the US to influence CS's rating so that the more attractive the US to which the CS is paired, the more positively the CS should be rated. In contrast with one of our past experiment (https://osf.io/ckgtv) relying on a similar procedure, we will make the attractiveness dimension salient in the instructions. Crucially, in line with the classic Halo effect, we expect selectivity as a function of the dimension--i.e., a larger influence on social competence- and vanity-related traits (here, negatively valenced) than on adjustment- and potency-related traits, themselves producing a larger effect than intellectual competence, integrity and concerns for others. abstract_r:

summary: We are preregistering a replication of a study that investigates how stereotype knowledge
about specific groups (e.g., the extent to which a person thinks that Black men are stereotyped as dominant) influences the cognitive process of person perception (e.g., perceiving a Black male target as dominant).

In this study, participants will categorize faces (Race: Asian, Black White; Gender: Female, Male) as either "Less" or "More" of one of six traits (Attractive, Dominant, Friendly, Intelligent, Strong, Trustworthy). The manipulation of faces is within-subject; the manipulation of trait is between-subject. This categorization will be performed using MouseTracker; our outcome variables measure deviation in trajectory (Area Under Curve, or AUC) and spatial complexity (Entropy). After completing this task, participants will report their stereotype knowledge for all six race-by-gender groups on all six traits (e.g., "To what extent are Black men stereotyped as dominant?"). 

We predict that people, as stereotype knowledge increases for a given target-trait combination (e.g., Black males being stereotyped as dominance; referred to as "stereotype congruence"), participants will show less deviation in trajectories (i.e., lower AUC) and simpler trajectories (i.e., lower Entropy) when categorizing faces as "more" of the relevant trait. Conversely, they will show more deviation in trajectories and more complex trajectories when categorizing faces as "less" of the relevant trait. 

We will test the robustness of our results by specifying three models with alternate specifications of random effects. We will explore whether specific traits and race-by-gender effects emerge after stereotype congruence is accounted for. Finally, we will test how much variance is shared between AUC and Entropy and whether the effects for each are maintained removing after removing their shared variance from the model. 

In our exploratory study, we analyzed the data of 220 people. We will collect 150 participants' responses for analysis in this replication. For our analyses, we will use the uploaded code.

title_r: Using fMRI to explore causal reasoning and abstract relational reasoning in the left lateral prefrontal cortex in the human brain
abstract_r: This study builds upon our earlier experiment (“Experiment 1”; https://osf.io/s54tb), which found a region in the left lateral prefrontal cortex that responded more strongly in causal reasoning about both physical and social causes compared to descriptive reasoning about physical and social situations. In Experiment 2 we test whether we can replicate the key finding from Experiment 1, namely that Physical Causal (PC) and Social Causal (SC) conditions will produce higher responses in a left frontal region than Physical Description (PD) and Social Description (SD) conditions. We further test the specificity of this region for causal reasoning per se, versus whether this region is also engaged in processing other abstract relationships like temporal order (TO) and part/whole relationships (PW), versus whether it is simply engaged during any demands on executive function broadly (EF). We also test whether the same region responds during a different causal task, when participants reason counterfactually about how an event could be prevented, for both physical (PCP) and social (SCP) conditions. In Experiment 3, we test whether the same region is more strongly engaged when participants read verbal vignettes of causal events of social or physical nature (SCn & PCn), and non-causal descriptions of either social or physical nature (SDn and PDn).

title_r: Experiment 3: AFRS accuracy of 92.9% (AFRS93), and 54.8% (AFRS55), unknown to participants.
abstract_r: Rationale: The current experiment is the third in our project about the use of Automated Facial Recognition Systems (AFRS) as decision-aids in one-to-one face matching tasks. The pre-registrations for Experiment 1 (https://osf.io/q7m8z) and Experiment 2 (https://osf.io/9evxk) can also be found in this project on the Open Science Framework. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants were told exactly how accurate the identity decisions made by the AFRS were (Experiment 1: 97.6%; Experiment 2: 92.9% or 54.8%). In both experiments, we found that human performance increased when the AFRS was highly accurate. However, there was no change in performance when the system had low accuracy (Experiment 2). In the current study, we will test whether the decisions made by the AFRS still influence performance on a face matching task when the participants are not told exactly how accurate the system is. The current study will be a direct replication of Experiment 2, with Aid condition (control, AFRS93, AFRS55) as a between-participants factor, and Test condition (baseline, aided) as a within-participants factor. The only change to the current experiment is that instead of telling participants the exact accuracy of the AFRS decisions (92.9%, 54.8%), all participants will simply be told that the AFRS gives the correct answer on “most trials”. Otherwise, the design, methods and procedure will be identical to Experiment 2. As such, the current pre-registration will only highlight differences with Experiment 2.

title_r: The hidden side of diversity: do students’ linguistic identities shape their emotions and belonging in class?
abstract_r: Universities have pledged to increase diversity, equity, and inclusion. Yet, language diversity (e.g., dialects, non-mainstream language varieties) and linguistic bias are rarely acknowledged. By assessing the perceptions of first language (L1) and non-first language (LX) users of English in an English-speaking context, this study examines students’ sense of belonging as well as their classroom anxiety and enjoyment in relation to their linguistic background. The objective is to aid the development of linguistically inclusive structures fostering intersectional learning and improving accessibility to allow every student to thrive. In a preliminary study, involving 186 undergraduate students enrolled at a U.S. higher education institution we found that, regardless of their English proficiency levels, LX users reported lower levels of perceived belonging and higher levels of anxiety when interacting in class, compared to L1 users. Additionally, high levels of proficiency, paired with high levels of enjoyment and low levels of anxiety, predicted increased belonging in class (variance = 43.4%) among all students. When answering open-ended questions, almost 70% stated that their English impacts their inclusion and participation in class. About 20% reported having experienced discrimination based on language. Of these respondents, most listed English as their L1. First-generation college students, as well as students from disadvantaged or minority backgrounds admitted feeling anxious about their English being considered ‘improper’ or not ‘polished’ enough, whereas LX users of English reported lack of socialisation with their peers. In their narratives, participants provided suggestions on how to improve their experience in class, such as reducing instructors’ over-reliance on active participation or favouring different dynamics, including work in small groups. These findings highlight the role of emotions in class when it comes to fostering belonging beyond the language barriers and setting the ground to develop a system for training instructors and students on inclusive practices that value every linguistic identity. The study reported below is a pre-registered replication of the preliminary study.

title_r: reinforcing nature of insight
abstract_r: In a correlational study, insight frequency and intensity (rated after each creative idea was generated) both correlated with self-reported positive reinforcement metrics (liking and motivation) and creative self-efficacy (feelings of creative confidence and higher self-rated creativity) during the creative process [while completing the alternate uses task]. We further found insight intensity largely drove these effects (i.e., in simultaneous regression that included both insight intensity and frequency). In this follow up study, we aim to compare the motivational potential of insight in both divergent thinking and convergent thinking contexts, and use a behavioral proxy for motivation in both. Specifially, in the divergent thinking task-- the alternate uses task-- participants will be given open-ended time to generate ideas. Time voluntarily spent on task will be used as a proxy for motivation. On the convergent thinking task-- anagrams-- two unsolvable anagrams are given at the end. Motivation is measured by how long they try to solve the unsolvable ones. It is predicted that greater reported experiences of insight intensity during these tasks will predict the motivational proxies, showing that experiencing insights is positively reinforcing, behaviorally. We will also replicate previous results showing that the tendency towards increased insight intensity (as an individual difference-- measured across participants) predicts greater creative behaviors in real life and greater creative achievements, and is predicted by atypical salience attribution and deprivation curiosity.

title_r: The influence of drinking consequences on alcohol expectancy likelihoods and valences: an item level multilevel approach
abstract_r: Theories of risk evaluation propose that experiencing an alcohol consequence should alter youth’s expectancies of that consequence occurring in the future. title_r: Attenuating Racial Stereotypes Through Babyfacedness: A Replication and Extension of the Teddy-Bear Effect
abstract_r: Facial features seemingly should not affect leadership assessments, yet research has consistently shown instant and robust judgments on physical appearance. Babyfacedness, a central attribute of facial inference, was originally found to be harmful for leaders. Through a survey of full-time employees in the United States (n = 269), non-White CEOs’ (Black, East Asian, and South Asian) increased babyfacedness was linked to higher leadership assessments mediated by warmth. This increased babyfacedness acted as a disarming mechanism by attenuating stereotypical perceptions of threat of non-White leaders. These findings stood despite non-White people being rated categorically less warm than White people in a separate survey of 50 participants. Collectively, these findings suggest non-White CEOs benefit from cues of warmth to compensate for racial stereotypes. Theoretical and practical implications, as well as future directions, are offered in the discussion section.

title_r: Evidence for Indirect Retrieval effects for an associated stimulus in a prime-probe paradigm using audiovisual stimulus associations.
abstract_r: This experiment investigates whether stimulus-response bindings can be indirectly transferred to a stimulus that has prior associations with a prime stimulus. To create stronger stimulus associations, audiovisual stimuli were used. Two words – German word and a pseudoword (representing a foreign language word) are paired together and learnt in the first phase of the study by means of contingency learning – 100% contingent audiovisual presentations of a stimulus (a german word, for example) followed by another stimulus (pseudoword) (S-S association formation phase). Two pairs were learnt (Haus – mank; Wald – dels) which were counterbalanced across the participants where half learnt the pairs of Haus-mank; Wald-dels and the other half learnt Haus-dels; Wald -mank. The order is also balanced within each participant so that for half the presentations, the name precedes the adjective and for the other half the names follow after an adjective. Both trial orders are presented randomly. Following this association phase, there will be a prime-probe sequence with a colour classification forced choice task. Here the stimuli from the association phase are presented as prime and probes in 4 different colours: green, yellow, blue and pink – 2 colours mapped to one response key, and participants press the relevant key based on the colour. For each prime-probe sequence, the probe will either be the identical stimulus, the associated stimulus from the previous S-S association phase or a different/unassociated stimulus from the other pairs in the association phase. Both the prime and the probe stimulus are presented both auditorily and visually. We investigate whether associated stimuli can access and retrieve bindings from the prime trial. This experiment is intended as a conceptual replication of a previous study preregistered under the same name but using audiovisual presentations of stimuli instead.

title_r: Does Proactive Policing Really Increase Major Crime? A Replication Study of Sullivan and O’Keeffe (Nature Human Behaviour, 2017)
abstract_r: In December 2014 and January 2015, police officers in New York City engaged in an organized slowdown of police work to protest the murder of two police officers who were targeted by a gunman while sitting in their patrol car. An influential 2017 article in Nature Human Behaviour studies the effect of the NYPD's work slowdown on major crimes and concludes that the slowdown led to a significant improvement in public safety. Contrary to the remainder of the literature, the authors conclude that proactive policing can cause an increase in crime. We re-evaluate this claim and point out several fatal weaknesses in the authors' analysis - which purports to be a difference- in-differences analysis but isn't - that call this finding into question. In particular, we note that there was considerable variation in the intensity of the slowdown across NYC communities and that the communities which experienced a more pronounced reduction in police proactivity did not experience the largest reductions in major crime. The authors' analysis constitutes a quintessential fallacy in statistical reasoning, a logical miscalculation in which inferences from aggregated data are mistakenly applied to a more granular phenomenon. We raise several additional and equally compelling concerns regarding the tests presented in the paper and conclude that there is little evidence that the slowdown led to short-term changes in major crimes in either direction

title_r: Size-based niche partitioning permits coexistence in natural populations of Nicrophorus spp.
abstract_r: When species compete over similar resources, niche partitioning can permit ecologically-similar species to coexist. Such coexistence should be a particular challenge for carrion-feeding invertebrates, with the ephemeral nature of carrion leading to intense competition over this nutrient-rich resource. Here we tested whether the carrion niche in four species of coexisting burying beetles (Nicrophorus spp.) is partitioned seasonally or by species size in seven ancient woodlands in the United Kingdom. We fail to replicate the results of previous studies in the UK that found a strict seasonal separation in the activity of competing burying beetle species. Instead, our data support the hypothesis that the niche is partitioned by species size. We present field evidence consistent with the hypothesis that smaller species are less successful at contested carcasses and confirm the existence of a sexual dimorphism in head width, a trait likely related to competitive ability, in several species of Nicrophorus. We discuss the considerable but as-of-yet unnoticed variation between different geographic populations of Nicrophorus spp. in how the carrion niche is partitioned.

title_r: Victoria MS Thesis_final vers.pdf
abstract_r:
Glucocorticoids (GC) play a critical role in regulating the physiological response to stress. Disruptions to baseline levels due to stress can have negative implications on a variety of factors including growth and development, physical body conditions, metabolism, immune functions, and expression of normal behaviors, although this list is not exhaustive. When birds are unable to adapt to the stressor and return to homeostasis, the energy expenditure associated with the failed attempt at coping can lead to significant declines in the overall health, welfare, production, and performance of the bird. This can go on to impact producers and consumers as well, indicating the extensive repercussions of stress. Recently, scientists have been investigating thorough and efficient methods of quantifying stress in birds, such as measuring heterophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (HLR) or detecting glucocorticoid levels through enzyme-linked immunoassays (ELISA). However, the precise mechanism behind HLR increase during stress is unknown and ELISAs may not provide accurate results depending on when the blood is being measured.
GC are differentially released and exert their effects in a manner that is dependent on sex, age, and time. However, before investigating this, it was critical to validate the GC kits to ensure that they were measuring cortisol and corticosterone separately along with zero cross reactions with other precursors. Chapter 2 had 4 experiments carried out. The objective of experiment 1 was to validate ELISAs to ensure that they were measuring the GC accurately and separately since both cortisol and corticosterone were being measured. To do this, duck serum was pooled and charcoal-stripped to remove the presence of steroids. 3 standard curves were run to confirm that there was no cross reactivity. The objective of experiment 2 was to further validate the ELISA kits with mass spectrometry by checking for both glucocorticoids in the pooled samples. Once the validation process was complete, experiment 3 was carried out to look at the effect of ACTH stimulation on GC release. 16-week-old drakes and hens were given either intramuscular (IM) injections of cosyntropin (0.06 mg/kg) or saline as control. The cosyntropin dose was chosen according to previous studies reporting relatively high physiological responses, therefore, we wanted to replicate this. N was 10/sex/treatment. Blood was then collected at 0, 1, and 2 hours after injections and serum was analyzed by ELISAs. Lastly for experiment 4, 14-week-old developer drakes and hens at Maple Leaf Farms were assessed for a transportation stress experiment. Blood from 10 ducks/sex/time/barn were collected at 24 hours before transport to the breeder barn, immediately after a 1-hour transport, 24 hours after, and 1 week after transport. The results from experiment 1 yielded that both cortisol and corticosterone can be measured without the presence of unwanted contaminants or other products. Experiment 2 identified the greater sensitivity of mass spectrometry when reading GC levels, although the differences were linear. Experiment 3 showed that serum corticosterone levels were significantly increased at 1 hour after ACTH injections in both drakes and hens, with levels continuing to increase for the drakes. Serum cortisol levels were significantly increased at 1 hour after ACTH injections in both sexes, however, the hens had greater levels compared to the drakes. Serum cortisol levels returned to levels similar to that of saline-injected ducks at the 2-hour mark. Lastly, the transportation stress portion showed that cortisol was released at about 1/3 of corticosterone levels in both sexes. Hens showed increased levels of serum corticosterone compared to drakes at all time points except for 1 week after transport, and also had significantly increased serum cortisol levels at all time points. In conclusion, the ELISA kits were verified for future use when measuring GC as well as mass spectrometry. GC were detected in the ACTH and transportation stress experiments with hens displaying a greater sensitivity to GC release due to increased circulating levels compared to drakes. Although it was nonsignificant, there was a trend for GC to increase in response to transport.
There are sex differences in GC release and HLR for Pekin ducks and various challenges from the studies support this. With hens showing increased sensitivity to stress and drakes with more transient and gradual levels, we have consistently seen that both GC have differential roles in the stress response and not only is it critical to study both hormones, the timing of when measurements are taken are important as well to get a clear understanding of when the stress response is initiated.
Chapter 3 went further to understand the response of GC and HLR. The objective was to investigate the release of cortisol and corticosterone in response to an ACTH dose response challenge. In Chapter 2, only one dose of cosyntropin was used and sample collection times only went to 2 hours after injections. In this study, 2 additional doses and an extra hour of sample collection were added to obtain more information. Pekin ducks were either given IM cosyntropin injections or saline for control, with an N of 10/sex/treatment. There were 3 treatment doses: High (0.06 mg/kg), medium (0.03 mg/kg), and low (0.015 mg/kg). All injections were given promptly at 0730 hours. Blood was collected at 0, 1, 2 and 3 hours after injections from the tibia veins to obtain serum for ELISAs. Blood smears were done to analyze HLR and sent to an independent lab to obtain values. The results indicated that both GC had significant sex x dose x time interactions. The low dose injection had no effect on corticosterone in hens with a slight increase for drakes at the first hour. The high dose for hens led to a spike in corticosterone levels at the first hour with a gradual decrease, and drakes had an increase that lasted for 2 hours until they returned to baseline at the last hour. The high dose in drakes stimulated cortisol release during the first 2 hours after injection with a similar effect in hens. However, hens had elevated levels compared to drakes. Finally, there was no dose response effect for HLR, although interestingly, the low dose injection elevated HLR even though there was no effect in GC. There were sex differences in the HLR response where the drakes given the high dose had levels that plateaued by the third hour, while the hens still had elevated levels. In conclusion, the ACTH dose-response test identified that ACTH has a dose-dependent effect in both GC and sex differences in their release. HLR also showed sex differences that did not depend on the dose given.
Chapter 4 observed acute exposure of GC in ducks. Pekin ducks were assigned 10/sex/treatment to receive either IM control, cortisol, or corticosterone injections. In addition, a low-dose cortisol treatment was given to represent the endogenous levels of cortisol compared to corticosterone. The control injections contained safflower oil, which was chosen as vehicle due to the low levels of genistein present. This is important as genistein is a plant estrogen and this could interact with the GC and alter the results. Blood was collected at 0, 1, 2, and 3 hours after injections for serum analysis with ELISAs, and blood smears were collected for complete blood count (CBC) differentials. Significant sex x treatment x time interactions were notable in both GC. Hens had significant increases at the first hour after injections in all treatments compared to controls, and drakes had increases at 2 hours after injections in all treatments except the low-dose cortisol.
After observing the effect of acute stress in ducks, the next step was to investigate the effects of chronic stress in chapter 5. Adult breeder Pekin ducks were randomly distributed into 3 groups: corticosterone, cortisol, or control treatments. The GC were in crystalline steroid form distributed through 2 capsules that were subcutaneously implanted on the backs of the neck. The ducks in the control group were given empty capsules. Blood smears, blood draws for serum, egg collection, body weights, and organ samples were collected over a period of 2 weeks. For the results, the corticosterone implants elevated corticosterone levels in both sexes. Interestingly, cortisol levels were elevated in both GC treatments in both sexes. Cortisol elevated HLR in drakes 1 day after implants with no effect from corticosterone. Hens had elevated HLR from both GC at all timepoints throughout the experiment. There were no significant differences in morphometrics in either sex. Corticosterone was not present in eggs, but cortisol was elevated in the albumen on day 7 and 14 of the experiment. Overall, there were sex differences in HLR where hens had greater levels in both GC treatments.

title_r: Learning by Evaluating Strategies in Design Education
abstract_r: This three-article dissertation explores Learning by Evaluating (LbE), an educational approach that enhances student learning through the process of assessing and providing feedback on peer work. Leveraging principles of comparative judgement, students evaluate pairs of exemplars side-by-side to determine which is better and provide a rational for their decision, actively engaging in the assessment process. Students engage in critical thinking to justify their decisions, enhancing their understanding of the task at hand by discerning quality where they can apply these principles to their own assignments. Teachers may use this as a formative assessment tool to elicit student insights and misconceptions to better utilize teaching strategies and address specific needs. Engaging students in feedback allows teachers and students to communicate about a shared value structure, making the design process more comprehensive and manageable. Importantly, teachers have control over the duration of student engagement with LbE in the classroom. Once students have started the decision-making process, teachers can use a website interface to bring the session to a close, ensuring that all students finish simultaneously. Once these sessions have been created, they can be reused, further enhancing the efficiency of LbE in the classroom.An important part of this process is the selection of exemplars for student evaluation. In my first paper, I engage in a systematic literature review of 33 articles on exemplars and their influence on the student learning experience in secondary and post-secondary education. Through this process, nine key themes were identified: clarity of instruction, learner focus, motivation for learning, student reflection on learning, building student self-efficacy, identifying instructional challenges, providing contrasting cases, the relationship between exemplar quality and student work quality, and raising the bar for learning outcomes. Findings suggest that the selection of exemplars has a significant influence over student motivation, understanding, and application, and that time should be taken not only to identify these items, but to use them as a means to discuss and clarify expectations to enhance the learning experience.After establishing the educational merits in the first paper, I explore how selected pre-engineering teachers integrate LbE into their classrooms. To do this I use a design-based research approach in my second paper to both analyze and optimize the implementation of this method in a secondary STEM education setting through an investigation of student comments and justifications throughout the design process for five teachers after the first year of piloting the program in their classrooms. Findings show diverse student engagement and decision-making patterns, highlighting the importance of strategic integration of Learning by Evaluating for both students and educators.In my final paper, recognizing that much of the research of Learning by Evaluating has focused on student outcomes in groups, I investigate the benefits on students as individuals. Using quasi-experimental research, a conceptual replication study was initiated to investigate the influence of Learning by Evaluating of 325 undergraduate students in an entry-level design thinking course as they prepare for and conduct qualitative research interviews. While the original study used LbE to have students develop PoV statements as a group, this replication study builds on that research by using the same methods and a similar sample of students from the same course, but shifts the focus to individual interviews to inform the PoV problem statement. The findings show that students in the treatment group prepared more open-ended questions, indicating improved interview preparation, however, the actual length of interviews showed no significant improvement. The study used random sampling and independent samples t-tests to compare treatment and control groups, with results suggesting that this is an effective pedagogical strategy for individualized work, highlighting its value for educators and researchers in optimizing comparative judgement to enhance student learning experiences.

title_r: TESS Experiments: Cross-National Replication of Questions Design Experiments
abstract_r: Time-sharing Experiments for the Social Sciences (TESS) offers researchers the opportunity to capture the internal validity of experiments. Investigators submit proposals, and TESS fields successful proposals for free on a representative sample of adults in the United States. This experiment was conducted as part of a larger international study to test whether the principles of question design, derived from primarily US American research a few decades ago, still apply and are generalizable outside the United States. Respondents were randomly assigned to different versions of 17 political and social issue questions which manipulated response option order, question order, question wording, the presence or absence of various ‘no opinion’ response options, and question balancing. Respondents were re-randomized for manipulation. A total of 1,029 respondents participated. This allowed for comparison of response behaviors across variations in question design and respondent demographics.

title_r: The Development of Implicit and Explicit Knowledge of Collocations: A Conceptual Replication and Extension of Sonbul and Schmitt (2013)
abstract_r: Sonbul and Schmitt (2013) showed that exposure to second language (L2) collocations in reading texts can produce gains in explicit knowledge, but they found no evidence of gains in implicit knowledge. This study is a conceptual replication and extension of Sonbul and Schmitt's research. Sixty-two advanced English as a second language (ESL) speakers read texts containing repeated occurrences of low-frequency medical collocations in three sessions over 2 days. The incidental learning treatments included reading only (no typographic enhancement), bolding, and bolding-plus-glossing. Collocational knowledge was assessed in tests of explicit knowledge (cued recall, form recognition) and a test of implicit knowledge (primed lexical decision). Repeated exposure to bolded collocations produced greater explicit knowledge than repeated exposure to typographically unenhanced collocations. Evidence of implicit knowledge development was observed in the unenhanced (reading only) treatment but not in the remaining treatments. These results replicated Sonbul and Schmitt's findings for explicit knowledge and extended their findings for implicit knowledge.
