title_r: More Conservative or Differently Moral? Moral Foundations and Populist Electoral Choice in Multiparty Competition
abstract_r: This project examines whether support for populist-right parties in a fragmented multiparty system is associated with a distinct configuration of moral priorities, or whether it mainly reflects a more intense version of mainstream-right ideology. The broader motivation is that populism is often described as a moralized vision of politics that opposes a virtuous people to a corrupt elite, yet most research has focused more strongly on elite rhetoric and communication than on the moral psychology of voters. Using Moral Foundations Theory as the main framework, this study investigates whether moral foundations help explain differences in party preference within the Dutch electorate, and especially whether they distinguish voters who are relatively more attracted to populist-right parties from those who prefer mainstream-right parties. This preregistration concerns the analysis of an independent 2025 Dutch election survey and is explicitly framed as a direct replication of exploratory analyses previously conducted on a separate 2023 election survey. The two studies contain the same key variables and were designed to make such replication possible. The 2023 analyses were exploratory and produced the expectations for the present study. The 2025 analyses are preregistered in order to test whether those patterns are robust in a new election context or whether they were more contingent on the 2023 case. The 2025 dataset serves as the replication only and will not be pooled with the 2023 data for confirmatory inference. Because the 2025 data have already been collected, this preregistration is prospective with respect to analysis and not data collection. Its purpose is to document, in advance, the hypotheses, variables, and statistical procedures that will be used for the confirmatory replication, while clearly separating these from any later exploratory follow-up analyses. The study relies on survey measures that are identical or directly comparable to those used in 2023. Moral foundations are measured using the same Dutch short version of the MFQ-2, covering the foundations of Care, Equality, Proportionality, Loyalty, Authority, and Purity. Electoral preference is operationalized with propensity-to-vote (PTV) scores for parties rather than a single vote-intention item, because PTV captures graded party preference and is especially appropriate in a multiparty system where voters may feel affinity with more than one party. The analysis further includes ideological self-placement, measured with left-right and conservative-progressive self-placement items, as well as people-centrism/populist attitudes, which are included to assess whether any moral differences between populist-right and mainstream-right preferences remain once broader ideological orientation and explicitly populist beliefs are taken into account. Standard demographic controls are also included. When the same construct is available in multiple waves, the earliest available 2025 measurement will be used to mirror the 2023 design and maximize comparability. The analytical strategy replicates the 2023 workflow as closely as possible. First, the study will map Dutch parties in a moral-foundations space by estimating party-specific regression models in which party PTV is predicted from the six moral foundations while controlling for relevant covariates. The resulting coefficient profiles will then be compared across parties using cosine similarity and community detection in order to assess whether the populist right forms a distinct moral bloc or whether it is internally heterogeneous. Second, the study will estimate within-right contrast models that predict relative preference for populist-right versus mainstream-right parties. These models test which moral foundations distinguish the two camps, first with baseline controls and then after adding ideology and people-centrism. As a third and secondary step, the study will estimate separate party-level models for the main right-wing parties in order to examine whether any bloc-level findings are broadly shared or instead driven by a subset of parties. The populist-right and mainstream-right classifications will follow the same party grouping used in the 2023 analyses so that the 2025 study functions as a direct replication rather than a redesigned extension. The project is observational and correlational. Its goal is not to make causal claims about the effect of morality on vote choice, but to test the reproducibility of previously observed associations. Based on the exploratory 2023 findings, the expected outcome is not a simple result in which the populist right appears as one coherent moral bloc that is cleanly separated from the mainstream right. Instead, the main expectation is a more differentiated pattern. In the full party system, populist-right parties are expected to show internal heterogeneity rather than clustering as a single unified moral community, while still showing some differentiation from the mainstream right. In the within-right comparison, relative preference for populist-right over mainstream-right parties is expected to be associated more strongly with Equality and Loyalty and less strongly with Authority, with the Loyalty association weakening once people-centrism is included in the model. At the party level, mainstream-right parties are expected to show a more coherent moral profile, especially with respect to higher Authority and lower Equality, whereas populist-right parties are expected to show more variation from party to party and a stronger link with Loyalty. These expectations are derived from the 2023 exploratory analyses and will be evaluated in the independent 2025 dataset. The main contribution of the project is therefore twofold. Substantively, it addresses whether moral foundations help explain populist electoral choice in a multiparty context beyond standard ideological self-placement and beyond explicitly populist attitudes. Methodologically, it provides a transparent, preregistered replication of an earlier exploratory study using an already collected independent dataset with matching measures. A successful replication would strengthen confidence that the previously observed moral patterns are robust rather than incidental. A weak or failed replication would be equally informative, because it would suggest that the moral correlates of populist-right electoral preference are more context-dependent or election-specific than the 2023 results implied. In either case, the study is intended to clarify the extent to which moral-foundation differences are stable features of populist electoral competition rather than one-off findings from a single election survey.

title_r: Sensitive windows, sensitive outcomes: Early or late-postnatal maternal separation differentially impacts puberty and behavior
abstract_r: Early-life adversity disrupts the maturation of neuroendocrine, cognitive, and emotional regulatory systems, yet outcomes likely depend on both the timing of development and sex. Maternal separation (MS) in rodents is a widely used model for studying these effects, yet the sex-specific consequences of distinct postnatal MS windows remain underexplored. Here, we investigated how early [postnatal day (P)2–P10], late (P11–P20), or prolonged MS (P2–P20) influences pubertal maturation, spatial memory, and anxiety-like behavior in male and female Sprague–Dawley rats. Pubertal development was assessed through daily visual inspection. Affective behavior was evaluated using dyadic social interaction and light-enhanced startle (LES), and spatial memory was evaluated in the delayed win-shift task during adolescence. Both postnatal timing of adversity exposure and sex influenced the measured outcomes. Females exposed to prolonged or early MS exhibited significantly earlier pubertal initiation, with no effect of MS on pubertal onset in males. Prolonged or early MS exposure also impaired spatial memory, with females affected by prolonged MS and males affected by early MS. Affective measures in males and females were differentially affected by early and late MS exposure. While only late MS exposure yielded more social approach-avoidance behavior in males, females exhibited approach-avoidance changes after both early and late MS. We replicated previous findings that PMS-exposed males display a blunted light-enhanced startle, and now show that late, but not early MS, yields reduced LES in males. Female adolescents, however, responded to early MS with enhanced LES. Together, these findings demonstrate that MS exerts distinct, sex-specific effects on pubertal maturation and behavior depending on the developmental window of adversity. By demonstrating window and sex-dependent effects on pubertal development, anxiety-like behavior, social interaction, and cognition, this work highlights developmental timing and sex as key determinants of early-life stress outcomes and underscores the importance of distinguishing discrete postnatal periods when modeling the consequences of early caregiving disruption. • Early and prolonged maternal separation accelerates pubertal onset in females • Maternal separation impacts startle modulation in a window- and sex-specific fashion • Social behavior and spatial memory are differentially sensitive to separation timing • Some behavioral effects of maternal separation are buffered by prolonged exposure

title_r: How Non-Linguistic Is the Indus Sign System? A Synthetic-Baseline Scorecard
abstract_r: Whether the Indus Valley sign system (c. 2600-1900 BCE) encodes spoken language has been debated for decades. This paper introduces a multi-metric discrimination framework that tests the observed Indus corpus against two kinds of computer-generated non-linguistic baseline -- one mimicking a heraldic emblem system, the other an administrative coding system -- each calibrated with Zipfian frequency distributions, positional constraints, and bigram dependencies derived from six attested non-linguistic corpora. The scorecard evaluates four properties central to the Farmer-Sproat-Witzel (2004) critique: text brevity, repeated formulaic phrases, hapax legomenon rate, and positional rigidity. Applying this framework to 1,916 deduplicated inscriptions (584 unique signs, 11,110 tokens) from the ICIT/Yajnadevam digitization, we find that the Indus corpus does not match either baseline cleanly. Across the four metrics examined, the Indus corpus occupies an intermediate position relative to the two baseline families, matching neither cleanly. Neither a heraldic nor an administrative generator can reproduce all four properties at once. We also compare against seven real-world non-linguistic corpora including Sproat's (2014) datasets, finding that no attested non-linguistic system reproduces the full Indus statistical profile either. We replicate key prior results including a Zipf slope of -1.49 and conditional entropy of 3.23 bits. All code and data are publicly available.

title_r: Targeting a host acidic lipase as a strategy to counteract West Nile virus: implications in replication.
abstract_r: West Nile virus (WNV) is a neurotropic flavivirus endemic in many regions of the world, representing a persistent global health concern. Although most WNV infections are asymptomatic or mild, the neuroinvasive form can cause severe inflammatory diseases that can lead to meningitis and encephalitis, with no specific antivirals or vaccines currently available for humans. Like other flaviviruses, WNV profoundly remodels host lipid metabolism to support its replication and evade immune responses. These viruses boost lipogenesys to shield the replication factories against the cellular defenses. In a previous work we showed that a key enzyme involved in lipid disruption, N- acylethanolamine acid amidase (NAAA), plays a crucial role in the replication of Zika virus (ZIKV). NAAA hydrolyzes the bioactive lipid palmitoylethanolamide (PEA), by lowering lipid availability and counteracting ZIKV replication and virus-associated inflammatory damage. Building on these previous studies, in this work, we explored NAAA therapeutic potential against WNV. Using a next-generation NAAA inhibitor, ARN19702, we demonstrated a marked reduction in WNV replication both in vitro and in vivo. Lipidomic profiling revealed that treatment restored sphingolipid levels, which are otherwise elevated during WNV infection. Moreover, in Golden Syrian hamster models, NAAA inhibition decreased viremia and provided significant protection to the central nervous system, reducing inflammation and virus-induced damage. Together, these findings highlight NAAA inhibition as a promising host-directed therapeutic strategy against WNV and potentially other flavivirus infections.

title_r: Understanding the mechanisms behind descriptive norm effects in emergency preparedness communication (Subject to change): Replication.
abstract_r: While emergency preparedness has been shown to reduce both loss of life and the economic costs resulting from disasters (Idris, 2018; United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction, 2025), the general emergency preparedness among citizens remains relatively low. Specifically in Europe, a survey from early 2024 showed that only 37% of European citizens’ considered themselves prepared for potential emergencies (European Commission, 2024). Accordingly, several international organizations stress the importance of increasing this number (e.g., European Commission, 2025; Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2014; World Health Organization, 2021). Many of these institutions also emphasize the role of policies and interventions aimed at improving preparedness at the citizen level. That said, policymakers might be less inclined to adopt or advocate for policies perceived as unpopular (Toshkov et al., 2020), potentially to avoid future electoral costs. This highlights the importance of understanding how public policy acceptability is shaped. A key part of this might be the influence of social norms which have received considerable attention in recent years and which inform individuals about the behaviors and attitudes of others (Cialdini et al., 1990). At the same time, research has shown that communicating high prevalence of undesirable behaviors can sometimes backfire (Bicchieri & Dimant, 2022; Schorn, 2024), as such messages communicate descriptive norms and may inadvertently signal that this undesirable behavior is common and, therefore, sensible (Cialdini, 2005). Consistent with this, our preliminary pilot data showed that presenting participants with information that a majority of people feel unprepared for emergencies led to decreased policy acceptability. As people are exposed to descriptive norms on a daily basis, it is important to better understand the mechanisms through which these norms operate, especially in order to mitigate their potentially undesirable effects. While the influence of social norms has been demonstrated across decades of research, many influential findings in the social norms literature have been explained at a theoretical level, often without direct tests of the underlying mechanisms. At the same time, operationalizations of social norms vary considerably across studies. It therefore remains uncertain which mechanisms drive the effects of descriptive norms. Some research suggests that descriptive norms operate through informational processes, distinct from the normative influence of injunctive norms (Cialdini & Jacobson, 2021), whereas other work points to potential overlap or interaction between these mechanisms (Eriksson et al., 2015). The present study aims to address these gaps by examining the mechanisms underlying descriptive social norm effects, specifically distinguishing between informational and normative influences, as originally conceptualized by Deutsch & Gerard (1955). Focusing on the context of emergency preparedness, it tests how exposure to descriptive norms shapes policy acceptability and whether these effects are driven by motivations to do the most efficient thing (informational influence) or to be approved of by others (normative influence). Understanding these mechanisms is particularly important, as certain types of norm communication may unintentionally undermine support for policies aimed at increasing preparedness, thereby slowing progress in an area where behavioral change is urgently needed.

title_r: Preparation for Disasters Among Nurse Leaders in New York State: A Replication Study and Guide for Preparation
abstract_r: OBJECTIVE: To assess the knowledge and confidence levels in emergency management and disaster preparedness among nurse leaders, and to provide recommendations for enhancing nurse leader preparedness. BACKGROUND: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed significant gaps in disaster preparedness among healthcare leaders, including deficiencies in disaster training, underscoring the need for better preparation. METHODS: This replication study used a prospective, cross-sectional design. Participants rated their confidence in managing disasters using the Emergency Preparedness Information Questionnaire. RESULTS: NYONL members (n=198) demonstrated moderate confidence in disaster preparedness (mean score: 3.11). Four major needs that emerged were education specific to emergency preparedness, supply management, infection prevention, and mental health and well-being. CONCLUSIONS: There is a critical need to better equip nurse leaders for future emergency situations. Overall, this study's findings suggest that targeted disaster training and educational opportunities, especially those emphasizing leadership and well-being, are critical to better equip nurse leaders for future emergency situations.

title_r: Replication Studies in TESOL
abstract_r: Abstract Replication studies are critical to the growth and credibility of the field of TESOL studies, including what we know about the teaching, learning, and use of English globally. Much of what we understand about TESOL is determined through empirical research evidence. However, we rarely revisit and probe at the stability of our claims about TESOL with new evidence. We can do this by conducting replication studies, in which a previous study's research design and methods are repeated, with or without changes, and the new findings are systematically compared with those from the previous study. In this paper, I review and discuss the key conceptual underpinnings and principles of replication research in TESOL, informed by prior scholarship published in this journal. I then examine the conduct and reporting of replication studies in TESOL Quarterly , drawing on three examples. Informed by this discussion and current methodological work in the field of applied linguistics more generally, I outline key guidelines for the conduct of rigorous replication research in TESOL. In doing so, this paper supports and invests in the conduct of high‐quality replication studies in TESOL to strengthen and invest in the future and credibility of the discipline.

title_r: Time is money! A replication and extension of Diaz-Salvat et al. (2020) evaluating the significance of training type and training time on resurgence
abstract_r: Resurgence is often defined in terms of previously reinforced responses returning after differential reinforcement strategies terminate (Lattal et al., 2017; Shahan & Craig, 2016). Existing literature on resurgence includes evaluations of using Single Training and Serial Training to teach alternative responses and then evaluating responding by eliminating or worsening conditions of reinforcement (Diaz-Salvat et al., 2020). Previous findings suggest that Serial Training, or training more than one alternative response, may be the most effective way to decrease resurgence (Lambert et al., 2015). This study sought to replicate the findings of Diaz-Salvat et al. and further explore the role of time and learning history on resurgence. Experiment 1 evaluated the influence of Single Training and Serial Training on resurgence by systematically replicating the initial experiment of Diaz-Salvat et al. (2020) to test the viability of the experimental arrangement using the PORTL apparatus (Hunter & Rosales-Ruiz, 2019). During Experiment 2, training type was manipulated again, and training time was doubled to extend learning histories and evaluate their influence on resurgence. In Experiment 3 training time was manipulated and the effects of short or long training time on resurgence was evaluated. Major findings of Diaz-Salvat et al. (2020) were replicated in Experiment 2. The present research found similar results to that of existing literature in that more research is necessary to understand how methodological and conceptual considerations impact resurgence.

title_r: Replication and Extension of an Evaluation of a Functional Analysis Decision-Making Model
abstract_r: The effectiveness of functional analysis (FA) has been demonstrated over the years (Melanson & Fahmie, 2023) however, FA is infrequently used in clinical practice (Oliver et al., 2015; Roscoe et al., 2015). Researchers have developed variations to the FA methodology originally described by Iwata et al. (1982/1994) to address behavioral and environmental constraints such as time, setting, dangerous behavior (e.g., self-injurious behavior), and session-resetting behaviors (e.g., elopement). In an unpublished thesis, Benson (2021) created, validated, and evaluated an FA decision-making model (DMM) for selecting an initial FA variation with graduate students. The majority of students needed additional training (i.e., CBT, rehearsal and feedback). The purposes of the current study were to replicate and extend Benson. Specifically, we were interested in evaluating the FA DMM with and without additional training with practicing, master’s- and doctoral-level Board Certified Behavior Analysts. Results of the study were similar to Benson and idiosyncratic across participants. One participant acquired the trained response following the introduction of the DMM, and three participants required additional training components. Similar to Benson, CBT and rehearsal and feedback were mostly ineffective. Thus, additional education and clinical experience did not impact participants responding using the DMM. title_r: Differential Accuracy Judgments of Matching Versus Mismatching Personality Feedback: Motivationally Inclined or Inferentially Obliged? (II)
abstract_r: THEORETICAL BACKGROUND [----------] Psychologists have proposed, and found evidence, that people do not only seek out the truth about themselves (Gregg, 2023). That is, they are guided by more than merely the motive to self-assess (Trope, 1980). At least two other motives show signs of biasing how people pursue and process self-relevant information, namely, the motives to self-enhance (Alicke & Sedikides, 2019) and to self-verify (Swann, 2012). Each motive is also embedded in a broader theoretical framework, which may be respectively labelled self-enhancement theory (SET) and self-verification theory (SVT). [----------] SET is ostensibly supported by findings such as the Better-Than-Average-Effect (BTAE; Zell et al., 2020). Here, defying statistical logic, most people rate themselves as better than most other people on many desirable commonplace traits. The inference is that the self-enhancement motive—to protect, maintain, or promote the positivity of one’s self-view—biases their perceptions. [----------] SVT is ostensibly supported by findings such as the Matching-Feedback-is-Accurate-Effect (MFAE; Seih et al. 2013). Here, people with positive and negative self-views rate feedback matching their self-view as more accurate than feedback mismatching it. The inference is that the self-verification motive—to maintain their existing view of oneself because of the sense of predictability, control, and coherence it provides—biases their perceptions. [----------] ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS OF THE MFAE [----------] The SVT explanation for the MFAE is nonetheless open to objection. Why should judgments of feedback accuracy be shaped solely by the motive to self-verify? Consider this thought experiment. If the motive did not operate, and people with positive and negative self-views made completely rational judgments, should one expect them to rate positive and negative feedback as equally accurate? Impartial inference based on prior presuppositions might still suffice to produce an MFAE. The burden of proof is arguably on an advocate of SVT to show that the motive to self-verify alone accounts for the MFAE. [----------] Nonetheless, one may empirically address the issue with an actual experiment. Self-verification theory is essentially about both the self and about verification. If feedback pertains to other people rather than self, then no motive to self-verify can operate by definition. So what happens when people judge the accuracy of feedback about other people? If the MFAE persists, then that would prove that (a) the motive to self-verify is unnecessary to produce the MFAE and (b) other factors are sufficient to produce the MFAE—which in principle would require ruling out before adopting a self-verification interpretation. abstract_r: THEORETICAL BACKGROUND [----------] Psychologists have proposed, and found evidence, that people do not only seek out the truth about themselves (Gregg, 2023). Each motive is also embedded in a broader theoretical framework, which may be respectively labelled self-enhancement theory (SET) and self-verification theory (SVT). title_r: Analysis of Two Metrics for Keynote and Invited Speaker Expertise: A Replication and Extension in Canada
abstract_r: ABSTRACT As an extension of a recent study on the two metrics of expertise for keynote and other invited speakers at behavior analytic conferences in the United States, this study evaluated 63 continuing education presentations provided by keynote and invited speakers at 17 conferences in Canada during 2021, 2022, and 2023. For each keynote and invited presentation, researchers used Google Scholar to count each speaker's (a) peer‐reviewed publications on their presentation topic and (b) total peer‐reviewed publications. Results across all 3 years indicate that over 50% of speakers had zero topic‐specific publications and the percentage of speakers with zero topic‐specific publications increased slightly across the 3 years. Results also indicate that over 50% of speakers with zero topic‐specific publications did not have any peer‐reviewed publications. We discuss the findings within the context of other recent studies and changes to guidelines for selecting speakers.

title_r: Evaluation of a Functional Analysis Decision-Making Model: A Systematic Replication
abstract_r: Functional analyses (FAs) are an experimental methodology in which variables are systematically manipulated to evoke the behavior of interest to determine the function. Although the literature suggests effectiveness of FA methodology, clinicians have reported environmental and behavioral constraints to their implementation. Researchers have made modifications to the standard FA to mitigate these constraints. We replicated and extended Benson (2021) by enhancing the computer-based training to identify an appropriate FA variation. Study 1 surveyed experts in FA to identify the point at which behavioral and environmental variables became constraints. These results were used to enhance the computer-based training. Study 2 evaluated the effects of the enhanced training with online graduate students in identifying an initial FA variation given hypothetical scenarios. Results of Study 2 suggest the training was effective for one participant; however, rehearsal and feedback was needed for two participants.Keywords: functional analysis, constraints, computer-based training, decision-making model

title_r: NO EVIDENCE SUPPORTING POST-ACTIVATION PERFORMANCE ENHANCEMENT: A PREREGISTERED, CONCEPTUAL REPLICATION, MULTI-CENTRE RANDOMISED CONTROL TRIAL
abstract_r: INTRODUCTION & AIMS: Concerns about the replicability of sport science findings have intensified. Particularly, performance-based interventions are susceptible to inflated effects due to methodological variability and selective reporting. Post-activation performance enhancement (PAPE) is widely applied to acutely improve ballistic performance, yet reported effects are inconsistent. This pre-registered study aimed to conceptually replicate a previously used PAPE protocol and investigate its acute effects on countermovement jump (CMJ) height and CMJ height variance. METHODS: Forty-nine trained athletes (31 men, 18 women) completed a multi-centre, randomised control trial across four separate sites. Following a familiarisation session, participants completed a standardised warm-up and two PAPE sessions involving a single set of barbell back-squats (3 × 90% 1RM) and two control sessions with time-matched active rest. Session order was counterbalanced, randomised, and separated by one-week periods. CMJ height was assessed with force platforms at baseline and immediately (time 0), 3, 6, 9, and 12 minutes after the set of barbell back-squats. A generalised additive mixed model for location, shape, and scale modelled the location (i.e. mean) and scale (i.e. standard deviation [SD]) of CMJ height across time. Baseline CMJ height was used as a covariate to account for regression-to-the-mean. RESULTS: Mean CMJ height for PAPE was significantly lower immediately after the intervention compared to control (32.75cm [95%CI: 32.29-33.14] vs. 33.86cm [95%CI: 33.65-34.14]). CMJ height SD for PAPE was significantly higher than control immediately after the intervention (2.00cm [95%CI: 1.60-2.37] vs. 1.38 [95%CI: 1.11-1.57]). Qualitatively, the time course of CMJ height is similar at minutes 3 through 12, and CMJ height SD is only similar by minute 12. CONCLUSION: The results indicate PAPE decreases CMJ jump height while nearly doubling CMJ height variance. Together with methodological variability and selective reporting (small samples, p-hacking, etc.), this increased variance is likely the cause of the widespread belief that PAPE exists.

title_r: Verifiability, Interestingness-if-True, Likelihood, and Belief in News Headlines: Replication Using Original Stimuli
abstract_r: This study is a pre-registered replication of prior work examining how verifiability, likelihood, and interestingness-if-true shape belief in news headlines. It builds on two earlier studies and a subsequent direct replication attempt. The first study (pre-registered at https://osf.io/t8adf/overview) found no overall main effect of verifiability on belief, but confirmed that perceived likelihood positively predicts belief when verifiability is controlled for, and revealed exploratory interactions between verifiability and truth status as well as between verifiability and likelihood. A follow-up study (pre-registered at https://osf.io/n6f24/overview) collected interestingness-if-true ratings from an independent sample and found a significant interaction between verifiability and interestingness-if-true; higher verifiability was associated with increased belief for headlines low in interestingness-if-true, but this positive association weakened or disappeared for headlines high in interestingness-if-true. A subsequent direct replication attempt (pre-registered at https://osf.io/7mx8e/overview), which used a new set of headlines and a new independent sample, did not replicate the key interaction: no interaction between verifiability and interestingness-if-true on belief was observed. Post-hoc analyses suggested this null result may have been due to a ceiling effect in verifiability ratings, which limited variability across headlines and reduced the ability to detect a possible interaction. The present study addresses this by returning to the original headline set used in the first two studies to determine whether the interaction can still be replicated with a new independent sample. All hypotheses are pre-registered prior to data collection and are identical to those from the prior replication.

title_r: Extinction of experience, perceptions of wildness and preferences for wild landscapes (Study 2)
abstract_r: The decline in human-nature interactions in people’s daily lives (i.e., extinction of experience), especially in childhood, is assumed to have adverse effects on human health and well-being as well as on pro-environmental behavior. The decline in interaction with wild nature during childhood in particular could diminish people’s ability to estimate the extent to which landscapes are impacted by humans (i.e. perceived wildness), which in turn could affect preferences for wild landscapes. The present study aims to replicate and extend findings from a previous study that found that age, but not interactions with wild nature in childhood, is related to perceived wildness of landscapes. Furthermore, we aim to replicate the finding that interactions with wild nature in childhood is related to preference for high wildness and that it mediates the effect of age on preference for high wildness. The present study will use a different set of landscape photographs and a within-subjects design. In addition, we will explore the role of exposure to wild nature in childhood in the relationship between age and perceived wildness.

title_r: Moral Threats and Extremism (Study 2)
abstract_r: Guided by research emphasizing the role of moral values in driving political extremism (Bandura, 2015; Fiske & Rai, 2014), we previously conducted a study comparing the effects of self-relevant moral and economic threats on extremism engagement, as measured by the RIS. Our previous study supported the thesis that threatened moral values elicit stronger intentions to engage in political extremism. However, we did not find the expected mediation effects, thus failing to find an explanatory mechanism for the effect. In this second study, we aim to replicate our results while testing agency of the transgressors and need for chaos as potential mediators. Additionally, we have refined our manipulation to more rigorously test the primacy effect of moral threats by removing any framing of the topics being threatened while maintaining their classification as moral or economic.

title_r: Replication Failure: U.S. Militarized Policy from Plan Colombia to the Mérida Initiative
abstract_r: Between 2000 and 2021, the United States invested more than $13 billion in militarized programs in Latin America, first through Plan Colombia and then with the Mérida Initiative. Despite independent evaluations raising concerns about the effectiveness and human rights violations, the U.S. used Plan Colombia as a model for the Mérida Initiative, with the primary goal of drug reduction, which neither program achieved. This thesis examines how U.S. agencies were able to replicate the program, overlooking reports from the Government Accountability Office (GAO) and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) showing that cocaine production, trafficking, and cartel-related violence didn’t decline. I use a two-step mixed-methods analysis, analyzing U.S. congressional testimony, GAO evaluations, declassified embassy cables, and UNODC data to argue that the replication wasn’t based on the evidence presented by the agencies responsible for implementing Plan Colombia, but rather from three institutional mechanisms. The securitization framework supports agencies’ belief that military enforcement is the correct approach to respond to drug trafficking. Bureaucratic politics then led agencies to use self-validating metrics as evidence of success, despite actual long-term outcomes. Lastly, coercive transfer brought the agency’s form of success to Mexico, seeking to replicate the same outcomes of success described in Colombia. Overall, this paper isn’t to document that these programs failed, but to explain the specific institutions that led to the replication.

title_r: Does graph format bias LLM forecasts? An exploratory replication of the format effect in a multimodal language model
abstract_r: Human forecasters are known to exhibit systematic biases based on how data is visually encoded, a phenomenon termed the format effect. Whether Large Language Models (LLMs) are susceptible to the same effect remained unexplored. In this study, a multimodal LLM (gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07) was tasked with forecasting eight future points based on a 50-point time series, presented across bar charts, line graphs, and point graphs, conceptually replicating the methodology of Reimers and Harvey. Bar chart forecasts were found lower than line and point-format forecasts in upward trends, under conventional ANOVA analysis, but remain insignificant under linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept for experimental cell. The format effect therefore constitutes a candidate observation motivating future work under designs with genuine between-cell independence. A reverse directional pattern was observed under downward trends, and further analysis show decaying format effect across time horizon. The primary driver of forecast error was function type instead of format. These results suggest that LLMs may reproduce certain directional format biases under specific conditions but constrained algorithmically that differs from human perceptual mechanisms.

title_r: A simulation study on coevolution of social opinions and the underlying social networks
abstract_r: Since the world connected to the Internet, networks have been increasingly socialized and have developed powerful functions for expressing and transmitting public opinion. New forms of communication such as YouTube and Twitter have grown rapidly, and the rise of new media has provided favorable conditions for the emergence of mass public opinion. Public opinion has a profound influence on people’s thoughts, actions, and social situation. Its forms and dissemination are complex and highly dynamic. Hence, research on public opinion dissemination has important theoretical and practical significance. For example, it can make progress in the development of opinion dynamics, or in organizational decision-making, government crisis management, and corporate marketing activities. In this thesis, based on the Deffuant model, we first introduce two parameters: the rewiring probability and the opinion mutation rate. Based on the existing research, we replicate and verify the influence of the confidence threshold, rewiring probability, and mutation rate on the final opinion distribution. The verification results are consistent with previous studies: the larger the confidence threshold is, the fewer the final opinion clusters will be, and it is easier to form a global consensus. The higher the rewiring probability is, the clearer the opinion clusters will be, and the faster the convergence speed will be. The larger the mutation rate is, the closer the connections between the opinion clusters will be, and the more scattered the opinion distribution will be. Secondly, in real society, individuals do not change their opinions without hesitation every time they have a chance to communicate. They also do not easily cut off relationships and find new friends whenever disagreements appear. Therefore, this the introduces two new constraints, named as the consensus formation constraint and the rewiring constraint, respectively. The consensus formation constraint means that before accepting an opinion update, an individual will estimate how many people still have opinions within his tolerance range after the update. These people are called “friends.” Only when the number of friends does not decrease, or does not fall below a certain proportion of the original number of friends, the individual updates the opinion. The rewiring constraint means that an individual will break a connection only when the opinion difference with the other person exceeds the tolerance range, and when that person also disagrees with most of the individual’s neighboring friends. Only in this case will the individual choose to disconnect and search for a new partner. This thesis mainly compares and studies the opinion evolution under two different cases: when consensus formation and rewiring are completely unconstrained and subject to the two constraints respectively. The research results show that the stricter the consensus formation constraint is, the more difficult it is to form large-scale opinion clusters and the more dispersed the opinions become. When there is no consensus formation constraint, the greater the rewiring constraints is, the more dispersed opinions become . However, when the consensus formation constraint is the strictest, the rewiring constraints have the opposite effect. In conclusion, this thesis replicates the previous research about rewiring and mutation rates, and contributes significantly to opinion evolution by introducing new concepts and methods of consensus formation constraint and rewiring constraint. This extended Deffuant model better reflects real human communication and therefore has greater practical significance.

title_r: Accuracy of repeated events recall: Warning against misinformation in the repeated events scenario. Conceptual replication.
abstract_r:
OSF registration template: Open-Ended Registration

This is a conceptual replication of a previously conducted study, preregistered as Accuracy of repeated events recall: Warning against misinformation in the repeated events scenario at https://osf.io/fjzdn/overview
We want to investigate potential explanations for the limited and irregular effects of warnings observed in the previous experiment. For that end, we introduced several changes to the experimental procedure. First, we plan to use a stronger, more specific warning against misinformation. Second, we reasoned that participants might have difficulty using a warning to improve responding when they struggle to monitor the source of specific event details. Therefore, the new experimental task is designed to be easier for the participants in that regard, thanks to presenting three instead of four event videos.

summary: Our hypotheses are essentially the same as in the primary study. However, previously, we measured the misinformation effect only by comparing the retrieval of correct responses in the misled and non-misled conditions, and only looked at misinformation endorsement in conditions where the item was presented as misinformation (internal or external). In the present study, we intend to also look at misinformation endorsement in the non-misled conditions (control and repeated OI). There are two important reasons for that change. First, the difference in misinformation endorsement rates between misled and non-misled conditions is one of the ways to measure the misinformation effect (I can cite e.g., mine and Hartmut’s paper): misinformation can sometimes be reported spontaneously, and therefore, a control condition misinformation endorsement serves as a useful baseline. When people report an item significantly more when exposed to it as misinformation, it demonstrates that misinformation exposure influences their responses. Second, in the context of repeated events, the difference in the retrieval of correct information in misled and non-misled conditions can be obscured by a higher frequency of reporting internal intrusions in the non-misled conditions, as we observed in the previous study. In sum, we believe that important aspects of changes in participants’ responding might not have been fully observed due to not examining the rates of misinformation reporting in the non-misled conditions, and therefore plan to test our predictions using this measure as well.
Reducing the number of instances of a repeated event presented to participants implicated changes to the content of misinformation narratives. The new set of manipulated details and their counterbalancing are presented in the xlsx file “exp2_Stimuli counterbalancing for the narratives”. However, the basic pattern of manipulating the four types of detail (repeated original information, control, internal misinformation, and external misinformation) remains the same, with full counterbalancing (each item serves as one of the four types of detail in one out of the four narratives presented to the participants).
A type of warning used also changed: we now intend to use a more specific, stronger warning. Instead of mentioning a possibility of distortions in the report provided by a post-event source, we now explicitly acknowledge their presence, which should significantly increase the warning’s efficacy (Blank & Launay, 2014). In both versions of a warning, however, we drew participants' attention to the fact that they should base their answers on what they remember from the event itself. To ensure that participants attend to a warning, we added two simple attention- and comprehension- check questions. The first question, “What should you be careful about when responding?” is open-ended. The second question, “Is the other agent’s report a fully accurate description of what happened in the first mission?”, requires choosing a “yes” or “no” response.

title_r: Depression advertisements and recommended help-seeking mode 2
abstract_r: This study is a conceptual replication of, and complement to, another pre-registered study (https://osf.io/v6gau/) . As public service announcements that aim to increase help-seeking for depression can backfire and given that people with depression often experience social anxiety, we aim to determine whether the mode of help-seeking recommended in public service announcements impacts the likelihood of seeking help. More specifically, we predict that people with depression may be more willing to engage in help-seeking behaviors through modes of communication that are less socially interactive. As such, we will investigate whether recommending texting (a less interactive mode) for help-seeking compared to video conferencing (a more interactive mode) will result in higher help-seeking intentions, more favorable help-seeking attitudes, and more favorable attitudes toward the advertisement itself. Without making any formal hypotheses, we will also examine whether the likelihood of seeking help through texting or video conferencing is affected.

title_r: A replication of Gross et al. (2024) in a brazilian sample
abstract_r: Mind-wandering refers to thinking about something other than what one is currently doing — for example, imagining going home during a busy workday. Although common to all humans, its effects on behavior and emotions are still being investigated. One key question is whether people who mind-wander less are happier, and how the content (or valence) of thoughts influences this relationship. This study aims to directly replicate Gross et al. (2024), itself a conceptual replication of Killingsworth and Gilbert (2010), with a Brazilian sample of 200 participants. Given the replication crisis, such studies are essential to assess the robustness of findings and estimate effect sizes. Data will be collected using the Expiwell app over seven days, with an initial questionnaire, a final one, and six experience sampling prompts per day. Participants will report on their current happiness, thought valence, mind-wandering, and other thought characteristics. Data will be analyzed using multilevel models in R to identify predictors of happiness. The study will be conducted as part of an undergraduate research project at the Laboratory for Replication in Psychology Studies (LAREPsi) and will follow open science practices, including preregistration and sharing data and code.

title_r: Revisiting Private Browsing Forensics: A 2026 Replication Study of Ohana & Shashidhar (2011)
abstract_r: This study replicates the 2011 work by Ohana and Shashidhar on private browsing forensics using modern systems and tools in 2026. The original methodology, including search queries and browsing scenarios, was preserved to ensure a valid longitudinal comparison. This replication is important to evaluate whether advancements in browser privacy have effectively mitigated forensic data leakage over time. The analysis was conducted using contemporary tools such as FTK Imager and Volatility 3 in a controlled virtual environment. Results show that while disk-based artifacts have significantly decreased, sensitive user data can still be recovered from system memory. This demonstrates that private browsing modes remain vulnerable to memory forensics and do not guarantee complete privacy.

title_r: PI-RADS v2 and Adverse Prostate Cancer Outcomes: A Cross-cohort Replication Study Across Three Centers
abstract_r: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) coupled with Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) provides standardization for assessing the clinical significance of prostate cancer (PCa). The association between PI-RADS and clinical endpoints has remained underexplored due to limited follow-up data. METHODS: Association of PI-RADS with prostate cancer-specific mortality (PCSM), overall survival (OS), metastasis-free survival (MFS), and biochemical recurrence (BCR) was investigated across three retrospective cohorts focusing on the PI-RADS v2 era. The Helsinki University Hospital included 4674 men with clinical suspicion of PCa (MRI during 2015-2019, median follow-up [mFU] 5.0 yr), Tampere University Hospital (N = 1159; 2016-2021, mFU 2.3 yr) with men diagnosed with PCa, and Lille University Hospital (N = 301; 2016-2024, mFU 6.2 yr) with radical prostatectomy-treated men with PCa. KEY FINDINGS AND LIMITATIONS: In Helsinki cohort, multivariable Cox regression found PI-RADS score 5 to be significantly associated with PCSM (hazard ratio 18.4, 95% confidence interval [6.62-51.1]), along with biopsy GG 5 (5.45 [1.82-16.3]), Charlson's Comorbidity Index (1.53 [1.42-1.7]), and prostate-specific antigen (1.28 [1.11-1.5]). PI-RADS score 5 associated with OS in the Helsinki and Tampere cohorts, and MFS and BCR in the Lille cohort. Main limitation of the work is that all data is retrospective. CONCLUSIONS AND CLINICAL IMPLICATIONS: PI-RADS score 5 is associated with elevated risk of adverse outcomes. The presented clinically strong endpoints have potential to affect decision-making in MRI-based PCa diagnosis and prognosis.

title_r: Identification of genomic copy number variations associated with obesity-related phenotypes
abstract_r: Obesity is a chronic disease with increasing prevalence worldwide. Recent advances in human genetics have led to the discovery of genetic variations underlying obesity, including copy number variants (CNVs). The overall aim of this thesis was to explore the contribution of CNVs to human obesity by (i) producing high quality CNV catalogues from various SNP genotyping datasets; (ii) identifying specific CNVs previously reported to be associated with obesity-related phenotypes (two rare deletion variants in the 16p11.2 region, and multi-allelic CNVs in the amylase gene region on chromosome 1) in 5 study cohorts in order to perform replication studies and extend understanding of their phenotypic effects; and (iii) to identify rare, novel CNVs in morbid obesity. The CNVs were predicted and quality-checked based on the signal intensity data from the SNP genotyping data, which yielded CNVs with consistent characteristics across the study cohorts, and comparable with other studies. Salivary amylase (AMY1) CNVs were genotyped by a collaborator using Paralogue Ratio Tests (PRTs) in a small intensively-phenotyped cohort of overweight-to-obese individuals. Statistical analyses indicated no significant associations for AMY1 CNVs with body mass index, waist-to-hip ratio, body fats and starch intake, further increasing the evidence that AMY1 CNVs are not associated with obesity, as reported in previous studies. Both 16p11.2 deletion variants (~600-kb and ~200-kb) were confirmed as associated with BMI and WHR in the UK Biobank and Northern Finland Birth Cohort 1966 participants: 600-kb deletion carriers had 12-fold increased risk of obesity in the UK Biobank. Finally, 3 potentially causative CNVs were discovered in 3 different morbidly obese people from the Northern Finland general population; duplications in 17p13 and 22q11.2 regions and a 5p14.3 deletion. The 3 CNVs spanned regions involving brain function and implicated in obesity. The findings are consistent with previous studies, highlighting the role of rare CNVs in the aetiology of obesity.

title_r: Highly automated vehicles' communicated intents to interact with pedestrians and pedestrians' appraisals - A study across different cultures
abstract_r: Highly automated vehicles (HAVs) introduce new challenges for safe pedestrian interaction, particularly in how vehicles communicate intent. This intent can be conveyed implicitly through vehicle kinematics or explicitly via external human-machine interfaces (eHMIs), such as light bands. Yet research comparing how these signals work together across cultures remains limited - knowledge that is essential for universal design and standardization. To address this gap, we replicated earlier experimental studies from Germany, Japan, and Singapore with new samples from the Netherlands and UK. Participants viewed HAVs that varied in explicit communication (intention-based eHMI, static eHMI, none) and implicit behavior (yielding, non-yielding). We measured pedestrians' willingness to cross, perceived safety, and trust in the eHMI. Across all five countries, intention-based light-bands increased willingness to cross and perceived safety, and were rated as more trustworthy and supportive. However, when explicit and implicit cues conflicted, participants tended to rely on the explicit signal, creating potentially unsafe situations. The degree of this overreliance varied slightly between national samples. Overall, the findings highlight both the benefits and risks of light-band eHMIs and reinforce the need for universal, standardized design guidelines that improve safety while reducing overreliance on explicit signals.

title_r: The verifiability approach to deception detection: A Pre-registered direct replication of the information protocol condition of Nahari, Vrij, and Fisher (2014)
abstract_r: Nahari, Vrij, and Fischer (2014) found that, when participants were forewarned that their statements would be checked for verifiable details, truth tellers gave much more verifiable details than liars (d = 1.14 [95% CI: 0.49; 1.78]). In this direct replication (n = 72), all participants wrote a statement claiming they had carried out their regular campus activities, whereas liars had actually stolen an exam. Statements were coded for verifiable details. Our primary prediction was confirmed: Truth tellers provided significantly more verifiable details than liars (d = 0.50 [95% CI: 0.02; 0.98]). Our secondary predictions - that liars would provide more unverifiable details than truth tellers, and that truth tellers would have a higher verifiable to unverifiable ratio score than liars - were not confirmed. We hope this will stimulate other independent investigations of VA to tell whether or not coding for verifiability will pass Ockham´s razor test.

title_r: When climate anxiety motivates versus paralyzes: A conceptual replication of the inverted U-shaped relationship between climate anxiety and pro-environmental behavior
abstract_r: While some studies have linked higher Climate Anxiety (CA) to higher levels of Pro-Environmental Behavior (PEB), other studies have found an inverted U-shaped relationship, with intermediate levels of CA relating to more PEB and high and low levels of CA being associated with less PEB. This suggests that high levels of CA may cause eco-paralysis, i.e., feeling so overwhelmed by environmental problems that it reduces PEB. However, given that only a few studies demonstrated this inverted U-shaped relationship between CA and PEB and due to the narrow range of operationalizations applied to these constructs, we wanted to replicate this pattern in a large, independent sample. Therefore, a convenience sample of 1205 Dutch participants completed the Climate Change Anxiety Scale (CCAS), the Pro-Environmental Behavior Scale (PEBS), and several other scales. Replicating previous findings, a regression analysis yielded a significant negative quadratic relationship between CCAS on PEBS ( b = -0.02, p < .001). Additionally, the quadratic model fitted the data better than a linear model. This study replicates previous reports about an inverted curvilinear relationship between CA and PEB, implying that moderate levels of CA are optimal for the reported expression of PEB, where low levels of CA are related to low reported expression of PEB, and high levels of CA indeed may hamper PEB. Implications and potential associations with eco-paralysis are discussed.

title_r: Partitioning Neural Co-Variability
abstract_r: Trial-to-trial variability of neural responses has been linked to important aspects of neural computation and is essential for understanding how neuronal populations respond. While current overdispersion models treat each neuron's gain as independent of each other, this assumption fails to capture the network statistics of neuronal populations. As no existing model can capture overdispersed structured spiking gain-modulation across a neural population, network-level gain covariance remains largely unstudied. We thus present the Poisson matrix-normal latent variable (PMNLV) model, which extends single-neuron overdispersion to neural populations by placing a matrix-normal prior over the latent gain with a Kronecker-factored covariance. Spike counts are Poisson-distributed with a rate equal to the sum of a per-neuron stimulus tuning term and a matrix-normal gain, passed through a quadratic soft-rectifying link. We derive two complementary estimation algorithms: a variational EM (VEM) with a matrix-normal posterior that recovers dense Kronecker factors without structural assumptions, and a Kernel Tournament Method (KTM) that performs data-driven selection over a biologically motivated kernel dictionary and composite likelihood. On simulated data, both algorithms recover the inter-neuron and temporal covariance factors and accurate tuning curves. Applying VEM to Neuropixel recordings across four cortical regions of mouse visual hierarchy, we replicate a previous finding that single-neuron marginal variability changes little across cortical areas. We then show that shared population co-variability, invisible to scalar summaries e.g., the Fano factor, peaks in primary visual cortex and declines in higher visual areas. The PMNLV framework is applicable to any simultaneously recorded population where structured gain covariance is of scientific interest.

title_r: Partitioning Neural Co-Variability
abstract_r: Trial-to-trial variability of neural responses has been linked to important aspects of neural computation and is essential for understanding how neuronal populations respond. While current overdispersion models treat each neuron's gain as independent of each other, this assumption fails to capture the network statistics of neuronal populations. As no existing model can capture overdispersed structured spiking gain-modulation across a neural population, network-level gain covariance remains largely unstudied. We thus present the Poisson matrix-normal latent variable (PMNLV) model, which extends single-neuron overdispersion to neural populations by placing a matrix-normal prior over the latent gain with a Kronecker-factored covariance. Spike counts are Poisson-distributed with a rate equal to the sum of a per-neuron stimulus tuning term and a matrix-normal gain, passed through a quadratic soft-rectifying link. We derive two complementary estimation algorithms: a variational EM (VEM) with a matrix-normal posterior that recovers dense Kronecker factors without structural assumptions, and a Kernel Tournament Method (KTM) that performs data-driven selection over a biologically motivated kernel dictionary and composite likelihood. On simulated data, both algorithms recover the inter-neuron and temporal covariance factors and accurate tuning curves. Applying VEM to Neuropixel recordings across four cortical regions of mouse visual hierarchy, we replicate a previous finding that single-neuron marginal variability changes little across cortical areas. We then show that shared population co-variability, invisible to scalar summaries e.g., the Fano factor, peaks in primary visual cortex and declines in higher visual areas. The PMNLV framework is applicable to any simultaneously recorded population where structured gain covariance is of scientific interest.

title_r: Spatiotemporal analysis of autism gene enrichment implicates cortex, thalamus, and hypothalamus
abstract_r: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable neurodevelopmental disorder. Sequencing analyses have identified 185 ASD-associated genes, which implicate neurons, but the specific brain regions through which these neurons influence neurodevelopment remain unclear. Here, we integrate over one million single-cell RNA sequencing profiles from 20 regions of the developing human brain (4-23 post-conceptual weeks) using a new framework, STARMAPS (Sparse Task-specific Analysis for Revealing Molecular Associations in Particular Single-cell datasets). STARMAPS accounts for coordinated regional and developmental perturbations in gene expression, enabling robust cross-region comparison. We replicate prior findings that ASD-associated genes are enriched in excitatory neurons during mid-fetal development, and we extend these results to reveal distinct spatial signatures. Across 26 excitatory neuron subtypes, six clusters showed significant enrichment for ASD-associated genes. These clusters localize to both cortical and subcortical regions, including the motor, temporal, and visual cortex, as well as the thalamus and hypothalamus. Our findings support a major role for excitatory neurons across distributed brain circuits, implicating previously underappreciated subcortical structures in ASD etiology. By providing a statistically rigorous framework for spatiotemporal integration of single-cell data, STARMAPS enables refined mapping of molecular vulnerability across the developing human brain.

title_r: "Gambling-like" mechanisms in video games
abstract_r:
Loot boxes are a type of small purchase (i.e., “microtransaction”) available in many video games that provide randomised virtual rewards of varying desirability. Loot boxes have garnered research attention for their psychological and structural similarities to bona fide gambling, and a consistent positive relationship between spending on loot boxes and problem gambling symptomatology is now well established. In this thesis, we report six-studies that examine loot boxes – investigating individual differences in spending behaviour and the efficacy of current consumer protection efforts to mitigate the risks of overspending – across three peer-reviewed, published papers.
Chapter 2 reports a single-study manuscript published in International Gambling Studies, where we reanalysed pre-existing data from Drummond et al. (2020a). This paper focusses on the potential interaction between yearly income and problem gambling severity in predicting spending on loot boxes. If the established relationship between loot box spending and problem gambling severity only persisted for high-income individuals, then potential negative financial effects would likely be attenuated (as these individuals would have a greater ability to absorb financial losses). However, we found that the model that best predicts loot box spending included both the main effects of income and problem gambling severity, but not the interaction between these factors. Fundamentally, the relationship between loot box spending and problem gambling symptomatology was consistent across income levels, meaning that individuals with elevated problem gambling scores consistently spend more money on loot boxes across each level of income. Importantly, this means that these increases in spending are not confined to populations with higher levels of disposable income, suggesting that lower-income individuals with elevated scores on problem gambling measures may be a specifically vulnerable population, as even low quantities of spending may be problematic.
Chapter 3 presents a manuscript published in Telematics and Informatics, where we examined whether a known predictor of problem gambling – impulsivity – also predicted loot box spending. This chapter includes samples from two studies: an initial sample collected from MTurk (n = 342), and a second direct replication with a larger sample collected from Prolific (n = 1142). Although impulsivity is consistently associated with gambling behaviour, four previous studies examining the role of impulsivity on loot box spending have found little evidence of an effect. However, all four studies shared the same potential shortcoming - conceptualising and measuring impulsivity as unidimensional - which past research suggests may underestimate the nuance and complexity of this construct. To advance this research, we implemented a multidimensional measure of impulsivity (short UPPS-P), supplemented with a measurement of reward/punishment sensitivity (BIS/BAS). The UPPS-P had a grounding in previous gambling research, with 3 of its 5 factors consistently implicated in problem gambling behaviours: Positive Urgency, Negative Urgency, and (lack of) Premeditation. Our key findings were that Positive Urgency and Sensation Seeking, as well as BAS-Drive (BIS/BAS), were positively correlated with loot box spending, but Negative Urgency, and (lack of) Premeditation were not. These findings demonstrate that a general positive reinforcement mechanism appears to underlie loot box spending. Ultimately, impulsivity appears to play a role in loot box engagement, but the underlying impulsive processes implicated differ in some ways from the processes relevant to problem gambling (i.e., Unlike gambling, Negative Urgency and (lack of) Premeditation not relevant to loot box spending).
Governmental and regulatory responses to loot boxes vary substantially around the world, ranging from outright bans to non-regulation. Chapter 4 reports a three-study manuscript published in Computers in Human Behavior investigating the efficacy of a loot box warning label - “In-Game Purchases (Includes Random Items)” - currently implemented by video game regulatory boards across some of North America (ESRB) and much of Europe (PEGI). This series of studies represents the first empirical evaluation of the ESRB/PEGI loot box warning. Using a consumer-oriented approach, we investigated two aspects of this warning: First, the comprehension of the warning for consumers (a basic requirement for a warning), and second, the overall efficacy of the warning. The first study in this program of research did not examine the warning itself, instead it assessed consumers’ perceptions of the potential harm that loot boxes represent, as although scholars had concerns related to these mechanisms, consumer perception had not been examined (i.e., Do non-academics consider loot boxes as potentially harmful?). We assessed consumers’ perceptions of harm (rated from 0 = not harmful at all – 100 = very harmful) related to loot box engagement, and then compared this with their perceptions of harm (rated on same scale) related to engagement with a variety of related activities, including bona fide gambling and non-randomised microtransactions. We found that consumers perceived that engagement with loot boxes has a greater potential for harm than engagement with non-randomised microtransactions, but a lower potential for harm than engagement with bona fide gambling activities. The second study in this chapter explicitly examined the efficacy of the ESRB/PEGI loot box warning with a mixed-methods design. Initially, participants were presented with the ESRB/PEGI warning (amongst other warnings) and asked what they believed the given warning meant, or what content they believed the warning referred to, with open responses permitted. Using these responses, a thematic analysis was completed, providing two key findings. First, the majority (75%) of participants identified the warning referenced financial expenditure, however, second, only 36% of participants identified the warning referenced chance-based outcomes. This suggests the ESRB/PEGI warning may fail to make the chance aspect salient, which is problematic considering this is the quintessential reason the warning exists (i.e., distinguishing it from the “In-Game Purchases” warning that is also used by the ESRB/PEGI). Next, a series of quantitative analyses comparing the ESRB/PEGI loot box warning with other warnings (including “Real Gambling”, “Simulated Gambling” and “In-Game Purchases”) across three factors: recommended age of access for games with a given warning, how severe the underlying context is denoted by a given warning, and the severity of potential gambling content underlying a given warning. We found that the ESRB/PEGI loot box warning was rated lower than the Real Gambling (i.e., gambling involving real currency) warning across all factors, higher than the In-Game Purchases (i.e., non-randomised microtransactions) warning across all factors, and similar to the Simulated Gambling (i.e., gambling not involving real currency) warning across all factors, except warning severity, where the loot box warning was rated as indicating more severe gambling content. The third study in this manuscript empirically examined how the ESRB/PEGI loot box warning performs at informing accurate consumer perceptions of harm. In the absence of objective data on harms, for a warning to facilitate an informed decision, we proposed it must convey a sense of harm that is similar with an individual’s perception of harm of the activity it represents, even if this perception is not indicative of the “true” potential harm of an activity. Given this, we examined if participants’ perceptions of harm as generated by the ESRB/PEGI loot box warning were commensurate with their perceptions of harm related to engagement with loot boxes. If these two perceptions were commensurate, this would establish the warning was effectively informing decision making. We found that the warning generated a perception of harm that was lower than perceptions of harm related to the activity itself: Participants rated the warning - In-Game Purchases (Includes Random Items) - as representing a lower potential for harm compared to their perception of harm related to engagement with loot boxes.
Overall, this thesis has advanced our understanding of the profiles of individuals who spend money on loot boxes, with evidence for the role of income being a minor factor when compared to problem gambling symptomatology. Using a more comprehensive measure of impulsivity compared to previous research, we have identified two impulsive subfactors that are correlated with loot box spending (Positive Urgency and Sensation Seeking). We have also empirically demonstrated that in terms of perceived potential for harm, consumers perceived loot boxes to be of greater potential harm than non-randomised microtransactions, but lesser potential harm than bona fide gambling. Further, we empirically evaluated the loot box warning implemented across some of North America and much of Europe, finding that is poorly comprehended by almost 2/3 of participants. Finally, this loot box warning fails to generate a perception of harm that is equivalent with perceptions of harm related to the activity that it represents (i.e., engaging with loot boxes). Combined, this raised questions over the ability of this warning to effectively inform consumer decision making.

title_r: Replication and extension of the study entitled “phonemic contrast exposure triggers brain lateralization for language perception on the day of birth”
abstract_r: This study is a replication and extension of a neonatal EEG study testing whether brief postnatal exposure to phonemic contrasts can modulate functional hemispheric lateralization for phoneme perception on the day of birth. In Experiment 1 (replication) neonates have their EEG recorded in a dichotic oddball paradigm involving repeated diotic presentation of the disyllable /tata/ (standard) interrupted by an infrequent dichotic stimulus (/tata/ in one ear and /dada/ or /kaka/ in the other, deviant). Baseline EEG testing will measure responses to unilateral changes in speech sounds presented to the left and right ear of the neonates before five hours of exposure to one phonemic contrast, e.g., /tata/ & /dada/ presented in alternance (exposure), followed by 12 hours of rest (consolidation). A second EEG session (test) will then measure selective changes in responsiveness to phonemic contrasts induced by exposure. During exposure, half of the participants will hear /tata/ and /dada/ and the other half will hear /tata/ and /kaka/, but all participants will be probed with both dichotic deviants at baseline and at test. To maximize statistical power within the constraints of the target sample size, the original three-group design (experimental, active control, passive control) is collapsed into a within-subject exposed/unexposed contrast. The purpose is to determine whether exposure to a consonantal contrast for a period of a few hours after birth induces a hemispheric shift of sensitivity from the right to the left hemisphere selective for that contrast, as reported in the original study. To determine whether the previous observation is language-selective, Experiment 2 will test another group of neonates using the exact same paradigm as Experiment 1 but featuring disyllables played backwards (reverse speech). Here, we expect to see a right-hemispheric advantage for dichotic oddballs that will not be affected by exposure. The predictions, if supported by the data, will be evidence that structured phonemic input can rapidly recruit left-hemispheric speech-processing mechanisms in newborns in a selective fashion.

title_r: Drivers of Attitudinal and Behavioral Outcomes in Streaming Consumption: A Cross-Context Replication and Extension
abstract_r: Addressing the scarcity of replication studies in marketing and consumer research, this study examines the drivers of attitudinal and behavioral outcomes in video streaming consumption. We replicate a prior model and cross-validate it in the market of commercial video streaming services and extend it by incorporating electronic word of mouth (eWOM), which has been largely overlooked in prior research into streaming service usage. An online survey will be analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results are expected to confirm the central role of habit and content quality in shaping actual usage, word of mouth (WOM), and brand perception in commercial video streaming services. Further, we expect eWOM to increase the explained variance of the three outcomes. Overall, the study will strengthen the empirical evidence for the original model and supports robustness across contexts.

title_r: Replication and Extension of the Organisational Health Improvement Questionnaire- Core (OHIQ-Core): Confirmatory Validation and Measurement Invariance in an Independent Sample
abstract_r: Background. The Organisational Health Improvement Questionnaire- Core (OHIQ-Core) is a brief 14-item measure of organisational psychological health developed for ongoing organisational use. Initial validation was previously conducted with 1,026 working adults, and supported a two-factor structure (Organisational Support and Work Design) and a higher-order unitary factor. Cross-validation in an independent sample, broader measurement invariance, and extended convergent validity evidence were the priorities for further validation work.Methods. The OHIQ-Core was tested in a new independent sample of 1,106 working adults. Confirmatory factor analysis compared single-factor, correlated two-factor, and higher-order models, with respecification replicated from the original validation. Measurement invariance was tested across gender, age, organisational size, disability status, and collapsed industry sectors. Convergent validity was examined against the WHO-5 Wellbeing Index, the Self-Rated Workplace Performance scale, and five single-item outcome indicators (n = 559).Results. The two-factor structure replicated, with the respecified model producing acceptable fit (CFI = .939, RMSEA = .072) and the higher-order solution yielding equivalent fit. Standardised loadings were significant and consistent with the original validation. Internal consistency was good for Organisational Support (ω = .90), the OHIQ-Core total (ω = .92), and acceptable for Work Design (ω = .77). Average variance extracted fell marginally below .50 for both subscales. Full scalar measurement invariance was established across all five grouping variables. Convergent validity replicated the original validation and was extended through the single-item outcomes. Organisational Support more strongly predicted attitudinal and wellbeing outcomes, while Work Design more strongly predicted self-rated performance.Conclusions. The OHIQ-Core's factor structure, reliability, and convergent validity replicate in an independent sample and demonstrate measurement equivalence across important demographic and organisational characteristics. The differential predictive pattern across subscales suggests distinct intervention targets for organisations seeking to improve relational and systemic versus structural and work-design aspects of organisational psychological health.

title_r: Curiosity tempts indulgence: a replication of Experiment 2 with need for cognitive closure as moderator
abstract_r: This study is a partial replication of Experiment 2 from Wiggin et al. (2019), examining whether unsatisfied curiosity increases indulgent consumer behaviour. We extend the original by replacing BAS sensitivity with Need for Cognitive Closure (NFC) as the moderator. Participants were randomly assigned to a high or low curiosity condition and reported willingness to pay for a luxury vacation package. We hypothesised that unsatisfied curiosity would increase WTP (H1) and that this effect would be stronger among individuals with higher NFC (H2). Data collection was conducted via online survey (N = 126).
